stork.name: Stork
stork.specimen: healthy adult male, 3.5 kg, about 110 cm from bill tip to tail and 115 cm tall when standing, with a wingspan near the middle of the 155–215 cm range.
stork.summary: A tall black-and-white wader with long red legs and a dagger-like red bill, the white stork stalks meadows for frogs, rodents and insects and soars thousands of kilometres between Europe and Africa each year. It is a superb long-distance traveller, but at about 3.5 kg it is a light and fragile fighter.
narrative: The white stork is one of Europe's best-loved birds, a metre-tall wader with white plumage, black flight feathers and brilliant red legs and bill. Pairs return each spring to huge stick nests on rooftops, church towers and poles, greeting each other by throwing their heads back and clattering their bills in a rattle like distant gunfire.

Its real talent is travel. Rather than flapping across the Mediterranean, storks ride rising columns of warm air, circling up over a kilometre and gliding on towards the next thermal, funnelling through Gibraltar or the Bosphorus by the hundreds of thousands. GPS tags show that young birds explore and waste energy, while experienced adults fly faster, straighter and even invent shortcuts.

On the ground it hunts by walking slowly and stabbing, taking insects, frogs, snakes and small mammals. In an Animal Battle Stats matchup, the stork has reach and a sharp bill that can hurt small opponents, and remarkable stamina, but its light bones, lack of talons and modest weight make it vulnerable to any serious predator.

sections.habitat: Breeds across much of Europe (about a quarter of the world population in Poland), north-west Africa and western Asia, and winters mainly in sub-Saharan Africa, with some birds in India. It prefers open farmland, wet meadows, grassland and shallow wetlands and avoids areas overgrown with tall grass and shrubs.
sections.diet: A carnivore eating insects (especially beetles, grasshoppers, locusts and crickets), earthworms, frogs, snakes, lizards and small mammals such as voles, moles and shrews, with occasional eggs, young birds, fish, molluscs, crustaceans and scorpions. Its nests host many other species, from house sparrows and starlings to kestrels and little owls.
sections.social: Gregarious: flocks of thousands gather on migration and in winter, and non-breeders form groups of 40–50. Breeding pairs are monogamous for the season and territorial around the nest, nesting in loose colonies.
sections.reproduction: The male arrives first and claims a nest. The female usually lays four eggs (one to seven), incubated for 33–34 days; chicks reach about 3.4 kg within 45 days and fledge at 58–64 days. First breeding is usually at about four years.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. It declined and disappeared from parts of western Europe in the 19th and 20th centuries because of wetland drainage and farming changes, then recovered through reintroduction and protection; a reintroduction project in Sussex, England, produced the first wild nests there in 2020, the first documented British breeding since 1416. Power-line collisions and changing migration habits linked to landfills are current concerns.
sections.features:
Long, straight, pointed red bill and long red legs.
Broad wings suited to thermal soaring.
Bill-clattering communication with a resonating throat pouch.
Urohidrosis: droppings on the legs cool the bird by evaporation.
Huge, long-used stick nests.
sections.humanInteraction: Welcomed as a bird of good luck in much of Europe, where it nests on houses and churches. Folklore that storks deliver babies is widespread, especially in Slavic cultures. A stork found in Klütz, Germany, in 1822 with an ornate African arrow embedded in its body (the Rostocker Pfeilstorch, now a mounted specimen at the University of Rostock) was early proof of long-distance bird migration.

funFacts: A stork found in Germany in 1822 with an African arrow embedded in its body helped prove that birds migrate to Africa.
Flapping flight burns about 23 times more fat per distance than soaring.
Storks returning to Latvia find frogs by listening to their mating calls.
A single stork nest can weigh up to 250 kg.
Storks cool off by directing their droppings onto their legs.
Older storks invent new shortcuts on their spring migration.
The oldest known wild white stork lived 39 years after being ringed.

abilities.name: Thermal Rider
abilities.description: it spirals up in rising warm air to 1,200–1,500 m and glides onward, using a fraction of the energy of flapping, which lets it cover thousands of kilometres and outlast most opponents in a long pursuit.

abilities.name: Dagger Bill
abilities.description: a long, straight, pointed bill on a long neck lets it strike at a distance, stab small animals and break larger prey apart before swallowing.

traits.name: Machine-Gun Clatter
traits.description: almost voiceless as an adult, it communicates by rapidly clattering its bill, amplified by its throat pouch into a sound likened to distant machine-gun fire.

traits.name: Rooftop Giant Nest
traits.description: pairs build stick nests 1–2 m deep and up to 250 kg on roofs, church towers, poles and trees, often reusing them for years.

combat.weapons: The white stork's weapon is its long, straight, pointed bill, driven by a long neck. It swallows small prey whole but kills and breaks apart larger prey first (Wikipedia). Prey includes insects, earthworms, frogs, snakes and lizards, voles, moles and shrews, and sometimes eggs, young birds and fish. The bill can deliver sharp jabs, but a 3.5 kg bird has little force behind it and no talons or hooked tip for holding struggling animals.
weaknesses: Low absolute mass and a fragile, light skeleton.
No talons, armor or hooked bill.
Slow on the ground and not built for tight aerial manoeuvres.
Needs thermals for efficient long flights; long sea crossings are costly.

sugar-glider.name: Sugar Glider
sugar-glider.specimen: healthy adult male, 0.14 kg, about 17 cm head-body with a tail of similar length, gliding membranes fully developed.
sugar-glider.summary: A 140-gram gliding possum that wins by leaving: the sugar glider can steer a 50-metre glide between trees, sees ultraviolet light at night and can drop into torpor to wait out storms. It is a real hunter of insects, lizards and nesting birds, but in a straight fight almost any larger animal overwhelms it.
narrative: The sugar glider is a pocket-sized specialist of the forest canopy. Weighing around 140 g, it has no meaningful armor, strength or reach, and on the absolute roster scale its Attack and Defense sit near the floor with other tiny mammals. What it does have is a furred membrane stretched from wrist to ankle. From a high trunk it can launch, hold its limbs out at right angles and steer a glide of 50 metres or more, adjusting its body angle through small limb movements that high-speed filming has captured in detail.

That mobility makes the glider very hard to pin down in the right habitat. An opponent on the ground or on a single trunk may never get a second chance at contact, because the glider has already crossed to the next tree. Its senses support the same strategy: large eyes, swivelling ears and, unusually for a nocturnal mammal, colour vision that reaches into the ultraviolet. At rest it shares a leaf-lined hollow with a clan of up to seven adults, and dominant males mark the group and territory with scent.

Its diet is broader and fiercer than its name. Gum and sap carry it through winter, but in summer it hunts insects, and it will kill lizards and small birds and raid eggs. Introduced gliders in Tasmania prey so heavily on nesting swift parrots that they threaten that species. Away from trees, though, the glider has few answers: owls, snakes, quolls and cats all take it, and any medium-sized opponent that catches it ends the contest immediately. In a battle ranking it is a textbook example of elite Agility and Special paired with near-minimum Attack and Defense.

sections.habitat: Sugar gliders live in forests and woodlands, nesting in tree hollows lined with leaves. Under the 2021 split, P. breviceps in the strict sense occurs only in coastal south-east Queensland and New South Wales east of the Great Dividing Range, up to about 2,000 m in the eastern ranges. Krefft's glider and the savanna glider cover much of the rest of eastern and northern Australia, and further glider populations occur in New Guinea and nearby islands. Captive and pet populations are kept worldwide.
sections.diet: A seasonal omnivore. In summer it eats mainly insects and other arthropods; in winter it relies on plant exudates such as acacia gum, eucalyptus sap, manna, honeydew and lerp, stripping bark or boring holes with its teeth to reach them. Nectar, pollen, acacia seeds, fungi, fruit, bird eggs, lizards and small birds are taken when available. Heavy pollen feeding makes it a likely pollinator of Banksia. It shares forests with squirrel gliders and yellow-bellied gliders by using food resources differently.
sections.social: Groups of up to seven adults and their young share a nest as a clan. Within the clan they are playful and social; toward other clans and intruders they are territorial. Dominant males scent-mark clan members and the nest area.
sections.reproduction: Females have a well-developed pouch and commonly raise twins, which stay in the pouch for just over two months and then begin foraging, usually with the mother (Australian Museum). Females mature late in their first year (Animal Diversity Web).
sections.conservation: The broad, pre-split species was assessed as Least Concern by the IUCN in 2016. The narrowly defined P. breviceps has a much smaller range, and Wikipedia notes it is sensitive to disasters such as the 2019–20 Australian bushfires; a formal reassessment of the split species is still needed.
sections.features:
Furred gliding membrane from the fifth finger to the ankle.
Long, partly prehensile tail used for steering and balance.
Opposable toe on each hind foot for a secure grip.
Elongated fourth finger for extracting insects from under bark.
Daily torpor and group huddling to save energy.
UV-sensitive trichromatic vision.
sections.humanInteraction: Sugar gliders are among the most widely kept exotic pets. Genetic work shows that European and US pet stock came from New Guinean gliders, not the eastern Australian animals that now carry the strict name. Introduced gliders in Tasmania are a serious predator of the critically endangered swift parrot.

funFacts: The Latin name Petaurus breviceps translates roughly as "short-headed rope-dancer", a nod to its canopy acrobatics.
A single glide can cover 50 m or more.
In a storm with cyclone-strength winds, wild gliders switched to deep torpor and all survived.
Its heart beats 200–300 times a minute.
Behavioural tests show it can see ultraviolet light as well as three colour channels, at night.
Pet "sugar gliders" in Europe and the US turn out to be New Guinean gliders, a different species from the eastern Australian P. breviceps under the 2021 split.
Introduced gliders in Tasmania kill so many nesting female swift parrots that the parrots' adult sex ratio has become male-biased.

abilities.name: Canopy Glide Escape
abilities.description: spreads the furred membranes between wrists and ankles to glide 50 m or more between trees, steering with its limbs and tail. Against ground or trunk-bound opponents it simply leaves the fight.

abilities.name: Storm Torpor
abilities.description: drops its body temperature and metabolism for hours at a time; wild gliders used deep torpor to sit out a cyclone-strength storm and all survived. It turns bad conditions into a waiting game rather than a crisis.

traits.name: Clan Scent Marker
traits.description: lives in nest-sharing clans of up to seven adults; dominant males mark group members and territory with forehead and chest glands, and clans defend their patch noisily against outsiders.

traits.name: Ultraviolet Night Vision
traits.description: a rod-dominated retina that still supports trichromatic colour vision with ultraviolet sensitivity, uncommon among nocturnal mammals.

combat.weapons: The sugar glider's only real weapons are sharp incisors and small claws on a 140 g body. It is a more active predator than its sweet-food name suggests: in summer it is mainly insectivorous, and it opportunistically takes lizards, small birds and eggs. In Tasmania, where gliders were introduced, they kill nesting swift parrot females and their clutches in tree hollows, and this predation has skewed the parrot's adult sex ratio (Wright 2019, summarising Heinsohn et al.). Under the 2021 split those Tasmanian gliders are treated as Krefft's glider, but the behaviour shows what this body plan can do to a trapped, smaller animal at night. Against anything larger than a small bird, the glider's absolute damage is close to nil.
weaknesses: Extremely low mass, power and durability.
Weapons are only small incisors and claws.
No armor; any solid bite from a medium predator is lethal.
Heavily dependent on trees for its main advantage.

sun-bear.name: Sun Bear
sun-bear.specimen: healthy prime adult male, 50.0 kg, about 70 cm at the shoulder and 130 cm head-body, representing a mainland or Sumatran animal rather than the lighter Bornean form.
sun-bear.summary: The smallest bear, but one of the fiercest for its size: the sun bear carries 10 cm sickle claws, a bite of about 2,000 N at the molars and loose skin that lets it twist round and bite anything that grabs it. It climbs better than any other bear, though at around 50 kg it is badly outmatched by tigers and big bears.
narrative: The sun bear looks like a compact, short-coated black bear with an oversized set of tools. Most adults weigh 25 to 65 kg, less than half the size of the black, sloth and spectacled bears on the roster, yet its claws are about 10 cm long and its bite is strong enough for its size that researchers have linked it to ripping open living hardwood trunks for bees and larvae. In a close fight those tools make it a costly opponent for any medium-sized predator.

Its defense is built around getting up a tree first and fighting back second. It is the most arboreal bear, climbing with inward-turned forefeet and bare soles and resting in branches several metres above the ground. When something does get hold of it, the loose skin gives it room to twist and bite, and zoo staff describe exactly that response. Tigers are its main natural enemy, and one recorded tiger–sun bear clash killed both animals, a sign of how expensive it can be to finish one off.

The sun bear is also smarter than its size suggests. Rescued bears housed together mimic one another's facial expressions with remarkable precision, and a captive bear once opened a locked cupboard with a claw. Its limits are real, though: it is slow and short-legged on open ground, it has no armor, and at around 50 kg it is simply outweighed by the big cats and larger bears that can overpower it.

sections.habitat: Tropical evergreen and lowland forests of South and Southeast Asia, from north-eastern India and Bangladesh through mainland Southeast Asia to Sumatra and Borneo. Mangroves are used near preferred forest. The species avoids heavily logged forest and areas near settlements.
sections.diet: An omnivore with a broad diet: ants, bees and bee larvae, beetles, termites, honey, fruit and seeds, plus occasional birds, rodents, lizards, deer and scavenged tiger kills. It tears open hollow trees for bees' nests and breaks termite mounds, licking and sucking out the contents while holding pieces with its forepaws. Several bears may gather at large fruiting trees.
sections.social: Solitary in the wild apart from mothers with cubs, though group-housed rescued bears form complex play relationships and mimic one another's facial expressions.
sections.reproduction: Breeding occurs year-round. Litters are one or two cubs of about 325 g, born in tree cavities. Cubs stay with the mother for about two to three years; sexual maturity comes at two to four years (Wikipedia; SDZWA gives three to five).
sections.conservation: Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and on CITES Appendix I. IBA reports a range-wide decline of more than 30% in 30 years, with populations in Bangladesh and China close to local extinction. Deforestation, forest fires and hunting for the pet and bear-part trade are the main threats; human–bear conflict is a smaller one.
sections.features:
Sickle-shaped foreclaws about 10 cm long.
Very large canines and a strong bite for its body size.
Loose skin that allows turning within a predator's grip.
Inward-turned front feet and hairless soles for climbing.
Exceptionally long tongue.
Pale chest patch on a short black coat.
sections.humanInteraction: Crop damage rose after the 1997–98 El Niño drought and fires in Borneo reduced forest fruit; farmers were most hostile when bears killed old coconut trees by climbing and feeding in them, and metal sheeting on trunks deterred bears for at least a few years (Fredriksson 2005). Cubs were often taken as pets because of their timid nature, and bear parts are still found for sale in traditional medicine shops in Sabah and Sarawak.

funFacts: It is the smallest bear species, yet its claws are comparable in size to a brown bear's.
A 50 kg sun bear was measured biting with about 2,000 N at the molars using a reward-driven bite plate.
Sun bears copy the exact facial expressions of their playmates, a precision previously reported mainly in humans and gorillas.
A captive sun bear watched sugar being locked away and later opened the lock with a claw.
One recorded fight between a tiger and a sun bear ended with both animals dead.
The Malay and Indonesian name beruang madu means "honey bear".

abilities.name: Loose-Skin Counterbite
abilities.description: the skin is loose enough that a bear gripped by a predator can twist around inside it and bite back, turning a hold into a close-range counterattack.

abilities.name: Hardwood Ripper
abilities.description: 10 cm sickle claws and a bite of about 2,000 N at the molars let it tear open living tree trunks and termite mounds, the same tools it swings in a fight.

traits.name: Smallest Bear
traits.description: the lightest living bear species at around 25–65 kg in most accounts, and the most arboreal, often resting and sunbathing in trees 2–7 m up.

traits.name: Longest Bear Tongue
traits.description: the longest tongue of any bear, used to lick insects, larvae and honey out of narrow cavities.

combat.weapons: The sun bear packs a strong weapon set into a small bear. Its bite is unusually strong for its size, with about 2,000 N measured at the molars in a 50 kg animal, and its canines are large. Its forepaws carry heavy, sickle-shaped claws around 10 cm long that it uses to rip open hardwood trunks and termite mounds. In a fight, it combines bites with claw swipes and grappling. It is not a specialised large-prey killer: vertebrates such as birds, rodents, lizards and the occasional deer are a minor part of the diet.
weaknesses: Small mass for a bear; outweighed by most large predators.
No evidence of speed on the ground.
No armor; defense depends on skin, coat and fighting back.
Primarily an insect and fruit eater, not a trained large-prey killer.

swan.name: Swan
swan.specimen: healthy adult male (cob), 11.0 kg, about 150 cm long with a wingspan of about 220 cm.
swan.summary: The mute swan is an 11-kilogram waterbird with a big temper. It defends its nest by hissing, raising its wings, then charging with wing blows and bites, and it can drown intruding birds and even attacking dogs in the water. On the full roster its small body and lack of claws or teeth keep its damage low, and it is clumsy on land.
narrative: The mute swan is one of the heaviest birds that can still fly. A typical cob weighs about 11 kg with a wingspan of more than two metres, and it needs a long, splashing run across the water to get airborne before cruising at up to about 88 km/h. That size makes it the heavyweight of most lakes and rivers it lives on, and it behaves accordingly.

Swans are famous for defending their nests and cygnets. A threatened cob hisses, arches its neck and raises its wings in the busking display. If that does not work it charges, beating with the bony joints of its wings and biting with its bill. Against other waterbirds it has a deadly move: it climbs onto the intruder's back and holds its head underwater. Swans have killed foxes and drowned dogs, and they will chase canoes away from their young.

On the absolute battle scale, though, a swan is still an 11 kg bird. It has no talons, no teeth and no armor, its long neck and legs are exposed, and on land it is slow and awkward. Its best fights happen on open water against animals that cannot swim well. Against real predators of medium size or larger, its courage outruns its weapons.

sections.habitat: Lakes, lagoons and slow-flowing rivers, preferring medium to large bodies of fresh water. Native across much of Europe and temperate Asia; introduced populations are established in North America, where numbers in the lower Great Lakes grew at over 10% a year between 1971 and 2000, doubling every seven to eight years.
sections.diet: Mainly aquatic plants, reached by plunging the head and neck underwater or up-ending, since mute swans do not dive; small invertebrates are taken too. Grazing can deplete river vegetation, and managers have modelled "sacrificial" feeding areas to protect valuable plant beds (Wood et al. 2014). Ducks and gulls often feed alongside swans on weed the swans bring to the surface.
sections.social: Breeding pairs hold territories, often a single pair on a small lake, of about 4–10 acres (ADW). Non-breeding birds up to three or four years old gather in flocks that can number several hundred at traditional sites. In a few rich areas pairs nest colonially.
sections.reproduction: Breeding usually begins at about four years of age (BTO). The large reed nest holds eggs of about 294–396 g each, and cygnets hatch at 180–248 g. Care lasts more than four months from laying to fledging; cygnets keep grey plumage until at least their first year and are driven away before the next breeding season.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. UK numbers fell from about 1960 to the early 1980s through lead poisoning from swallowed fishing weights and shot, then recovered quickly after lead was replaced. The UK wintering population is internationally important, and the species is on the UK amber list (BTO). Whooper swans spreading into central Europe now compete with mute swans for nest sites.
sections.features:
Orange bill with a black basal knob, larger in males.
Bony wing joints used as striking points.
Very long neck for reaching submerged plants.
Loud, throbbing wingbeat noise in flight.
Among the heaviest flying birds.
sections.humanInteraction: Mute swans are familiar park birds. A UK community-science study found that 22% of systematic observations recorded people feeding swans (Maréchal et al. 2025). Cobs can attack people, boats and dogs that come near nests. Introduced North American populations have grown rapidly, doubling every seven to eight years in the lower Great Lakes between 1971 and 2000.

funFacts: One Polish cob weighed almost 23 kg, the heaviest verified weight for a flying bird.
The oldest ringed mute swan in Britain lived over 29 years.
Mute swans are not silent: their wingbeats throb loudly enough to be heard 1–2 km away.
They run across the water at about 48 km/h to get airborne.
Swans can kill intruding waterbirds by climbing on them and holding them underwater.
The story that a swan's wing can break a man's leg is a myth, although the blows are powerful.
Cygnets often ride on a parent's back between its wings.

abilities.name: Drowning Hold
abilities.description: climbs onto an intruding bird's back and pecks at its head to force it underwater until it drowns; the same approach has overwhelmed attacking dogs in water.

abilities.name: Wing Bludgeon
abilities.description: hisses, raises its wings in the busking threat pose and then charges, striking with the bony wrist joints of its wings while biting with its bill.

traits.name: Heavyweight Flyer
traits.description: one of the heaviest flying birds, with cobs averaging about 11 kg; it needs a long running take-off across the water but then reaches about 88 km/h in flight.

traits.name: Singing Wings
traits.description: despite the "mute" name, its wingbeats make a loud throbbing sound audible 1–2 km away, used as a contact signal in flight.

combat.weapons: A mute swan attacks with its wings and bill. Defense usually starts with a loud hiss and the "busking" threat pose, neck curved back and wings half raised. If that fails, the swan charges, strikes with the bony wrist area of its wings and bites. Against other waterbirds it has a specific killing technique: it climbs onto the intruder's back and pecks at the head until it forces the bird underwater and drowns it (Wikipedia). Swans can kill red foxes and have overwhelmed and drowned dogs attacking them or their cygnets. Absolute damage is still limited by an 11 kg body with no claws, talons or teeth.
weaknesses: Low absolute mass and power on the full roster.
No claws, talons or teeth; bill and wing blows only.
Long, exposed neck and legs.
Poor land mobility and slow take-off.

swordfish.name: Swordfish
swordfish.specimen: healthy large adult female, 200.0 kg, about 300 cm total length including the sword.
swordfish.summary: The swordfish is a 200-kilogram ocean hunter armed with a long, flat sword that has killed blue sharks and makos. It heats its eyes and brain to see fast prey in cold water hundreds of metres down and migrates thousands of kilometres, but it has no scales or armor and loses to orcas and the biggest sharks.
narrative: The swordfish is a deep-diving, heat-assisted hunter built around a single weapon. Its flat, broad sword makes up a large share of its three-metre length, and it uses it to slash through squid and fish before swallowing them. The sword is not only for feeding: blue sharks stranded in the Mediterranean have been found with sword fragments in their brains and eyes, some of them healed over from earlier encounters, and dead shortfin makos have turned up with broken swords in their heads.

What sets the swordfish apart is its physiology. A heater tissue keeps its eyes and brain 10 to 15 °C warmer than the surrounding water, which makes its vision many times better at following fast movement in the cold, dark depths where it spends the day. It commonly hunts at around 500 m and has been recorded below 2,800 m, then rises toward the surface at night. A gland at the base of the sword oils the skin of the head, probably helping it slip through the water.

In a battle, the swordfish is dangerous head-on and very hard to follow into the deep, and it has the stamina to migrate thousands of kilometres. Its limits are just as clear: adults have no scales or armor, the sword can snap off, and it has no bite to fall back on. Killer whales and big toothed sharks that manage to close the distance can overpower it, and outside open water it has nothing to offer.

sections.habitat: Worldwide in tropical and temperate parts of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans and the Mediterranean, from roughly 45°N to 45°S. Usually from the surface to 550 m, exceptionally to 2,878 m. Preferred temperatures are 18–22 °C, but it tolerates 5–27 °C and moves toward colder regions to feed in summer.
sections.diet: An opportunistic predator feeding from the surface to the bottom. In the north-western Atlantic, 82% of 168 stomachs held squid and 53% held fish such as gadids, mackerels, butterfish, bluefish and sand lance (Wikipedia). Other prey include barracudinas, hake, rockfish, herring, lanternfish and crustaceans. It feeds mostly at night near the surface. Almost 50 parasite species are recorded, including remoras, lampreys and cookiecutter sharks.
sections.social: Solitary or in very loose aggregations, with individuals up to 10 m apart. Males and females pair only to spawn.
sections.reproduction: Spawning is external, in warm surface waters (about 24 °C or more) down to 75 m. Females mature at 4–5 years and produce 1–29 million eggs depending on size (NOAA). Young fish are voracious predators from an early age.
sections.conservation: FishBase lists the global IUCN status as Near Threatened (assessed 2021). The North Atlantic stock is not overfished and not subject to overfishing under the 2022 ICCAT assessment (NOAA). Longline fisheries target it across all oceans.
sections.features:
Long, flat, broad sword-like bill.
Heater tissue warming the eyes and brain.
Oil gland and pores on the head.
No teeth or scales in adults; no pelvic fins.
sections.humanInteraction: A major commercial and sport fish, taken by longlines, harpoons and rod and reel. As a top predator it accumulates mercury: in the western equatorial Atlantic, swordfish had the second-highest mercury levels among the sharks and pelagic fish sampled, after the shortfin mako, and the authors set limits on safe monthly meals (de Alencar Goyanna et al. 2025). Sword strikes on sharks may be increasing as fishing reduces shared prey (Wikipedia).

funFacts: Swordfish heat their eyes and brain up to 15 °C above the surrounding water.
They have been recorded as deep as 2,878 m.
A gland at the base of the sword oils the front of the head.
Adults have no teeth and no scales.
One tagged swordfish swam 3,275 km from Tasmania toward the Coral Sea.
Stranded blue sharks in the Mediterranean have been found with pieces of swordfish sword in their brains.
The famous 100 km/h swordfish speed has no reliable measurement behind it.

abilities.name: Broadsword Slash
abilities.description: a long, flat rostrum used to slash and wound prey and to stab large sharks; stranded blue sharks have been found with sword fragments lodged in their brains and eyes.

abilities.name: Heated Deep Vision
abilities.description: a heater tissue warms the eyes and brain 10–15 °C above the water, giving more than ten times better tracking of fast movement while hunting hundreds of metres down.

traits.name: Oil-Slick Head
traits.description: a gland at the base of the sword pumps oil to pores on the head, which with tiny denticles probably forms a water-repellent layer that cuts drag.

traits.name: Sole Broadbill
traits.description: the only living member of its family, with no teeth or scales as an adult and a flat sword instead of a marlin's rounded spear.

combat.weapons: The sword is the weapon. Swordfish slash large prey with it and swallow small prey whole (Wikipedia), and FishBase states that they use the sword to kill prey. The popular image of skewering prey is based on little evidence; slashing to injure is more likely. The sword is also used against sharks. Campos-Sosa et al. (2025) examined ten blue sharks stranded in the western Mediterranean after fatal encounters with swordfish: every shark carried rostral fragments, the brain was the most damaged organ, and some fragments were already surrounded by fibrous tissue, showing earlier non-fatal clashes. Dead or dying shortfin makos have also been found with broken-off swords in their heads (Wikipedia). This is one of the best-documented lethal weapon uses of any fish on the roster.
weaknesses: No armor or scales in adults.
The sword is a single frontal weapon and can snap off inside a target.
No bite weapon; nothing to fight with at close quarters once the sword is used.
Loses to large toothed predators such as orcas and big sharks that can close in.

tapir.name: Tapir
tapir.specimen: healthy adult female, 230.0 kg, about 95 cm at the shoulder and 200 cm head-body. Females are the larger sex in this species.
tapir.summary: The lowland tapir is a 230-kilogram forest browser that prefers running to fighting. It crashes through undergrowth, swims and dives well and can breathe through its trunk while hiding underwater. When cornered its bite can be deadly, as a fatal 2005 attack in Brazil showed, but it has no horns, tusks or claws and jaguars can still bring it down.
narrative: The lowland tapir is the largest native land mammal of the Amazon, a heavy, rounded browser with a short trunk made from its nose and upper lip. It looks slow, but it moves quickly through dense forest, climbs steep ground and is an excellent swimmer and diver. Its body tapers at the front, letting it push through tangled undergrowth that slows pursuers.

Its strategy against predators is to leave. At the first sign of danger a tapir bolts into thick cover or plunges into water, where it can stay submerged with just the tip of its trunk above the surface. Thick skin on the back of the neck gives some protection against a jaguar's bite, the classic attack on a tapir resting on a riverbank at night.

When there is nowhere to run, the tapir fights with its teeth. In 2005 a Brazilian farmer who stabbed a tapir in his cornfield was bitten repeatedly on the legs and neck and died. That shows real defensive danger, but the tapir remains a single-weapon herbivore: no horns, tusks or claws, poor eyesight and a strong preference for avoiding conflict. On the absolute scale it sits in the moderate middle, with Defense a little above Attack.

sections.habitat: Tropical forests, swamps and river margins of South America east of the Andes, from Venezuela, Colombia and the Guianas south through Brazil to Paraguay, Bolivia and northern Argentina, and west to Peru and Ecuador. It is most common in dense forest near water and less common in open pasture. ADW records the species from sea level to high elevations and describes it as an adept climber. In 2024 it was seen in Rio de Janeiro state for the first time since 1914.
sections.diet: A generalist browser of leaves, buds, shoots, small branches, fruit, grasses and aquatic plants, using its trunk to pull food to its mouth. DNA metabarcoding of dung from 31 latrines in Brazil's Atlantic Forest found 61 plant species from 46 families, chosen across a wide home range rather than from the most common local plants (Lautenschlager et al. 2026). Tapirs swallow and spread large numbers of seeds, making them important seed dispersers.
sections.social: Largely solitary and mainly nocturnal. Mothers and calves stay together, and pairs meet to breed. Social behaviour in the wild is still poorly studied.
sections.reproduction: Mating peaks in April to June. Gestation lasts about 13 months (390–395 days), and females usually have one calf every two years. Newborns weigh about 6.8 kg, carry white spots and stripes that fade after about seven months, and are weaned at around six months. Sexual maturity comes in the third year.
sections.conservation: Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Habitat loss and fragmentation are the main threats highlighted by recent field studies, which find tapirs depend on dense forest and water networks (Alviz et al. 2025). Lautenschlager et al. (2026) describe Atlantic Forest tapirs as threatened megafauna whose broad diet helps maintain forest plant diversity.
sections.features:
Short, flexible, prehensile proboscis used as a snorkel.
Thick hide, especially on the back of the neck.
Low crest and short mane along the neck.
Teardrop-shaped body for pushing through dense undergrowth.
sections.humanInteraction: Serious attacks on people are rare and follow cornering or injury, such as the fatal 2005 case in Brazil. They sometimes feed in smallholder crops; in Colombia, occupancy was positively linked to crop areas used for household food (Alviz et al. 2025).

funFacts: A tapir's trunk is made from its nose and upper lip and works as a snorkel.
It can explore a circle of ground about 30 cm across with its trunk without moving its head.
Tapir calves are born with white spots and stripes, like a watermelon.
Pregnancy lasts about 13 months (390–395 days), and a female usually raises one calf every two years.
Competing tapirs bite at each other's feet.
The name "tapir" comes from a Tupi word linked to "thick", after its tough hide.
In 2024 a lowland tapir was recorded in Rio de Janeiro state for the first time in 110 years.

abilities.name: Snorkel Escape
abilities.description: flees into rivers and swamps, swims and dives well, and can breathe through its raised trunk while the body stays submerged, leaving land predators on the bank.

abilities.name: Cornered Bite
abilities.description: when trapped, bites hard and repeatedly with chisel-like incisors; a provoked lowland tapir caused fatal bite wounds to a farmer in Brazil.

traits.name: Prehensile Proboscis
traits.description: a short, flexible trunk formed from the nose and upper lip, made of soft tissue, used to grab branches, pluck fruit and sample scents.

traits.name: Amazon Heavyweight
traits.description: the largest native land mammal of the Amazon, with females outweighing the other sex and adults averaging around 225 kg.

combat.weapons: The tapir is a browsing herbivore with one weapon: a strong bite backed by a 230 kg body. It uses it when cornered. In 2005 a farmer in south-eastern Brazil surprised and stabbed a lowland tapir in his corn plantation; the tapir inflicted deep bites to his thighs, neck and cervical region and he died of haemorrhage, the first recorded fatal tapir attack (Haddad et al. 2005). Wikipedia adds that the tapir, a female of about 180 kg, also died of its wounds. Males competing for a receptive female bite each other on the feet (ADW). The tapir also has shoving mass, but no horns, tusks or claws.
weaknesses: Only one weapon, the bite, with no reach.
Poor eyesight.
No armor beyond thick skin.
Prefers flight to fighting; low willingness to press an attack.

tarantula-hawk.name: Tarantula Hawk
tarantula-hawk.specimen: healthy adult female P. grossa, about 4.5 cm body length and about 1 g. Only females hunt and only females carry a sting.
tarantula-hawk.summary: The tarantula hawk is a 1 g spider wasp whose female hunts tarantulas many times her size, paralyzing them with a precise sting to feed her larva. Its sting ranks among the most painful of any insect but is barely toxic to vertebrates, so it dominates arthropod matchups and deters predators while doing little real damage to large animals.
narrative: The tarantula hawk is a specialist built around one weapon. A female Pepsis grossa is about 4.5 cm long and weighs roughly a gram, yet her whole life's work is hunting tarantulas that can outweigh her many times over. She finds an occupied burrow by sight or scent, drives or provokes the spider into the open, and makes it rear into its threat posture. Then she seizes a leg and slips her long sting into the soft membrane beside the first leg, the route taken in more than eight of ten recorded attacks. The spider may stay paralyzed for months while her single larva feeds on it.

That precision is why the wasp tops the roster's small-animal Special tier. In an arthropod matchup, one clean sting ends the contest, and field work shows that experienced females complete the approach and paralysis faster than novices. The same sting doubles as a defensive shield. Justin Schmidt rated its pain at the top of his scale, and he found that the pain alone gives the wasp near-complete immunity from vertebrate predators: bright warning colors, a strong smell and a crowd of mimics reinforce the message.

The limits are just as clear. The venom is among the least lethal of all stinging insects, with mouse LD50 values of 65–120 mg/kg, and a 1 g body cannot overpower anything that is not an arthropod. A lizard, bird or mammal that ignores the pain can crush the wasp in one bite. On the absolute roster scale the tarantula hawk therefore keeps a very low Attack and Defense, capable Agility, and one of the highest Special scores among tiny animals.

sections.habitat: Pepsis is confined to the Americas, from Utah and Kansas south to Argentina, with at least 250 species in South America. In the United States tarantula hawks are most common in the southwestern deserts. P. grossa ranges from the southern United States through Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean to northern South America. Tarantula hawks as a group (including Hemipepsis) occur on every continent except Europe and Antarctica.
sections.diet: Adults drink nectar. In Big Bend Ranch State Park, Texas, four plants supplied 73.6% of adult P. grossa feeding: two milkweeds, Mexican buckeye and honey mesquite, and the wasps are important milkweed pollinators. Larvae are carnivorous parasitoids: each develops on a single paralyzed tarantula, feeding while avoiding vital organs for as long as possible. In Texas the preferred prey of P. grossa is Aphonopelma hentzi.
sections.social: Solitary hunters. Males defend hilltop perches to meet females, and P. grossa forms mixed-species, mixed-sex aggregations that appear defensive and may help in finding resources and mates.
sections.reproduction: A female lays one egg on each paralyzed spider in a sealed burrow. Fertilized eggs become females and are usually placed on larger (often female) spiders; unfertilized eggs become males. The larva feeds for weeks, spins a cocoon and pupates. Punzo recorded 41 days from egg to adult for P. thisbe in the laboratory, and eggs and larvae died under very dry (10% relative humidity) conditions.
sections.conservation: No IUCN Red List assessment of P. grossa was located, so it is treated here as Not Evaluated. The species is widespread and common in parts of its range. Its prey tarantulas and its nectar plants are its main ecological dependencies.
sections.features:
Long, curved sting with a large venom supply.
Paralytic venom able to immobilize spiders for months.
Hooked tarsal claws for grappling and dragging prey.
Aposematic coloration and odor.
Female-only sting; males are harmless.
sections.humanInteraction: Stings happen almost only when a wasp is handled or stepped on. Aside from allergic reactions, the sting is not medically dangerous, and redness can last up to a week after the pain fades. In 1989 New Mexico schoolchildren voted P. formosa (now P. grossa) the official state insect.

funFacts: The tarantula hawk's sting is rated 4 on the Schmidt pain index, level with the bullet ant, yet its venom is roughly 45 to 65 times less lethal to mice (LD50 65–90 versus 1.4 mg/kg).
Entomologist Justin Schmidt described the pain as "blinding, fierce, shockingly electric".
One Pepsis sting dissected in a 2018 study measured 14.33 mm, the longest actual sting of 39 non-velvet-ant wasps measured.
Tarantulas paralyzed by large spider wasps have survived eight months of paralysis.
Only females sting; males spend their days guarding hilltop perches.
The greater roadrunner is one of the few animals that eats them, beating each wasp against the ground first.
Many flies, beetles and moths survive by copying the tarantula hawk's orange-and-blue warning colors.

abilities.name: Nerve-Center Sting
abilities.description: the female drives her long sting through the soft membrane between a spider's sternum and first leg (over 80% of recorded stings in P. thisbe), producing paralysis that can last months. Against arthropods this ends the fight in one strike.

abilities.name: Blinding Pain Venom
abilities.description: a sting rated 4 of 4 on the Schmidt pain index that incapacitates people for minutes while carrying very low lethality (mouse LD50 65–120 mg/kg). Against vertebrates it is a deterrent that can force a disengagement, not a killing weapon.

traits.name: Tarantula Specialist Parasitoid
traits.description: each female hunts and paralyzes tarantulas to feed a single larva, routinely overpowering an armed spider far heavier than herself.

traits.name: Warning-Color Immunity
traits.description: metallic blue-black body, bright orange wings and a strong odor advertise the sting so well that few animals eat tarantula hawks, and many harmless insects mimic them.

combat.weapons:
The primary weapon is the female sting: a long, curved lancet (7–14 mm in published measurements) backed by a large venom supply. Against arthropods, especially tarantulas, the venom is a precision paralytic. Punzo (1994) found that more than 80% of stings on P. thisbe prey went through the soft membrane between the sternum and the base of the first leg, straight toward the spider's central nerve mass. The result is paralysis that can last months, which is decisive in any arthropod matchup.

Against vertebrates the same sting is a pain weapon rather than a killing weapon. Its lethality to mice (65–120 mg/kg) is among the lowest of all stinging insects, so a 1 g wasp cannot deliver a toxic dose to a large animal. What it can deliver is some of the most intense pain recorded for any insect. The mandibles and hooked claws grapple and drag prey but have negligible absolute force.
weaknesses: About 1 g of body mass: negligible absolute force against any vertebrate.
Venom has very low vertebrate toxicity; a large animal suffers pain, not disablement.
A clean bite, peck or crush ends the fight.
Males are unarmed.
Activity drops in extreme heat and in cold.

tasmanian-devil.name: Tasmanian Devil
tasmanian-devil.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 9.0 kg, about 65 cm head-body length plus a 25–26 cm tail and about 30 cm at the shoulder.
tasmanian-devil.summary: The Tasmanian devil is a stocky 6–12 kg marsupial scavenger with the strongest bite for its size of any living mammalian carnivore. It crushes bone, eats whole carcasses and can kill wallabies and wombats, but its small body, slow gallop and lack of armor keep it far below the big predators in a straight fight.
narrative: The Tasmanian devil is a jaw on legs. A mature male weighs about 9 kg, yet its massive head and jaw muscles produce the highest bite force relative to body size of any living mammalian carnivore that has been measured. That bite lets it crush bones, swallow fur and hide, and clean a carcass so thoroughly that little remains. When it hunts, it kills with a crushing bite to the head or neck and can take animals heavier than itself, including wallabies and wombats.

The rest of the body supports that weapon rather than adding new ones. Devils amble and gallop instead of sprinting, so they rarely catch healthy fast prey. Their strength is endurance: they patrol trails for up to 16 km in a night, find carcasses by smell and hearing, and settle disputes with a chorus of growls, screeches and wide-mouthed gapes. Most encounters end without contact, but when devils do fight, especially during mating, they bite each other hard, which is how devil facial tumour disease spreads.

In a matchup the devil is dangerous to anything its own size or smaller that lets it close in. Its bite is far stronger than its mass suggests, and it tolerates wounds. Against large predators, armored animals or fast opponents, its small body, limited speed and single weapon leave it outmatched. On the absolute roster scale it sits among small carnivores such as badgers and honey badgers, with a notable Special score for its bone-crushing specialization.

sections.habitat: Found only on the island of Tasmania, where it uses almost all habitats, including coastal heath, dry forest, wet forest and farmland edges. It disappeared from mainland Australia about 3,500 years ago. Insurance populations are kept in zoos and disease-free sites under the Save the Tasmanian Devil Program, and a small group has been returned to the Australian mainland for the first time in over 3,000 years (Wikipedia).
sections.diet: A scavenger and hunter that eats whatever animal food is available. Favorite prey and carrion include wallabies, possums and wombats; small mammals and birds are eaten as prey or carrion, and seabird feathers and fur-seal fur have turned up in scats. Collared devils spent more time scavenging than hunting. By clearing carcasses quickly, devils help limit insects that could otherwise harm livestock (Wikipedia).
sections.social: Solitary, with overlapping home ranges of about 2,500 ha at one study site; Wikipedia gives two-to-four-week home ranges of 4–27 km². Devils gather at large carcasses, where they compete with noise and posture, and meet during the mating season (recent studies place it between February and June), when biting is most frequent. Contact-network studies found all devils in one population linked into a single network.
sections.reproduction: Gestation lasts about 21 days. A female gives birth to 20–30 tiny young of about 0.2 g, but has only four nipples in the pouch, so no more than four can be raised. Young leave the pouch at about 100–105 days, weighing around 200 g, and are fully grown at about two years. In populations with DFTD, females often begin breeding at one year instead of two.
sections.conservation: Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2008), under Tasmania's Threatened Species Protection Act and under Australia's EPBC Act. Devil facial tumour disease, a fatal, contagious cancer spread by biting, has reached about 95% of the species' range in two decades. The Save the Tasmanian Devil Program manages insurance populations and disease-free sites.
sections.features:
Highest bite force for body mass among living mammalian carnivores.
Teeth that keep erupting throughout life.
75–80 degree jaw gape.
Long whiskers from chin to the rear of the jaw.
Forelegs slightly longer than hind legs.
sections.humanInteraction: Believed to kill livestock, the devil was targeted by a bounty scheme as early as 1830; it is now a Tasmanian icon and a flagship conservation species. Roadkill is a significant local mortality cause because devils feed on carcasses along roads.

funFacts: Pound for pound, the devil has the strongest bite of any living mammalian carnivore measured, with a bite force quotient of 181.
A newborn devil weighs about 0.2 g, roughly the weight of a raisin.
A female gives birth to 20–30 young but has only four nipples in her pouch.
Devils can eat up to 40% of their body weight in 30 minutes.
Their teeth are never replaced but keep erupting slowly through life.
DFTD is one of only a handful of contagious cancers known in nature.
Devils can travel up to 16 km in a single night.

abilities.name: Bone-Crusher Bite
abilities.description: a large head, heavy jaw muscles and 75–80 degree gape give the highest bite force relative to body mass of any living mammalian carnivore measured (BFQ 181). It lets the devil crush bone and deliver a killing bite to the head or neck of wallabies and wombats.

abilities.name: Screech-and-Gape Standoff
abilities.description: growls, screeches and the wide open-mouthed gape settle most carcass disputes without contact. In a matchup it can make a rival or scavenger hesitate, but it does not add damage.

traits.name: Largest Carnivorous Marsupial
traits.description: the biggest surviving meat-eating marsupial, a stocky 6–12 kg animal found only in Tasmania.

traits.name: Whole-Carcass Scavenger
traits.description: eats meat, bone and fur, typically about 15% of its body weight a day and up to 40% in 30 minutes when food is plentiful.

combat.weapons:
The devil's weapon is its jaw. A large head, heavy jaw muscles and robust teeth give it the highest bite force for its body size of any living mammalian carnivore measured by Wroe et al. The absolute figure, about 418 N at the canine for a 12 kg animal, is roughly what a medium dog produces. It lets a devil crush bone, consume whole carcasses including fur, and kill prey larger than itself. Andersen et al. (2020) note that hunting is rarely seen but that devils can kill Bennett's wallabies and bare-nosed wombats, using a crushing bite to the head or neck. Wikipedia describes attacks on wombats up to 30 kg.

Forelimbs are used for holding and digging; the claws are not the main weapon. With only a 9 kg body behind it, the bite can maim a medium animal but cannot overpower a large predator head-on.
weaknesses: Small absolute mass (9 kg).
Slow for a predator; poor at pursuing fast prey.
No armor; relies on a single close-range weapon.
Highly vulnerable to DFTD, a transmissible cancer.

tiger-shark.name: Tiger Shark
tiger-shark.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 4.0 m total length and about 500 kg.
tiger-shark.summary: The tiger shark is a 4 m, 500 kg generalist predator with serrated, sideways-hooked teeth that saw through sea-turtle shells. A stealthy, persistent hunter that eats almost anything, it ranks second only to the white shark in attacks on people, though it lacks the speed of lamnid sharks and is outclassed by orcas.
narrative: The tiger shark is the ocean's great generalist. A mature female commonly reaches around 4 m and 500 kg, and she will eat almost anything: fish, rays, seabirds, dolphins, dugongs, other sharks, whale carcasses and, most famously, sea turtles. The key is her teeth. Each is broad, finely serrated and hooked to one side, and a shake of the head turns a row of them into a saw that cuts through shell and bone.

Tiger sharks hunt by patience rather than raw speed. Tagged sharks swim continuously, rising and falling through the water column in a yo-yo pattern that researchers read as a search strategy. The dark striped back blends with deep water or reef, letting the shark close in slowly before a short burst. When it misses, it tries again: at albatross colonies in Hawaii, strike efficiency is low, but repeated attacks make predation successful overall. Tiger sharks also time their movements to seasonal food, arriving at fledging colonies ahead of peak numbers and gathering in diffuse aggregations during the mating season.

In a matchup, the tiger shark brings mass, cutting teeth and persistence. It is heavier than the bull and mako sharks and better equipped to cut hard prey, but it is less agile than lamnid sharks and smaller and less specialized than the great white. Orcas and the largest marine mammals remain out of its reach. On the absolute roster scale it sits in the elite marine-predator tier, just below the white shark in Attack and above most other sharks.

sections.habitat: Tropical and warm-temperate seas worldwide, especially coastal waters, reefs, lagoons, seagrass beds and river mouths, with regular trips into open ocean and deep water. Fuvahmulah Island in the Maldives hosts the largest known aggregation of tiger sharks.
sections.diet: A generalist apex predator and scavenger. Prey includes sea turtles, rays, other sharks, bony fishes, seabirds, dolphins, dugongs, seals, squid, crustaceans and carrion. Juveniles take smaller prey; the diet broadens sharply at about 2.3 m. Dolphins and dugongs shift their habitat use when tiger sharks are abundant, so the shark shapes the behavior of its prey.
sections.social: Mostly solitary, but tiger sharks gather at predictable food pulses and at mating aggregations. Mature females at Fuvahmulah form a size-based dominance hierarchy.
sections.reproduction: The tiger shark is ovoviviparous: eggs hatch inside the mother and fully developed young are born live, in litters of 10 to 80 pups. Newborns measure 51–76 cm. Females reach median maturity at 261.4 cm FL and 11.6 years, males at 258.9 cm FL and 9.5 years (western North Atlantic). Females are reported to breed once every three years.
sections.conservation: Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List, mainly because of fishing and finning pressure.
sections.features:
Serrated, sideways-hooked teeth shaped for cutting hard prey.
Broad, heavily calcified jaws and a nearly terminal mouth.
Ampullae of Lorenzini and lateral line.
Reflective retinal layer for low-light vision.
Long upper tail lobe for bursts and long pectoral fins for lift.
sections.humanInteraction: Second only to the white shark in confirmed unprovoked attacks and fatalities. Hawaii typically records three to four shark bites a year, a very low rate given the number of people in the water. Tiger sharks are also a major dive-tourism draw at provisioning sites such as Fuvahmulah and the Bahamas.

funFacts: Tiger sharks have been found with cans, plastic bottles and burlap sacks in their stomachs.
Adult sea turtles have made up as much as 20.8% of stomach contents in some tiger shark studies.
At Kure Atoll, tiger sharks arrive at albatross colonies about four weeks before peak fledging, when young birds are most vulnerable.
Their stripes fade as they grow, so the oldest tiger sharks are often the least striped.
Tagged tiger sharks swim continuously, rising and diving through the water column in a yo-yo pattern.
Tiger sharks have been recorded at depths approaching 900 m.
Orcas are among the few animals that prey on adult tiger sharks.

abilities.name: Shell-Saw Bite
abilities.description: broad, serrated teeth with a sideways hook, set in a heavily calcified jaw and worked by side-to-side head shaking, slice through sea-turtle shells and carve chunks from animals far larger than the shark.

abilities.name: Stripe-Shadow Ambush
abilities.description: a dark striped back hides the shark against dark water or reef; it approaches slowly, then bursts in, and keeps striking after misses until it connects.

traits.name: Ocean's Widest Menu
traits.description: the widest food spectrum of any shark, from crustaceans, fish and seabirds to sea turtles, dolphins, dugongs and whale carcasses, plus inedible objects such as cans and sacks.

traits.name: Tiger-Striped Giant
traits.description: bold bars and spots on young sharks fade with age on a body that commonly reaches 3.3–4.3 m and 385–635 kg.

combat.weapons:
The tiger shark's weapon is a broad, heavy jaw lined with serrated, hook-cusped teeth. It can bite through the shells of large sea turtles and remove chunks from large animals by shaking its head. Adults regularly eat sea turtles (found in up to 20.8% of stomachs in some studies), dolphins, dugongs, seals, seabirds, rays and other sharks, and they scavenge whale carcasses. Wikipedia describes its food spectrum as the widest of any shark.

In a matchup, this combination of mass, bite and cutting teeth is enough to maim or kill most marine animals short of great whales and orcas. It is below the great white in size and bite specialization but above the bull, mako and oceanic whitetip in weight and hard-prey cutting ability.
weaknesses: No armor; gills, eyes and belly are vulnerable.
Relatively slow and not built for long high-speed chases.
Cannot match orcas, great whales or the largest crocodilians in mass and power.

toucan.name: Toucan
toucan.specimen: healthy adult male, 0.6 kg and about 58 cm long, with a bill of about 20 cm.
toucan.summary: The toco toucan is a 0.6 kg South American fruit-eater with the largest bill for its body of any bird. The foam-cored bill works as a reach tool and a heat radiator, and toucans use it to raid nests and kill nestlings, but with little body mass or force, the bird is outmatched by almost any real predator.
narrative: The toco toucan looks like a bird built around its bill, and in a sense it is. The bright orange bill makes up about a third of the bird's length and up to half of its surface area, yet it is so light that it adds only a few percent to the bird's roughly 0.6 kg weight. Inside, a thin shell of keratin tiles surrounds a foam of bony struts, a structure engineers study for its stiffness at low weight. That design lets the toucan perch on slender branches and reach out for fruit that heavier birds cannot get.

The bill is more than a fruit picker. Toco toucans can pump blood into it to dump heat or shut the flow down to keep warm, a thermal control system that rivals an elephant's ears. And the serrated bill makes the toucan a skilled nest raider. In central Brazil, toco toucans have been filmed taking eggs from buff-necked ibis nests and killing chicks weighing 200–300 g by grabbing their heads and shaking. They also take a large share of hyacinth macaw eggs, even while planting the seeds of the trees those macaws nest in.

In a battle, however, the toucan's bill is more reach than weapon. It cannot crush like a macaw's beak or pierce like a raptor's talons, and the bird itself is light, lightly muscled and not especially fast in the air. On the absolute roster scale it sits near other small birds in Attack and Defense, with good canopy agility and a Special score driven by its unusual bill rather than by combat power.

sections.habitat: South America from the Guianas south to northern Argentina and Uruguay, including much of Brazil, Bolivia and far southeastern Peru. ADW describes dry, semi-open areas such as woodland, savanna, cerrado, plantations and gallery forest, up to about 1,750 m near the Andes. The species' range may be expanding into deforested parts of the Amazon.
sections.diet: A generalist frugivore that eats figs, guavas, peppers and many other fleshy fruits, plus insects (mainly caterpillars and termites), lizards, amphibians, eggs, nestlings and small birds. Toco toucans disperse more than 83% of the seeds of the manduvi tree, the main nesting tree of the endangered hyacinth macaw, while also accounting for over half of hyacinth macaw egg predation.
sections.social: Usually alone, in pairs or small groups at fruiting trees; group members preen one another. After breeding, larger flocks may roam in search of fruit.
sections.reproduction: Monogamous pairs nest in tree hollows. The female lays 2–4 eggs, both parents incubate for 17–18 days, and both care for the altricial chicks. Juveniles have duller colors and shorter bills. Sexual maturity comes at 3–4 years (ADW).
sections.conservation: Least Concern (BirdLife International, as reported on Wikipedia). The species is listed on CITES Appendix II because of the bird trade.
sections.features:
Largest bill relative to body size of any bird.
Keratin-and-foam sandwich bill structure.
Controllable blood flow to the bill for heat exchange.
Serrated bill edges for gripping and peeling food.
Nearly bill-length flat tongue.
sections.humanInteraction: A popular zoo and aviary bird and an icon of South American wildlife. Captive toucans are prone to iron-storage disease on iron-rich diets (ADW). The trade in wild birds is regulated under CITES.

funFacts: The toco toucan's bill can make up one-third of its length but only a few percent of its weight.
Its bill works like a radiator; relative to its size it sheds heat about as well as an elephant's ears.
Toucans sleep with their bills tucked under a wing to keep warm.
The earliest European writer to describe it, Pierre Belon in 1555, owned only a bill and guessed the toucan was a web-footed fish-eater.
Toco toucans spread more than 83% of the seeds of the manduvi tree, yet they also eat many hyacinth macaw eggs laid in those same trees.
The heaviest prey recorded for a toucan are buff-necked ibis nestlings of 200–300 g.
Toco toucans can fly across bodies of water more than 5 km wide.

abilities.name: Long-Reach Nest Raid
abilities.description: a 16–22 cm serrated bill reaches deep into tree holes and out to thin branch tips; toco toucans use it to seize eggs and kill nestlings of ibises, macaws and other birds by gripping and shaking.

abilities.name: Radiator Bill
abilities.description: the toucan can open or close blood flow to its bill to shed or keep body heat, making the bill one of the largest thermal windows relative to size in the animal kingdom. It helps the bird stay active in heat.

traits.name: Biggest Bill for Its Body
traits.description: the largest bill relative to body size of any bird, about one-third of total length and 30–50% of the body surface, yet only a few percent of body weight.

traits.name: Foam-Core Beak
traits.description: a sandwich of thin keratin tiles over a bony foam gives stiffness at very low density (about 0.1–0.25 g/cm³).

combat.weapons:
The toucan's only real weapon is its long, serrated bill. It gives reach and a grasping edge rather than crushing power: the bill is a lightweight foam-filled structure built for reaching fruit at the tips of thin branches, not a nut-cracking vise like a macaw's. Even so, the toco toucan is a capable nest predator. Moroni et al. (2017) watched toco toucans raid buff-necked ibis nests, carrying off an egg and killing 10–15-day-old nestlings by gripping the head in the bill and shaking vigorously, probably breaking the neck. The nestlings snapped back with their own bills. These 200–300 g chicks are the heaviest birds known to be taken by a toucan.

In a matchup this means the toucan can kill small, vulnerable animals but has little to offer against a healthy predator of its own size or larger.
weaknesses: About 0.6 kg with little muscle power.
Light, foam-cored bill that can crack or deform.
No talons or crushing bite.
Heavy, undulating flight is less evasive than a parrot's or raptor's.

tuna.name: Tuna
tuna.specimen: healthy large adult, 2.0 m fork length and about 150 kg, sex unspecified because the sources used give no sex-specific size difference.
tuna.summary: The Pacific bluefin tuna is a 2 m, 150 kg warm-bodied fish built for speed and endurance, crossing the North Pacific and turning sharply despite its torpedo shape. It hunts small schooling prey and has no real weapon, so it wins by outlasting and outrunning rather than by fighting.
narrative: The Pacific bluefin tuna is an engine in the shape of a fish. A common large adult is about 2 m long and 150 kg, most of it swimming muscle. Heat exchangers in its circulation hold that muscle, along with its eyes and brain, well above the temperature of the surrounding sea, so the bluefin can keep swimming hard in cold water where other fish slow down. That warm engine powers some of the longest migrations of any fish: young bluefin hatched off Japan cross the whole North Pacific to feed off California, as shown when fish carrying Fukushima-derived cesium turned up there within months.

The same body is surprisingly nimble. Its front half is stiff and streamlined, but the narrow tail stalk and crescent tail flex hard. Filming of captive bluefin showed turns of up to 302 degrees per second and turn radii under half a body length, achieved with rapid ratchet-like tail strokes. Combined with its size, this lets the tuna run down fast squid and schooling fish, which it swallows whole.

In a battle, though, the bluefin has little to hurt an opponent with. Its teeth are small and meant for gripping, it has no bill like a marlin or sailfish, and it carries no armor. Its best tactic is to use its speed and stamina to escape. On the absolute roster scale it scores near the top in Stamina and high in Agility and Special, but its Attack stays far below the billfish and sharks it shares the ocean with.

sections.habitat: The North Pacific, from the coasts of East Asia to western North America, with occasional records in the South Pacific; a genetically confirmed Pacific bluefin has even been caught off Brazil. Usually in the upper 200 m of open water, down to 550 m.
sections.diet: An open-water predator of schooling squids and fishes (anchovies, sardines, saury, mackerels, hake, other tunas) that also takes pelagic red crabs and krill. Diet studies in the southern California Current show its feeding niche shifting with the abundance of prey such as northern anchovy.
sections.social: Schooling fish that migrate in groups; no territorial or ritualized fighting behavior is known.
sections.reproduction: Spawning takes place in the western Pacific, mainly the East China Sea and the Sea of Japan. Fish mature at about five years, around 1.5 m and 60 kg. The generation length is about 7–9 years. Many juveniles make a trans-Pacific crossing during their first years and feed in the California Current before returning west.
sections.conservation: Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List. Wikipedia notes that this listing has not been updated since a 2024 stock assessment found the population had risen from about 2% of historic levels in 2010 to about 23% in 2020. NOAA Fisheries and several international commissions manage the fishery.
sections.features:
Regional endothermy through retia mirabilia.
Thunniform swimming with a crescent tail, finlets and keels.
Rigid, streamlined body with exceptional turning ability for its shape.
Warm eyes and brain for cold-water vision.
sections.humanInteraction: One of the most valuable fish in the world. About 80% of Pacific and Atlantic bluefin is eaten in Japan, and New Year auction prices can reach millions of dollars: a 278 kg Pacific bluefin sold for 333.6 million yen in 2019. Recreational anglers also target the species off California.

funFacts: Pacific bluefin carried traces of the 2011 Fukushima release across the entire North Pacific to California within months.
A 278 kg Pacific bluefin sold for 333.6 million yen (about US$3.1 million) at a Tokyo auction in 2019.
Bluefin can keep their muscles up to 20 °C warmer than the surrounding sea.
Despite a stiff body, a bluefin can turn at up to 302 degrees per second.
Juvenile bluefin start holding their own body temperature at about 40 cm long.
During a marine heatwave, young bluefin moved their feeding migration about 900 km toward the pole.

abilities.name: Warm-Blooded Engine
abilities.description: counter-current heat exchangers keep swimming muscle, eyes and brain up to 20 °C warmer than cold water, sustaining power and vision where cold-bodied fish slow down.

abilities.name: Ratchet Turn
abilities.description: a rapid series of small tail strokes swings the stiff body around at up to 302 degrees per second in less than half a body length, letting a torpedo-shaped fish change direction sharply.

traits.name: Ocean-Crossing Migrant
traits.description: young Pacific bluefin cross the entire North Pacific from Japan to California and return years later to spawn in the western Pacific.

traits.name: Living Torpedo
traits.description: a rigid, streamlined body, crescent tail, finlets and keels make the bluefin one of the most specialized fast-swimming body plans among fishes.

combat.weapons: The Pacific bluefin is a fast, powerful predator of small schooling animals: squids, sardines, anchovies, saury, mackerels, hake, other tunas, pelagic red crabs and krill. It catches prey by speed and swallows it whole; its small teeth grip rather than cut. It has no bill like a marlin, no cutting teeth like a shark and no defensive spines. In a matchup its main assets are momentum and endurance, not a weapon, so Attack stays low for a 150 kg animal.
weaknesses: No meaningful weapon; small gripping teeth only.
No armor; ordinary scaled skin.
Must keep moving in open water; poor in shallow, cluttered or confined habitats.
Heavy fishing pressure has made populations far smaller than their historic size.

vulture.name: Vulture
vulture.specimen: healthy adult of about 8.0 kg, 105 cm long, with a 2.6 m wingspan.
vulture.summary: The griffon vulture is a big 8 kg scavenger with a 2.6 m wingspan that soars for hours at almost no energy cost while scanning thousands of square kilometres for carcasses. It has a strong tearing beak and an acid gut, but its weak feet and light, unarmored body make it a poor fighter against anything healthy.
narrative: The griffon vulture is built around soaring. With broad wings spanning up to 2.8 m and a body of about 8 kg, it rides thermals over mountains and plains at barely more than its resting metabolic rate, covering foraging ranges of around 10,000 km² from its cliff colonies. Take-off is the hard part: a triple-speed heartbeat and heavy flapping lift it into the first thermal, after which it can glide between updrafts at close to 19 m/s.

Its tools are those of a carcass specialist. A heavy hooked beak rips open hides, the bare head and neck stay clean inside the body cavity, and an extremely acidic gut handles decaying meat. Griffons find food by sight and by watching each other, and a feeding crowd strips a carcass in minutes, with older adults bullying their way to the best places. Occasionally, when food is short, griffons have attacked newborn or weakened livestock.

In a fight, the griffon is outclassed by almost any predator of similar size. It cannot grip or kill with its feet, it is slow to get airborne, and its body offers no armor. Its ABS profile therefore stays low in Attack and Defense while scoring high in Stamina and Special, reflecting an animal that wins by outlasting and out-searching rivals, not by overpowering them.

sections.habitat: Resident in the Iberian Peninsula, the eastern Atlas Mountains, the eastern Alps and Balkans, Anatolia, the Caucasus, parts of Arabia and the Iranian plateau, and east to the Tian Shan and Altai Mountains. It breeds on crags and cliffs and forages over open landscapes of scrub, grassland and small woods where carcasses can be spotted. Spain held an estimated 30,946 breeding pairs in 2018; Crete has the largest island population.
sections.diet: An obligate scavenger of large carcasses, historically wild ungulates and now largely livestock. Birds eat from the mouth and anus inward, and food at supplementary feeding stations is preferred when natural food is scarce or flight conditions are poor. Mean foraging radius on Crete was about 15 km, with livestock carrion up to 9 km from a colony used with little competition. Carcass removal is an important ecosystem service that reduces disease transmission.
sections.social: Highly social. Birds nest in loose colonies, roost together and forage in mixed-age groups, following one another to food. At carcasses older adults dominate younger birds.
sections.reproduction: One egg per breeding attempt, laid on a cliff ledge or in a cave; sheltered sites produce more fledglings. Strong natal philopatry: many birds recruit as breeders in the colony, and sometimes on the same cliff, where they hatched. The captive longevity record is 41.4 years.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (BirdLife International 2021), with a growing Spanish population. Threats include illegal poison baits, veterinary drugs such as NSAIDs in carcasses, food shortages after EU carcass-removal rules brought in over BSE, collisions with wind turbines, and outbreaks such as the 2022 H5N1 avian influenza outbreak in Spain and France. Reintroductions and releases have restored or reinforced colonies in France, Bulgaria and Sardinia.
sections.features:
Wingspan 2.3–2.8 m and wing loading of about 9 kg/m².
Soaring flight at about 1.43 times basal metabolic rate.
Bare head and neck with a pale neck ruff.
Strong hooked beak with cutting edges; ground-walking feet.
Digestive tract pH about 1–1.5.
Can fast for up to two weeks.
sections.humanInteraction: Griffons clear livestock carcasses, and supplementary feeding stations are the main management tool supporting them today. In parts of Spain, farmer complaints of vulture attacks on newborn or weak livestock have grown since sanitary rules cut food supplies. Griffons are highly vulnerable to poison baits and wind turbines because they feed in groups and cannot see ahead while scanning the ground.

funFacts: A griffon in soaring flight uses only about 1.4 times its resting energy.
Heart rate triples at take-off but drops back near resting levels within 10 minutes of soaring.
About 30 griffons can finish a sheep carcass in half an hour.
Their gut acid has a pH of about 1–1.5.
When foraging, a griffon is often blind straight ahead, which is why it hits wind turbines.
Spain holds more than 90% of Europe's griffon vultures.
A captive griffon lived to 41.4 years.

abilities.name: Thermal Marathon
abilities.description: soaring flight costs about 1.43 times resting metabolism and lets a griffon search foraging ranges of around 10,000 km² with almost no flapping; it wins long searching or waiting contests, not short fights.

abilities.name: Carcass Crew Descent
abilities.description: a vulture lowering its legs to land signals a find to others, and a crowd of about 30 can strip a sheep in half an hour; a group arrival quickly overwhelms smaller scavengers at food.

traits.name: Acid Gut Shield
traits.description: a digestive tract with a pH of about 1–1.5 and a protective gut microbiota let it eat decaying carcasses that would sicken most animals.

traits.name: Bare-Head Thermostat
traits.description: the bare head and neck stay clean inside carcasses and act as radiators; posture changes raise bare-skin exposure from about 7% to 32%.

combat.weapons: The griffon is a scavenger, not a hunter. Its one real weapon is a heavy hooked beak made for ripping open carcasses, backed by strong neck muscles for pulling tissue. Its feet are suited to walking on the ground rather than catching prey, so it cannot grip and kill like an eagle. It "does not normally attack larger living prey", but Spanish griffons have been reported killing weak, young or sick animals when carrion was scarce. In Catalonia, 683 farmer complaints of "vulture attacks" were logged from 1996 to 2020, 80% during the birthing season and mostly involving cattle, which points to newborn or birthing livestock rather than healthy adults.
weaknesses: Weak, walking feet; no killing grip.
Expensive, slow take-off and poor performance in weak thermals, cloud or rain.
Light, unarmored body on the full-roster scale.
Blind spot in the direction of travel when foraging.
Low willingness to fight healthy animals.
