wallaby.name: Wallaby
wallaby.specimen: healthy adult male of about 17 kg, 76 cm head-body length and a tail of about the same length.
wallaby.summary: The swamp wallaby is a 17 kg, dark-furred browser of eastern Australian undergrowth that hops with its head low and its tail straight out. It eats plants poisonous to many animals and finds food by smell, but with weak kicks, no armor and a strong preference for fleeing, it is easy prey for dingoes and dogs.
narrative: The swamp wallaby is a stocky, dark wallaby of about 17 kg in an adult male, with a rusty chest, a pale cheek stripe and a long tail often tipped white. It is the only living member of its genus and moves unlike other wallabies, bounding through ferns and scrub with its head low and tail held stiffly behind it.

It is a browser, feeding on shrubs, ferns and fungi, and it tolerates plants such as bracken, hemlock and lantana that poison many other herbivores. It finds seedlings by their leaf odour, a skill grazing kangaroos lack, and spends the day hidden in thick cover before moving out at night, even into farmland and suburbs. Its reproduction has been described as unique among mammals: a female forms a new embryo while still pregnant with a full-term fetus, so she is pregnant and suckling young throughout her adult life.

In a fight the swamp wallaby has little to offer. It can kick and push like other macropods, but at 17 kg its blows are light, its skull is built for leaves, and it has no armor. Dingoes and wild dogs eat it regularly. Its ABS profile therefore has low Attack and Defense, with good Agility for escape through dense undergrowth.

sections.habitat: Eastern Australia, from the tip of Cape York Peninsula in Queensland down the east coast to western Victoria and south-eastern South Australia, where its range has expanded greatly in recent decades. It lives in thick forest and woodland undergrowth, fern gullies, swamps and sandstone heath, and also uses farmland, mallee and sand hills; brigalow scrub in Queensland is a favoured habitat. It has been introduced to New Zealand.
sections.diet: A browser rather than a grazer: shrubs, ferns, pasture plants, crops and native and introduced vegetation, including plants toxic to many other animals. It also eats fungi and disperses the spores of mycorrhizal fungi, which live in partnership with trees, hundreds of metres through the forest. It browses palatable tree seedlings such as blackbutt eucalypts, finding them by smell.
sections.social: Solitary and mainly nocturnal. Unrelated animals may gather at shared food without territorial behavior.
sections.reproduction: Breeds year-round. Gestation is 33–38 days; the single young spends 8–9 months in the pouch and suckles until about 15 months. Because its pregnancy is longer than its oestrous cycle, a female ovulates, mates and forms a new embryo before the current fetus is born; the embryo then pauses its development (embryonic diapause) until the newborn leaves the pouch about nine months later. Males have an unusual sex-chromosome system with one X and two Y chromosomes.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2016). It is common and has expanded its range, but many are killed on roads, and dingoes, wild dogs and eagles prey on it.
sections.features:
Hops with head low and tail held straight out.
Browsing teeth with a lifelong cutting premolar.
Tolerates bracken, hemlock and lantana.
Finds food by leaf odour.
Continuous overlapping pregnancies.
Only living member of the genus Wallabia.
sections.humanInteraction: The swamp wallaby lives in bushland close to towns and farms, is often seen by roads and is frequently hit by vehicles. In Queensland and New South Wales it is nicknamed "stinker" for its swampy smell. Livestock guardian dogs exclude swamp wallabies from grazing properties.

funFacts: Female swamp wallabies are pregnant almost continuously, carrying a new embryo while still pregnant with a full-term fetus.
Males have two different Y chromosomes.
Swamp wallabies can eat bracken, hemlock and lantana, plants that poison many animals.
They can find hidden seedlings using smell alone.
A rare golden form lives on Stradbroke Island.
It is sometimes called the "stinker" because of its swampy odour.
Swamp wallabies spread the spores of tree-partner fungi through the forest in their droppings, sometimes more than a kilometre away.

abilities.name: Undergrowth Bolt
abilities.description: hops fast with its head held low and tail straight out, a posture suited to bursting through ferns and thick scrub where larger animals cannot follow easily.

abilities.name: Scent-Tracking Browser
abilities.description: finds hidden seedlings by leaf odour alone, a skill grazing kangaroos lack; in a battle this means strong awareness at close range rather than extra damage.

traits.name: Always Pregnant
traits.description: females mate and form a new embryo one to two days before giving birth, so they carry two pregnancies at once and stay pregnant and lactating throughout their reproductive life.

traits.name: Toxic-Plant Diet
traits.description: browses shrubs and ferns and tolerates plants poisonous to many animals, including bracken, hemlock and lantana.

combat.weapons: The swamp wallaby is a browsing herbivore with no specialized weapons. Its only real striking tools are its long hind feet, which in macropods can deliver kicks, but at 17 kg any such blow is far weaker than a large kangaroo's. Its skull is built for chewing leaves, not for biting hard. It is not known to attack other animals, and its whole defensive strategy is to avoid being seen and to bolt.
weaknesses: Small absolute size and weak kicks and bite.
No armor or dangerous weapon.
Low willingness to fight.
Vulnerable to dogs and dingoes in the open.
Often killed on roads.

walrus.name: Walrus
walrus.specimen: healthy adult bull of about 1,200 kg and 300 cm long, with tusks of about 50–70 cm.
walrus.summary: The walrus is a 1.2-tonne Arctic giant armed with ivory tusks up to a metre long, protected by skin up to 10 cm thick and blubber, and equipped with a carpet of super-sensitive whiskers. Slow on land but dangerous in water, it can fatally wound a polar bear, though herds usually flee from danger.
narrative: A walrus bull is a mountain of wrinkled brown skin: around 1,200 kg, three metres long, with a broad whiskered muzzle and two ivory tusks that can reach a metre. Its hide alone makes up about a fifth of its weight, and on the neck and shoulders it thickens to 10 cm, a shield against the tusks of rival bulls that fight for mates every breeding season and leave each other scarred and sometimes dying.

Most of its life, though, is spent feeding. A walrus dives to the seabed, rests its tusks on the mud like sledge runners, sweeps the bottom with hundreds of sensitive whiskers, blasts sediment away with jets of water or strokes of a flipper, and sucks clams out of their shells with suction strong enough to pull a metal plug from a pool floor. Between feeding trips it hauls out on ice floes or beaches in herds of thousands, levering itself up with its tusks.

On the ABS scale the walrus is a heavy tank with a genuinely dangerous weapon. Polar bears prefer to stampede herds and pick off the crushed and weak, because a healthy adult walrus in the water can kill a bear. Its Defense and Raw Power rank among the roster's large marine mammals, but its slowness on land, short reach and tendency to flee keep its Attack and Agility well below the elite predators.

sections.habitat: Arctic and sub-Arctic seas around the North Pole. The Pacific walrus lives in the Bering and Chukchi Seas, summering north of the Bering Strait around Wrangel Island and the coasts of Siberia and Alaska. The Atlantic walrus ranges from the Canadian Arctic across Greenland, Svalbard and the Barents and Kara Seas. It uses shallow continental shelf waters close to sea ice or coasts where it can haul out.
sections.diet: A benthic forager on more than 60 genera of marine animals, mainly clams, plus snails, worms, crabs, shrimp, sea cucumbers and slow fish, occasionally seals and seabirds. It locates prey with its whiskers, clears sediment with water jets and flipper strokes, and sucks the soft parts out of shells. Feeding on the seabed stirs large areas of sediment.
sections.social: Gregarious, forming herds of hundreds to thousands on ice floes and beaches. Hierarchies depend on age, body size and tusk length, and the strongest bulls with the largest tusks dominate.
sections.reproduction: Females begin breeding at about 6–7 years and usually give birth every two to three years, the lowest reproductive rate of any pinniped. Calves weigh 45–75 kg at birth, can swim immediately, and stay with the mother for about two years, the longest mother-calf bond among pinnipeds. Males are mature at about 8–10 years but rarely win mates before about 15 years, when they are fully grown.
sections.conservation: Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2016). Commercial hunting in the 18th–20th centuries cut populations severely; the Pacific population was estimated at about 129,000 in 2006. The main modern threat is loss of summer sea ice, which forces walruses onto crowded coastal haul-outs where disturbance-caused stampedes can kill hundreds to thousands in a year. Indigenous subsistence hunting continues under management.
sections.features:
Tusks in both sexes, up to about 1 m and 5.4 kg.
400–700 whiskers in 13–15 rows.
Neck and shoulder skin up to 10 cm thick in bulls; blubber up to 10–15 cm.
Oral suction as low as −118.8 kPa underwater.
Throat air sacs for floating and sleeping upright in water.
Can walk on all four flippers.
sections.humanInteraction: Walrus meat, fat, skin, bone and ivory have been central to many Arctic Indigenous cultures, and walrus ivory was a prized trade good in medieval Europe. Aircraft, boats, tourists and hunters can trigger deadly stampedes at haul-outs, so managers now protect major haul-out sites from disturbance.

funFacts: The name Odobenus means "tooth-walker", after walruses using their tusks to pull themselves out of the water.
A walrus can suck the meat out of a clam and even sucked a 2.3 kg metal plug out of a pool floor.
Its whiskers can tell apart objects only 3 mm thick.
A bull's hide can make up about 20% of its body weight.
Walruses sleep floating upright by inflating air sacs in their throats.
Walruses show a preference for the right flipper when digging for food.
Mother and calf stay together for about two years, longer than any other pinniped pair.

abilities.name: Ivory Tusk Stab
abilities.description: tusks up to about 1 m, driven down by more than a tonne of body, stab rivals and predators; walruses have fatally injured polar bears in the water.

abilities.name: Vacuum Suction Feeding
abilities.description: a vaulted palate and piston-like tongue produce mouth pressures as low as −118.8 kPa underwater, enough to suck clams from their shells and a 2.3 kg plug out of a pool floor.

traits.name: Whisker Carpet
traits.description: 400–700 stiff, nerve-rich whiskers up to 30 cm long can tell apart shapes just 3 mm thick in dark, murky water.

traits.name: Tusk-Walker Hide
traits.description: walruses haul themselves onto ice with their tusks, and bulls carry neck and shoulder skin up to 10 cm thick that shields them from tusk jabs.

combat.weapons: The walrus's weapons are its tusks, driven downward by a massive neck and a body of more than a tonne. Bulls threaten by raising and turning their heads to show their tusks; when tusks are matched, they fight and stab each other, causing bruises, punctures and lacerations on the neck and shoulders. SeaWorld notes that many males die each year from injuries received in breeding-season fights. Against predators, adults use the tusks as weapons: walruses have fatally injured polar bears that followed them into the water, and are believed to have fought off orcas. Walruses occasionally kill and eat seals, including bearded seals of up to about 200 kg, and rarely seabirds. The weakness is delivery: the tusks strike mainly downward and forward, and on land the walrus is slow and heavy.
weaknesses: Slow and clumsy on land; charges are short.
Tusks mainly strike downward, with limited reach to the sides.
Short dives compared with deep-diving seals.
Herds panic into stampedes that crush calves and small animals.
Calves and injured adults are vulnerable to orcas and bears.

warthog.name: Warthog
warthog.specimen: healthy adult boar of about 85 kg, 75 cm at the shoulder and 130 cm head-body length, with upper tusks of about 25 cm.
warthog.summary: The common warthog is an 85 kg African pig with long curved tusks, razor-edged lower tusks and padded facial warts. It is a fast sprinter that dives into burrows backwards and bursts out tusks-first, dangerous when cornered but still regular prey for lions, leopards and hyenas.
narrative: A warthog boar looks built for trouble: a broad, flat head with two long upper tusks curving out of the snout, a pair of shorter lower tusks sharpened like knives, big cartilage warts on its face, and a bristly mane down its back. At about 85 kg and 75 cm at the shoulder, it is longer-legged than most pigs and can outrun many threats over a short distance, tail held high.

Its survival strategy is built around the burrow. Warthogs sleep, give birth and hide in abandoned aardvark holes, always reversing in so their tusks face the entrance, and they leave at a run in case a predator is waiting. In the open they graze on their knees, dig for roots in the dry season and keep an ear and nose out for danger, since their eyesight is poor. Boars fight each other with head blows and the blunt upper tusks, cushioned by their warts, saving the razor-edged lower tusks for predators.

On the ABS scale the warthog is a mid-weight scrapper. It is better armed than most antelope of similar size, and a cornered warthog fights back with its sharp lower tusks, but it remains a staple prey species for lions, hyenas and wild dogs. Its Attack and Defense sit well below the giant forest hog and the big predators, while its Agility and burrow tactics give it a real chance to escape.

sections.habitat: Sub-Saharan Africa, from West Africa through East Africa to southern Africa, in savanna, open woodland and grassland, often near waterholes and marshy ground. It is widespread in parks such as Kruger in South Africa, where its range tracks open woodland savanna. A genome study of 35 common warthogs from throughout the range found that the species interbred with the desert warthog in eastern Africa.
sections.diet: Mainly a grazer of short grasses, switching in the dry season to digging up bulbs, tubers, rhizomes and roots with its snout and tusks. Warthogs wallow in mud at waterholes and rely on burrows dug by aardvarks and others. The soft ticks in their burrows and the warthogs themselves maintain African swine fever virus in a sylvatic cycle in eastern and southern Africa.
sections.social: Sounders of sows and their young, sometimes several females together; adult boars live apart and join sounders only to mate. Sows are much more social than boars. Home ranges are about 0.6–3.3 km².
sections.reproduction: Sows give birth in burrows and stay underground for several weeks nursing the piglets. Young may stay with the mother for up to two years. Boars wait near burrows for sows to emerge in the mating season, and males rarely mate before about four years old. Wild warthogs live about 7–11 years on average.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Warthogs are hunted for meat and trophies and killed for raiding crops. In Gonarezhou National Park, Zimbabwe, warthog and other herbivores under 140 kg declined after 2013, probably because of predation.
sections.features:
Upper tusks up to about 25.5 cm, curving 90 degrees or more.
Lower tusks honed to a sharp edge.
Three pairs of cartilage facial warts, the largest up to 15 cm.
Calloused wrist pads for kneeling.
Runs with its tail held straight up.
sections.humanInteraction: Warthogs are among the best-known animals of African safari parks. They are hunted for meat, which is lean (under 2% fat) and about 32% protein, and for tusk trophies; tusks are carved for the tourist trade. They are also killed as crop raiders, and they matter to veterinarians as carriers of African swine fever virus.

funFacts: Warthogs back into their burrows so their tusks face any intruder.
Their "warts" are not warts at all but cartilage pads that cushion blows.
Warthogs often kneel to graze, on calloused wrist pads.
They run with their tails straight up like a flag.
Banded mongooses and vervet monkeys groom ticks off warthogs.
Warthogs rarely dig their own homes, preferring old aardvark burrows.
The dangerous lower tusks are rarely used in fights between boars.

abilities.name: Burrow Ambush Exit
abilities.description: reverses into aardvark burrows with its head toward the opening, then bursts out at full speed with tusks forward if a predator waits outside.

abilities.name: Lower-Tusk Slash
abilities.description: the short lower tusks are honed to a cutting edge against the uppers and inflict severe wounds on predators while the long uppers push and strike.

traits.name: Cushion Warts
traits.description: thick cartilage "warts" on the face, the suborbital pair up to 15 cm long in boars, pad the blows of head-to-head fights so injuries are rare.

traits.name: Kneeling Grazer
traits.description: calloused, padded wrists let it graze short grass on its knees and even shuffle forward in that position.

combat.weapons: The warthog has two tusk pairs. The long, curved upper tusks are blunt and used for pushing and striking with the head in fights between boars. The lower tusks are shorter but honed to a sharp edge against the uppers, and are used to slash predators. San Diego Zoo describes warthogs as "not afraid to fight", slashing with the lower tusks while squealing loudly. A warthog cornered in or near its burrow bursts out head first with its tusks forward. It never attacks animals as prey: it is a grazer and rooter, and all its fighting is defensive or between rivals.
weaknesses: Poor eyesight.
Short-range sprinter with little stamina for long chases.
No armor; sparse hair on the body.
Vulnerable when kneeling to graze.
Mid-sized prey for all of Africa's large carnivores.

wild-boar.name: Wild Boar
wild-boar.specimen: healthy adult European male ("boar") of about 100 kg, 80 cm at the shoulder and 150 cm head-body length, with lower tusks exposed about 10 cm.
wild-boar.summary: The wild boar is a 100 kg Eurasian pig with sharp, ever-growing tusks, a rut shield of tough tissue over its shoulders and an excellent nose. It charges from cover with its tusks, which can kill dogs and have even killed tigers, though wolves and tigers still prey on young and weakened boar.
narrative: A wild boar is a compact wedge of muscle and bristle: around 100 kg in a big European male, 80 cm at the shoulder, with a long snout, small eyes and tusks that never stop growing. The sharp lower tusks are the main weapons, and a charging boar drives them into legs and flanks. Every autumn, males grow a shield of tough tissue up to 3 cm thick over their shoulders before fighting rivals for access to sows.

The species is spectacularly versatile. Boar live from Mediterranean scrub to Siberian taiga, dig through frozen ground with their snouts, swim between islands and have moved into the suburbs of many European cities. They learn from hunting pressure, tolerate crowds of people while staying alert, and have shown striking problem solving, as when a sow freed trapped young from a cage trap. Their sense of smell is keen enough for drug detection, even if their eyesight is poor.

On the ABS scale the boar is a strong mid-weight brawler. It is lighter than the giant forest hog and a large black bear and cannot match a wolf pack or a tiger, but its tusks, toughness and temper make it one of the most dangerous animals of its size to confront in dense cover. Its ratings sit in the roster's moderate middle, with Ferocity and Senses as standout substats.

sections.habitat: One of the most widely distributed land mammals: native across Europe, North Africa and much of Asia, east to the Russian Far East and the Lesser Sunda Islands, in forests, reed beds, scrub, farmland and mountains. Introduced and feral populations, often mixed with domestic pigs, occur in the Americas, including 44 US states. It lives increasingly in and around cities such as Kraków, Bordeaux, Budapest and the suburbs of Prague.
sections.diet: An omnivore that roots for underground plant parts and burrowing animals, feeds on acorns and beech mast in fruiting years and raids crops. Its rooting upturns large amounts of soil. Boar are also an important prey for wolves and tigers, and invasive feral pigs raid turtle nests where they have been introduced.
sections.social: Matriarchal sounders of related sows and young, typically about 6–20 animals. Adult males are mostly solitary outside the rut. Sows in a sounder protect all the young together, and piglets can nurse from other sows.
sections.reproduction: Sows usually first breed at about two years; males rarely take part in the rut before 4–5 years because older males keep them away. Piglets weigh about 0.6–1.0 kg at birth. Heavy juvenile mortality means the average boar lives only 1–2 years, and few pass 4–5 years in the wild.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Numbers are growing in much of Europe, where driven hunts with dogs are used to manage them, bringing crop damage, urban conflict and concern over African swine fever. Outside its native range feral pigs are a damaging invasive animal.
sections.features:
Ever-growing tusks; lower tusks exposed 10–12 cm.
Seasonal 2–3 cm shoulder-to-rump shield in rutting males.
Excellent sense of smell, weak eyesight.
Can jump 140–150 cm and swim more than 10 km.
Pig muscle receptors resist snake α-neurotoxins.
sections.humanInteraction: Boar have been hunted for thousands of years and appear in cave art and in the myths of many cultures. Today they are a major game animal, and driven hunts with dogs are common in Europe. Attacks on people are rare; in one urban case series most wounds were on the legs and only one of 34 patients had a complication.

funFacts: Wild boar have been used as drug-sniffing animals in Germany.
A boar swam about 11 km from France to the island of Alderney in 2013.
Rutting males grow a natural shield up to 3 cm thick over their shoulders.
A mother boar once freed two trapped young by working the logs that held a trap door shut.
A boar's snout can turn over rocks of 40–50 kg.
Some Far Eastern boar weigh as much as a brown bear, up to about 300 kg.
Domestic pigs were bred from wild boar.

abilities.name: Tusk-Point Charge
abilities.description: a charge from cover with the tusks pointed at the target; the sharp lower tusks, exposed 10–12 cm, cause penetrating wounds, mostly to the legs, and kill a share of the hunting dogs they strike.

abilities.name: Rut Shield
abilities.description: before the breeding season males grow a 2–3 cm layer of tough subcutaneous tissue from the shoulder blades to the rump that protects vital organs from a rival's tusks.

traits.name: Detection-Dog Nose
traits.description: the boar's sense of smell is good enough that boar have been used for drug detection in Germany, and wild boar keep more olfaction gene activity than domestic pigs.

traits.name: Venom-Blocking Receptor
traits.description: pigs carry amino-acid changes in the snake α-neurotoxin binding site of the muscle nicotinic receptor, functionally equivalent to those of honey badgers and hedgehogs, which resist cobra-type venom.

combat.weapons: A boar attacks by charging and pointing its tusks at the target. Human injuries are typically penetrating wounds to the thigh and lower limbs; in a Spanish emergency department series of 34 patients, 50% had superficial wounds, 38.2% penetrating wounds and 71.9% of wounds were on the legs. Hunting dogs take the brunt of this weapon: over 797 driven hunts in Czechia, boars inflicted 150 injuries on dogs, of which 18.8% were severe and 7.4% fatal. Old boars have been recorded goring a small tiger and a tigress to death in self-defense, and a large male tiger died of wounds from a boar it killed. A group of boar was once seen killing and eating an adult axis deer, but boar do not normally hunt large animals.
weaknesses: Poor eyesight and no color vision.
Deep snow badly limits movement.
Short-range weapon that requires a head-on charge.
Shield is seasonal and covers only the shoulders and flanks.
Piglets and young are easy prey.

wild-horse.name: Wild Horse
wild-horse.specimen: healthy mature adult male (harem stallion), 320.0 kg, 135.0 cm at the withers and 210.0 cm head-body length.
wild-horse.summary: Przewalski's horse is a stocky, dun steppe horse and the last truly wild horse. A 320 kg stallion defends his family with rearing strikes, bites and powerful hind kicks and survives brutal winters by throttling his own metabolism, but he has no horns or armor and relies on open ground to see and escape danger.
narrative: Przewalski's horse is the steppe version of the horse: shorter-legged and heavier-necked than a racehorse, dun-coated, with a stiff upright mane and a pale muzzle. It came close to vanishing. The wild population faded under hunting, livestock competition and hard winters, and after 1969 the only takhi left were in zoos. Careful studbook breeding from about a dozen founders rebuilt the population, and reintroduced herds now graze the Mongolian Gobi and grasslands again.

In a fight the takhi stallion is the dangerous member of the family. He herds the mares, faces down rivals and meets threats with a full equid arsenal: rearing forefoot strikes, gripping bites to the neck and legs, and hind kicks that can break bone. Wolves, the main modern predator, mostly target foals rather than healthy adults. Yet the horse has no horn, tusk or claw, so every blow needs close range, and a large cat or bear that controls its neck faces no armor at all.

Its most unusual strength is quieter. Heart-rate loggers on free-roaming takhi show the body running at roughly half speed in midwinter, with lower activity and cooler tissues, so the horse spends less energy when food is scarce. That makes the takhi a durable, patient survivor rather than a sprinter or a brawler, and on the absolute scale it sits alongside other mid-sized hoofed animals: tougher and stronger than a donkey, far below the heavy bovids and big predators.

sections.habitat: Historically the steppes and semi-deserts of Central Asia, with the last wild animals surviving between the Takhiin Shar Nuruu and Bajtag-Bogdo ranges of the Dzungarian Gobi. Today free-ranging horses live at reintroduction sites in Mongolia (Great Gobi B, Hustai, Khomiin Tal), in Xinjiang and Gansu in China, in Kazakhstan, and in the Chernobyl exclusion zone, with semi-wild herds in Europe such as Hortobágy in Hungary and Döberitzer Heide in Germany.
sections.diet: A grazer of grasses and sedges that also takes leaves of shrubby plants. Its winter diet resembles that of domestic horses; isotope work on the historical population suggests a switch to browsing shrubs in winter under heavy habitat pressure. It shares Gobi ranges with Asiatic wild asses and livestock and is prey for wolves.
sections.social: Harem groups of one adult stallion, mares and offspring, plus bachelor groups. Young stay until two or three years old; young females join other harems and young males join bachelor groups. Mares often lead group movement, while the stallion herds and defends. Harem sizes in the 15-year Hortobágy dataset stayed stable even as the number of harems grew from three to 23.
sections.reproduction: Sexual maturity at about two years, though stallions rarely hold mates before about five. Single foals; foal mortality near 25% in one study, much of it from infanticide by incoming stallions.
sections.conservation: Endangered on the IUCN Red List. The species was listed as Extinct in the Wild for over 30 years after the last sighting of a lone stallion in 1969, then downlisted from Critically Endangered to Endangered in 2011 as free-ranging numbers in Mongolia reached about 350. Threats include low genetic diversity, hybridization with domestic horses, disease, wolf predation, habitat degradation and catastrophic winters. Hunting has been banned in Mongolia since 1930.
sections.features:
Seasonal hypometabolism with a halving of winter heart rate.
Woolly winter coat and erect mane suited to cold, dry steppe.
Stocky, short-legged equid frame with hard single hooves.
Stallion fighting repertoire of rearing, biting and kicking.
Stable, long-term family bonds.
sections.humanInteraction: Captured for zoos around 1900, the horse survived in captivity through a narrow bottleneck that included World War II losses. International studbook management, zoo exchanges and airlifts to Mongolia from 1992 onward restored wild herds. In China reintroduced horses still depend on winter feeding.

funFacts: "Takhi," the Mongolian name, is usually translated as "spirit."
Every living Przewalski's horse traces to roughly 12–16 founder animals.
The last confirmed wild individual before reintroduction was a single stallion seen in 1969.
Free-roaming takhi drop their winter heart rate to about 44 beats per minute, half their spring rate.
More than 100 Przewalski's horses were estimated to live in the Chernobyl exclusion zone in 2019.
The 2009/2010 Mongolian winter killed about 60% of the Gobi B population on average, with large differences between east and west.
Its mane stands upright and it has no forelock, unlike most domestic horses.

abilities.name: Harem Stallion Onslaught
abilities.description: a defending stallion rears, strikes with the forefeet, bites at the head and neck and wheels into hind kicks, the same repertoire used in fights for harems. It makes close approach costly for medium predators.

abilities.name: Winter Metabolic Throttle
abilities.description: in late winter heart rate falls to about half its spring level, activity drops and subcutaneous temperature declines, letting the horse conserve energy through long food shortages.

traits.name: Last Truly Wild Horse
traits.description: the only horse regarded as never successfully domesticated, lost from the wild in the late 1960s and returned from zoo stock bred from about a dozen founders.

traits.name: Steppe Dun Build
traits.description: a stocky dun body, short erect mane with no forelock, pale mealy muzzle, dark lower legs and a tail with a short-haired dock.

combat.weapons: A Przewalski's stallion fights with its whole body. Rival stallions rear and strike with the forefeet, bite at the neck, head and legs, and wheel to deliver double-barrelled hind kicks. Against predators the same repertoire is used defensively: ADW's horse account records that the dominant stallion may attack a predator by biting and kicking. A 320 kg equid landing a clean hind kick can inflict serious blunt trauma on a medium carnivore, but the horse has no horns, tusks or cutting teeth, and every blow requires the attacker to be inside a narrow reach.
weaknesses: No horns, tusks or cutting weapons; kicks need precise range and angle.
No armor; the neck, flanks and legs are exposed to grappling predators.
Heavy snow cover, confinement and dense forest remove its running options.
Foals are vulnerable, and a stallion defending them must engage at close range.
Conservative space use in catastrophic winters.

wildebeest.name: Wildebeest
wildebeest.specimen: healthy mature territorial adult male (bull), 250.0 kg, 140.0 cm at the shoulder and 220.0 cm head-body length, horns up to about 83 cm.
wildebeest.summary: The blue wildebeest is a 250 kg horned antelope built for distance. Bulls clash on their knees with hooked horns and herds mob lone predators, but its real edge is endurance: highly efficient muscle lets it walk for days without water. Lions and hyena clans still kill adults, and it has no armor.
narrative: The blue wildebeest looks assembled from spare parts, with the forequarters of an ox, the legs of an antelope and the tail of a horse, but every part serves travel. A mature bull weighs about 250 kg, carries a pair of smooth horns that sweep out and up like brackets, and spends much of the year either defending a small patch of plain or walking toward the next rains.

Its fighting style is modest for its size. Rival bulls kneel and push, and a bull or a mother will charge and chase a lone hyena, cheetah or wild dog. Hooked horns and 250 kg of forequarters can injure a medium predator, but they do not stab like an oryx's horns, and nothing protects the neck and legs from lions or a hyena clan. Predation, not starvation, is what usually kills adult wildebeest.

Endurance is where it stands out on the roster. GPS collars in Botswana recorded animals walking up to 80 km in five days without drinking, and muscle biopsies found the most efficient mammalian muscle contraction measured in that comparison. Add mass migration, synchronized calving and shared vigilance with zebras, and the wildebeest becomes an animal that survives by outlasting and outnumbering danger rather than by beating it.

sections.habitat: Short- and medium-grass savannas, open woodland edges and floodplains of eastern and southern Africa, from Kenya and Tanzania to Zambia, Botswana, Namibia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and South Africa. Wildebeest avoid dense forest and depend on access to water and grazing.
sections.diet: A grazer of short grasses, following rainfall and new growth. Wildebeest are a keystone prey species: a 2026 analysis of Mara predation networks found the wildebeest to be the most influential species across most metrics. In drought, water-dependent grazers such as wildebeest and zebra may decline or move away while drought-tolerant gazelles and impala hold on.
sections.social: Herds of females and young, bachelor herds and territorial bulls. Nursery herds are often around eight females and their calves in resident populations (ADW), merging into huge aggregations during migration. Transient cows may be driven out by territorial bulls.
sections.reproduction: Males are sexually mature at about two years, females can conceive at 16 months if well fed. Gestation is about 8.5 months, and 80–90% of calves are born within a three-week period; single calves weigh about 19 kg at birth and stand within minutes. Calving is timed to the rains and migration to fertile plains. In Liuwa, first-year survival was estimated at 56%.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, with around 1.5 million animals and a stable overall trend. Many migrations have been lost; only the Serengeti, Tarangire and Kafue systems remain among the long-distance ones listed by Wikipedia. Fences that cut migration routes have caused mass die-offs, and the Maasai Mara population fell by about 80% between 1977 and the late 1990s. Modelling for the Greater Mara found 39–54% connectivity gains from removing 15–140 km of fences.
sections.features:
Forelimb muscle with unusually high mechanical efficiency.
Long-distance travel without drinking.
Horns in both sexes, much larger in bulls.
Synchronized calving and fast-standing calves.
Mass migration and mixed herds with zebras.
sections.humanInteraction: Wildebeest herds are a centerpiece of East African wildlife tourism. Fencing, agricultural expansion that removes wet-season grazing and calving ranges, and blocked migration routes are the main human pressures.

funFacts: Blue wildebeest in Botswana walked up to 80 km in five days without drinking.
Wildebeest muscle converts energy to work at about 62.6% efficiency, far above cattle muscle (41.8%).
A territorial bull may neither eat nor rest while a female is in his territory.
Newborn calves weigh about 19 kg and can stand within minutes.
At high density, one square kilometre of plain can hold 270 territorial bulls.
The species name taurinus comes from the Greek word for bull.
Mothers often chase off lone hyenas and cheetahs to save their calves.

abilities.name: Kneeling Horn Clash
abilities.description: bulls drop to their knees and drive their parenthesis-shaped horns into a rival or threat, and herds trail and mob predators to push them away. Most useful against lone mid-sized hunters.

abilities.name: Efficient-Muscle March
abilities.description: forelimb muscle that turns energy into work at about 62.6% efficiency lets wildebeest walk up to 80 km over five days without drinking, outlasting opponents in long, hot contests.

traits.name: Great Migration Grazer
traits.description: three long-distance migrations survive (Serengeti, Tarangire and Kafue), timed to the rains and grass growth; migratory populations grow far larger than resident ones because they reach nutrient-rich calving plains.

traits.name: Synchronized Calving
traits.description: 80–90% of calves are born within about three weeks, and calves stand within minutes of birth, flooding predators with more newborns than they can take.

combat.weapons: The wildebeest's weapon is its horned head driven by heavy forequarters. Territorial bulls face each other with bent knees and exchange horn thrusts, grunt, paw the ground and dig their horns into the soil in display. Against predators the horns are used in short threat charges; ADW notes that wildebeest often trail or follow predators to drive them off, and that mothers often defend calves successfully against individual hyenas or cheetahs. The horns hook sideways and upward rather than stabbing forward like an oryx's, so their penetrating power is moderate.
weaknesses: Horns hook rather than stab, and the neck and legs are exposed.
No armor; lions and hyena clans kill adults.
River crossings and fences cause mass deaths.
A lone animal loses the herd's vigilance and confusion effect.

wolverine.name: Wolverine
wolverine.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 16.0 kg, 42.0 cm at the shoulder and 90.0 cm head-body length, tail excluded.
wolverine.summary: The wolverine is a 16 kg snow-country powerhouse with bone-crushing jaws, crampon claws and snowshoe paws. It travels enormous distances, plans routes from memory and will face down larger predators over a carcass, but wolves and bears can still kill it and it is slow on open ground.
narrative: The wolverine looks like a small bear and behaves like a much larger animal. A mature male weighs about 16 kg, yet it hunts reindeer and moose trapped in deep snow, cracks frozen bones that other scavengers leave, and sometimes drives much bigger predators off their kills. Its paws are broad and furred, its claws hooked like climbing spikes, and its coat thick enough for Arctic winters.

That reputation needs context on the absolute scale. Wolves are its main natural killer, bears and cougars also kill wolverines, and a clean fight against a 50 kg wolf or a big cat is a losing one. What makes the wolverine formidable is the combination of a heavy bite, raw toughness for its size and a readiness to fight when food or life is at stake, not raw mass.

Its most remarkable features are endurance and mind. Wolverines cover 20 to 45 km in a day, disperse hundreds of kilometres, and one tracked male travelled more than 1,300 km. A 2025 study showed they plan routes through rugged mountains from memory, aiming at places several kilometres out of sight. Those abilities, together with its snow specialization, give the wolverine high Stamina, Intelligence and Special ratings while its Attack and Defense stay in line with other mid-sized carnivores.

sections.habitat: Boreal forest, taiga, alpine tundra and Arctic tundra across northern Eurasia and North America, from Scandinavia and Russia to Alaska, Canada and the northern Rocky Mountains. In the contiguous United States it survives mainly in high mountains, and wolverines are returning to areas such as Mount Rainier, with a reintroduction program planned in Colorado. Year-round occupation is limited to areas where snow persists into late spring.
sections.diet: An opportunistic predator and scavenger. In Norway, diet in tundra was 40% reindeer, 39% moose and 9% rodents; in forest with wolves it shifted to 76% moose, 18% reindeer and 5% rodents, because wolf kills supplied moose carcasses. Prey ranges from voles, lemmings, hares, marmots, beavers and porcupines to caribou, deer, moose and livestock. Vegetation, including whitebark pine nuts in Yellowstone, is eaten occasionally.
sections.social: Solitary. Males hold large territories overlapping several females. Densities are very low: 0.71–6.74 wolverines per 1,000 km² across Alberta landscapes, for an estimated 955 animals in the province.
sections.reproduction: Females give birth in dens dug into deep snow, often in alternate years, to litters averaging about three kits born between January and April. Young stay in the mother's territory until they can hunt; FEIS records juveniles and subadults dispersing 30–378 km.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List because of its wide range and large northern populations. In 2023 the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service listed the North American wolverine in the contiguous United States as threatened. Main concerns are loss of spring snowpack for denning, human development, trapping and low genetic connectivity. In the Arctic, reduced snow and sea ice, changing prey and increased human access are research priorities.
sections.features:
Snowshoe-like five-toed paws with semi-retractable, crampon-like claws.
Heavy jaws and teeth able to crush bone and frozen meat.
Dense, thick fur over a thick hide.
Potent anal scent glands used to mark territory and caches.
Spatial memory used to plan efficient mountain routes.
sections.humanInteraction: Trapped for fur and persecuted in reindeer-herding and livestock areas, especially in Fennoscandia, where it takes semi-domestic reindeer. They are rarely seen, and climate change models predict shrinking spring snowpack in much of the western United States by 2050.

funFacts: A young male wolverine tracked from near Grand Teton National Park travelled about 800 km south, and his journey eventually exceeded 1,300 km.
Wolverines plan routes from memory, often to places 5.3–9.8 km away.
Wolverine scent-gland secretions contained 123 different compounds in one six-animal study.
Females give birth in dens tunnelled into deep spring snow.
Where wolves returned in Norway, wolverine diet switched to about 76% moose from wolf kills.
Wolverines follow wolf and lynx trails to scavenge what those hunters leave behind.
It is the largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family.

abilities.name: Frozen-Carcass Crusher
abilities.description: a heavy bite and robust teeth crack bone and frozen meat, and a neck bite kills prey many times the wolverine's own weight once the prey is stuck in snow.

abilities.name: Deep-Snow Hunter
abilities.description: large, wide paws spread its weight and crampon-like claws grip ice and rock, so the wolverine stays on top of snow where hoofed prey sinks and cannot escape.

traits.name: Mountain Route Planner
traits.description: GPS tracks show wolverines plan routes to places 5.3–9.8 km ahead from memory, saving energy in rugged terrain.

traits.name: Largest Land Weasel
traits.description: the largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family, stocky and bear-like, with potent scent glands that earned it the name "skunk bear."

combat.weapons: The wolverine's main weapon is a heavy mustelid bite able to crack bone and frozen meat, backed by strong forelimbs and long, hooked claws. It kills small and medium prey outright and takes large ungulates, including reindeer, caribou, deer and even adult moose and elk, when they are weakened by winter or floundering in deep snow, usually with a bite to the neck. It also takes over carcasses from other predators; ADW notes it can drive bears, cougars and even wolf packs from kills. In captive reindeer herds held in deep snow, wolverines have killed many animals at once.
weaknesses: Small absolute size; wolves, bears and cougars can kill it.
Slow straight-line speed on firm ground.
Relies on persistent spring snow for dens; lower snowpack threatens southern populations.
No armor; its bite is its main damaging weapon.

wombat.name: Wombat
wombat.specimen: healthy mature adult male of the mainland subspecies, 28.0 kg and 100.0 cm head-body length.
wombat.summary: The common wombat is a 28 kg burrowing marsupial with ever-growing teeth, powerful digging claws and a cartilage-backed rump it uses to plug its tunnel against predators. It can sprint over 40 km/h and bite hard, but away from its burrow it is a slow, unarmored herbivore.
narrative: The common wombat is a low, barrel-shaped digger about a metre long and near 28 kg, built around its burrow. Short, heavy legs with long claws excavate tunnels up to 20 m long, and a single pair of chisel-like incisors backed by unusually large jaw muscles crops tough grasses. Every tooth keeps growing throughout life, a feature no other marsupial shares.

Its best-known defense faces backwards. Most of the wombat's rear is cartilage covered by toughened hide, and it has almost no tail, so when a dingo, fox or devil follows it underground the attacker meets a hard wall that is difficult to bite. Some sources describe wombats crushing an intruder's skull against the tunnel roof; others call that a legend, so it is not counted here. In the open the wombat can sprint over 40 km/h for a short distance and will bite, claw or charge when cornered.

On the absolute roster scale the wombat is a small defender rather than a fighter. Its Attack stays low because its weapons are defensive and it weighs under 30 kg, its Defense is boosted by the rump shield, and its Special score reflects how much the burrow-and-plug strategy changes fights against pursuing predators. Away from cover, against a large carnivore, it has few answers.

sections.habitat: Temperate forests, woodlands, heath and grassy areas of southeastern Australia with soil suitable for burrowing. At European settlement it ranged from southeastern Queensland along the Great Dividing Range of New South Wales to most of Victoria (Australian Museum); it also lives in Tasmania and on Flinders Island, with an introduced population on Maria Island. Wombats often live in riparian areas because they prefer to dig burrows there (ADW).
sections.diet: A grazer of mainly native grasses. Its efficient digestion lets it spend much of its time in burrows. Common wombats are ecosystem engineers: their burrows turn over soil and shelter many other species. A camera-trap study in southeastern Australia found small mammals and birds more active at burrow sites, and those associations persisted or strengthened in areas burned by the 2019–20 Black Summer fires.
sections.social: Solitary, with overlapping home ranges and occasional burrow sharing. Wombats use several burrows and switch sleeping burrows every 1–9 days.
sections.reproduction: Wombats breed about every two years and produce a single joey. Joeys leave the pouch weighing 3.5–6.5 kg. Sexual maturity comes at about two years.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Sarcoptic mange is the most serious problem, along with roadkill and habitat loss. Spotlight surveys estimated about 71,800 wombats on Flinders Island in 2020, with densities of 0.42 per hectare there and 0.11 per hectare on mainland Tasmania; both populations grew over the 19-year survey period. A Victorian bounty paid from 1926 to 1966 treated wombats as agricultural pests.
sections.features:
Cartilage-backed, toughened rump used to block burrows.
Single pair of upper and lower incisors; all teeth grow continuously.
Greatly enlarged jaw-closing muscles on a broad, flat skull.
Powerful digging claws and short, strong legs.
Cube-shaped droppings formed in the final part of the intestine.
sections.humanInteraction: Wombats dig under rabbit fences and are sometimes treated as pests. Most encounters are harmless, but startled or mange-affected wombats have bitten, clawed and knocked people over. Wildlife carers treat mange in the field using burrow flaps that dose animals as they pass; one semi-isolated population was temporarily cleared of mange for about 20 months this way.

funFacts: Wombat droppings are cube-shaped, and the physics of how they form won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2019.
The cubes form within the last 17% of the intestine.
A wombat can run at over 40 km/h in short bursts.
Wombats switch the burrow they sleep in every 1–9 days.
The common wombat is the only marsupial whose teeth grow throughout life.
Many small animals use wombat burrows, and these burrows stayed activity hotspots after the Black Summer fires.
One naturalist was bitten 2 cm deep through a rubber boot, trousers and woollen socks.

abilities.name: Rump Shield Plug
abilities.description: the wombat dives into its tunnel and blocks it with a cartilage-backed rump under toughened hide, leaving a pursuer facing a hard, almost tailless wall that is difficult to bite. Crushing an attacker against the tunnel roof is reported by some sources but not confirmed.

abilities.name: Bulldozer Burrower
abilities.description: powerful claws and short, strong limbs dig tunnel systems 2–20 m long with several entrances and side tunnels, giving the wombat a network of refuges across its range.

traits.name: Cube-Shaped Scat
traits.description: the common wombat produces cube-shaped droppings; dissections show the cubes form in the last 17% of the intestine, where varying intestinal wall stiffness shapes the corners.

traits.name: Ever-Growing Teeth
traits.description: the only marsupial whose teeth grow continuously, with a single pair of upper and lower incisors and self-sharpening molars.

combat.weapons: The wombat is a herbivore, so its offense is defensive. Chisel-like, ever-growing incisors driven by very large jaw muscles give a strong bite, the long digging claws can puncture skin, and a startled wombat will charge and bowl a person over, risking broken bones from the fall (Wikipedia). A 2010 report described a Victorian man needing hospital treatment for cuts and bite wounds after a wombat attack. None of these tools is a dedicated killing weapon.
weaknesses: Slow over distance; far from a burrow it must rely on a short sprint and a bite.
Low absolute mass and no dedicated killing weapons.
Head, neck and belly are exposed if flipped or caught in the open.
Sarcoptic mange weakens many animals.

yak.name: Yak
yak.specimen: healthy mature adult male (domestic bull), 450.0 kg, 130.0 cm at the withers and 160.0 cm body length (FAO trunk-length convention; see below).
yak.summary: The domestic yak is a 450 kg high-altitude ox with sweeping horns, a ground-length coat and a heart and lungs built for thin air. Bulls charge head-down in the rut and herds bunch against wolves, but domestic yaks are usually docile, slow to turn and badly suited to heat.
narrative: The yak is the cattle of the roof of the world. A domestic bull stands about 130 cm at the withers and weighs around 450 kg, with a hump over the shoulders, long horns sweeping outward and back, and a coat so long that it hangs in a skirt below the belly. Beneath the hair lies a dense undercoat and a thick layer of fat, and inside is an oversized heart and pair of lungs suited to air that holds a third less oxygen than at sea level.

As a fighter, the domestic yak is capable but not eager. Bulls charge and spar with lowered horns during the rut, and a 450 kg charge is dangerous to any wolf-sized predator. But domestic breeding has made most yaks tractable, many Mongolian yaks carry no horns at all, and their first response to danger is to bunch together or run. Their wild relatives are another matter: wild yak bulls weigh about a tonne, carry horns averaging over 75 cm and will attack intruders when cornered.

The yak's real advantage is where it lives. At 4,000 to 5,500 m, in temperatures that fall to −40 °C, it keeps working when lowland cattle struggle to breathe, which is why it scores high in Stamina and Special. Take it down to warm lowlands and it begins to overheat at 16 °C. On the absolute scale it sits among heavy hoofed animals like the musk ox and fighting bull, below the tonne-class bison, buffalo and gaur.

sections.habitat: Domestic yaks live across the Himalayan region, the Tibetan Plateau, the Pamirs, Tajikistan, Mongolia and southern Siberia, mostly above 3,000 m in cold, semi-arid to semi-humid uplands; the further north, the lower the altitude at which they live. Small herds are kept in North America, Europe and New Zealand. Wild yaks survive on treeless uplands of the Tibetan Plateau between about 3,000 and 5,500 m, especially alpine tundra with grasses and sedges.
sections.diet: Grazers of grasses and sedges, with herbs, dwarf shrubs, lichens and mosses. In snow they break through the cover to reach wilted grass. Yaks have a large rumen for fermenting poor forage. Wild yaks are an important prey species for wolves.
sections.social: Wild yaks live in large female-and-young herds and smaller bull groups; bulls wander alone outside the rut. Domestic herds are managed by herders, with bulls kept for breeding and steers for work.
sections.reproduction: Mating occurs mainly from July to September. Gestation lasts about 257–270 days and produces a single calf, which can walk within about ten minutes of birth. Females usually calve every other year, first at three or four years of age.
sections.conservation: Domesticated; the domestic yak is common across its range. The wild yak (Bos mutus) is Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, with the 2008 assessment suggesting no more than 10,000 mature individuals. Poaching is its most serious threat, followed by interbreeding and disease risk from domestic herds. A 2015 study found female wild yaks now depend on winter snow patches 20 times more than males, and use steeper terrain than in the past.
sections.features:
Large chest, lungs and heart for low-oxygen air.
Hemoglobin with high oxygen affinity.
Long hair skirt, dense undercoat and thick subcutaneous fat.
Few functional sweat glands, conserving heat.
Rounded hooves suited to steep and marshy ground.
sections.humanInteraction: Yaks have long supplied milk, butter, cheese, meat, fibre and transport to Tibetan, Himalayan and Mongolian herders. Dried yak dung is an important fuel on the treeless Tibetan Plateau. Yak steers carry packs, are ridden and in some areas plough fields, and they accompany trekking and climbing expeditions. The yak genome, sequenced in 2012, shows expanded gene families linked to sensing, energy metabolism and hypoxia.

funFacts: Bos grunniens means "grunting ox": yaks grunt rather than moo.
Przewalski named the wild yak Bos mutus, "mute ox," thinking it made no sound, but it does.
A Zhongdian yak's heart averages about 1.3 kg, half again as heavy as a local cow's.
Yaks start to overheat at about 16 °C.
Yaks normally live as high as about 5,500 m.
Wild yak bulls can weigh about a tonne, roughly one and a half times a domestic bull from the same area.
Dried yak dung is often the only fuel available on the high Tibetan Plateau.

abilities.name: Thin-Air Engine
abilities.description: a large chest, large lungs, a heart about 1.5 times the mass of local cattle hearts and oxygen-hungry hemoglobin let the yak work hard where the air holds about a third less oxygen than at sea level.

abilities.name: Lowered-Horn Charge
abilities.description: bulls charge with heads down and spar with long, outward-sweeping horns, putting 450 kg behind the impact.

traits.name: Ground-Sweeping Skirt
traits.description: long outer hair hangs below the belly, sometimes to the ground, over a dense winter undercoat and thick fat, protecting the yak in temperatures down to −40 °C.

traits.name: Grunting Ox
traits.description: yaks grunt instead of lowing like cattle, which gave the domestic yak its scientific name grunniens, "grunting."

combat.weapons: The yak fights like other wild cattle: head down, horns forward, mass behind. During the rut bulls bellow, scrape the ground with their horns, and compete directly by charging each other with lowered heads and sparring with their horns (Wikipedia). A 450 kg bull with 50–100 cm horns can gore and knock down medium predators. Domestic yaks, however, are bred for tractability and often avoid conflict; many Mongolian yaks have no horns at all.
weaknesses: Poor heat tolerance; performance drops above about 15 °C.
Domestic yaks are often docile or polled.
Not fast; limited agility for its mass.
No armor on the neck and belly beneath the hair.

zebra.name: Zebra
zebra.specimen: healthy mature adult male (harem stallion), 300.0 kg, 135.0 cm at the shoulder and 230.0 cm head-body length.
zebra.summary: The plains zebra is a 300 kg striped equid and one of the most combative prey animals on the savanna. Stallions fight with bites, wrestling and kicks, attack hyenas and wild dogs, and families mob predators together. It migrates farther than any other African large mammal, but it has no armor and lions kill it regularly.
narrative: The plains zebra is a horse-sized grazer of the African savannas, a stallion weighing about 300 kg and standing about 135 cm at the shoulder. Its stripes are its signature, and the best experimental evidence says they stop biting flies from landing. Whatever else they do, they have not made zebras hard for lions to catch: lions and spotted hyenas remain its main killers.

What makes the zebra formidable is its temperament. Harem stallions fight each other violently, biting at necks and legs, wrestling rivals to the ground and kicking, and sometimes faking surrender before striking again. The same stallions charge hyenas and wild dogs, and a harem will close around a predator that has wounded one of its own, biting and kicking until it leaves. Against a lion, though, the zebra's hooves and teeth are rarely enough; lions most often kill lone, older males.

Zebras are also travellers. Collared zebras in Namibia and Botswana make a 500 km round trip each year, and models suggest they steer by remembered conditions, not just what they can see. That endurance and memory lift the zebra's Stamina and Intelligence, while its lack of horns and armor keeps Attack and Defense in the middle of the roster, alongside other mid-sized hoofed animals.

sections.habitat: Grasslands, savannas and open woodland of eastern and southern Africa, from Uganda (its most northern and most genetically distinct population) through Kenya and Tanzania to Botswana, Namibia, Zimbabwe and South Africa. Populations may be sedentary in dense, small ranges or migratory between separate wet- and dry-season ranges.
sections.diet: A grazer of grasses. Zebras and wildebeest often graze and migrate together, as in the Maasai Mara. In drought, water-dependent grazers such as zebras may decline or move away.
sections.social: Highly social. Harems of one stallion, several mares and young; bachelor groups of young and older males. Many harems and bachelor groups gather into herds of hundreds, especially on migration. Mares have a dominance hierarchy, and the top mare leads group movement.
sections.reproduction: Females reach puberty before three years, males after five or six. Foals weigh 30–35 kg at birth and stay with their mothers, learning to watch for predators and to follow migration routes. Stallions that take over a harem may kill foals that are not theirs.
sections.conservation: Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2016). Threats include competition with livestock for food and fences that block migration routes. The quagga, a southern form, was lost to hunting in South Africa.
sections.features:
Black and white stripes that deter biting flies.
Violent stallion fighting style of biting, wrestling and kicking.
Cooperative harem defense and graded predator responses.
Memory-guided long-distance migration.
Sturdy equid frame with hard single hooves.
sections.humanInteraction: Zebras are major attractions in African parks. They compete with livestock for grazing, and fences interrupt migrations. The zebra is a totem animal for the Shona people of Zimbabwe, and zebras appear in southern African rock art.

funFacts: Eight collared zebras revealed a 500 km round-trip migration, longer than the Serengeti wildebeest's straight-line journey.
Horseflies approach zebras fast and fail to slow down, so many just bump the coat instead of landing.
A fighting stallion may pretend to give up, then attack again.
Zebras watch lions from 50–100 m away but let a single hyena come within a few metres.
At night at least one harem member stays awake on guard.
Foals weigh 30–35 kg at birth.
Zebra vigilance rises when they hear recorded lion roars, even where lions are rarely seen.

abilities.name: Harem Mob Defense
abilities.description: when a family member is attacked, the harem closes around the predator, biting and kicking, and the stallion charges hyenas and wild dogs head-on.

abilities.name: Playing-Dead Counterstrike
abilities.description: a fighting stallion may lie still as if beaten and then strike again when the rival lets up, part of a violent biting, wrestling and kicking fight style.

traits.name: Fly-Proof Stripes
traits.description: experiments show horseflies fail to make controlled landings on striped coats; far fewer land on zebras than on plain-coated horses.

traits.name: Longest African Migrant
traits.description: plains zebras travelling between the Chobe River and Nxai Pan make a 500 km straight-line round trip, the longest recorded large-mammal migration in Africa.

combat.weapons: The plains zebra is one of the more combative hoofed prey animals. Stallion fights "often become very violent," with biting at the neck, head and legs, wrestling to the ground and occasional kicking; a stallion may even lie still as if surrendering and strike again when the rival relaxes (Wikipedia). Against predators the harem stallion goes on the offensive against hyenas and wild dogs, and stallions sometimes bluff-charge lions. ADW describes harems surrounding a predator that has wounded a member and biting and kicking until it flees or dies. The weapons are blunt hooves and strong incisors on a 300 kg body; there are no horns or claws.
weaknesses: No horns, claws or armor; kicks need precise range.
Exposed neck and legs for lions and crocodiles.
Dependent on water; drought and fences cut migrations.
A lone zebra loses the group's vigilance and defense.

aardvark.name: Aardvark
aardvark.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 65.0 kg, 120.0 cm head-body length, about 60 cm at the shoulder.
aardvark.summary: The aardvark is a 65 kg African digging specialist that tears open termite mounds with spade-like claws and finds food with one of the most powerful noses among mammals. It fights only when cornered, clawing and kicking hard, but its real defense is digging itself underground faster than most attackers can react.
narrative: The aardvark looks like a mix of several animals, with a pig-like snout, rabbit-like ears and a kangaroo-like tail, but it is its own thing: the only living species in its order. A healthy adult weighs around 65 kg and stands about 60 cm at the shoulder, and almost everything about its body is built around finding and digging out ants and termites. Its nose is packed with more turbinate bones than any other mammal's, its ears swivel independently and fold shut while it digs, and its teeth are unique enamel-free tubes of dentine.

In a battle, the aardvark is a reluctant fighter with real tools. Its four spade-like foreclaws can break open termite mounds that feel like concrete, and its heavy hind legs can deliver strong kicks. Predators that try to pin it in the open risk being clawed and kicked. Still, those claws are broad digging spades rather than long slashing hooks, and it has no bite to speak of, so lions, leopards, hyenas and large pythons can and do kill it.

Its best move is to leave. Aardvarks keep burrows and bolt-holes across their home range and can reportedly dig in and cover themselves within minutes. That makes the terrain decisive: on soft savanna soil near a burrow, it is a hard animal to finish; on rock or in the open, it is a slow, heavy target. Its main weakness is energy. A Kalahari study found that a hot, dry summer starved most of the tracked animals, showing how thin its margin is when insects become scarce.

sections.habitat: Found across most of sub-Saharan Africa wherever there is diggable soil and enough ants and termites: savanna, grassland, open woodland, scrub and semi-arid Karoo and Kalahari landscapes. It avoids very rocky ground and dense rainforest.
sections.diet: A specialist insectivore feeding mainly on termites and ants, located by smell and extracted with claws and a long, sticky tongue. By digging burrows and breaking open mounds, it turns over soil and creates shelters used by a wide range of other animals, which is why researchers describe it as an ecosystem engineer.
sections.social: Solitary and nocturnal. Individuals forage alone over home ranges reported at roughly 2–5 km² and use several burrows within them.
sections.reproduction: Females usually raise a single young, which stays with the mother for months before moving to its own burrow. Adults are reported to live up to about 18 years in the wild and a little over 20 years in zoos.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List because it is widespread and occurs in many protected areas, although numbers have declined in some countries. The South African Red List also treats it as Least Concern. Drought and rising temperatures are an emerging threat: a 2017 Kalahari study documented starvation deaths during a hot, dry summer.
sections.features:
Spade-like foreclaws on four front toes and clawed five-toed hind feet.
Enamel-free, tube-structured teeth; adults lack incisors and canines.
Nasal turbinates more numerous than in other mammals, for exceptional smell.
Long, independently mobile ears that fold shut during digging.
Thick, sparsely haired skin.
sections.humanInteraction: Rarely seen because it is nocturnal and secretive. Burrowing on farmland can bring it into conflict with landowners, and it is hunted locally. Its burrows are important refuges for other wildlife, so its loss would affect many species.

funFacts: The name aardvark comes from Afrikaans for "earth pig."
It is the only living species in its entire order, Tubulidentata.
Its teeth have no enamel and are built from bundles of tiny dentine tubes.
It can reportedly dig a hole about 0.6 m deep in around 15 seconds.
Its nose holds more turbinate bones than any other mammal's, often cited as 9–11 versus 4–5 in dogs.
It can fold its long ears shut while digging.
Old aardvark burrows shelter porcupines, warthogs, hyenas, bats, birds and even the rare blue swallow, which nests in them.

abilities.name: Emergency Burrow
abilities.description: spade-like foreclaws and powerful limbs let the aardvark dig in at exceptional speed and vanish into its own tunnel network, turning an open-ground fight into a chase it can end underground.

abilities.name: Spade-Claw Kickback
abilities.description: when cornered it slashes with its broad foreclaws and kicks with its heavy hind legs, a defensive combination that can injure predators that try to pin it.

traits.name: Tube-Toothed Oddity
traits.description: the only living member of its order; its enamel-free teeth are made of densely packed dentine tubules, and adults have no incisors or canines.

traits.name: Savanna Burrow Engineer
traits.description: its large burrows, which can exceed 12 m with several chambers, become shelters for porcupines, warthogs, hyenas, foxes, birds and many other animals.

combat.weapons: The aardvark has no offensive predatory weapons in the usual sense. Its damage comes from the same tools it uses to dig: four spade-like foreclaws driven by a heavily muscled forelimb, and strong hind legs that can kick. Species accounts and conservation organizations describe cornered aardvarks slashing with their claws and kicking with the back legs to drive off predators. These are blunt, broad digging claws, not the long hooked slashing claws of a giant anteater, so they are better at bruising and tearing than at deep puncture.
weaknesses: No bite weapon; offense depends on close-range claws and kicks.
Thin energy margin; vulnerable to drought and heat.
Poor eyesight and a heavy, low-slung body that is not built for pursuit or long chases.
Rock-hard or rocky ground removes its best escape.

aardwolf.name: Aardwolf
aardwolf.specimen: healthy adult of about 10.0 kg, head-body about 70 cm, shoulder height about 47.5 cm. Males are used as the nominal specimen because they scent mark more and fight other males in the mating season, but there is little size difference between the sexes.
aardwolf.summary: The aardwolf is a slender, 10 kg member of the hyena family that eats termites instead of meat, licking up hundreds of thousands in a night. It can raise a mane and release a foul scent to bluff predators, but with a weak jaw, peg-like teeth and no speed, it is one of the least dangerous fighters of its size.
narrative: The aardwolf looks like a small, thin striped hyena with a long mane, big ears and slender legs. A typical adult weighs about 10 kg. Despite its name and its family, it is a specialist insect-eater: its cheek teeth are reduced to little pegs, and it feeds by licking harvester termites off the ground with a long, broad, sticky tongue, taking hundreds of thousands in a night.

Its life is tied to those termites. It forages alone through the night at about 1 km per hour, finding termite columns by sound and smell, and in cold southern winters it can lose a fifth of its weight. Pairs share small territories of 1–4 km², mark them with hundreds of scent pastes a night and chase out intruders, and fathers stand guard at the den against jackals.

In a battle context the aardwolf is weak. Its canines are its only real weapons, its bite-force quotient is a fraction of the other hyenas', and it is neither fast nor armored. Its survival relies on bluff: a raised mane that makes it look far larger, a foul anal secretion and a burrow to dive into. It sits near the bottom of the medium-small mammals in Attack and Defense, with its Special score coming from its unusual feeding specialization and defensive display.

sections.habitat: Two separate populations: one in East and Northeast Africa and one in southern Africa, split by wetter woodlands in Zambia and southern Tanzania. It prefers open, grassy plains and savanna with 100–800 mm of rain a year, avoids forest and pure desert, and does not need to drink. It thrives in heavily grazed grassland and farmland where harvester termites are common.
sections.diet: Feeds almost entirely on one or a few local species of nasute harvester termites (Trinervitermes), licked from the soil surface as they forage in dense patches. In southern African winters it switches to the pigmented harvester termite Hodotermes, and in the East African rains to other termites. It does not destroy mounds, so colonies keep supplying food. In the Serengeti aardwolves and aardvarks overlap heavily in space and time, and aardwolves appear to benefit from aardvark activity.
sections.social: Socially monogamous pairs with their latest offspring share a territory of about 1–4 km², marked with anal-gland paste. Young stay about a year and leave around the time the next litter is born.
sections.reproduction: In South Africa mating is in early July and cubs are born from October to December after a gestation of about 91 days. Litters average 2.5 cubs (1–4). Cubs first leave the den at about one month, forage near it at about nine weeks, and are weaned at about four months.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Most southern African aardwolves live on farmland, where the main threat is indirect poisoning from pesticide spraying against locusts; other threats are persecution by people who mistake it for a livestock predator, dogs trained to hunt jackals, roads and drought. Camera trapping in southern Tanzania estimated 9.2–13.3 aardwolves per 100 km².
sections.features:
Long, broad, sticky tongue.
Peg-like cheek teeth and retained canines.
Five toes on the front feet.
Erectile mane along the back.
Anal-gland scent paste used about 200 times a night.
sections.humanInteraction: Harmless to livestock and a useful consumer of harvester termites on grazing land, but sometimes killed by farmers who mistake it for a jackal or hyena that kills stock. It suffers indirectly from locust poisoning campaigns.

funFacts: One aardwolf can lap up about 250,000–300,000 termites in a single night.
It is the only African termite-eater known to tolerate the chemical defences of Trinervitermes soldier termites.
Its cheek teeth are tiny pegs, yet it belongs to the hyena family.
It has five toes on its front feet, while other hyenas have four.
A pair may leave about 200 scent marks in one night.
Fathers can guard the den for up to six hours a night.

abilities.name: Termite Vacuum Tongue
abilities.description: a long, broad, sticky tongue laps up to about 250,000–300,000 termites in a night, and it is the only African termite-eater known to tolerate the terpene defence secretions of Trinervitermes soldiers.

abilities.name: Mane Bluff
abilities.description: when threatened it raises the long mane along its back to look much larger and can release a foul-smelling liquid from its anal glands, then retreat into a burrow.

traits.name: Peg-Toothed Hyena
traits.description: a member of the hyena family whose cheek teeth are reduced to small pegs; it keeps its canines for fighting and swallows sand with its termites.

traits.name: Den-Guarding Father
traits.description: pairs share a territory, and males may guard the den for up to six hours a night against jackals; females with a guarding male raise about three times as many cubs.

combat.weapons: The aardwolf is a termite specialist, not a predator of vertebrates. Its only real weapons are its canines, which are kept for fights with other aardwolves and for defense, backed by a light jaw with a very low bite-force quotient. It does not dig into termite mounds; it licks harvester termites off the soil surface with a long, broad, sticky tongue.
weaknesses: Only about 10 kg, lightly built.
Weak jaw and peg-like cheek teeth.
Slow runner with no armor.
Seasonal weight loss and dependence on one food type.
