african-grey-parrot.name: African Grey Parrot
african-grey-parrot.specimen: healthy adult male, 400 g (0.4 kg) and 33 cm long, with a 46–52 cm wingspan, matching Wikipedia's typical 400 g and the World Parrot Trust's 400 g and 33 cm; ADW gives up to 407 g.
african-grey-parrot.summary: The African grey parrot is one of the smartest animals alive, a 400-gram forest parrot that can use words for objects, colours and numbers and track hidden objects better than young children. Its hooked bill bites hard for its size, but on the absolute scale it is a small, unarmoured bird that wins by staying alert and flying away.
narrative: The African grey parrot is a medium-sized, red-tailed parrot of the African rainforest, and it has become the model for what a bird's mind can do. Decades of work with Alex showed that a parrot could learn English labels for objects, colours, shapes and quantities and use them to ask for things, refuse them and sort them into categories. Later tests found a grey parrot matching adult humans at a shell game, and captive greys voluntarily helping partners obtain food.

In the wild, those abilities serve a cautious forest life. Greys roost in large, noisy flocks over water, fan out by day to feed on oil-palm nuts and fruit, and drop into forest clearings in careful waves while sentinels watch the edges. Young birds stay with their families for years, learning which foods are safe and how to avoid palm-nut vultures and hawks. That same intelligence made the species a prized pet, and trapping has driven it to Endangered status.

As a fighter, the grey parrot is limited by size. Its bill produces about 84 newtons, enough to crack palm nuts and hurt a hand, but it is a 400-gram bird without armour or talons. It rates at the very top of the roster for Intelligence and well above average for Agility, while its Attack and Defense sit among the small birds.

sections.habitat: The grey parrot lives in the forest belt of central and West Africa, from the eastern border of Côte d'Ivoire through Ghana, Cameroon, Gabon and the Congo Basin to Uganda and Kenya, plus the island of Príncipe (ADW; Wikipedia). It prefers moist lowland forest but also uses forest edges, clearings, gallery forest, mangroves, wooded savanna, farmland and gardens, up to 2,200 m (ADW; World Parrot Trust). Escaped or released birds have been seen in South Florida since at least 1984, without evidence of breeding (Wikipedia).
sections.diet: Mainly fruit and nuts, especially oil-palm, supplemented with seeds, leaves, bark, flowers and some insects (ADW). The grey parrot is partly a ground feeder and regularly visits natural forest clearings: at one Congolese clearing an average of 40 birds arrived each day, perched and called in the surrounding trees, then landed to feed, drink and interact, with arrival times shaped by weather and season (Fastré et al. 2024). Natural predators include palm-nut vultures and several raptors (Wikipedia).
sections.social: Highly social. Large single-species flocks roost together and break into smaller foraging groups by day. Each breeding pair holds its own tree within a loose colony. Young birds remain in family groups for years, socialize in "nursery trees", and learn food, water, predator and nest skills from adults (ADW).
sections.reproduction: Pairs form lifelong monogamous bonds at sexual maturity, at 3–5 years. Females lay 3–5 eggs in tree cavities, sometimes old woodpecker holes; incubation takes about 30 days while the male feeds the female, chicks leave the nest at about 12 weeks and reach independence at about 3 years (ADW).
sections.conservation: Endangered on the IUCN Red List since 2016 (Wikipedia; World Parrot Trust), with a decreasing and unknown wild population. More than 359,000 grey parrots were traded internationally between 1994 and 2003, and about 21% of the wild population was harvested each year; in 2016 CITES moved the species to Appendix I (Wikipedia). In Ghana, surveys found greys in only 10 of 42 forest areas, and roosts that once held 700–1,200 birds held 18 in total (Wikipedia).
sections.features:
Heavy hooked bill with an 84 N calculated bite.
Referential use of learned human labels in trained birds.
Visual working memory rivalling adult humans in a shell-game task.
Very large vocal repertoire, including imitations of other species in the wild.
Flock vigilance and staggered descents to feeding clearings.
sections.humanInteraction: One of the most popular pet parrots because of its speech; companion greys have the largest mimicry repertoires of any parrot species surveyed (Benedict et al. 2022). The intelligence that makes them popular also makes them hard to keep well: they need intensive social and behavioural enrichment or become distressed (Wikipedia). Trapping for the pet trade, together with timber felling, is the main cause of wild declines.

funFacts: Alex the grey parrot could label about 50 objects, 7 colours and 5 shapes, and count up to six.
A grey parrot named Griffin beat 6- to 8-year-old children at a shell game and matched adults on most rounds.
Grey parrots will hand a token to a partner so the partner can buy a treat, even with no reward for themselves.
Two wild greys recorded at a roost in Congo used over 200 different calls, including nine imitations of other birds and one of a bat.
A grey parrot can live 40–60 years in captivity.
Flocks drop into forest clearings in waves so that the whole group is never on the ground at once.
Wild greys once roosted in groups of 700–1,200 at Ghanaian sites that now hold only a handful.

abilities.name: Referential Speech
abilities.description: grey parrots do not just copy sounds: Alex used English labels for objects, colours, shapes and quantities to request, refuse and categorize, and trained greys have tried to direct their trainers as a problem-solving strategy (ADW). In a matchup this is situational awareness and flock communication, not damage.

abilities.name: Nutcracker Bill
abilities.description: a heavy hooked bill with an 84 N calculated bite (61–96 N by finite-element modelling) cracks oil-palm nuts and hard seeds and can deliver a painful defensive bite at close range.

traits.name: Shell-Game Memory
traits.description: a grey parrot outperformed 6- to 8-year-old children at tracking hidden objects through a series of swaps, matching adult humans on most test conditions.

traits.name: Red-Tailed Forest Voice
traits.description: wild greys roost in large, noisy flocks and have been recorded with repertoires of over 200 call types, including imitations of other forest birds and a bat.

combat.weapons: The weapon is a heavy, hooked black bill backed by a calculated bite of about 84 N, used to crack oil-palm nuts and other hard seeds. That is roughly half the sulphur-crested cockatoo's calculated 167 N and a fifth of the scarlet macaw's 444 N. Zygodactyl feet grip and manipulate but are not talons. The bill can crush a finger or damage a small animal, but a 400 g bird cannot deliver much absolute force.
weaknesses: Only 400 g; far below any serious predator in absolute power.
No protection beyond feathers.
Partly a ground feeder, which exposes it at clearings.
Wild populations are heavily depleted by trapping.

africanized-honey-bee.name: Africanized Honey Bee
africanized-honey-bee.specimen: a healthy adult female worker acting as a guard or forager. Workers are the only caste that defends the nest by stinging; queens rarely sting outside fights with rival queens, and drones have no sting. Following the hornet and ant reports, all ratings describe one worker, not the colony.
africanized-honey-bee.summary: The Africanized honey bee is a hybrid of African and European honey bees that has spread from Brazil across the Americas. One worker carries only a small venom dose and dies after stinging, but its tear-away sting keeps pumping and marks the target with banana-scented alarm pheromone. Its reputation comes from colonies that attack in huge numbers and pursue for hundreds of metres.
narrative: The Africanized honey bee began with an accident. In 1957, 26 swarms of African honey bees escaped from a research apiary in Brazil and bred with local European bees. Their descendants spread through South and Central America and Mexico and reached Texas in 1990. They look almost identical to European honey bees, a little smaller, and they make honey and pollinate crops in the same way.

The difference is behaviour. Disturb an Africanized colony and it reacts faster, sends 10–30 times more bees, stings 4–10 times more often and chases for up to about 400 m. Each worker's barbed sting tears away and keeps pumping venom, while the sting apparatus releases isopentyl acetate, an alarm scent that marks the victim for the next wave. Research shows the venom per bee is actually smaller than a European bee's; people are hurt by the sheer number of stings.

On the absolute battle scale, the ratings describe one worker, and one worker is a tiny, fragile insect with a single small dose of venom. It gets low Attack and Defense but strong Agility, high Ferocity and one of the best insect Intelligence scores, thanks to the learning and waggle-dance communication honey bees are famous for. The colony-scale threat is recorded in the profile and traits rather than inflated into one bee's physical ratings.

sections.habitat: The pure African subspecies A. m. scutellata lives in the savannas and open country of eastern and southern Africa. The Africanized hybrid spread from southern Brazil after 1957 through much of South America, Central America and Mexico, and has been in the southern United States since 1990. It does best in warm climates and nests in cavities, including in and around buildings.
sections.diet: Workers collect nectar (stored as honey) and pollen, plus water and plant resins. As pollinators they visit many crops and wild plants. Predators include birds and other insects that eat bees, and the honey and brood attract nest raiders.
sections.social: A colony has one egg-laying queen, thousands of female workers and seasonal male drones. Workers change jobs with age, from nursing and nest work to guarding and foraging. Africanized colonies swarm very often, up to 16 times a year, and readily abscond.
sections.reproduction: The queen lays the eggs; workers raise larvae in wax cells. New colonies form by swarming, when the old queen leaves with part of the workforce. Summer workers live about a month; queens live for years.
sections.conservation: Not Evaluated: no IUCN Red List assessment of the Africanized hybrid was located in this pass. It is an abundant, widespread and in many places invasive hybrid; in the Americas it is managed as a public-safety issue and also kept by beekeepers.
sections.features:
Barbed sting that tears free and keeps pumping venom.
Alarm pheromone (mainly isopentyl acetate) that marks targets.
Very high colony defensiveness and long pursuit distance.
Waggle dance communication.
Frequent swarming and absconding.
Smaller body and smaller venom load per bee than European honey bees.
sections.humanInteraction: Africanized bees are responsible for many serious mass-stinging incidents in the Americas, and tertiary sources credit them with around 1,000 human deaths since their arrival. Research shows their venom is not stronger than European bee venom; the danger comes from the number of bees and stings. Public-safety agencies, including the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, publish guidance on avoiding colonies and escaping attacks. Many beekeepers in Latin America keep Africanized bees for honey and pollination.

funFacts: Africanized bees came from 26 swarms that escaped a Brazilian research apiary in 1957.
Each Africanized worker carries less venom than a European honey bee: about 94 µg versus 147 µg.
Their danger lies in numbers: colonies send up to 10–30 times more bees after a threat.
They may chase a threat for about 400 m.
The alarm pheromone smells like bananas.
A detached sting keeps pumping venom after the bee flies off.
Africanized colonies can swarm up to 16 times a year.

abilities.name: Tear-Away Venom Pump
abilities.description: the barbed sting lodges in skin and tears free with the venom sac, muscles and nerve ganglion, which keep pumping venom after the bee has gone.

abilities.name: Banana-Scent Target Marking
abilities.description: the sting apparatus releases alarm pheromone, mainly isopentyl acetate, that marks the victim and brings guards and other workers to the same spot.

traits.name: Long-Range Pursuit
traits.description: Africanized colonies chase threats up to about 400 m, sting 4–10 times more often and send 10–30 times more bees than European colonies.

traits.name: Waggle Dance Navigator
traits.description: workers tell nestmates the direction and distance of food with a dance, and young bees get better at it by following experienced dancers.

combat.weapons: The primary weapon is the barbed venom sting, which can be used once against a mammal. The secondary weapon is chemical: the alarm pheromone, mainly isopentyl acetate (smelling like banana oil), released from the sting apparatus marks the target and recruits more defenders. The mandibles can nip but do little.
weaknesses: Each worker can sting a mammal only once and then dies.
Small venom dose per bee; one sting rarely matters to a large animal.
Tiny, fragile body.
Poorer tolerance of cold climates than European bees, which limits its spread north.
Colony defense is strongest near the nest and fades with distance.

alligator-snapping-turtle.name: Alligator Snapping Turtle
alligator-snapping-turtle.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 45.0 kg with a 58.0 cm straight carapace length, representing a large prime male rather than a record animal.
alligator-snapping-turtle.summary: The alligator snapping turtle is North America's heaviest freshwater turtle and a patient ambush specialist. A 45 kg adult male lies still on the river bottom, wriggles a worm-shaped lure on its tongue and snaps its huge hooked beak shut on anything that comes close. Its ridged shell is strong armor, but it is very slow and can only hurt what comes within reach of its head.
narrative: On the bottom of a muddy southern river, a large alligator snapping turtle can pass for a log or a rock. Algae coats the three ridged rows of its shell, and it may not move for long stretches. Its mouth hangs open, and on the floor of that mouth a pink, worm-shaped appendage twitches. When a fish comes to inspect the "worm", the jaws close faster than the fish can turn.

That ambush is the whole fighting style. The head is huge, the beak is sharply hooked, and bite tests on 62 animals showed that alligator snapping turtles out-bite common snapping turtles at every size. A big male weighs several times as much as the common snapper on the roster, so the bite is correspondingly more dangerous. The shell adds real protection from above, but the plastron is small, the head cannot be pulled in, and the animal is very slow. An opponent that avoids the front of the head and attacks from the side, or simply walks away, faces little danger.

In ABS terms the alligator snapping turtle is an armored close-range trap. It earns solid Attack and good Defense, a low Agility score and modest Stamina and Intelligence. Its Special is high because the tongue lure is a genuine one-of-a-kind hunting mechanism. The species is now Endangered, and much of its recent history has been shaped by harvest for meat.

sections.habitat: Alligator snapping turtles live in large rivers, oxbow lakes, bayous, swamps and reservoirs in the Mississippi River basin and neighbouring Gulf of Mexico drainages of the south-central and southeastern United States, north to Indiana. Radio-tracked adults preferred areas with submerged cover combined with a high percentage of overhead canopy.
sections.diet: The diet is broad. Studies from Arkansas and Louisiana and species accounts list fish, molluscs and other turtles, especially musk turtles, as frequent prey, along with plant food such as acorns. Medium-sized mammals, including opossums, raccoons and armadillos, are taken occasionally.
sections.social: Solitary. Adults do not form groups, and contact between individuals is mainly during mating.
sections.reproduction: Only nesting females regularly leave the water. Nests are dug in sandy soil usually within about 20 m of water, and females lay about 17–52 eggs in a single clutch each year. With only one clutch a year and a population decline measured over three generations, losses of adults take a long time to recover.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2025 assessment), based on a population reduction of at least 50% over three generations. Threats named in the assessment summary include pollution, residential and commercial development, climate change, and invasive species and diseases; historical harvest for meat also reduced many populations. In the United States, the Fish and Wildlife Service proposed listing it as threatened under the Endangered Species Act in 2021; the Suwannee species was listed as threatened in 2024. The final rule for M. temminckii was still pending in the sources found in this run.
sections.features:
Worm-like lure on the floor of the mouth.
Very large head with a sharply hooked beak.
Thick carapace with three rows of raised keels.
Small plastron and a head that cannot be withdrawn into the shell.
Long, thick tail and heavy clawed limbs.
Algae often grows on the shell, adding camouflage on the river bottom.
sections.humanInteraction: Past harvest for meat contributed to its decline. Federal and state agencies now manage it as a species of conservation concern, and the Fish and Wildlife Service has publicized releases of the species back into the wild. A bite from a large adult can cause serious injury to hands.

funFacts: Its tongue lure is the only prey-catching lure inside the mouth of any living reptile.
Newly hatched turtles already use the lure; experiments described a four-phase hunt of waiting, luring, attack and handling.
A 2023 study measured the bites of 62 alligator snapping turtles and found they out-bite common snapping turtles at every size.
Record weights above 110 kg make it one of the heaviest freshwater turtles in the world.
Nesting females are usually the only adults that ever come onto land.
Algae growing on its ridged shell helps it look like a mossy rock or log.

abilities.name: Tongue-Worm Lure
abilities.description: a pink, worm-like appendage on the floor of the mouth is wriggled while the turtle lies still with its jaws open. Fish swim into the mouth to investigate and the jaws snap shut. In battle this lets it strike first at anything that approaches its head.

abilities.name: Beak-Trap Bite
abilities.description: a massive head and hooked beak deliver a bite measured stronger than the common snapping turtle's at every body size. It punishes any opponent that puts a limb, head or snout within reach.

traits.name: Ridged River Fortress
traits.description: a thick carapace with three rows of raised keels gives it the look of a spiked boulder and strong protection from above.

traits.name: North America's Heaviest Freshwater Turtle
traits.description: adult males can exceed 90 kg, with record weights above 110 kg, far larger than any other freshwater turtle on the continent.

combat.weapons: The main weapon is a massive head with a hooked beak and powerful jaw muscles. The turtle lies still on the bottom with its mouth open and wriggles a pink, worm-like appendage on the floor of its mouth. When a fish investigates the lure, the jaws snap shut. The same bite is used on other turtles, molluscs and occasional mammals. Measured bite forces exceed those of the common snapping turtle at every size, and a 45 kg male bites far harder than the 12 kg common snapper on the roster. The weakness is delivery: the bite reaches only what comes within range of the head.
weaknesses: Very slow whole-body movement on land and in water.
Small plastron and exposed head, limbs and tail.
Offense depends entirely on the opponent coming within reach.
Limited sustained high-output effort.
Almost no tactical options beyond ambush and defensive biting.

american-pit-bull-terrier.name: American Pit Bull Terrier
american-pit-bull-terrier.specimen: healthy adult male in good working condition, 23.0 kg, 50.0 cm at the withers.
american-pit-bull-terrier.summary: The American Pit Bull Terrier is a muscular 23 kg bulldog-terrier breed made to grip and hold. It fights with a committed catch-and-shake bite and remarkable persistence, which makes it formidable against dogs of its size, but its small frame and thin coat leave it far below wolves, big guardian dogs and every large predator in absolute power.
narrative: The American Pit Bull Terrier comes from 19th-century British crosses between bulldogs and terriers, made to combine the bulldog's strength with the terrier's drive. After bull-baiting was outlawed in 1835, these dogs were pitted against each other, and immigrants brought them to North America, where the United Kennel Club registered the breed in 1898. A fit male weighs about 23 kg and stands about 50 cm tall, with a wide, deep jaw and thick, well-muscled thighs.

Its fighting method is simple: close in, take a grip and hold. The UKC standard says the breed must be able to catch, hold, push and pull while breathing easily, the job farmers used it for on semi-wild cattle and hogs. That grip, backed by a bred tendency to keep going when hurt, is why the breed is feared in dog fights. But there is no "locking jaw", and the viral bite-force numbers trace back to a television demonstration, not a study.

On the absolute scale, the APBT sits among the medium wild canids. It is heavier and more committed than a coyote or dingo, roughly level with an African wild dog in attack, and clearly below the 50 kg Kangal, Rottweiler and Gray Wolf. Against big cats, bears or large hoofed animals its grip does not make up for being several times smaller, and its short coat gives no protection against teeth or claws.

sections.habitat: A domestic breed kept as a companion and working dog, mostly in North America but also elsewhere. It lives in homes and on farms. Twelve European countries, Australia, Canada, parts of the United States and several other countries restrict or ban pit bull-type dogs.
sections.diet: Fed by its owners on commercial dog food, meat and household scraps. It does not hunt for a living, though catch dogs are used on hogs and cattle.
sections.ecology: As a domestic animal it has no wild ecological role. Its working roles have included catch dog for semi-wild cattle and hogs, farm dog and, increasingly, sport and therapy work.
sections.social: Strongly bonded to its people and generally friendly toward strangers, according to the UKC standard. Many individuals are intolerant of other dogs, so they are often kept as single dogs or carefully managed with other pets.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is managed by people. Litters of about 5–10 pups are typical (Wikipedia).
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed.
sections.features:
Wide, deep lower jaw and prominent cheek muscles.
Short, smooth, stiff single coat in many colors (merle not accepted).
Muscular, athletic build that should never look bulky or fine-boned.
Strong grip-holding behavior and persistence.
Friendly toward people but often aggressive toward other dogs.
sections.humanInteraction: The APBT is one of the most debated dog breeds. A CDC-linked study of 238 US dog bite-related deaths from 1979 to 1998 found pit bull-type dogs and Rottweilers were involved in more than half, while warning that breed is hard to determine and that fatal attacks should not drive dangerous-dog policy alone. A later study of 256 US deaths from 2000 to 2009 found that valid breed identification was possible in only 17.6% of cases and that most deaths shared preventable factors such as isolation from people and poor management. The breed's own standards treat aggression toward people as a serious fault.

funFacts: The UKC registered the American Pit Bull Terrier in 1898, but the American Kennel Club has never recognized it.
Its UKC standard says it is "not the best choice for a guard dog" because it is so friendly with strangers.
The "locking jaw" is a myth: holding on is behavior, not a special joint.
APBTs compete in weight pulling, dock jumping, lure coursing and French Ring sport.
In 1996 the San Francisco SPCA tried to rename pit bull terriers "St. Francis Terriers" to counter their fighting reputation.
In a study of 120 shelter dogs, staff labelled 52% "pit bull-type", but DNA tests confirmed only 21%.

abilities.name: Catch-Dog Grip
abilities.description: takes hold and keeps holding while pushing and pulling, the job the UKC standard says the breed must be built to do. In a matchup it can pin and wear down an opponent of similar size, but it also locks the dog into close contact.

abilities.name: Game Persistence
abilities.description: a bred tendency to keep fighting while injured and not break off, rooted in its dog-fighting history. It raises Ferocity and Toughness but does not add armor or raw power.

traits.name: Bulldog-Terrier Build
traits.description: a medium, smooth-coated dog with a wide, deep lower jaw, prominent cheek muscles and thick thighs, bred from bulldog and terrier crosses to combine strength with agility.

traits.name: Most-Regulated Breed Type
traits.description: the target of breed-specific legislation in many countries, while the "pit bull" label itself is applied so inconsistently that DNA tests often disagree with it.

combat.weapons: The APBT's weapon is the canid bite used as a catch-and-hold. The UKC standard says the dog "must have the functional capability to be a catch dog that can hold, wrestle (push and pull), and breathe easily while doing its job". Its style is to close, take a grip, and then shake, push and pull while holding. Farmers used APBTs as catch dogs for semi-wild cattle and hogs, which means gripping and holding animals much heavier than itself until handlers arrive.
weaknesses: Small absolute mass; large carnivores and ungulates outweigh it many times over.
Short single coat with no protection over the neck and limbs.
Grip-and-hold style commits it to close contact and leaves little room to disengage.
Its short single coat gives little insulation in severe cold.
No measured speed or bite data to support the viral claims made about it.

arapaima.name: Arapaima
arapaima.specimen: healthy mature large adult, 100.0 kg and 210.0 cm total length. Sex is left unspecified because no consistent size difference between the sexes was found; males differ mainly in breeding colour and in providing most parental care.
arapaima.summary: The arapaima is a giant air-breathing fish of Amazon floodplain lakes, reaching over 2 m and 100 kg. It ambushes fish with a sudden vacuum-like gulp and crushes them on a bony, toothed tongue. Its scales are so tough that piranha teeth fail against them, but it must surface to breathe every 10–20 minutes and has little offensive power against large animals.
narrative: In a warm, still Amazon lake at low water, the oxygen can run so low that most large fish cannot cope. The arapaima can. Every ten to twenty minutes it rises, gulps air with an audible splash and sinks again. Between breaths it hangs near the surface or among flooded trees, waiting for smaller fish to come close. Then its huge mouth opens so fast that water and prey rush in, and the prey is crushed against the toothed "bony tongue" and palate.

The arapaima's scales are one of the best-studied natural armors. Engineers testing them found a hard mineralized outer layer over a flexible base of collagen fibres stacked like plywood, and a piranha tooth driven into a scale broke before it could get through. Those scales let a large fish share its lakes with shoals of piranhas. They are not proof against everything: caimans share the same lakes, and a crushing crocodilian bite or a fisher's spear is a different problem from a piranha's cutting teeth.

In ABS terms the arapaima is a large, well-armored fish with modest weapons. Its Defense is solid because its armor is scientifically demonstrated, its Attack is low for its size because suction feeding does little to big opponents, and its Special reflects air breathing and remarkable parental care. Its story also includes one of conservation's success stories, as fishing communities that count the fish at their breathing rises have helped several populations recover.

sections.habitat: Arapaima live in the Amazon basin in Brazil, Peru and neighbouring countries, in floodplain lakes, slow rivers, flooded forest and swamps. Populations also occur in Guyana, and introduced populations exist outside South America, including in Indonesia where the species is considered invasive.
sections.diet: Adults are mainly piscivorous, taking other fish, and also eat crustaceans and occasionally birds, frogs, small mammals and plant matter. As one of the largest predators in floodplain lakes, the arapaima is itself hunted mainly by people; caimans also live in the same lakes.
sections.social: Adults are usually solitary. During breeding a male and female pair, and the male guards the brood. Young fish school tightly around the guarding parent as rising water carries them into flooded forest or savanna.
sections.reproduction: Spawning takes place in the rainy season. Males, which develop red coloration when breeding, dig nests about 50–60 cm across and 15–20 cm deep in shallow water, and a female lays thousands of eggs. Males guard the young for up to about three months. Both sexes carry gland-like tissue on the head that releases a secretion, and a proteome study found that this cephalic fluid changes during parental care; it is used for communication with the young and may partly feed the fry. Fish reach maturity at 4–5 years and about 1.6–1.85 m.
sections.conservation: Arapaima gigas is listed as Data Deficient on the IUCN Red List. Overfishing has caused severe local declines in parts of the Brazilian Amazon, and a 2020 review called the species endangered in its native range in Brazil while invasive in Indonesia. Community-based management has produced striking recoveries: at the Mamirauá reserve, fishers counting arapaima at their breathing rises helped the population grow about nine-fold, from roughly 2,200 to 20,650 fish, between 1999 and 2006. Similar recoveries have been reported on the Juruá and Purus rivers.
sections.features:
Obligate air breathing through a modified, lung-like swim bladder.
Large scales with a hard mineralized surface over a flexible collagen base.
Toothed "bony tongue" and palate for crushing prey.
Suction feeding that pulls prey in within a fraction of a second.
Head glands that release a secretion used in parental care.
Red breeding coloration in males.
sections.humanInteraction: Arapaima are among the most valuable food fishes of the Amazon and are farmed and exported. Their need to surface makes them easy targets for fishers, which drove declines, but it also makes them easy to count, the basis of successful community management with fishing quotas.

funFacts: In lab tests, a piranha tooth broke before it could get through an arapaima scale.
Arapaima must breathe air and surface about every 10–20 minutes.
Fishers at Mamirauá count arapaima by watching them rise to breathe, and the managed population grew about nine-fold in eight years.
Male arapaima guard their young for up to about three months.
Glands on the parents' heads release a fluid used to communicate with the fry.
Until 2013 all arapaima were treated as one species; a revision showed there are several.

abilities.name: Piranha-Proof Scales
abilities.description: each scale pairs a hard mineralized outer layer with a flexible, plywood-like collagen base. In lab tests, piranha teeth could not puncture the scales. In a battle this blunts attacks from cutting and puncturing teeth.

abilities.name: Gulp-Air Survival
abilities.description: an obligate air breather that rises every 10–20 minutes to gulp air, letting it hunt and live in warm, oxygen-poor lakes that drive other large fish away.

traits.name: Giant of the Bonytongues
traits.description: one of the largest freshwater fishes in the world, with published maximums near 3 m and 200 kg, and a toothed "bony tongue" that crushes prey inside the mouth.

traits.name: Devoted Father
traits.description: males build nests, guard eggs and lead schools of fry for up to about three months, communicating with the young through secretions from glands on the head.

combat.weapons: The arapaima is a suction-feeding ambush predator. It hovers near the surface or among flooded vegetation, then opens its large mouth suddenly so that prey is sucked in within a fraction of a second. Prey is gripped and crushed against the toothed tongue and palate. Most prey is fish, with crustaceans and sometimes birds, frogs or small mammals taken near the surface. Against large opponents this system offers little damage: it has no large teeth, claws or venom. Its most dangerous physical asset beyond feeding is the thrust of a 100 kg muscular body, which males use to clear nest hollows with their tails.
weaknesses: Must surface to breathe every 10–20 minutes.
Weak offensive weapons against large or armored opponents.
Scale armor resists cutting teeth but not crushing crocodilian bites.
Large, predictable fish that is easy to locate at the surface.
Poor performance outside slow, warm fresh water.

asian-elephant.name: Asian Elephant
asian-elephant.specimen: healthy mature adult male (bull) of about 4,500 kg and 275 cm shoulder height, carrying tusks. This is a representative prime mainland bull, not a record captive or historical giant.
asian-elephant.summary: The Asian elephant is a multi-tonne forest giant whose prime bulls combine crushing mass, tusks, a powerful grasping trunk and the testosterone-fuelled aggression of musth. Slightly smaller and less heavily tusked than its African cousin, it is still one of the roster's strongest land animals, and it pairs that power with some of the best-documented intelligence of any non-primate.
narrative: A mature Asian bull weighs around four and a half tonnes and stands close to three metres at the shoulder. That mass is the core of its fighting ability. It can shove over trees, pin an opponent and trample with feet that carry a tonne each, and a tusked bull adds a stabbing weapon driven by the whole body. The trunk works like a strong, precise extra limb, able to deliver a blow or seize a limb. Almost nothing on land can absorb a committed charge from an animal this heavy.

The species is not simply a smaller African elephant. Tusks are shorter and far less universal: many males, especially in Sri Lanka, carry none at all and fight with head, trunk and bulk. Asian elephants live mostly in forest and forest-grassland mosaics rather than open savanna, and they are skilled at climbing wooded slopes, crossing rivers and moving quietly through cover. Their measured top speed of about 25 km/h is enough to catch a running person but far below any predator's sprint.

Its mind is its other great weapon. Asian elephants have passed the mirror mark test, cooperated in rope-pulling experiments and discriminated between the growls of tigers and leopards according to the danger each poses. In musth, adult bulls become intensely aggressive, and a smaller bull in musth can drive off a larger rival. For ABS purposes the Asian elephant sits just below the African savanna elephant in size, power and weaponry, close to it in cognition, and well above rhinoceros and bovid heavyweights in overall defense.

sections.habitat: Asian elephants live in 13 range countries across South and Southeast Asia, from India and Sri Lanka through Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia. They use dense tropical evergreen forest, dry and wet deciduous forest, scrubland and grassland, often moving between forest cover and open feeding areas.
sections.diet: They are bulk herbivores that eat grasses, bark, roots, leaves, stems and fruit, needing around 150 kg of food a day. By opening forest paths, dispersing seeds and shaping vegetation, they act as important ecosystem engineers. Crops near forest edges attract them and drive conflict with people.
sections.social: Family groups of related females and their young are led by an older matriarch. Adult bulls leave their birth group and live alone or in loose associations, joining family groups mainly to breed. Communication uses rumbles, trumpets, touch and scent.
sections.reproduction: Females give birth to a single calf after a long pregnancy of close to two years, and calves depend on their mothers and aunts for years. Males reach full body size and competitive status late, typically in their twenties or later, which is why prime bulls are the canonical specimen.
sections.conservation: Endangered on the IUCN Red List, a status held since 1986, after declines of at least 50% over three generations. An IUCN-compiled 2018 set of national estimates totalled roughly 48,000–52,000 wild elephants, with wide uncertainty. Habitat loss and fragmentation, conflict with people, and poaching for ivory and other body parts are the main threats. Removing tuskers through poaching also skews sex ratios in some populations.
sections.features:
Only males carry tusks; many males are tuskless makhnas.
Highly muscular, boneless trunk used for feeding, touch, smell, drinking and fighting.
Instrumented running speed up to 6.8 m/s without a true aerial phase.
Low-frequency rumbles, part of which travel through the ground.
Musth in adult bulls.
Very large brain and strong evidence for self-recognition and cooperation.
sections.humanInteraction: Asian elephants have been captured and trained for timber work, transport, ceremony and war for thousands of years, and many still live in captivity in Myanmar, Thailand and India. Human-elephant conflict kills about 500 people a year in India alone, and around 100 elephants die in retaliation each year. Mitigation focuses on corridors, early-warning systems, crop protection and barriers.

funFacts: A 2003 Nature study timed Asian elephants at up to 25 km/h and found they "run" with a bouncing body but never lift all four feet at once.
An Asian elephant at the Bronx Zoo passed a mirror mark test, one of very few animals to do so.
In a cooperative rope task, elephants waited up to 45 seconds for a partner before pulling.
Only about 7% of Sri Lankan males carry tusks.
Wild Asian elephants react differently to tiger and leopard growls, retreating quietly from tigers but confronting leopards.
An adult can eat around 150 kg of food in a day.
The trunk contains 17 major muscles made of up to 150,000 muscle fascicles; the popular "40,000 muscles" figure counts these bundles differently.

abilities.name: Musth Surge
abilities.description: periodic testosterone-driven state in adult bulls that sharply raises aggression and fighting drive; a smaller bull in musth can defeat a larger one that is not. In a matchup it names a real escalation of commitment, not extra strength from nowhere.

abilities.name: Trunk Strike and Grip
abilities.description: the boneless, highly muscular trunk can strike, grab, lift and throw, giving the elephant a precise close-range tool on top of its tusks and mass.

traits.name: Tusker or Makhna
traits.description: only males carry tusks, and in some populations most males are tuskless makhnas; the species' weapon kit varies more between individuals than in almost any other roster animal.

traits.name: Mirror-Aware Mind
traits.description: the Asian elephant is one of the few animals shown to pass a mirror mark test, alongside strong evidence for cooperative problem solving.

combat.weapons:
The Asian bull's offense is built on mass. A 4.5-tonne animal can shove, butt, pin and trample almost any terrestrial opponent, and a tusked bull adds a stabbing and levering weapon backed by that whole body. The trunk is a strong, precise limb that can strike, grab and throw. Against predators the practical threats are a charge, a tusk thrust, a trunk blow and crushing under the feet.

Tusks are smaller and less universal than in African savanna bulls. Many bulls in Sri Lanka and some mainland regions are tuskless makhnas, which still fight effectively with head, trunk and mass but lose the penetrating weapon.
weaknesses: Low absolute agility and no jumping; slow to turn at speed.
Heat and water dependence limit prolonged exertion.
Many bulls lack tusks, removing the penetrating weapon.
Large target; calves are vulnerable to tigers.
Weaker eyesight than hearing and smell.

ball-python.name: Ball Python
ball-python.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 1.3 kg and 125.0 cm total length, representing a well-grown wild female rather than a record or captive-fattened animal.
ball-python.summary: The ball python is a small, stocky constrictor from the savannas and farmland of West and Central Africa. A 1.3 kg adult female hunts rats and other small animals at night, finding them with heat-sensing pits and killing them by constriction. When threatened it would rather roll into a ball with its head hidden than bite, which makes it a gentle pet and a weak fighter.
narrative: In the West African savanna, a ball python spends its day underground, often in a burrow dug by a rodent. At night it waits near a trail or burrow entrance. The pits along its lips pick up the heat of a passing rat, and the snake strikes, grips with rows of curved teeth and throws its coils around the prey. It is an efficient hunter of small mammals and birds, and not much more.

Its defense is what made it famous. When a predator or a person grabs it, the ball python usually does not bite. It rolls into a tight ball with its head buried in the middle, protecting its skull and neck. That makes it easy to handle, and it is now the most popular pet snake in the world, bred into thousands of colour morphs. The same pet trade weighs on the wild population: the species is Near Threatened, and hunters in Togo alone collected thousands of snakes and eggs in a single year.

In ABS terms the ball python is a small constrictor with modest Attack, low Defense and middling Agility and Stamina. Its heat pits and constriction give it a solid Special score, but at about 1.3 kg it is far below the roster's big pythons, and its reluctance to bite means it rarely presses a fight.

sections.habitat: The ball python lives in grassland, savanna, open woodland and farmland across West and Central Africa, from Senegal through Cameroon to Sudan and Uganda. It favours mammal burrows and other underground hiding places, and it tolerates land cleared for farming.
sections.diet: It eats mainly small mammals, including Gambian pouched rats, soft-furred and striped grass mice, bats, forest giant squirrels and Demidoff's bushbabies, plus birds such as young grey parrots. Young snakes under 70 cm feed mostly on small birds, and snakes over 100 cm mostly on mammals.
sections.social: Solitary. It is nocturnal or crepuscular. Males are more often found climbing and females on the ground.
sections.reproduction: Females lay 3–11 large, leathery eggs and care for them until they hatch after about 55–60 days; the young then fend for themselves. Males mature at 11–18 months and females at 20–36 months, with body weight as important as age. Parthenogenesis has been confirmed in a pet female.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2022) and is on CITES Appendix II. Wild populations are believed to be declining in most of West Africa, mainly because of collection for the international pet trade, along with hunting for skin, meat and traditional medicine and habitat loss. In southern Togo, 58 interviewed hunters collected 3,000 live ball pythons and 5,000 eggs in 2019 alone for sale to snake ranches.
sections.features:
Infrared-sensing lip pits.
Coiling ball defense with the head hidden.
Pelvic spurs on both sexes, larger in males and used to grip during mating.
Stocky body with a short tail and small head.
Recurved teeth for holding prey.
sections.humanInteraction: The ball python is the most popular pet snake. Breeders have produced more than 7,500 colour and pattern morphs; the "spider" morph is linked to malformations of the inner ear that cause head wobbling, and one herpetological society banned its sale at events. The Igbo people of southeastern Nigeria revere the ball python, and in many communities an accidentally killed python is given a funeral.

funFacts: It gets its name from rolling into a ball with its head tucked in the middle when scared.
A ball python at the Saint Louis Zoo lived to 62, the oldest known snake in captivity.
Breeders have produced more than 7,500 different morphs.
Its lip pits can sense the body heat of prey in darkness.
A pet female produced embryos without ever meeting a male.
In Togo, hunters collected 3,000 live ball pythons and 5,000 eggs in a single year.

abilities.name: Heat-Pit Strike
abilities.description: pits along the lips sense the body heat of prey, guiding a fast strike in darkness that is followed by constriction. Against warm-blooded prey at night it can find and hit targets it cannot see.

abilities.name: Ball Guard
abilities.description: when threatened it coils into a tight ball with the head hidden in the centre, protecting its most vulnerable part instead of biting back.

traits.name: Burrow Lodger
traits.description: it spends much of its time in mammal burrows and other underground refuges, where it also waits out the dry season.

traits.name: Virgin Birth
traits.description: a wild-caught pet female with no contact with a male laid eggs containing embryos that genetic tests showed came from her alone, demonstrating parthenogenesis in the species.

combat.weapons: The ball python is an ambush constrictor. It strikes, holds with its recurved teeth and wraps coils around the prey. Its prey is small: rats, mice, shrews, bats, squirrels, bushbabies and birds such as young grey parrots. Juveniles strike as fast as much larger snakes relative to their size, but a three-year study found strike performance fell steeply during the first 18 months of life. At 1.3 kg its constriction is only a threat to small animals.
weaknesses: Small absolute size for a python.
Slow on the ground.
Rarely counterattacks; the ball defense can be pried open by large predators.
No armor.

basking-shark.name: Basking Shark
basking-shark.specimen: healthy mature adult, 790 cm total length and 4,000 kg, representing an average adult rather than the 12.27 m Bay of Fundy record.
basking-shark.summary: The basking shark is the second-largest fish alive, a 7.9-metre, 4-tonne filter feeder that cruises open-mouthed through plankton. It has no weapons and never fights, but its thick, rough skin and huge size protect it, and it can burst out of the sea as fast as a great white shark.
narrative: The basking shark spends summer days at the surface with its mouth stretched open like a giant net, straining tiny copepods from the water. An average adult is about 7.9 metres long and weighs around four tonnes, yet it feeds at a slow walking pace and barely reacts to passing boats. That calm made it an easy target for centuries of harpoon fisheries hunting its oily liver.

Its lazy image hides surprising power. Loggers attached to basking sharks show them rushing up from around 20 metres and leaping clear of the sea at about 5 m/s, the same vertical speed as a great white shark, and doing so hundreds of times a year. Satellite tags show them crossing oceans and even the equator, diving hundreds of metres into the twilight zone and staying there for weeks.

In a battle, the basking shark is a pure endurer. It has no bite worth the name and no inclination to fight, but its thick, abrasive skin and massive body make it a very hard target for anything smaller than a killer whale. Orcas, working together, are the one predator known to take them, and against such opponents its only real options are its bulk and a dive into deep water.

sections.habitat: Basking sharks live in boreal to warm-temperate waters around the world, on continental shelves and in the open ocean, and occasionally enter brackish water. They prefer water of about 8–14.5 °C, are often seen at the surface in summer at hotspots such as western Scotland, the Isle of Man and the continental shelf off the north-east United States and Canada, and move deeper, to about 900 m, in winter. Some cross the tropics at depth.
sections.diet: A filter feeder on zooplankton, especially calanoid copepods, along with fish eggs, larvae and small invertebrates. It feeds selectively in the densest plankton patches, often along ocean fronts, and continues foraging during long migrations, including in the deep scattering layers of the mesopelagic.
sections.social: Usually solitary but gathers in summer where plankton is dense. It forms small sex-segregated groups, and courtship tori of several sharks circling together have been documented in the eastern North Atlantic.
sections.reproduction: Ovoviviparous; embryos may use their tiny teeth to feed on unfertilised eggs in the womb. Only the right ovary appears to work in females. Maturity is thought to come at 6–13 years and 4.6–6 m, breeding every two to four years, with a long gestation. Lifespan is estimated at about 50 years.
sections.conservation: Listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2019, amended 2021) and on CITES Appendix II. Centuries of harpoon and net fisheries for its liver oil, fins and meat collapsed several populations. It is fully protected in the United Kingdom and in the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico waters of the United States.
sections.features:
Mouth up to about 1 m wide and gill slits almost encircling the head.
Gill rakers shed and regrown continuously.
Tiny, unused teeth about 5–6 mm long.
Rough skin with large denticles and a mucus layer.
Able to breach at the same vertical speed as a great white shark.
sections.humanInteraction: A popular ecotourism species at summer hotspots such as western Scotland. Its slow speed and habit of not avoiding boats made it easy to harpoon and still expose it to boat strikes. Decomposing basking shark carcasses have been mistaken for sea monsters, including the "Stronsay Beast" of the early 1800s and the Zuiyo-maru carcass hauled up in 1977.

funFacts: A basking shark can burst out of the water at about 5 m/s, as fast as a breaching great white.
One logger study counted 577 breaches by four sharks in a year.
A 5 m basking shark can filter about 450 tonnes of seawater an hour.
It has the smallest brain for its body weight of any shark.
Rotting basking sharks have been mistaken for sea serpents and plesiosaurs.
Some basking sharks cross the equator, travelling from New England to South America.
Its skin denticles are rough enough to injure divers.

abilities.name: Latent Breach Power
abilities.description: despite feeding at under 1 m/s, a basking shark can rush up from about 20 m and leave the water at about 5 m/s, matching a great white shark. Four tonnes arriving at that speed is a real hazard to anything in the way.

abilities.name: Transequatorial Deep Run
abilities.description: tagged basking sharks have crossed from North America to South America, spending weeks to months hundreds of metres down, and Scottish-tagged sharks travelled a median of more than 3,600 km. It can leave a fight for waters few opponents would follow.

traits.name: Cavernous Filter Mouth
traits.description: a mouth up to about 1 m wide and gill slits that nearly encircle the head, with bristle-like gill rakers that are constantly shed and replaced.

traits.name: Abrasive Giant
traits.description: skin so rough with large denticles that it has injured divers who brushed against it.

combat.weapons: The basking shark has no feeding weapon. Its tiny teeth are unused, it has no spines or venom, and it never attacks other animals. What it does have is mass and hidden power. A 4-tonne body is dangerous to anything it collides with, and breaching data show that this apparently lazy fish can generate the same vertical speed as a great white shark: about 5 m/s, with a mass-specific power output of about 5.5 W/kg (Johnston et al. 2018). Its rough skin also scrapes anything that rubs against it.
weaknesses: No weapon and no attacking behavior.
Slow routine speed and wide turning.
Very small brain for its size.
Docile; does not flee boats and was easily harpooned.
Vulnerable to coordinated predators such as orcas.

bearded-dragon.name: Bearded Dragon
bearded-dragon.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 0.40 kg, about 50.0 cm total length with a snout-vent length near 25 cm, representing a well-grown wild adult.
bearded-dragon.summary: The bearded dragon is a sturdy, spiny lizard from the dry woodlands and deserts of inland Australia. A 0.4 kg adult male bites harder than a female and puts on a dramatic threat display, inflating a dark spiny beard and gaping, but its spines are soft and its bite is only dangerous to insects and small animals. It stands out for its brain, not its brawn: it was the first reptile shown to learn by imitation.
narrative: On a fence post in inland Australia, a male bearded dragon sits high in the morning sun, darkening its back to warm up faster. When a rival approaches, it bobs its head rapidly and swells its throat into a black, spiny beard. A lower-ranking dragon answers by slowly waving an arm in a circle, and the standoff ends without a bite. Most of bearded dragon life is decided this way, by signals rather than fights.

The dragon's weapons are modest. Males have broader heads and bite harder than females, and the diet ranges from termites and beetles to flowers and the odd small lizard or rodent. When a predator appears, the dragon flattens itself, inflates its beard, opens its yellow-lined mouth, hisses and hops forward. That bluff can work on a small predator, but the spines are soft and the whole animal weighs about 400 g, so birds of prey, snakes, foxes and cats all take them.

What sets the bearded dragon apart on the roster is its mind. In a trap-door experiment, dragons that watched another dragon open a door copied the same movement, the first clear case of imitation in a reptile, and it outperformed tortoises in a test of self-control. In ABS terms it is a low-Attack, low-Defense lizard with solid Agility, a notably high Intelligence for a reptile, and a moderate Special built on its threat display and colour change.

sections.habitat: The central bearded dragon lives in semi-arid and arid woodland, scrub, grassland and rocky desert across inland eastern Australia, from eastern South Australia and the southeastern Northern Territory through inland Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria. It tolerates cleared farmland and perches on fence posts and even picnic tables. It retreats to shade or burrows in the hottest part of the day.
sections.diet: It is an opportunistic omnivore. In a stomach-content study of 14 free-roaming adults, animal food made up 61% of dry matter, termite alates made up 95% of all prey items, and plants made up 16% of dry matter. Wikipedia's summary of the same work states plant matter was 54% of the diet by volume, so the plant share depends on how it is measured. Adults also eat beetles, grasshoppers, caterpillars, flowers and the occasional small lizard or rodent.
sections.social: Mostly solitary, but dragons gather at prime basking and feeding spots, where a clear hierarchy appears. Communication is visual: head bobs of different speeds signal dominance, submission and courtship, and arm waving signals submission.
sections.reproduction: Females dig a nest and lay about 11–30 eggs per clutch, and can lay several clutches in a season. Sex is normally set by ZZ/ZW chromosomes, but hot incubation (above about 32 °C) reverses genetic males into fertile females. Sexual maturity is estimated at one to three years and depends more on body size than on age.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2018 assessment). It is common and widespread in its range and tolerates considerable habitat change. Australia has banned the export of native wildlife since the 1960s; most of the world's captive dragons come from stock exported illegally between 1974 and 1990, and a captive-bred pet population was established by the early 1990s.
sections.features:
Expandable spiny throat pouch (the "beard") that darkens in displays.
Parietal "third eye" that senses light.
Daily and mood-linked colour change.
Head-bob and arm-wave signalling.
Temperature-triggered sex reversal.
Straight-legged posture that lifts the body off hot ground.
sections.humanInteraction: A 2021 Google Trends study found the bearded dragon was by far the most popular pet reptile of the previous decade, ahead of ball pythons and leopard geckos. Captive breeding has produced many colour morphs and scale-reduced lines; scaleless "silkback" dragons lose water about twice as fast as normal dragons. Without UVB light and dietary calcium, captive dragons develop metabolic bone disease.

funFacts: Bearded dragons were the first reptiles shown to learn by imitation.
Termite alates made up 95% of the prey items found in wild dragons' stomachs.
Heat can turn a genetically male embryo into a fertile female, and such females lay more eggs than normal females.
A dragon waves one arm in a slow circle to tell a dominant dragon it gives up.
Its skin gets darker in sunlight and lighter at night on a built-in daily rhythm.
It is the most popular pet reptile in the world by online search interest.

abilities.name: Beard Threat Display
abilities.description: when threatened it flattens and widens its body, inflates and darkens its spiny throat pouch, gapes to show the yellow mouth lining, hisses and hops toward the attacker. The display can stop a small predator without contact.

abilities.name: Solar Colour Shift
abilities.description: the skin darkens in sunlight and lightens in darkness on an internal daily rhythm, and it changes colour with mood and during displays. Darker skin absorbs heat faster, helping it warm up for action.

traits.name: Copycat Lizard
traits.description: in a 2015 experiment, dragons that watched another dragon open a trap door opened it the same way, the first evidence of learning by imitation in a reptile.

traits.name: Heat-Switched Sex
traits.description: eggs incubated above about 32 °C turn genetic males into fertile females, and a 2015 study made the first report of reptile sex reversal in the wild in this species.

combat.weapons: The weapon is a bite from a broad, triangular head, stronger in adult males. The bearded dragon is an opportunistic omnivore: stomach flushing of 14 wild adults found that 61% of dry-matter intake was animal food, dominated by termite alates, with plants making up much of the rest. It will also take small lizards and rodents when it can. Against anything beyond insect and small-vertebrate size, its offense is minimal.
weaknesses: Very small absolute mass and a weak bite on the roster scale.
Soft spines and no armor.
Performance falls when cold.
Preyed on by birds of prey, snakes, foxes and feral cats.

bearded-vulture.name: Bearded Vulture
bearded-vulture.specimen: healthy adult female, 6.2 kg, 110.0 cm total length, wingspan about 2.7 m.
bearded-vulture.summary: The bearded vulture is a 6 kg mountain vulture with a 2.7 m wingspan that lives mostly on bones, dropping them onto rocks to smash them and dissolving the pieces in stomach acid below pH 1. It is a graceful, far-ranging flier but a poor fighter, with weak talons and little appetite for conflict.
narrative: The bearded vulture is described as the only animal whose diet is based mainly on bone. Where other scavengers leave off, it arrives, swallowing ribs, vertebrae and leg bones whole. Anything too big it carries into the air and drops onto rocks, often at favorite smashing sites, until the bone shatters. Its stomach acid, below pH 1, dissolves bone within about a day, turning an almost useless food into a steady supply of fat-rich marrow and minerals.

It is also one of the most striking birds in the mountains. Adults have long, narrow wings spanning about 2.7 m, a diamond-shaped tail, a black "beard" under the bill and rusty orange underparts. That orange is not natural color: the birds bathe in iron-rich mud and springs to stain their white feathers, a rare cosmetic habit that researchers still debate.

As a fighter, the bearded vulture has little to offer. Its talons are weak, its beak is built for bones, and it avoids conflict. Its combat value lies in agile, low-cost soaring, excellent eyesight, and a clever drop technique that can kill small prey such as tortoises. Persecution once wiped it from most of Europe; today reintroduction and GPS tracking are bringing it back to the Alps and other ranges.

sections.habitat: Lives in high mountains and gorges: the Pyrenees, Alps (through reintroduction), Corsica, Crete, the Atlas, Ethiopian Highlands and eastern and southern Africa's mountains, the Caucasus, Middle East, and across Central Asia to the Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau. It needs cliffs for nesting and open slopes with wild or domestic grazing animals.
sections.diet: A bone specialist: about 70–90% of its diet is bone, supplemented by meat, skin and occasional live prey such as tortoises and small mammals. It feeds after other scavengers have stripped a carcass, filling a niche no other bird uses. Bones too large to swallow are dropped from height onto rocky ossuaries to break them.
sections.social: Lives in territorial pairs, sometimes with a helper, that defend large mountain territories. Non-breeding young birds wander widely over thousands of square kilometres.
sections.reproduction: Breeds in winter, laying one or two eggs in a cliff nest; usually only one chick is raised. It is long-lived, with individuals reported to live over 30 years in the wild and about 45 years in captivity.
sections.conservation: Listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List since 2014, with a decreasing global population estimated at roughly 1,675–6,700 birds. It was wiped out from most of Europe by persecution in the 19th and 20th centuries, surviving mainly in the Pyrenees, and has returned to the Alps and other ranges through reintroduction. Threats include poisoning (including veterinary drugs), power-line collisions, disturbance and falling food supply.
sections.features:
Stomach acid with pH below 1 that dissolves bone.
Stretchy esophagus that swallows bones up to about 30 cm long.
Long, narrow wings and a wedge-shaped tail for agile slope soaring.
Black "beard" of bristles under the bill.
Rust-orange cosmetic staining from iron-oxide bathing.
sections.humanInteraction: Once feared and persecuted in Europe as a supposed killer of lambs and even children, it is now the focus of major reintroduction projects in the Alps and other mountains, coordinated by groups such as the Vulture Conservation Foundation. GPS tracking of released and wild birds guides conservation planning.

funFacts: Bones make up about 70–90% of its diet.
Its stomach acid is below pH 1 and can dissolve bone within about a day.
It can swallow bones up to about 30 cm long whole.
It drops bones onto rocks from height to smash them, often at favorite sites.
Its orange color is cosmetic: it stains its white feathers by bathing in iron-rich mud.
One old name, "ossifrage," means "bone breaker."
Young non-breeding birds can roam over about 10,000 km² of mountains.

abilities.name: Bone Bomber
abilities.description: carries bones and live prey such as tortoises high into the air and drops them onto rocks at chosen sites, repeating until they shatter.

abilities.name: Acid Gut
abilities.description: a stomach with pH below 1 dissolves swallowed bones up to about 30 cm long within about a day, letting it live on food no other animal can use.

traits.name: Bone Eater
traits.description: bones make up about 70–90% of its diet, described as the only animal whose diet is based mainly on bone.

traits.name: Rust-Stained Plumage
traits.description: bathes in iron-rich mud and springs to dye its white underparts rusty orange, a rare cosmetic behavior in birds.

combat.weapons: The bearded vulture is a bone specialist, not a fighter. Its hooked beak handles and swallows bones and its feet can carry heavy loads, but its talons are weak compared with an eagle's. Its most dangerous tool is height: it carries bones and live prey into the air and drops them onto rocks. Tortoises, often nearly as heavy as the vulture itself, are a favored live prey where common, and rock hyraxes, hares, marmots and, in one case, a 62 cm monitor lizard have been reported seized and dropped. Popular accounts also claim it sometimes knocks large animals off ledges with its wings; this is anecdotal and not scored.
weaknesses: Weak talons and a beak built for bones rather than killing.
No armor; grounded, it is clumsy.
Depends on mountain updrafts and on carcasses left by other animals.
Low willingness to fight.

belgian-malinois.name: Belgian Malinois
belgian-malinois.specimen: healthy adult male working dog, 30.0 kg, 62.0 cm at the withers.
belgian-malinois.summary: The Belgian Malinois is a lean, 30 kg Belgian working shepherd built for explosive speed, leaping and relentless drive. Measured police dogs reach about 41 km/h in 25 m and hit with a flying grip, but its bite is moderate and its frame light, so it wins on agility and commitment rather than power and is outclassed by large predators.
narrative: The Belgian Malinois is the short-haired fawn variety of the Belgian Shepherd, a herding dog type that Belgian breeders began to standardize in 1891. A working male weighs about 30 kg and stands about 62 cm, a square, lean dog with a black mask. Its breed standard describes a dog "bursting with energy, and always ready to leap into action", and that energy has made it the police and military dog of choice for forces from the United States to Israel and Australia.

Science has measured what that looks like. Finnish police Malinois sprinted to about 40 km/h in 25 m, and IGP Malinois hit the helper's sleeve at about 7.6 m/s, carrying some 842 J of energy into the impact. The grip that follows is less dramatic: a median of 247 N on a sensor sleeve, lower than police German Shepherds. The Malinois is a missile first and a crusher second.

On the absolute scale that makes it one of the most agile and driven domestic dogs, rated above the German Shepherd in Agility, Stamina and Intelligence, but below it in Attack and Defense because it is lighter and bites less hard. Against coyotes and other light canids it is dangerous; against wolves, heavy guardian dogs and any large predator its 30 kg frame is simply too small.

sections.habitat: A domestic breed from Belgium, now kept worldwide in police, military and sport kennels as well as homes.
sections.diet: Fed by its owners on commercial dog food, meat and household scraps.
sections.ecology: No wild ecological role. Working roles include herding, police patrol, detection, military and anti-poaching work, search-and-rescue, guarding and assistance work.
sections.social: Bonds intensely with its handler; alert and watchful toward strangers. It needs a great deal of work and exercise.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is managed by people. The Finnish police Malinois measured by Hyytiäinen et al. had a median age of 35 months, and the IGP dogs studied by Vilar et al. averaged 4.4 years.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed.
sections.features:
Square build with body length equal to withers height.
Short, fawn coat with black overlay and a pronounced black mask.
Explosive acceleration and leaping.
Very high working drive.
Widely used scent-detection ability.
sections.humanInteraction: The Malinois is one of the most prized police and military dogs, but its energy and drive make it a demanding pet. Its popularity in military service has made it famous; the breed standard still calls for a calm, confident dog without unprovoked aggression.

funFacts: In 1891 a team led by Adolphe Reul gathered 117 Belgian shepherd dogs to sort them into varieties; the Malinois is the short-haired fawn one.
Finnish police Malinois reached up to 41 km/h within 25 m before biting.
In a 2026 study, Malinois hit the bite sleeve carrying about 842 J of kinetic energy.
Their measured median bite on a sensor sleeve was only 247 N, lower than that of police German Shepherds.
Diesel, a French police Malinois killed in the 2015 Saint-Denis raid, was posthumously awarded the PDSA Dickin Medal.
The FCI counts the Malinois as one variety of the Belgian Shepherd, while the AKC treats it as a separate breed.

abilities.name: Spring-Loaded Launch
abilities.description: sprints to about 40 km/h within 25 m and leaps into a full grip, hitting at about 7.6 m/s with roughly 842 J of kinetic energy. Against a similar-size opponent the impact alone can knock it down.

abilities.name: Relentless Work Drive
abilities.description: the FCI's "bursting with energy, always ready to leap into action" temperament, trained into sustained, handler-directed engagement. It keeps the Malinois pressing an attack long after many dogs would disengage.

traits.name: Short-Coated Belgian Shepherd
traits.description: the short-haired fawn variety of the four Belgian Shepherds, with black overlay and a pronounced black mask, square in build with body length equal to withers height.

traits.name: Special Operations Dog
traits.description: used by the US Armed Forces, the US Secret Service, Israel's Oketz Unit, the Australian Defence Force and Kruger National Park's anti-poaching unit; the French police Malinois Diesel was posthumously awarded the PDSA Dickin Medal in 2015.

combat.weapons: The Malinois attacks with a running, leaping full-mouth grip. Two independent studies put numbers on it. Finnish police Malinois reached about 40 km/h within 25 m and hit with peak accelerations around 7 g and deceleration spikes over 11 g across the study dogs. IGP Malinois hit the sleeve at about 7.6 m/s carrying about 842 J of kinetic energy. The impact is the main weapon; the grip itself measured a median of only 247 N on the sleeve.
weaknesses: Low mass for close-range grappling with large animals.
Short coat, little padding and no armor.
Moderate measured grip force.
Far outmatched by bears, big cats and large ungulates.

bengal-tiger.name: Bengal Tiger
bengal-tiger.specimen: healthy prime adult male from a mainland population (central India, Terai), 200.0 kg, about 285.0 cm total nose-to-tail length and 100.0 cm shoulder height. This sits between the central-India male mean (190 kg) and the heavier Chitwan sample (235 kg) and deliberately avoids record animals.
bengal-tiger.summary: The Bengal tiger is the big cat of South Asia's forests, grasslands and mangroves, a roughly 200 kg ambush hunter that kills sambar, wild pig and even adult gaur alone. It wins with stealth, an explosive grapple, long claws and a crushing throat bite. It lacks armor and tires quickly in a prolonged fight.
narrative: The Bengal tiger is built for one decisive moment. A prime male of around 200 kg spends most of a hunt unseen, working through tall grass or forest shade until the prey is within a few bounds. Then the charge, the forelimb strike and the bite arrive almost together. Broad paws with hooked retractile claws anchor the cat to an animal that may outweigh it several times, and the long canines hold the throat or nape until the struggle ends. Field studies in southern India show that tigers take the largest prey available, above the leopards and dholes that share their forests.

That power comes with clear limits. The tiger is a sprinter, not a runner, and a failed ambush usually ends within a short distance. There is no armor under the striped coat, and the animals tigers hunt fight back with horns, tusks and weight. Gaur, wild boar and rival males all wound tigers, and a solitary cat carrying a serious injury has no pride or pack to cover for it. Heat on the plains also limits how long a tiger can keep working, which is why so much of its activity is at dawn, dusk and night.

Compared with its northern cousin in the roster, the Amur tiger, the Bengal tiger is at least as heavy in its mainland populations, carries a thinner coat, and is equally comfortable in water. In a matchup it is one of the most dangerous close-range predators on land: it should overwhelm most medium-sized animals and trouble large ones, while armor, overwhelming mass or a long open-ground fight turn the odds against it.

sections.habitat: Bengal tigers live across India, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh in tropical moist and dry deciduous forest, Terai grassland, hill forest and the Sundarbans mangroves. They need dense cover, water and a large base of hoofed prey.
sections.diet: Tigers are hypercarnivores. Principal prey are sambar, chital, wild pig and gaur, with smaller mammals, livestock and occasionally other predators taken. In Nagarahole, tigers selected larger prey than co-occurring leopards and dholes, which lets the three predators share the same forest.
sections.social: Solitary and territorial. A male's territory overlaps several females, and residents defend them against transient males. Adults meet mainly to mate or at shared kills.
sections.reproduction: Females give birth to litters usually of two to four cubs after roughly a three-and-a-half-month gestation. Cubs stay with their mother for about two years while learning to hunt. New resident males may kill cubs sired by previous males.
sections.conservation: The tiger (Panthera tigris) is assessed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022, criteria A2abcd). The 2021 global estimate was roughly 3,726–5,578 tigers, with about 3,140 mature individuals, and most live in India. Main threats are poaching, prey depletion, habitat loss and fragmentation, and conflict with people.
sections.features:
Retractile claws up to about 10 cm, kept sharp inside sheaths.
Long canines for a sustained throat or nape hold.
Broad forepaws and dewclaws for seizing large prey.
Striped coat that breaks up the outline in grass and forest shade.
Strong swimming and horizontal leaping ability.
sections.humanInteraction: Tigers are a flagship species for Indian wildlife protection and tourism. Conflict arises where tigers kill livestock or people, especially in the Sundarbans and in forest-edge villages; management focuses on protected-area design, compensation and relocation of problem animals.

funFacts: Chitwan National Park produced the heaviest free-ranging tigers ever recorded, including two males above 270 kg.
Sundarbans tigresses can weigh only about 75–80 kg, less than half of a large mainland male.
A tiger can leap roughly 5.5–6 m horizontally, according to the Smithsonian's National Zoo.
In Thailand, radio-tracked tigers killed gaur of which about 45% were adults.
Tigers readily swim and can cross wide rivers and tidal channels.
India's 2022 tiger estimate put the national population at about 3,167–3,682.

abilities.name: Tall-Grass Ambush
abilities.description: vertical striping that breaks up the outline in grass and dappled forest, padded silent feet and patient stalking let the tiger close to a few metres before a single explosive rush. In cover, the tiger usually lands the first strike.

abilities.name: Mangrove Swimmer
abilities.description: tigers swim strongly and hunt across rivers and tidal channels; Sundarbans tigers cross open water routinely. Water that stops many land predators is part of the Bengal tiger's hunting ground.

traits.name: Wild-Cattle Killer
traits.description: the South Asian tiger is the only land predator in its range that regularly kills adult gaur and sambar alone, taking the largest prey in its predator guild.

traits.name: Subcontinent Stronghold
traits.description: India holds most of the world's wild tigers, with the 2022 national estimate at roughly 3,167–3,682 animals.

combat.weapons: The Bengal tiger kills with an integrated system: a short explosive rush from cover, forelimb seizure with hooked retractile claws, and a sustained killing bite to the throat or nape. Broad forepaws and a dewclaw let the cat anchor itself to a struggling animal while the jaws find position. Karanth and Sunquist's Nagarahole studies show tigers taking the largest prey in the local guild (sambar, gaur and adult wild pig) while leopards and dholes take smaller prey, which is the clearest field evidence for its absolute killing power.
weaknesses: Burst physiology: poor sustained chase capacity.
No armor; horns, tusks and quills can cause disabling wounds.
Solitary: an injured tiger has no support.
Heavy reliance on a successful first strike.
