betta-fish.name: Betta Fish
betta-fish.specimen: healthy adult wild-type male, 6.0 cm total length and about 2 g (0.002 kg). FishBase gives a maximum of 6.5 cm TL and Wikipedia a usual 6–8 cm (often including long domestic fins); the mass is estimated from FishBase's body-shape length-weight relationship (W = 0.00977 × L^2.97, about 2.0 g at 6 cm) because no weighed wild sample was found.
betta-fish.summary: The betta, or Siamese fighting fish, is a 2-gram paddy fish that breathes air and fights with a ferocity bred into it for centuries. It flares, rams and bites rival males, but on the absolute scale it is among the smallest and weakest fighters on the roster.
narrative: In the shallow, sun-baked rice paddies and marshes of Thailand, the water can be warm, stagnant and nearly empty of oxygen. The wild betta, a small, dull green-brown fish, thrives there because it can breathe air through its labyrinth organ. Males stake out patches of dense plants, build floating bubble nests, and chase off any rival male that comes near.

Their contests are ritualized. Two males flare their gill covers, spread their fins and flush with colour before escalating into ramming and biting at fins and scales. In the wild, most fights end within minutes when one fish backs away. People in Thailand and Malaysia began collecting these fish centuries ago and breeding the winners of staged fights, producing domestic fighting strains that attack faster and keep going for an hour or more, as well as the flowing, jewel-coloured show bettas sold today.

For all its reputation, the betta is a 2-gram fish with a tiny mouth. Its ferocity is real and scores near the top of the roster, but its Attack and Defense sit near the floor. Its genuine edge is survival: in foul, oxygen-poor water, where rivals suffocate, the betta simply rises to the surface and takes a breath.

sections.habitat: Native to mainland Southeast Asia, centred on the central plain of Thailand from the Mae Khlong to Chao Phraya basins, the eastern Cardamom Mountains of Cambodia and the Isthmus of Kra, with records from Laos, Vietnam, Myanmar and Malaysia (Wikipedia); FishBase lists the Mekong basin. It lives in shallow, heavily vegetated standing waters: marshes, floodplains, canals, rice paddies and slow parts of rivers (FishBase; Wikipedia). Air temperatures there range from about 15 to 40 °C and water pH from 6.9 to 8.2 (Wikipedia).
sections.diet: Carnivorous surface and mid-water feeder on zooplankton, small crustaceans, mosquito and other insect larvae, and fallen insects (FishBase; Wikipedia). It helps control mosquito larvae in paddies. Introduced populations can threaten native fish, frogs and other wetland animals (Wikipedia).
sections.social: Solitary and territorial. Males space themselves among dense plants; females and fry use vegetation for protection (Wikipedia).
sections.reproduction: The male builds a bubble nest at the surface, often anchored to plants. After a courtship "dance", he wraps around the female, fertilizes eggs as she releases a few at a time, catches the sinking eggs in his mouth and places them in the nest, then drives the female away and guards the brood. Eggs hatch in 24–48 hours; fry depend on their gills until the labyrinth organ develops at three to six weeks (ADW; Wikipedia).
sections.conservation: Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (Wikipedia; assessment by Vidthayanon), threatened by agricultural and chemical runoff, pharmaceutical pollution and conversion of wetlands, including to oil-palm plantations. Captive bettas are extremely abundant, and ornamental strains have hybridized with wild populations of related species (Kwon et al. 2022).
sections.features:
Labyrinth organ for breathing atmospheric air.
Ritualized flaring display before contact.
Male-built bubble nests and paternal egg care.
Can survive the dry season in moist mud cavities, but not complete drying (ADW).
Enormous colour and fin variety in domestic strains, controlled by a few genes of large effect (Kwon et al. 2022).
sections.humanInteraction: Among the most popular and varied pet fish in the world and the national aquatic animal of Thailand, which remains the main breeder and exporter (Wikipedia). Fish fighting for wagers has a long history in Thailand and Malaysia, and FishBase discourages keeping males in very small containers.

funFacts: Genetic analysis suggests bettas were domesticated at least 1,000 years ago, among the earliest of any fish.
The Thai name pla kat means "biting fish".
Wild bettas rarely fight for more than 15 minutes, but a bred fighting fish was judged poor if it quit within an hour.
During a fight, the brain gene activity of two rival males synchronizes.
A betta breathes air: it gulps oxygen at the surface with its labyrinth organ.
The father builds a bubble nest and catches falling eggs in his mouth.
A mirror is enough to make a male betta flare and display.

abilities.name: Labyrinth Lung
abilities.description: an accessory labyrinth organ lets the betta gulp air at the surface, so it thrives in hot, shallow, oxygen-starved paddies; during fights it meets its extra oxygen demand by taking more air rather than working its gills harder.

abilities.name: Flare Display
abilities.description: males flare their gill covers, spread their fins and intensify colour before escalating to ramming and biting, letting rivals size each other up; in a matchup this can deter an evenly matched rival without contact.

traits.name: Bred to Fight
traits.description: domesticated in Thailand at least 1,000 years ago and bred for staged fights for centuries; fighter strains are more aggressive than wild fish in every measured behaviour.

traits.name: Bubble-Nest Father
traits.description: the male builds a floating nest of mucus-coated air bubbles, catches sinking eggs in his mouth, places them in the nest and guards the eggs and fry alone.

combat.weapons: The betta's only weapon is its small mouth. Male fights consist of display, then ramming and biting at the opponent's fins, flanks and scales; confined fish without an escape route can kill each other (Wikipedia). In the wild it feeds on zooplankton, small crustaceans, mosquito and other insect larvae, and insects that fall onto the water surface (FishBase; Wikipedia). Against anything larger than another small fish, the bite is meaningless.
weaknesses: About 2 g; negligible absolute power and durability.
Needs access to surface air; displaying males must interrupt displays to breathe.
Long domestic fins reduce agility.
Aggression drives it into costly fights with its own kind.

binturong.name: Binturong
binturong.specimen: healthy mature adult female of about 16.0 kg, head-body about 80 cm, with a tail of similar length. Females are the larger and dominant sex.
binturong.summary: The binturong, or bearcat, is a shaggy 16 kg tree-dweller of Asian rainforests that smells like popcorn and climbs with a grasping tail. It has sharp teeth and claws but eats mostly figs, moves slowly and avoids fights, so it relies on the canopy and its grip rather than speed or aggression.
narrative: The binturong looks like something assembled from spare parts: a cat-like face with stiff white whiskers, a bear-like body covered in long, shaggy black hair, and a thick tail as long as its body that can grip branches like a hand. A grown female weighs around 16 kg and is larger than the males and in charge of them.

Most of its life is spent slowly moving through the canopy of South and Southeast Asian forests, feeding on fruit, especially figs. It climbs along the tops of branches or hangs beneath them, turns its ankles around to climb down head-first, and wraps its tail around branches for security. It marks its path with scent, and its urine carries the same compound that makes popcorn smell the way it does.

In a fight the binturong is better armed than its gentle habits suggest, with long canines and sharp claws on a heavy body. But it is slow, rarely leaps and is not a practised predator, and on the ground it is vulnerable to tigers and dholes. It rates in the low range for Attack and Defense, with low Agility for a climber because of its slowness, and a solid Special score for its prehensile tail, rotating ankles and unusual scent chemistry.

sections.habitat: Tropical forest in South and Southeast Asia, including India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, China, Indonesia and the Philippines (Palawan). On Palawan it uses primary and secondary lowland forest and grassland–forest mosaic up to about 400 m. It is essentially arboreal and depends on forest canopy.
sections.diet: Mostly fruit, especially figs, plus leaves and shoots, eggs, birds, small mammals and occasional fish. It is an important seed disperser, especially of strangler figs, and its fast digestion is similar to that of highly fruit-eating monkeys. Because it moves seeds within the canopy, its loss may reduce fig recruitment.
sections.social: Solitary or in small family groups of a female and her young. Females are about 20% larger than males and dominant. Both sexes scent mark with glands and urine; males produce a richer set of scent compounds.
sections.reproduction: Mating can happen year-round because females can delay implantation of the fertilised egg until conditions are good. Females mature at about 30 months. Young may stay with the mother until they are ready to breed.
sections.conservation: Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and listed on CITES Appendix III. ADW reports that populations have declined by more than 30% over about 30 years. The main threat is forest degradation through logging and conversion to plantations; it is also hunted for meat and skins used as food and in traditional medicine, and juveniles are captured for the pet trade and for kopi luwak coffee production. In zoos, cancers such as renal carcinoma are a leading cause of death.
sections.features:
Prehensile tail with a leathery gripping tip.
Ankles that rotate about 180 degrees.
Popcorn-scented urine from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline.
Long, coarse black coat and white whiskers.
Delayed implantation in females.
sections.humanInteraction: Hunted and traded in parts of its range and sometimes kept as a pet. It is a popular zoo animal, in part because of its smell and prehensile tail, and zoo records show kidney and other cancers are common in older animals. It is not considered dangerous to people when left alone.

funFacts: It smells like hot buttered popcorn, thanks to the same chemical found in popcorn.
It is one of only two carnivores with a prehensile tail, and the only one outside the Americas.
Its ankles turn 180 degrees so it can climb down trees head-first.
Females are about 20% bigger than males and are the boss.
Young binturongs can hang by their tails alone.
Its gut moves fruit through in about six and a half hours.
It is a key gardener for strangler figs in the rainforest canopy.

abilities.name: Fifth-Limb Tail
abilities.description: the last third of its thick, muscular tail is prehensile, with a leathery tip for grip. It can anchor itself to a branch, freeing its paws, and it is one of only two carnivorans (with the kinkajou) that have such a tail.

abilities.name: Reverse-Ankle Descent
abilities.description: its ankles turn about 180 degrees, so the hind claws keep gripping when it climbs down a trunk head-first, letting it retreat or descend under control.

traits.name: Popcorn Musk
traits.description: its urine contains 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the compound that gives popcorn its smell. The compound was found in every animal tested, more in males, and its level rises with the hormone androstenedione.

traits.name: Strangler Fig Gardener
traits.description: figs are a major food, and radio-tracked binturongs in Borneo were by far the most effective canopy dispersers of hemi-epiphytic fig seeds, depositing droppings on the branch sites where the seeds can grow.

combat.weapons: The binturong has the teeth and claws of a carnivore, with a long, sharp canine in each jaw quadrant and long claws, but it lives mostly on fruit, especially figs. It also takes birds, small mammals, eggs and occasionally fish when it finds them. Nothing in its anatomy or behavior marks it as a specialist killer, so its weapons are mainly defensive in practice.
weaknesses: Slow, rarely leaps, and must often descend to the ground to move between trees.
Low stamina for intense activity.
Not a practised fighter or predator.
Vulnerable to tigers, dholes and other large predators on the ground.

black-caiman.name: Black Caiman
black-caiman.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 300.0 kg and 420.0 cm total length, representing a large fighting-age male rather than a record giant.
black-caiman.summary: The black caiman is the Amazon's largest predator and the biggest member of the alligator family. A 300 kg adult male combines an elite crocodilian bite, dense bony armor and a dark body built for night ambush at the water's edge, where it drags capybara-sized prey under to drown. It is formidable at the shoreline but tires quickly and is far less dangerous on open land.
narrative: After dark, a big black caiman is close to invisible. Its black scales merge with the tea-coloured water of Amazon lakes and flooded forest, and only the eyes and nostrils break the surface. Pressure-sensitive organs in its skin pick up ripples as fish move or a capybara wades in to drink. When the moment comes, the tail drives a short, violent lunge, the conical teeth close, and the fight moves into deep water where the caiman holds and rolls until the prey drowns.

This is a heavyweight crocodilian built on the same plan as the Nile crocodile and the American alligator. A mid-sized 103 kg animal was measured biting at 4,310 N, and a full-grown male is about three times heavier. Dense osteoderms cover its back, and its skull is massive. Yet the species also shows the limits of that plan. Like all crocodilians it is a burst animal, strong for seconds rather than minutes, and it has soft spots on the belly, eyes and joints. Jaguars on the Amazon floodplain kill caimans and dig up their eggs, a reminder that a powerful, agile cat can win at the water's edge.

In ABS terms the black caiman sits between the alligator and the Nile crocodile. It earns elite Attack and very strong Defense from its bite, mass and armor, while Agility and Stamina stay moderate. Its Intelligence is competent but narrow, and its Special reflects the night ambush and pressure-sensing skin shared with other crocodilians rather than a unique weapon. Near water at night it is one of the most dangerous animals in South America; on open ground it is far easier to avoid.

sections.habitat: Black caimans live in slow-moving rivers, lakes, flooded forest (várzea) and seasonally flooded savannas across the Amazon basin and neighbouring South American freshwater systems, with records from Brazil, Ecuador, Bolivia and Suriname among other countries. During the dry season they gather in lakes and deeper channels as floodplain water drains away.
sections.diet: Hatchlings and juveniles eat insects, crustaceans and other invertebrates, which are largely replaced by vertebrate prey as they grow. Adults eat mainly fish, plus water birds and mammals that come near the water, such as capybara. Carrion is taken. Species summaries repeat reports of black caimans eating anacondas and even jaguars, but these are anecdotal. The relationship with jaguars runs both ways: jaguars prey on caimans in the Mamirauá reserve and are among the main predators of black caiman eggs.
sections.social: Adults are mostly solitary hunters but tolerate one another where food and water concentrate in the dry season. Males defend space during breeding. Females guard nests, and hatchlings stay together in pods that may mix young from several nests, often with an adult female nearby.
sections.reproduction: Females build mound nests of leaf litter, twigs and decaying vegetation in the dry season, usually a few metres to tens of metres from water. Clutches average around 40 eggs. Females defend the nest aggressively, yet eggs are still taken by jaguars, tegu lizards, capuchin monkeys and people. Maturity is reported at around 8 years or about 2 m length.
sections.conservation: Current species summaries list the black caiman as Least Concern (IUCN 3.1). Older assessments placed it in higher-risk categories, including Endangered, after commercial hide hunting caused steep declines. The IUCN Crocodile Specialist Group now describes the species as widespread and locally abundant, with substantial recovery in several parts of its range. Caiman meat is still harvested in parts of the Amazon, and egg collection by people can affect nest success.
sections.features:
Black, lightly patterned body that is hard to see in dark water at night.
Dense dorsal osteoderms and a heavy skull.
Large eyes suited to night hunting.
Pressure-sensitive skin organs typical of crocodilians.
Powerful tail for swimming and lunging.
Conical gripping teeth that are replaced through life.
sections.humanInteraction: The species was hunted heavily for its hide and is still taken for meat. Study of commercial hunting in the Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve estimated an annual harvest of about 5,230 black caiman and found that hunters mostly take subadult and small adult males. Fatal attacks on people are documented but rare. In 2004 Amazonas State agencies ran an experimental, authorized caiman harvest in the Mamirauá reserve as a trial of regulated use.

funFacts: It is the largest member of the alligator family, larger than the American alligator.
A 3 m, 103 kg black caiman bit with a measured 4,310 N in crocodilian bite tests.
Hunters at Mamirauá were estimated to take about 5,230 black caiman a year, mostly subadult and small adult males.
Hatchlings from different nests can join into one pod guarded by an adult female.
Jaguars both hunt caimans and raid black caiman nests on the Amazon floodplain.
Its nest is a mound of leaves and twigs, often around half a metre to 80 cm tall.

abilities.name: Blackwater Night Ambush
abilities.description: hunts mainly after dark, lying low in dark Amazon water with its black body almost invisible, then lunges at fish, birds and mammals at the bank. In a battle this gives it first-strike advantage at night and at the water's edge.

abilities.name: Capybara Takedown
abilities.description: seizes large mammals such as capybara, drags them into deep water and holds or rolls until they drown. This turns any shoreline into a trap for land animals of up to several times human size.

traits.name: Amazon's Largest Predator
traits.description: the biggest predator in the Amazon basin and the largest member of the alligator family, with adults commonly 4–5 m long and males over 300 kg.

traits.name: Night-Black Armor
traits.description: dark scales and osteoderms described as denser than those of the spectacled caiman give it both concealment in dark water and strong dorsal protection.

combat.weapons: The jaws are the main weapon. A black caiman hunts mainly at night, lying low in the water near the bank, then lunges with a tail-driven burst, seizes with conical teeth and pulls the victim into deeper water. Fish make up much of the diet, but adults take water birds and mammals at the water's edge, including capybara. Secondary accounts report that adults over about 2 m attack capybara-sized mammals when the chance arises. The measured 4,310 N bite of a mid-sized 103 kg animal, scaled up in a 300 kg male, places this species in the elite crocodilian bite class.
weaknesses: Softer belly, eyes, throat and limb joints.
Short limbs and poor dry-land pursuit.
Offense depends on landing the first bite.
Limited sustained high-output effort.
Jaguars are documented predators of caimans in the Amazon floodplain, showing that a powerful cat can overcome caimans, at least smaller ones, at the water's edge.

black-footed-cat.name: Black-footed Cat
black-footed-cat.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 1.9 kg, matching the Animal Diversity Web male average of 1.93 kg and sitting inside Wikipedia's 1.6–2.45 kg male range.
black-footed-cat.summary: Africa's smallest wild cat, the black-footed cat weighs under 2 kg yet catches prey on roughly six of every ten attempts and hunts all night long. It is a superb killer of mice and small birds, but its tiny body gives it almost no absolute power or protection against larger animals.
narrative: The black-footed cat is a study in efficiency. A male weighing about 1.9 kg leaves its termite-mound den at dusk and spends the whole night on the move, trotting through Karoo grassland, pausing to watch rodent burrows and switching between fast searching, slow stalking and motionless waiting. Field studies in South Africa recorded a kill about every 50 minutes and up to 14 kills in a night, and its hunting success of around 60% is often cited as the best of any cat.

That reputation for deadliness has to be read on the absolute scale. The prey it kills so reliably averages about 24 grams. Its weapons are the same as a house cat's (claws, dewclaws and a neck bite), carried on a body less than half the size. Against a jackal, a caracal or an eagle-owl it is prey, and its survival depends on staying close to burrows and termite mounds where it can vanish instantly.

In a matchup the black-footed cat is therefore dangerous only to animals far smaller than itself. Its strengths are stamina, reflexes and a hunting routine that rarely wastes effort; its weaknesses are size, power and protection. It belongs well below the serval and caracal in every physical category, a little below the house cat in Attack, and above the house cat in sustained Stamina.

sections.habitat: Endemic to southern Africa: arid and semi-arid short grassland, Karoo scrub and savanna with sparse bush cover, mainly in South Africa, with records in southern Botswana and only a few in Namibia, southern Angola and southern Zimbabwe. Daytime refuges are hollow termite mounds and old burrows of springhares, aardvarks and Cape porcupines, which it digs to enlarge.
sections.diet: A specialist hunter of small vertebrates. Wikipedia lists 54 prey species, with small rodents such as the gerbil mouse among the most important, followed by mammals over 100 g and small birds; insects such as harvester termites make up only about 2% of prey mass. Average prey weighs about 24 g. It scavenges occasionally. It can meet its daily water needs from prey but drinks when water is available.
sections.social: Solitary. Males range over larger areas that overlap several females. Scent marking is used throughout its range; receptive females were seen spraying urine up to 41 times along 685 m, and it also rubs objects, rakes with its claws and leaves faeces in visible places. Its calls are louder than those of other cats its size, presumably to carry over long distances, and it uses quieter purrs and gurgles at close range and hisses and growls when threatened.
sections.reproduction: Kittens weigh 60–93 g at birth and are born blind in springhare burrows or hollow termite mounds. Captive males mature at about nine months and females at about seven months. Mothers bring back live prey for kittens to practice on from about three weeks of age (ADW).
sections.conservation: Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (latest assessment 2026) and on CITES Appendix I. The Black-footed Cat Working Group estimates fewer than 10,000 mature individuals in the wild. Threats include bait poisoning and steel-jaw traps set for other predators, overgrazing, declining springhare numbers, predation by jackals and caracals, disease and road traffic. The PNAS genome study found high inbreeding that may raise the risk of AA amyloidosis, which causes about 70% of deaths in captive animals.
sections.features:
Tiny, compact body with short legs and a round head.
Black soles and black bars on the legs; small dark spots on a sandy coat.
Very high metabolic rate that drives near-continuous night hunting.
Three hunting modes and bird-catching leaps of up to 1.4 m.
Heavy reliance on termite mounds and burrows for shelter.
sections.humanInteraction: It kills rodents that damage crops and stores, and is harmless to people. It suffers from indiscriminate poison and trap campaigns aimed at jackals and caracals. It is kept in a small number of zoos, where amyloidosis is a major health problem.

funFacts: It is Africa's smallest wild cat; a big male weighs under 2.5 kg.
About 60% of its hunts succeed, one of the highest success rates recorded for any cat.
It can kill up to 14 small animals in one night.
It eats roughly a sixth of its own body weight in prey every night.
It can leap about 1.4 m straight up and snatch birds out of the air.
A San legend says it can kill a giraffe by biting its jugular; this is folklore, not fact.
It spends the day inside hollow termite mounds or old springhare burrows, and captive mothers move their kittens to a new hiding place every six to ten days.

abilities.name: Sixty-Percent Strike
abilities.description: field observation shows roughly six successful catches from every ten attempts, a kill about every 50 minutes and up to 14 kills in a night. In a matchup against small prey this reliability is its real weapon; against larger opponents it adds nothing to raw damage.

abilities.name: Termite-Mound Bolt
abilities.description: it rests in hollow termite mounds and old burrows and dives into cover at the slightest disturbance, which makes it very hard for larger predators to corner in its own habitat.

traits.name: Africa's Smallest Wild Cat
traits.description: adult males weigh only 1.6–2.45 kg and stand under 25 cm at the shoulder, making it the smallest wild cat on the African continent.

traits.name: Night-Long Hunter
traits.description: it eats about a sixth of its body weight in prey each night and hunts through the whole night in temperatures from −10 to 35 °C.

combat.weapons: The black-footed cat is a miniature but extremely efficient killer. It stalks, rushes and pins prey from behind with its forepaws and dewclaws, then kills with a bite to the neck or head. Its prey averages only about 24 g, but it also takes Cape hares heavier than itself and was once seen pouncing on a resting lamb before giving up when the lamb stood. The PNAS genome paper cites a hunting success of about 60%, and a 622-hour field watch recorded a kill roughly every 50 minutes and up to 14 small animals in one night. All of this is lethal to mice, gerbils, shrews and larks; at 1.9 kg it is almost meaningless against a medium-sized opponent in absolute terms.
weaknesses: Tiny absolute mass and power.
No armor; one bite from a jackal or caracal can be fatal.
Short stocky legs; not a climber.
Very high energy demand; it must keep hunting.
Kittens and subadults are taken by black-backed jackals, caracals and owls.

black-necked-spitting-cobra.name: Black-necked Spitting Cobra
black-necked-spitting-cobra.specimen: healthy adult, 1.5 kg (estimate) and 150 cm total length, sex unspecified. No reliable size difference between the sexes was verified in this pass.
black-necked-spitting-cobra.summary: The black-necked spitting cobra is an African cobra that defends itself by spraying venom at an attacker's eyes, tracking its target and aiming at the face. Its bite delivers a large dose of tissue-destroying venom. At about 1.5 m it is light and unarmored, but its blinding spit makes it one of the hardest snakes to attack.
narrative: The black-necked spitting cobra fights at a distance. When threatened it rears up, spreads its hood and sprays venom from its fangs toward the attacker's face. The stream leaves in about 50 milliseconds, and laboratory studies show that spitting cobras follow a moving target and anticipate where it will go, rapidly swinging the head to spread venom over the face. The snake matches its spray to the size of the target and aims at the center of the nearest body part, which is usually the face, so at least one eye is usually hit.

Venom in the eyes causes intense burning pain and can cause permanent blindness if it is not washed out. The bite adds another layer: 200–350 mg of venom dominated by cytotoxins that destroy skin and muscle, with enzymes that make the pain worse. It kills far less often than many cobras, with untreated mortality around 5–10%, but it can leave lasting tissue damage.

For battle ratings, the spit gives this cobra a genuinely unique ranged defense and the roster's first ranged venom attack, earning a very high Special. Its body is still that of a 1.5 kg snake, with no armor and little strength, and a bird of prey striking from above or an opponent with protected eyes can overcome it.

sections.habitat: The black-necked spitting cobra is widespread across sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal and Mauritania east to Ethiopia and Somalia and south to Angola, Zambia and Tanzania, entering southern Africa only in northern Namibia. It is absent from the Congo Basin rainforest. It prefers savanna and semi-desert but also lives in moist savanna, cleared former forest, coastal scrub and dry grassland up to 1,800 m, often near water. It shelters in termite mounds, rodent holes and especially hollow tree trunks.
sections.diet: It eats mainly small rodents, plus birds, fish, lizards, eggs and other snakes. Snake eagles, including the short-toed snake eagle, and other snakes prey on it.
sections.social: Solitary.
sections.reproduction: Egg-laying. Mating runs from about September to December. Females lay about 10–15 eggs (range 8–22), which hatch after 60–70 days at 28–30 °C. Hatchlings are 20–25 cm long and independent.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (as reported by Wikipedia). It is common and widespread, and in southern Nigeria it has done well where rainforest has been replaced by farmland and plantations.
sections.features:
Fangs that can spray venom as well as inject it.
Target-tracking and face-aiming spit.
Cytotoxic venom with pain-enhancing PLA2s.
Hood display with a black neck band in many populations.
Good climbing and flexible day or night activity.
sections.humanInteraction: Because it is common around villages and towns, it often meets people. Bites cause pain, swelling, blistering and tissue death; untreated mortality is about 5–10% and under 1% in some endemic regions. Venom spat into the eyes causes painful venom ophthalmia that can lead to corneal damage and blindness without prompt washing. In 1944 the ophthalmic surgeon Harold Ridley described a Ghanaian labourer spat on from about four or five feet away; the eye recovered in about a week. It is one of the main causes of snakebite in Nigeria, alongside the carpet viper and puff adder.

funFacts: It can spray venom at an attacker's eyes from more than a metre away.
A spit stream is released in about 50 thousandths of a second.
It tracks where an attacker's face is about to move and aims there.
It spits most at round or oval shapes, like faces.
Its venom has extra enzymes that make its cytotoxins more painful.
Eye-surgery pioneer Harold Ridley wrote about a spitting-cobra eye injury in 1944.
Some individuals are black with a red belly, others coppery brown without a neck band.

abilities.name: Aimed Venom Spray
abilities.description: it sprays venom from its fangs toward an attacker's face, releasing the stream in about 50 ms, tracking and anticipating the target's movement, and matching the spray to the target's size. Venom in the eyes causes intense pain and can cause permanent blindness.

abilities.name: Flesh-Melting Bite
abilities.description: its bite delivers 200–350 mg of venom dominated by cytotoxins that destroy skin and muscle, with phospholipase A2s that boost pain and some neurotoxic effect.

traits.name: Face-Finding Aim
traits.description: tests with artificial targets show it spits most at oval or round shapes and aims at the center of the nearest body part, usually the face, so at least one eye is usually hit.

traits.name: Day-or-Night Cobra
traits.description: it shifts between daytime and night-time activity with season, location and temperature, and in Nigeria has spread from rainforest edges into farmland and drier areas.

combat.weapons: Its first weapon is a ranged one: it can spray venom from its fangs at an attacker's face, causing blinding pain. Its second is the bite, which delivers a large dose of cytotoxic venom that destroys tissue, with some neurotoxic effect.
weaknesses: No armor and a light body.
Bite lethality is low compared with many cobras; the venom mostly destroys tissue.
Spitting deters but does not kill; a determined or protected attacker can close in.
Preyed on by snake eagles and other snakes.

blue-ringed-octopus.name: Blue-Ringed Octopus
blue-ringed-octopus.specimen: healthy adult, sex not specified, 0.05 kg (50 g), about 12.0 cm total length with arms extended and a mantle of about 4–5 cm.
blue-ringed-octopus.summary: The greater blue-ringed octopus is a 50 g reef octopus whose bite carries tetrodotoxin, a nerve toxin with no antidote that can paralyze a human's breathing. It flashes glowing blue rings as a warning, but its tiny, soft body means it wins only if it gets a bite in first.
narrative: The greater blue-ringed octopus is small enough to sit in the palm of a hand, weighing about as much as a hen's egg. Most of the time it looks drab, hiding in rock pools, rubble and empty shells on shallow Indo-Pacific reefs. When it is disturbed, it changes: about 60 rings across its body flash electric blue, switched on and off in about a third of a second by muscles that pull the skin away from mirror-like reflector cells.

That warning is honest. Its saliva carries tetrodotoxin, a nerve poison produced with the help of bacteria in its salivary glands. In Japanese specimens, the salivary glands were strongly toxic, and lower levels were found in the arms, organs and even the eggs. The octopus uses its bite to paralyze crabs and shrimp, and a human bite can shut down the breathing muscles. There is no antidote, but people who get rescue breathing quickly usually survive, and recorded deaths are very few.

In a battle, the blue-ringed octopus is a pure specialist. It has almost no strength, no armor and little stamina, and it must touch an opponent to bite. Anything that crushes it first, or never comes close, is safe. But any animal that grabs it risks a paralyzing bite, which is why its Special rating sits near the top of the roster while its physical ratings sit near the bottom.

sections.habitat: Shallow coral reefs, rubble, seagrass and tide pools of the tropical Indo-West Pacific, from northern Australia north to Japan and across Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, the Philippines and Indonesia, west to Sri Lanka, usually at 0–20 m. It is often seen in rock pools after storms, digging for crabs.
sections.diet: Carnivorous: small crabs, hermit crabs, shrimp, small mollusks and fish. It hunts mainly by day, pouncing on or luring prey and paralyzing it with a venomous bite.
sections.social: Solitary. Individuals come together only to mate.
sections.reproduction: Short-lived and semelparous: females lay a single clutch, carry and brood the eggs under their arms, usually stop feeding while brooding and die soon after the young hatch. Mothers pass tetrodotoxin into their eggs, and hatchlings appear to add their own toxin as they grow. Typical lifespan is about 2 years.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern in widely used summaries (IUCN 3.1), and it is not considered threatened. Some sources state that no Hapalochlaena species has been formally assessed on the IUCN Red List, so this status is recorded with low confidence. Its small size and hiding habits make surveys difficult.
sections.features:
Tetrodotoxin-laden saliva produced with the help of symbiotic bacteria.
About 60 iridescent blue rings exposed by muscle action in about a third of a second.
Stacked reflector cells with no pigment cells above the rings.
Toxic arms, organs and eggs.
Soft, flexible body able to squeeze into tiny shelters.
sections.humanInteraction: Dangerous only when handled: most bites happen when people pick one up from a rock pool or step on it. First aid is supportive, with rescue breathing and mechanical ventilation until the toxin wears off, and people who receive fast breathing support usually survive. Divers and tide-poolers are advised never to touch it.

funFacts: It can flash its blue rings on and off in about a third of a second.
Its rings shine from stacked reflector cells, not pigment.
Its venom is tetrodotoxin, the same toxin found in pufferfish, made with the help of bacteria.
Its bite can be painless, so victims may not notice it at first.
Its hatchlings are already toxic, carrying about 150 nanograms of tetrodotoxin each.
It often hides in empty shells and discarded bottles.
A whole adult weighs only about as much as a hen's egg.

abilities.name: Tetrodotoxin Bite
abilities.description: a small beak injects saliva carrying bacterial tetrodotoxin that blocks nerve signals and can paralyze the breathing muscles of a human; there is no antidote.

abilities.name: Blue Ring Flash
abilities.description: muscles under direct nerve control expose about 60 iridescent blue rings in about a third of a second, a fast warning display unlike other cephalopod color changes.

traits.name: Toxic From Birth
traits.description: tetrodotoxin runs through its arms, organs and eggs, and newly hatched young already carry about 150 nanograms each.

traits.name: Bottle-Hiding Reef Dweller
traits.description: shelters in crevices, empty shells and even discarded bottles and cans on shallow reefs and tide pools.

combat.weapons: The blue-ringed octopus kills with a venomous bite. It grabs prey with its arms, draws it to its beak and bites, injecting saliva laden with tetrodotoxin. TTX blocks the sodium channels that nerves and muscles need to fire, so the victim is paralyzed. A human bite is often painless and may go unnoticed until numbness and weakness begin; paralysis can start within minutes or take an hour or more, and death, when it happens, comes from paralysis of the breathing muscles. There is no antidote.
weaknesses: Tiny, soft body.
Must make direct bite contact to use its venom.
Low stamina and speed.
Completely tied to water.

bombardier-beetle.name: Bombardier Beetle
bombardier-beetle.specimen: healthy adult, 8 mm long, sex unspecified. No consistent size difference between the sexes was documented in the sources located.
bombardier-beetle.summary: The bombardier beetle is an 8 mm ground beetle that defends itself with a chemical explosion. When grabbed, it mixes stored chemicals with enzymes in a reaction chamber and fires a pulsed spray at about 100 °C, aimed precisely at the attacker. It is a superb small-scale defender but has almost no power to hurt large animals.
narrative: The bombardier beetle looks like an ordinary little ground beetle, red at the front and dark behind, hiding under stones on chalk grassland. Its secret is in its abdomen. Two glands store hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide. When something seizes the beetle, the mix flows into a reaction chamber lined with catalase and peroxidase, and the reaction releases oxygen, irritating benzoquinones and enough heat to bring the spray to about 100 °C.

The spray does not come out as one blast. It is a rapid series of small explosions, hundreds per second, controlled by a flexible membrane and a valve inside the chamber, as X-ray filming of living beetles has shown. The beetle can swivel its abdomen tip to hit the exact spot where it is being attacked, even over its own back. Experiments with a related bombardier beetle showed the weapon working from inside a predator: toads that swallowed the beetles often vomited them up again, and the beetles walked away.

On the absolute battle scale, the bombardier beetle is a tiny specialist. Its spray earns it one of the higher Special scores among insects and a Defense score above armoured beetles of much greater mass, but its Attack and Size sit near the floor. It wins by making itself too unpleasant to eat, not by harming large opponents, and anything big enough to crush it without hesitating wins easily.

sections.habitat: In Britain, Brachinus crepitans lives under stones and leaf rosettes in short, dry grassland, usually on chalk or limestone, including chalk quarries and arable field margins. It is mainly southern, with most modern records from coastal areas of southern England and South Wales, plus inland sites on the Cotswold and Northamptonshire limestones and Huntingdonshire boulder clays. It is also widespread in continental Europe.
sections.diet: Larvae are specialised ectoparasitoids of Amara ground-beetle pupae; adult activity peaks in June, matching the activity of their hosts. The adult diet was not resolved in the sources found in this pass. Adults are preyed on by many small predators but are well protected by their spray.
sections.social: Solitary during the active season; adults overwinter in groups under stones, often with other ground beetles.
sections.reproduction: Females lay eggs in the soil, each in a small mud cell. The first-stage larva searches for a host pupa, bites it and feeds on its fluid; the second stage continues this; the third stage fastens the pupa to its back and eats it completely within about two days. Laboratory development from hatching to adult took about 20 days, with speed depending on temperature.
sections.conservation: Not Evaluated: no IUCN Red List assessment was located in this pass. In Britain the species is listed as Nationally Scarce (B), with a much reduced inland distribution compared with older records.
sections.features:
Paired pygidial glands with a storage reservoir and a reaction chamber.
Catalase and peroxidase enzymes that trigger an explosive reaction.
Spray at about 100 °C, delivered as a pulsed jet.
Turnable abdomen tip for aimed spraying.
Red head and thorax with dark greenish or bluish-black wing cases.
sections.humanInteraction: Harmless to people apart from a brief sting, burn-like irritation or brown staining if handled. Its pulsed spray has attracted engineering interest as a model for efficient jets and sprays. In Britain it is a species of conservation interest on chalk and limestone grassland.

funFacts: Its spray reaches about 100 °C, close to the boiling point of water.
Each discharge is a string of tiny explosions, hundreds per second.
Scientists watched the explosions happen inside living beetles using synchrotron X-rays filmed at 2,000 frames per second.
It can aim the spray in many directions, even forward over its own back.
Toads that swallow bombardier beetles sometimes vomit them back up, alive.
Its larvae are parasitoids that eat the pupae of other ground beetles.
Its species name crepitans means "crackling", after the popping sound of the spray.

abilities.name: Boiling Pulse-Jet Spray
abilities.description: hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide are mixed with catalase and peroxidase in a reaction chamber, producing irritating benzoquinones at about 100 °C that are fired in a rapid train of small explosions, hundreds per second.

abilities.name: Swivel-Tip Aiming
abilities.description: the abdomen tip can be turned so the spray hits the exact spot being attacked, in many directions and even forward over the beetle's back.

traits.name: Stomach Escape Artist
traits.description: in experiments with a related bombardier beetle, 43% of toads that swallowed one vomited it back up, and every vomited beetle was still alive and active.

traits.name: Parasitoid Childhood
traits.description: its larvae hunt down the pupae of Amara ground beetles in the soil, feed on them and finish growing in about 20 days.

combat.weapons: The primary weapon is the hot, pulsed benzoquinone spray fired from the tip of the abdomen. In photographic studies of bombardier beetles, Eisner and Aneshansley showed that the abdomen tip can be turned to aim the spray at a stimulus in many directions, including forward over the beetle's own back. The mandibles are a minor secondary tool.
weaknesses: Tiny body with negligible absolute strength.
Spray is limited in range and supply.
A large animal can crush it without ever being sprayed effectively.
No active offensive weapon against anything bigger than small invertebrates.

bonobo.name: Bonobo
bonobo.specimen: healthy mature wild adult male of about 42.0 kg, head-body about 80 cm, able to stand about 115 cm tall.
bonobo.summary: The bonobo is a slim, long-legged great ape of the Congo rainforest, nearly as clever as the chimpanzee but built lighter and armed with smaller canines. It relies on climbing skill, grasping hands and powerful female coalitions rather than brute force, and its fights are frequent but seldom deadly.
narrative: Bonobos look like slender chimpanzees with long legs, a small head and a dark face framed by hair parted down the middle. They live only south of the Congo River, in swampy and lowland rainforest, and spend their days feeding on fruit in trees and moving between patches on the ground, often walking upright to carry food.

Their social life is what makes them famous. Females band together and use coalitions to keep males in check, so in many communities females hold the top ranks. Tension is often defused with social and sexual contact, and across decades of study only one bonobo killing was even suspected. Recent work has added nuance: male bonobos squabble more often than male chimpanzees, and in 2026 researchers documented an infant dying after an intergroup attack. The bonobo is peaceful by chimpanzee standards, not harmless.

In ABS terms the bonobo sits just below the chimpanzee on physical ratings, because it is lighter, more gracile and has smaller canines, and just below it on Intelligence and Special because wild bonobos use fewer tools. Its cognitive capacity is still elite: Kanzi's symbol use and stone-flake making show what a bonobo mind can do. In a matchup, its best assets are climbing, dexterity and allies, not raw damage.

sections.habitat: Lowland rainforest and swamp forest south of the Congo River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with some forest-savanna mosaic at the range edge. The river separates bonobos from chimpanzees.
sections.diet: Mainly ripe fruit, plus leaves, stems, seeds, flowers, mushrooms, invertebrates and occasional meat. Hunting of duikers and small primates is more frequent at some newer study sites than once believed, and meat is often shared.
sections.social: Fission-fusion communities of several dozen animals that split into smaller parties during the day. Females move to a new community at maturity and build alliances there. Female coalitions give females high social rank relative to males.
sections.reproduction: Females usually give birth to a single infant, and infants depend on their mothers for years. Long intervals between births mean populations recover slowly from losses.
sections.conservation: Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Population estimates range roughly from 5,000 to 17,000 animals but are very uncertain because conflict has limited survey work. Main threats are hunting for bushmeat, habitat loss and civil unrest.
sections.features:
Slim build with long legs suited to upright walking.
Grasping hands and feet.
Small canines and wide face compared with the chimpanzee.
Rich vocal and gestural communication.
Female-dominated coalition social system.
sections.humanInteraction: Bonobos are threatened by hunting and habitat loss in the Congo Basin. Sanctuaries such as Lola ya Bonobo care for orphans from the bushmeat trade. Research with captive bonobos, including Kanzi, has been central to studies of ape language and tool making.

funFacts: Bonobos live only south of the Congo River; the river keeps them apart from chimpanzees.
In a comparison of killings across the genus Pan, chimpanzees accounted for 152 while bonobos had just one suspected case.
Male bonobos were found to be about three times more physically aggressive than male chimpanzees, though fights were rarely serious.
Female bonobos outranked about 70% of males in their communities in one study.
Kanzi the bonobo learned hundreds of lexigram symbols and made stone tools.
Bonobos have been seen sharing meat with members of a different community.

abilities.name: Sisterhood Coalition
abilities.description: females team up against males in the large majority of their coalitions, allowing them to outrank most males in some communities; in a fight this means an attacker can face several allies at once.

abilities.name: Stone-Flake Craft
abilities.description: captive bonobos Kanzi and Panbanisha struck flint cores to make sharp flakes and used them for specific tasks such as cutting and digging, showing a capacity for making and using tools.

traits.name: Peacemaking Ape
traits.description: conflict is common but usually low in severity, and tension is often defused through social and sexual contact; across decades of study only a single suspected killing was recorded.

traits.name: Upright Long-Legged Build
traits.description: a slim upper body, narrow shoulders and long legs make the bonobo more at ease walking upright than the chimpanzee.

combat.weapons: A bonobo fights with its hands, arms and teeth: it grabs, pulls, hits and bites. Its canines are smaller than a chimpanzee's and it is more lightly built, so its damage output is lower. Male bonobos are nonetheless physically aggressive: a 2024 study found male bonobos engaged in about 2.8 times as many aggressive encounters and about three times as many physical attacks as male chimpanzees, although these fights were rarely severe. Bonobos also hunt: at LuiKotale and other sites they catch forest antelope (duikers) and occasionally monkeys.
weaknesses: Light build and small canines for an ape.
No armor and low body fat.
Tends to de-escalate rather than press a lethal fight.
Much less powerful than gorillas or large predators.

boomslang.name: Boomslang
boomslang.specimen: healthy adult, 0.3 kg and 140 cm total length, sex unspecified. The sexes differ in color (most males green, females brown) but no reliable size difference was verified, so no sex-based modifier is applied.
boomslang.summary: The boomslang is a slender, sharp-eyed African tree snake whose small doses of rear-fang venom cause deadly bleeding hours after a bite. It is fast and precise in the branches but timid and fragile, weighing only about 300 g, so in a fight its venom is too slow to protect it.
narrative: The boomslang looks like a harmless green tree snake, and for a long time experts treated it like one. Its fangs sit at the back of its mouth, and it produces only a few milligrams of venom. Then, in 1957, the herpetologist Karl Schmidt was bitten by a juvenile and died about a day later, after writing down his symptoms almost to the end. The venom, rich in enzymes that switch on the body's own clotting factors, causes widespread tiny clots and then uncontrolled bleeding, but only after hours of little warning.

In life the boomslang is a hunter of chameleons, tree lizards and nestling birds. It stalks slowly through branches using its exceptionally large eyes, swaying its head to judge distance, then bites and holds so its rear fangs can work. Its jaws open to about 170°. When threatened by something too large to eat, it usually slips away through the canopy; if cornered, it inflates its neck and takes an S-shaped strike pose.

For battle ratings, the boomslang's venom is dangerous but works on the wrong timescale for a fight: an opponent could keep fighting for hours before bleeding begins. Its body is tiny and fragile, and it is very reluctant to bite. Its genuine strengths are tree agility, vision and a venom system unlike that of any front-fanged snake.

sections.habitat: The boomslang lives across sub-Saharan Africa, from Senegal and The Gambia through West, Central and East Africa to southern Africa, with dense populations in Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe. It uses karoo scrub, savanna, lowland forest and grassland, living mainly in shrubs and trees and avoiding very dry desert.
sections.diet: Chameleons and other tree lizards are its main prey, along with frogs, nestling birds and eggs, small mammals and other snakes, including boomslangs. It hunts by day, stalking through branches.
sections.social: Solitary; conspecifics may be eaten.
sections.reproduction: Egg-laying. Mating is recorded in December and January; females lay about 8–14 leathery eggs (up to 27) in a hollow tree trunk or rotting log. Incubation averages about three months. Hatchlings are 29–38 cm and become dangerously venomous at around 45 cm.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (as reported by Wikipedia). It is widespread across much of sub-Saharan Africa.
sections.features:
Three large grooved rear fangs on each side of the upper jaw.
170° gape.
Exceptionally large eyes and excellent vision.
Slender, fast, highly arboreal body.
Strong color difference between males and females.
sections.humanInteraction: Bites are rare and almost always happen when people handle or try to kill the snake. Karl Patterson Schmidt, a leading American herpetologist, died in 1957 after a bite from a juvenile boomslang he doubted could deliver a fatal dose, and kept notes on his symptoms nearly to the end. D. S. Chapman recorded eight serious boomslang envenomings between 1919 and 1962, two fatal. Many hospitals do not stock the monovalent antivenom because bites are so rare. Dogs are also bitten occasionally.

funFacts: Its name means "tree snake" in Afrikaans and Dutch.
It can open its mouth to about 170°.
Juveniles have a huge emerald-green eye compared with their head.
Karl Schmidt kept a diary of his symptoms after being bitten, almost until he died the next day.
Its venom was once so underrated that many experts thought rear-fanged snakes could not kill people.
It sometimes spends cool spells curled up inside a weaver bird's nest.
Most males are green and females brown, so a pair can look like two different species.

abilities.name: Silent Clot Venom
abilities.description: metalloproteinases in its venom activate prothrombin and factor X, causing widespread tiny clots and then uncontrolled bleeding. Symptoms can take many hours to appear, which misled the herpetologist Karl Schmidt into thinking his 1957 bite was harmless; he died about a day later.

abilities.name: 170-Degree Rear-Fang Bite
abilities.description: it can open its jaws to about 170°, bringing three large grooved fangs on each side into contact, then holds on to work the venom in.

traits.name: Emerald-Eyed Sharpshooter
traits.description: its eyes are exceptionally large, and it sways its head from side to side to judge distance, giving it some of the best vision of any snake.

traits.name: Two-Tone Tree Snake
traits.description: most males are bright green and females brown, and it changes from a grey juvenile with a huge green eye into adult colors at around 1 m long.

combat.weapons: The primary weapon is a bite with three large grooved fangs on each side at the back of the upper jaw, delivering a small amount of an extremely potent clotting venom. The very wide 170° gape lets it bring these rear fangs into play. The secondary assets are sharp vision and speed in the branches, which it uses both to catch prey and to escape.
weaknesses: Very light, fragile body.
Rear fangs need a firm, held bite.
Tiny venom doses and slow onset.
Much weaker on open ground than in trees.

bowhead-whale.name: Bowhead Whale
bowhead-whale.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 16.0 m long and 75,000 kg.
bowhead-whale.summary: The bowhead whale is a 75-tonne Arctic giant that smashes through sea ice with its massive skull, wears the thickest blubber of any whale and can live over 200 years. It is slow and toothless, so it wins by being almost impossible to hurt and by retreating under the ice, not by chasing or striking.
narrative: The bowhead is built like an icebreaker. A third of its 16-metre body is head, arched into the bow shape that names it, and it uses that skull to punch up through sea ice to breathe. Wrapped around the body is a layer of blubber around 45 cm thick, the thickest of any whale, which keeps it warm in near-freezing water and puts a huge depth of fat between any attacker and its vital organs.

Bowheads are slow, cruising at walking pace and managing only about 10 km/h when fleeing, so they cannot outrun killer whales. Instead they belong to the "fight" group of baleen whales and, above all, they use the ice. A bowhead can slip beneath a floe where orcas are reluctant to follow and break through to breathe. Only a small share of Western Arctic bowheads carry killer whale scars, fewer than in other whales studied, though that share is rising as the open-water season lengthens.

Their long life is remarkable. Eye-lens aging put several males past 100 years, traditional harpoon heads have been recovered from recently harvested whales, and bowhead cells repair DNA damage unusually well. Males sing an ever-changing library of songs, with 184 types recorded in one population over three years. In battle terms the bowhead is a near-ceiling defender with very low agility and an attack limited by slowness and the lack of any real weapon beyond its colossal mass and skull.

sections.habitat: Bowheads live almost exclusively in Arctic and subarctic waters with seasonal sea ice, mainly between 60° and 75° north (NOAA). They follow the ice edge as it advances and retreats (ADW), and are the only baleen whale that spends its whole life in these waters.
sections.diet: Bowheads filter small crustaceans such as copepods and krill, plus other invertebrates and small fish, straining huge volumes of water through the longest baleen of any whale; each needs about 100 metric tons of prey a year (NOAA). Tagged whales off West Greenland swam slowly at depth with the mouth open, filtering continuously (Simon et al. 2009).
sections.social: Bowheads usually travel alone or in small groups of up to six (Wikipedia) and sometimes feed side by side in echelons (ADW). Males sing long, complex and changing songs during the breeding season (Stafford et al. 2018).
sections.reproduction: Bowheads reach sexual maturity at about 25 years, at 35 to 45 feet long (NOAA; George et al. 1999). Females have one calf every 3 to 4 years after a gestation of about 13 to 14 months; calves are about 13 feet long and 2,000 pounds and can swim at birth (NOAA).
sections.conservation: Globally the bowhead is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2018 assessment, as summarized by Wikipedia), though some stocks are listed as endangered. All bowheads are listed as endangered under the US Endangered Species Act (NOAA). Commercial whaling reduced the world population to under 3,000 by 1921; the Western Arctic stock has recovered to about 15,229 (NOAA). Threats now include loss of sea ice, rising killer whale predation, vessel strikes, entanglement, noise and oil and gas development (NOAA).
sections.features:
Bow-shaped skull about a third of the body length, used to break sea ice.
Blubber 43–48 cm thick, the thickest of any whale.
Largest mouth of any animal and the longest baleen.
No dorsal fin, unlike most whales (NOAA).
Exceptionally long life with enhanced DNA repair.
sections.humanInteraction: Bowheads were a prime target of commercial whalers because they are slow and float when killed (NOAA). Alaska Native communities continue a regulated subsistence hunt, and harvested whales have yielded traditional harpoon points that help show how long bowheads live (George et al. 1999).

funFacts: Bowheads may live more than 200 years, longer than any other mammal known.
A bowhead can break through sea ice about 20 cm thick with its head.
Its blubber can be about 48 cm thick, the thickest of any whale.
Spitsbergen bowheads sang 184 different song types in just three years.
A feeding bowhead can filter roughly 2,000 tonnes of water in a single dive.
Unlike most whales, bowheads have no dorsal fin.

abilities.name: Icebreaker Skull
abilities.description: a bow-shaped skull about a third of the body length lets the bowhead smash up through sea ice 20 cm thick, with reports of 60 cm. In a battle it can retreat under the ice where most attackers cannot follow and still breathe.

abilities.name: Arctic Blubber Armor
abilities.description: a blubber layer 43–48 cm thick, the thickest of any whale, insulates the body and gives a great depth of tissue before any attacker reaches vital organs.

traits.name: Two-Century Whale
traits.description: bowheads can live over 200 years; old harpoon points found in harvested whales and eye-lens aging both support lifespans beyond a century, and their cells repair DNA damage unusually well.

traits.name: Largest Mouth on Earth
traits.description: the bowhead has the largest mouth of any animal and the longest baleen plates of any whale, up to about 4.5 m, filtering around 2,000 tonnes of water in a single dive.

combat.weapons: The bowhead has no teeth. Its tools are sheer mass, broad flukes and a massive, arched skull that takes up a third of its body and can smash through sea ice 20 cm thick or more (NOAA). Ford & Reeves (2008) list the bowhead among five "fight" species that defend themselves physically against killer whales rather than fleeing. A 75-tonne whale that can ram through ice has real blunt-impact potential, but it delivers it slowly: this is one of the slowest large whales.
weaknesses: Very slow; cannot flee from fast predators in open water.
No teeth or cutting weapon.
Small flippers and a heavy body make tight turns difficult.
Calves and young whales are more exposed to killer whales.
Loss of sea ice removes its main refuge (NOAA notes rising orca scarring as open-water seasons lengthen).

brazilian-wandering-spider.name: Brazilian Wandering Spider
brazilian-wandering-spider.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 3.5 cm body length (prosoma plus opisthosoma), roughly 13–15 cm leg span, estimated about 4 g live mass.
brazilian-wandering-spider.summary: A fast, webless night hunter from Brazil's forests, the Brazilian wandering spider backs its dramatic rearing threat display with one of the most medically significant spider venoms. The venom is a multi-toxin nerve cocktail, but a 4 g body, a small per-bite dose and a soft exoskeleton keep its absolute Attack and Defense low on the full roster.
narrative: The Brazilian wandering spider earns its reputation from chemistry, not size. An adult female has a body about the length of a thumb joint and legs spanning a hand's width, and she weighs only a few grams. Her advantage is a venom that combines several nerve-targeting toxins: one fraction blocks calcium channels and neurotransmitter release, and others act on sodium channels and nitric-oxide signalling, producing intense pain and, in rare severe cases, cardiovascular collapse and pulmonary oedema.

Its fighting style follows from its lifestyle. Instead of waiting in a web, it walks the forest floor and foliage at night, finds prey through touch and vibration, grips it with brush-tipped pedipalps and bites. When something large threatens it, it rears up, lifts its banded front legs and sways with its fangs ready. The display is a warning, and the spider does not bluff.

On an absolute roster these strengths have hard limits. Clinical records show that nine in ten human bites are mild, so the dose from one bite is usually small. A bird, mammal or reptile that strikes first can crush the spider before any venom matters, and armour, scales or dense fur can stop the fangs entirely. The result is a profile with low Attack and very low Defense but high Agility and a near-elite Special: dangerous at close range and fragile at every range.

sections.habitat: Phoneutria is a Central and South American genus, and P. nigriventer is a Brazilian species of forest and forest-edge habitats that also lives around plantations, gardens and houses. In one Brazilian clinical series, 54.5% of bites happened inside homes and 76.5% during daytime, when hidden spiders were disturbed. Commercially shipped bananas occasionally carry Phoneutria, but UF/IFAS notes that the most potent species, P. nigriventer and P. keyserlingi, are rarely exported because most of Brazil's banana crop is consumed domestically.
sections.diet: A nocturnal generalist predator of insects and other arthropods, also taking small vertebrates such as frogs when available. Its own predators were not quantified in the sources reviewed; nocturnal activity and daytime hiding are its main ways of avoiding them.
sections.social: Solitary. Adults meet mainly for courtship and mating, and there is no cooperative hunting or group defence.
sections.reproduction: Females produce silk egg sacs. In the congener P. boliviensis, females laid up to four sacs, 430–1300 spiderlings emerged after 28–34 days, and spiders matured after 14–17 molts at 300–465 days. Venom composition shifts during development, so adult venom differs from juvenile venom.
sections.conservation: No IUCN Red List assessment of P. nigriventer was found in this research pass, so its status is treated as Not Evaluated. It remains common in parts of its range, including human-modified landscapes.
sections.features:
Complex neurotoxic venom with calcium- and sodium-channel-active fractions.
Dense prolateral scopulae on the pedipalps for gripping prey.
Conspicuous banded leg undersides shown during the rearing threat display.
Webless, nocturnal, roaming hunting mode.
Venom composition that changes with age and differs between the sexes.
sections.humanInteraction: Brazil records many Phoneutria bites, most of them mild and mainly painful; only about 0.5–1% become severe, mostly in children, who need hospital care. Bites mainly hit feet and hands (40.9% and 34.3% in one series), which fits spiders hidden around the home being disturbed. The venom is also a research source: the peptide Phα1β is being studied as a non-opioid analgesic.

funFacts: The genus name Phoneutria comes from Greek for "murderess".
In one Brazilian case series, 89.8% of bites were mild and only 0.5% were severe.
Adult females produce nearly three times the venom of equal-sized males.
The toxin Tx2-6 causes priapism in laboratory mice, which is why the species turns up in toxin-mechanism research.
Over half the bites in one clinical study happened indoors, usually when a hiding spider was disturbed.
A venom peptide, Phα1β, is being tested as a painkiller.
A congener needs about 14–17 molts to reach adulthood.

abilities.name: Armadeira Threat Stance
abilities.description: the spider rears up, raises its front two leg pairs to flash the banded undersides and sways while keeping its fangs forward. The display often ends an encounter without contact, and if it does not, the spider is already in striking position.

abilities.name: Multi-Channel Neurotoxin
abilities.description: the venom mixes toxin fractions that hit calcium and sodium channels and nitric-oxide pathways (PhTx3, Tx2-5, Tx2-6). One bite can cause intense pain and, in rare severe cases, cardiovascular and respiratory effects.

traits.name: Webless Night Roamer
traits.description: instead of waiting in a web, it hunts by walking the forest floor and foliage at night and hides in crevices, leaves or buildings by day. That habit also brings it into houses and cargo.

traits.name: Female-Weighted Arsenal
traits.description: adult females yield about three times more venom than equal-sized males, and their venom is more lethal in laboratory tests. The larger sex also carries the stronger weapon.

combat.weapons: The main weapon is a pair of fangs delivering a complex neurotoxic venom. P. nigriventer venom contains several toxin fractions (PhTx1–PhTx4) with different targets. PhTx3 is a broad-spectrum calcium-channel blocker that inhibits glutamate release, and the Tx2 fraction includes Tx2-5 and Tx2-6, which cause priapism through a nitric-oxide pathway and can kill mice. PhTx1, PhTx2 and PhTx3 all act on mammals. This multi-target cocktail is the reason the spider is medically important and why it rates highly in Special.
weaknesses: Tiny absolute mass and negligible raw force.
Soft abdomen and thin exoskeleton.
Small venom dose per bite; many bites cause only local pain.
Must make fang contact to do any damage.
goodMatchups: Insects, other spiders and small frogs or lizards within its prey range.
Small, thin-skinned animals that must engage at close range.
badMatchups: Any mammal, bird or reptile large enough to crush it before venom acts.
Armoured arthropods and animals with protective hair, scales or shells that block fang penetration.
Fast aerial predators that strike from above.

brown-hyena.name: Brown Hyena
brown-hyena.specimen: healthy mature adult male of about 43.0 kg, head-body about 115 cm, shoulder height about 79 cm. This is at the top of the usual adult range without using the exceptional 60–72 kg animals on record.
brown-hyena.summary: The brown hyena is a shaggy 43 kg desert scavenger of southern Africa that can smell carrion from 2 km away and walk more than 50 km in a night. Its heavy bone-cracking bite and bold temper let it drive leopards off their kills, but it rarely hunts successfully and cannot match lions or spotted hyena clans.
narrative: The brown hyena looks like a large, long-haired dog with a sloping back: dark brown to black, with a cream mantle around the neck and shoulders and a coat that bristles up to 30 cm when it is excited. A mature male weighs around 43 kg. It is the hyena of the Kalahari and the Namib, where rain can be less than 100 mm a year and food is thinly spread.

Its answer to scarcity is distance and a nose. Brown hyenas spend most of the night on the move, averaging about 31 km, and can find even dried carcasses by scent from 2 km away. On the Namib coast they patrol beaches for dead seal pups and washed-up marine life. They hunt only occasionally and rarely succeed, taking springhares, lambs and bat-eared foxes, so most of what they eat comes from carcasses and from kills they steal.

Stealing is where its fighting ability shows. A lone brown hyena will charge a leopard with its jaws open and can force an adult male up a tree, and it routinely displaces cheetahs and jackals. Its skull is among the largest in the hyena family and its bite-force quotient is close to the spotted hyena's. On the absolute roster scale it sits slightly above the striped hyena, just below the gray wolf in Attack and well below the spotted hyena, with very high Stamina from its long desert walks.

sections.habitat: Southern Africa's arid west: Namibia, Botswana, western and southern Zimbabwe, southern Mozambique and South Africa. It lives in desert with under 100 mm of rain, especially along the coast, and in semi-desert, open scrub and open woodland savanna up to about 650 mm of rain. It is independent of drinking water but needs cover to lie up in by day, and it can survive close to farms and towns.
sections.diet: A scavenger of a wide range of vertebrate remains, supplemented by wild fruits such as tsama melons, insects, birds' eggs and the occasional small animal it kills. In farming areas of South Africa it scavenges cattle carcasses and medium and small wild animals. It caches food and steals kills from jackals, cheetahs and leopards.
sections.social: Lives in clans that share and defend a territory but usually forage alone. Clans have separate male and female dominance hierarchies. Many males are nomads that roam between clan territories, and both nomadic and immigrant males may mate with clan females.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is non-seasonal. Gestation is about 97 days and litters average 2.3 cubs (range 1–5), each weighing about 1 kg. Dens are narrow holes, often in remote sand dunes away from lions and spotted hyenas. The denning period lasts about 15 months, cubs are moved between several dens, and all clan members bring food to the den.
sections.conservation: Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List, with a global population estimated at 4,000–10,000. Main threats are persecution by livestock farmers, poisoning, road deaths and disease from domestic dogs; 43% of Namib Desert brown hyenas sampled had antibodies to canine distemper virus. Density estimates in fenced South African reserves varied almost tenfold depending on whether fences were assumed to be permeable, showing how uncertain population numbers are.
sections.features:
Large skull with robust, bone-cracking teeth.
Long, shaggy coat with erectile neck and back hair up to about 30 cm.
Pale mantle around the neck and shoulders.
Two-part anal-gland scent paste.
Very long nightly foraging range.
sections.humanInteraction: Farmers often blame brown hyenas for livestock losses, but most damage comes from a few individuals, and removing a single culprit has stopped stock killing even with other hyenas present. Finding a brown hyena at a carcass does not prove it made the kill. It lives near people in some agricultural areas and near towns.

funFacts: It can smell an old, dried-out carcass from 2 km downwind.
One Kalahari brown hyena walked 54.4 km in a single night.
Only about 1 in 20 of its hunts succeed, so it relies on scavenging.
A single brown hyena can chase an adult male leopard up a tree.
On the Namib coast it lives on seal pups and has been seen in abandoned diamond mining towns.
Its white scent paste keeps its smell for more than a month.
Females in a clan may suckle each other's cubs.

abilities.name: Carcass Radar
abilities.description: carrion is located mainly by smell, and even old, dry carcasses can be detected from 2 km downwind. This lets it find food and rivals' kills across huge desert territories.

abilities.name: Leopard Charge
abilities.description: a lone brown hyena will rush a leopard with its jaws wide open and can drive an adult male leopard up a tree, then take its kill. Its heavy bite and thick-necked build back up the bluff.

traits.name: Strandwolf of the Namib
traits.description: on the Namib Desert coast it patrols beaches and seal colonies, living largely on Cape fur seal pups and other washed-up marine animals, and even uses abandoned diamond mining towns.

traits.name: Two-Tone Scent Paste
traits.description: each time it pastes a grass stalk it leaves a thin black smear and a thick white blob whose smell lasts over 30 days; marks are so dense that a hyena is rarely more than 500 m from one.

combat.weapons: The brown hyena's main weapon is a heavy bone-cracking bite from a large, robust skull. It is overwhelmingly a scavenger: in the southern Kalahari, vertebrates it killed made up only 4.2% of food items, and of 128 observed hunts only six (4.7%) succeeded, mostly on springhare, springbok lambs and bat-eared foxes. On the Namib coast it feeds mainly on Cape fur seal pups, nearly all found dead. Where it does use its bite on other animals, it is mainly in contests over food.
weaknesses: About 43 kg; outclassed by lions and spotted hyena groups.
A poor, rarely successful hunter; little experience subduing healthy prey.
No armor; its bite is its only serious weapon.
Heavy teeth wear down with age, reducing bite effectiveness in old animals.
