budgerigar.name: Budgerigar
budgerigar.specimen: healthy adult wild-type male, 30 g (0.03 kg), 18 cm long, matching the Animal Diversity Web average mass of 30 g and BirdLife Australia's average of 18 cm and 28 g.
budgerigar.summary: A 30-gram nomad of the Australian outback, the budgerigar survives on flight skill, flock vigilance and water-thrifty physiology rather than any weapon. It can thread gaps a quarter of its wingspan and switch flight speeds on the fly, but its tiny bill and body make it harmless to anything larger than an insect.
narrative: The budgerigar is a small parrot built for a harsh, unpredictable country. Wild flocks follow rain across inland Australia, feeding on fallen grass seed in the cool of the morning, sheltering motionless in shade through the midday heat, and wheeling around roost trees at dusk. When rain brings a flush of seed, pairs breed at once in tree hollows, and flocks can swell to tens of thousands of birds.

Its strengths are all about getting away. Laboratory work has shown that it flies in two distinct gears, a fast energy-efficient cruise and a slower maneuvering speed, and that it changes gear before it reaches a tight spot. It can fold its wings to slip through openings far narrower than its wingspan, and flock-mates watch for danger and give sharp alarm calls. Its ultraviolet-fluorescent plumage and finely tuned hearing make it one of the most studied birds in sensory science.

In a fight, none of this adds up to much. At 30 grams, with a bill that produces roughly 12 newtons, the budgerigar cannot seriously injure any vertebrate larger than itself, and it has no protection beyond its feathers. Its best result in any matchup is a clean escape into the air or into cover, and against a raptor, snake or cat that gets close, it has no answer.

sections.habitat: Wild budgerigars live across the drier parts of mainland Australia, in open grassland, mulga and mallee scrub, open woodland and farmland, seldom far from water. They are absent from the far south-west, the far north of the Northern Territory, Tasmania and most of the east coast (Australian Museum). Drought can push flocks into wooded or coastal areas. Pet birds are kept worldwide; ADW records an introduced population established in southwest Florida.
sections.diet: Budgerigars feed almost entirely on the seeds of native grasses and herbs such as spinifex, tussock grasses and saltbush, mostly picked from the ground, with drinking and feeding concentrated in the morning (Australian Museum; ADW). They drink about 5.5% of their body weight each day. Predators of such small flock birds include raptors, but no species-specific predation study was read in this pass.
sections.social: Strongly social flock birds. Flockmates preen and feed one another by regurgitating seed. Flocks range from a few birds to 100 or more and can reach tens of thousands after rain. There is little evidence of a dominance hierarchy (ADW).
sections.reproduction: Pairs are monogamous and nest in tree hollows, logs and fence posts, often a few metres apart. Breeding is triggered by rain and seeding grasses rather than a fixed season. Clutches average about 5 eggs (ADW; the Australian Museum gives 6–8), hatching after about 18 days; chicks leave the nest at about 35 days, and birds can breed at about 6 months (ADW; Australian Museum).
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (BirdLife International assessment, as reported by Wikipedia and BirdLife Australia). Wild numbers fluctuate with rainfall, and farm water points have increased populations in some areas.
sections.features:
Two preferred flight speeds, switched in anticipation of clutter.
Wing-folding postures for passing gaps narrower than the wingspan.
UV-fluorescent plumage used in mate choice.
Inner-ear hair cells that regrow after damage, restoring hearing.
Regulated evaporative water loss suited to the arid interior.
sections.humanInteraction: The budgerigar is the most widely kept pet bird in the world (ADW), valued for its small size, low cost and ability to mimic speech. It is also a major laboratory model for hearing, vocal learning and flight. Large wild flocks can damage cereal crops.

funFacts: Wild flocks can number in the tens of thousands after a season of abundant rain.
A budgerigar has flown through gaps only a quarter of its wingspan wide, with as little as 6 mm to spare on each side.
Budgerigars fly at two fixed "gears", about 9.4 m/s and 5.4 m/s, and switch abruptly between them.
Female budgerigars became more interested in males after watching them solve food puzzles.
Yawning is contagious between budgerigars that can see each other.
If their inner-ear hair cells are damaged, the cells regrow and the bird's hearing and song precision recover.
Their plumage glows under ultraviolet light.

abilities.name: Two-Gear Flight
abilities.description: budgerigars hold one of two fixed flight speeds, about 9.4 m/s in open space and about 5.4 m/s in clutter, and switch before they reach a narrowing passage. Combined with folding its wings to pass gaps a quarter of its wingspan, this lets it escape into cover where larger fliers cannot follow.

abilities.name: Warbling Mimicry
abilities.description: a lifelong vocal learner that copies flockmates, other sounds and human speech. In a matchup this is a communication and alarm system, not a damage source.

traits.name: Outback Nomad
traits.description: flocks follow rain across the arid interior, swelling to tens of thousands after good seasons, and breed opportunistically whenever grass seed is abundant.

traits.name: Ultraviolet Plumage
traits.description: its feathers fluoresce under UV light and UV signals are used in mate choice, a channel most mammalian predators cannot see.

combat.weapons: The only weapon is a small hooked bill with a calculated bite of about 12 N, used to dehusk grass seeds and, in disputes, to nip flockmates or a human finger. The feet are zygodactyl climbing feet, not talons. Against any vertebrate larger than itself the budgerigar has no way to cause serious injury; its offense is limited to pecks and bites in squabbles over nest hollows and perches.
weaknesses: Negligible mass (30 g) and no meaningful weapon.
No protection; a single strike from a predator is decisive.
Needs regular access to drinking water in the wild (ADW: about 5.5% of body weight per day).
Flock-based defense disappears in a one-on-one matchup.

canary.name: Canary
canary.specimen: healthy adult male common domestic canary, 0.02 kg, 13.0 cm total length. Males are used because they sing, hold breeding territories and fight other males, sometimes with bloody beak fights. The value also sits inside the wild weight range.
canary.summary: The Canary is a 20 g finch from the Canary Islands, Azores and Madeira, bred for centuries into the world's best-known songbird pet. It is a master of learned song and a famous brain-science model, but in a fight it has only a tiny seed-cracking bill and is one of the lightest, most fragile animals on the roster.
narrative: The canary began as a small, streaky green-yellow finch in the laurel forests, pine woods and gardens of the Atlantic islands. Sailors and colonists brought it to Europe, where its song made it a treasured pet by the 1600s. Breeders then shaped it into hundreds of forms: bright yellow and red birds, crested and frilled birds, and song breeds trained to roll, bubble or ring.

Its voice is the canary's real specialty. A male learns his song over most of his first year, building 30–40 syllable types on an inborn framework, and uses both sides of his voice box independently to produce rapid two-note syllables that females find especially attractive. Rival males hold song duels, overlapping and stretching their songs. Research on canary brains showed that adult birds keep adding neurons to their song-control centre, changing how scientists think about the adult brain.

In an absolute matchup the canary has almost nothing to fight with. It weighs about 20 g, its bill is built for seeds, and it is so sensitive to toxic air that it served for nearly a century as a living gas alarm. Its survival strategy is to hide, flock and fly.

sections.habitat: The wild Atlantic canary is found only in Macaronesia in the eastern Atlantic: the Canary Islands, the Azores and Madeira. It lives in a wide variety of habitats from pine and laurel forests to sand dunes, most commonly in semi-open areas with small trees such as orchards and copses, and in parks and gardens, from sea level to above 1,500 m in the Canary Islands (Wikipedia). It has been introduced to Midway Atoll (since 1911); a Bermuda population founded in 1930 died out by the 1960s.
sections.diet: It feeds in flocks on the ground or in low vegetation, mainly on seeds of weeds and grasses and on figs, plus other plant material and small insects (Wikipedia). Domestic canaries eat seed mixes plus greens, egg food and calcium sources.
sections.social: Gregarious; wild canaries often nest in loose groups, each pair defending a small territory. Domestic canaries can live in aviary groups outside the breeding season, where a hierarchy forms and fights become rare.
sections.reproduction: The cup nest is built 1–6 m up in a tree or bush, well hidden in leaves. Clutches are 3–4 (sometimes 5) pale blue eggs, incubated for 13–14 days; chicks leave the nest after about 14–21 days, and pairs raise 2–3 broods a year (Wikipedia). Male canaries learn their full song over their first year.
sections.conservation: The Atlantic canary is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. Populations are estimated at 80,000–90,000 pairs in the Canary Islands, 30,000–60,000 pairs in the Azores and 4,000–5,000 pairs in Madeira. The domestic canary is one of the most widely kept cage birds in the world.
sections.features:
Complex learned song of 30–40 syllable types.
Two-sided syrinx producing low and high notes independently.
Adult neurogenesis in the song-control centre.
Rapid breathing that makes it a sensitive detector of toxic gases.
Hundreds of domestic colour, song and type breeds.
sections.humanInteraction: Canaries were taken into captivity after the European conquest of the islands and became prized pets in 17th-century Europe. They were bred into song breeds such as the Harz Roller, Belgian Waterslager and Spanish Timbrado; colour breeds including the red factor canary; and type breeds from the tiny Fife Fancy to the large Lancashire. From 1896, after work by physiologist John Scott Haldane, miners in Britain, the United States and Canada used canaries to detect carbon monoxide, and Britain ended the practice in December 1986. Canaries remain a major laboratory animal for the study of song learning and the brain.

funFacts: The colour "canary yellow" is named after the domestic canary; wild canaries are mostly green-yellow with brown streaks.
British coal mines used canaries as gas detectors until December 1986.
Adult canaries grow new brain cells in their song-control centre.
A canary can sing two notes at once, one from each side of its voice box.
Rival male canaries hold song duels, trying to outlast each other's songs.
The Harz Roller sings with its beak closed at 40 or more notes per second.
A domestic canary in 1960s Leningrad learned to weave its owner's words into its song.

abilities.name: Two-Voice Song
abilities.description: the canary sings with both sides of its syrinx, the left side producing low notes and the right side high notes, and can alternate them so fast that it produces special high-repetition "sexy" syllables that females prefer.

abilities.name: Song Duel
abilities.description: rival males overlap their songs in aggressive vocal exchanges, and the leader stretches his songs to outlast the follower, settling contests without always coming to blows.

traits.name: Canary in the Coal Mine
traits.description: because canaries breathe rapidly and react to toxic gases quickly, miners carried them underground as carbon monoxide alarms from 1896 until Britain ended the practice in December 1986.

traits.name: Brain That Adds Neurons
traits.description: adult canaries keep producing new neurons in their song-control centre, a discovery that helped overturn the old belief that adult brains cannot add neurons.

combat.weapons: The canary has almost no weapons. Its small conical bill husks seeds and can peck, and during the breeding season males defend territories fiercely, which can lead to beak fights and chases that draw blood (Wikipedia). Outside the breeding season, flocks settle into a hierarchy and most disputes end with threats: an open bill and raised wings, after which the weaker bird gives way.
weaknesses: About 20 g; among the lightest vertebrates on the roster.
No armor and no real weapon.
Very sensitive to airborne toxins.
Domestic birds lack wild survival skills.

caucasian-shepherd-dog.name: Caucasian Shepherd Dog
caucasian-shepherd-dog.specimen: healthy adult male, 60.0 kg, 72.0 cm at the withers.
caucasian-shepherd-dog.summary: The Caucasian Shepherd Dog is a massive 60 kg mountain guardian from the Caucasus, with a long maned coat and thick skin. It fights by standing its ground and charging head-on, which makes it one of the strongest and best-padded dogs on the roster, but it is slow to turn, has no armor and is still far below bears and big cats.
narrative: For centuries shepherds in the Caucasus Mountains kept big, heavy-coated dogs to defend their flocks from wolves and thieves. In the 20th century Soviet breeders gathered these regional dogs, from Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Dagestan and the southern Russian steppe, into a single breed, the Caucasian Ovcharka, which the FCI accepted in 1984. A mature male weighs around 60 kg and stands about 72 cm, with a massive broad head and a coarse coat that forms a mane around its neck.

Its approach to a fight is to hold its ground. It warns, postures and then charges, relying on mass and a heavy bite. The mane and thick skin over its neck blunt the bites that decide most dog and wolf fights, and its coat lets it work through the harshest winters. Soviet state kennels used it to guard factories and government sites, and it still guards prisons in Russia.

That makes it the heaviest and best-protected dog in this batch, rated slightly above the Kangal and Tibetan Mastiff in Attack and Defense. But mass comes at a cost: it is the slowest dog here to turn and accelerate, and it has no armor. Against wolves and hyenas it is an even contest; against bears, big cats and large hoofed animals it is outmatched.

sections.habitat: Native to the Caucasus Mountains and the steppe of southern Russia, especially Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Dagestan. It is now kept in Russia, Europe and North America as a guardian and companion.
sections.diet: Fed by its owners on meat, dog food and household scraps. It does not hunt for its living.
sections.ecology: In its working role it guards flocks and villages against wolves and thieves. In the Soviet Union and Russia it has also been used to guard factories, government sites and prisons.
sections.social: Bonds closely with its family and flock; suspicious of strangers and strange dogs. It works independently rather than under constant command.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is managed by people. No breed-specific growth or maturity data were located; the FCI standard notes that males are more massive and often shorter in body than females.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed.
sections.features:
Large, massive, broad-cheeked head.
Coarse stand-off coat with undercoat, each at least 5 cm, forming a neck mane and "trousers".
Thick, elastic skin without folds.
Body 3–8% longer than tall; heavy bone.
Fearless, independent guarding temperament.
sections.humanInteraction: A serious guardian that needs experienced handling. The AKC warns that it "should never be taken lightly". It is prized in Russia and the Caucasus as a flock and property guard.

funFacts: The FCI accepted the breed in 1984 under the patronage of the Soviet Union; Russia is its patron country today.
The breed standard requires its guard coat and undercoat to be at least 5 cm long.
Soviet state kennels used Caucasian Shepherd Dogs to guard factories and government facilities.
They still work as prison guard dogs in Russia.
Dogs from different parts of the Caucasus look quite different: tall and light in Azerbaijan, compact in Dagestan, very large in Chechnya and Ingushetia.
A 2024 UK study found a median lifespan of just 5.4 years, but it included only 22 dogs.

abilities.name: Maned Neck Guard
abilities.description: a mane of long, coarse coat over thick, elastic skin covers the neck and shoulders, the targets wolves and other dogs aim for. It blunts bites there without being true armor.

abilities.name: Frontline Charge
abilities.description: meets intruders head-on with warning, posture and a heavy charge, the style shepherds kept it for against wolves and thieves. Its 60 kg mass makes the charge hard for lighter animals to stand.

traits.name: Bear-Like Mountain Guardian
traits.description: a massive, broad-headed dog whose stand-off coat on the cheeks and backskull gives it the bear-like look the UKC standard describes.

traits.name: Soviet-Standardized Caucasus Dog
traits.description: shaped in the 20th-century Soviet Union from the flock guardians of Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Dagestan and the southern Russian steppe, and accepted by the FCI in 1984.

combat.weapons: The weapon is the bite, delivered from a large, massive, broad-cheeked head (FCI) on a 60 kg frame. Like other mountain guardians, it confronts intruders with warning, posture and a charge before biting. Its mass lets it push and hold, but it has no second weapon system.
weaknesses: Heavy and slow to turn; the least agile dog in this batch.
No armor; one bite weapon.
Heat is a poor fit for the heavy coat.
Possibly short-lived, although lifespan data are thin.
Far outmatched by bears, big cats and large ungulates.

chinchilla.name: Chinchilla
chinchilla.specimen: healthy adult female of about 0.6 kg in domestic condition.
chinchilla.summary: The chinchilla is a 0.6 kg Andean rock-hopper wrapped in the densest fur of any land mammal, which it can shed in clumps to escape a predator's bite. It is agile, social and wary, but its bite is weak even by rodent standards, so it survives by leaping away rather than fighting.
narrative: The chinchilla is built for escape on broken rock. Long hind legs launch it across gaps of nearly two metres, big ears and eyes watch for predators at dusk, and colonies of dozens of animals share the job of spotting danger. When a fox, cat or bird of prey does close in, the chinchilla has two last tricks: it sprays urine, and if bitten it releases a clump of its extraordinarily dense fur and bolts.

What it lacks is any real weapon. Its incisor bite, measured at about 23.5 N, is weak even compared with other South American rodents, and its jaw is poorly built for hard biting. In ABS terms that means very low Attack and Defense, high Agility, and a Special score lifted by the unusual fur-slip escape rather than by any capacity to hurt an opponent.

That same fur nearly wiped the species out. Hunted for centuries for pelts, the long-tailed chinchilla now survives in the wild only in a few colonies in northern Chile and is listed as Endangered, even as domestic chinchillas bred from it live in homes and on farms around the world.

sections.habitat: Wild long-tailed chinchillas survive only in northern Chile, in arid, rocky mountain country where they den in crevices and holes among rocks; known colonies include Aucó near Illapel (Reserva Nacional Las Chinchillas) and La Higuera north of Coquimbo. Historically the genus ranged across the Andes of Chile, Peru, Bolivia and Argentina. Domestic chinchillas live worldwide.
sections.diet: Mainly herbivorous: grasses, herbs, sedges, seeds, lichens and mosses, with occasional insects and bird eggs. They sit upright and hold food in their forepaws. The native climate swings from about 30 °C by day in summer to below freezing on winter nights.
sections.social: Colonies (herds) of 14 to more than 100 animals, matriarchal, with dominant females and mostly monogamous pairs.
sections.reproduction: Gestation is long for a rodent, about 111 days, producing one to six (usually two) fully furred young with open eyes that can run almost at once. Females usually have two litters a year; young mature at about 8 months. Chinchillas can live about 10 years in the wild and up to 20 in human care.
sections.conservation: The long-tailed chinchilla is Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2025 assessment) and on CITES Appendix I. Centuries of hunting for fur, including dynamiting of burrow systems, destroyed most wild populations, and poaching continues. Domestic chinchillas are not covered by CITES.
sections.features:
Densest fur of any land mammal (about 20,000 hairs per cm²).
Fur slip escape reaction.
Long, muscular hind limbs for jumping.
Greatly expanded middle-ear bullae and large ears.
Vertical slit pupils and very long whiskers.
sections.humanInteraction: The Chincha people of the Andes wore chinchilla fur and ate the meat, and the Inca kept chinchillas. Commercial hunting in northern Chile began in earnest in 1828 and drove the wild animals to near extinction. Farm-raised chinchillas now supply the fur trade and the pet market; pet chinchillas need cool, dry housing and regular dust baths.

funFacts: A single chinchilla hair follicle can sprout 50–75 hairs; a human follicle grows two or three.
If a predator bites, a chinchilla can shed a patch of fur and escape, a reaction called fur slip.
Chinchillas bathe in fine volcanic dust, not water.
They can jump up to about 1.8 m.
Newborn chinchillas are fully furred with open eyes and can run almost immediately.
Chinchilla hearing, measured at 50 Hz to 33 kHz, is closer to a human's than most rodents' hearing is.

abilities.name: Fur Slip
abilities.description: when bitten or roughly grabbed, a chinchilla releases a large patch of fur, exposing clean skin and leaving the attacker holding hair while it escapes. It can break a predator's first grip but does nothing against a crushing or killing bite.

abilities.name: Rock-Hopper Leap
abilities.description: long, muscular hind limbs let it bound across rocks and clear gaps of up to about 1.8 m, darting into crevices where most predators cannot follow.

traits.name: Densest Fur on Land
traits.description: about 20,000 hairs per square centimetre, with 50–75 hairs sprouting from each follicle compared with two or three in humans; chinchillas keep it clean by rolling in fine volcanic dust instead of water.

traits.name: Hunted to the Brink
traits.description: its fur made it the target of an international trade that emptied most of its range; one full-length coat can need about 150 pelts, and the wild species is now Endangered and listed on CITES Appendix I.

combat.weapons: The chinchilla is a grazing and seed-eating rodent with a notably weak incisor bite for its family, measured at about 23.5 N. It fights mainly within its own species: females threaten with growls, teeth chattering and urine, and group-housed chinchillas can inflict bite wounds that cost each other pieces of ear and toe. Against predators it does not fight back meaningfully.
weaknesses: Very weak bite and tiny absolute mass.
Overheats easily; cannot pant or sweat.
Fragile ear pinnae easily injured.
Flat, open ground removes its rock refuges.

cockatiel.name: Cockatiel
cockatiel.specimen: healthy adult wild-type male, 90 g (0.09 kg) and 32 cm long including the tail, matching ADW's 80–90 g average and AnAge's 90 g, and inside Wikipedia's 30–33 cm length.
cockatiel.summary: The cockatiel is the smallest cockatoo, a 90-gram grey nomad of inland Australia that answers every threat by flying. Fast, direct flight and tight flocks keep it safe in open country, but its small bill and timid nature make it harmless in a real fight.
narrative: The cockatiel is a cockatoo in miniature: the same erectile crest, powder down and loud voice as the larger cockatoos, packed into a slim 90-gram body with a tail as long as the rest of the bird. Wild flocks roam the dry interior of Australia in search of seeding Acacia and grasses, never straying far from water, and pairs breed in eucalypt hollows whenever rain brings food.

Everything about the cockatiel points toward escape. Animal Diversity Web describes it as timid, with no natural defense beyond flight, and its long pointed wings and fanned tail make it one of the faster small parrots. Researchers use it as a model for bird flight, flying cockatiels in wind tunnels at up to 16 metres per second. Its crest works as a signal to flockmates, and its alarm calls change in pitch with the size of the threat.

As a pet it is known for whistled tunes rather than speech, and it has been recorded singing in time with human music. None of that helps in a fight. A 90-gram bird with a small bill and no protection cannot hurt a vertebrate predator; its best outcome in any matchup is a fast, clean getaway.

sections.habitat: Cockatiels live across mainland Australia, mostly in arid and semi-arid open country but always near water: open woodland, savanna around waterholes, shrubland and farmland (Wikipedia; ADW). They are absent from the fertile south-west and south-east corners, the deepest Western Australian deserts and Cape York (Wikipedia). BirdLife Australia lists woodland, desert and grassland habitats.
sections.diet: Wild cockatiels eat mainly seeds, especially Acacia, as well as wheat, sunflower and sorghum, and often feed on crops, to the dismay of farmers (Wikipedia; ADW). They forage on the ground, where their grey plumage makes them hard for aerial predators to spot.
sections.social: Gregarious throughout the year. Flocks usually hold up to 30 birds but may reach hundreds or thousands; small flocks fly in tight formation and flocks roost communally at night (BirdLife Australia). Pair bonds form early and persist all year (ADW).
sections.reproduction: Breeding is triggered mainly by rainfall. Pairs nest in tree hollows, usually in dead eucalypts near water, about 1–2 m above the ground. Males sing, strut and inspect the hollow before the female enters; both parents care for the young (ADW).
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (BirdLife International assessment, as reported by Wikipedia and BirdLife Australia). The species is widespread and common.
sections.features:
Erectile crest that signals mood and folds flat in flight.
Long, pointed tail that fans out to control altitude and stability.
Powder down that waterproofs the plumage and rises as dust when the bird shakes.
Fast, direct flight studied across 0–16 m/s in wind tunnels.
Loud, graded alarm calls and learned whistled songs.
sections.humanInteraction: One of the five most popular pet bird species; an estimated 4.8 million US households keep cockatiels (Wikipedia). Pet birds are valued for their crests, whistling and tameness. Wild flocks raid cereal and sunflower crops. Cockatiels are also a standard laboratory species for flight mechanics.

funFacts: The cockatiel is the smallest cockatoo in the world.
Its crest is a mood meter: upright when startled, angled when relaxed, flat when angry.
Cockatiels have been flown in wind tunnels at up to 16 m/s so scientists could measure how their flight muscle works.
A cockatiel study found birds spontaneously singing along in time with a melody of human music.
In a citizen-science test, budgerigars and cockatiels imitated simple R2-D2 beeps more accurately than grey parrots.
Cockatiels shed so much powder down that a cloud of dust rises when they shake after preening.
Their tail makes up about half of their total length.

abilities.name: Fan-Tail Sprint
abilities.description: a long tail that fans out to control altitude and stability, a crest folded flat to cut drag, and wind-tunnel flight up to 16 m/s make the cockatiel's first and only move a fast, controlled escape.

abilities.name: Melody Sync
abilities.description: a vocal learner that copies whistled tunes and has been recorded singing in time with human music; in a matchup this helps flock contact and alarm signalling, not damage.

traits.name: Mood Crest
traits.description: the erectile crest stands vertical when startled, sits at an angle when relaxed and lies flat when angry or defensive, a readable signal shared with the larger cockatoos.

traits.name: Smallest Cockatoo
traits.description: at about 30–33 cm and 90 g it is the smallest member of the cockatoo family, with the family's powder down and crest on a slim, long-tailed frame.

combat.weapons: A small hooked cockatoo bill, used to dehusk Acacia and grass seeds and to bite in defense, is the cockatiel's only weapon. It has no measured bite force and no talons. Against anything larger than itself it can deliver only nips; its whole response to danger is to fly.
weaknesses: 90 g body with a weak bill.
No protection; timid temperament.
Depends on fresh water.
Flock protection disappears in a one-on-one matchup.

common-death-adder.name: Common Death Adder
common-death-adder.specimen: healthy adult female, 0.4 kg and 70 cm total length. Females grow about 20% longer than males in mean adult snout-vent length (Shine et al. 2014), so a female is used as the representative larger adult.
common-death-adder.summary: The common death adder is a short, thick Australian elapid that hides in leaf litter and twitches a grub-like tail tip to lure prey. Its fast strike delivers a potent cobra-like neurotoxin that can paralyze a person over several hours. At about 0.4 kg and 70 cm it is tiny, slow and fragile, so it wins only when prey comes to it.
narrative: The common death adder looks like a viper and hunts like one, yet it belongs to the cobra family. It is short and wide, with a broad triangular head and a thin tail ending in a pale, grub-like tip. Hidden under leaves, it coils and waits, sometimes for days, twitching that tail tip near its head. When a lizard, frog, bird or mouse comes to investigate, the adder strikes, injects its venom and waits for its prey to die.

The venom is unusual among Australian snakes. Most Australian elapid venoms are rich in clotting toxins, but the death adder's is dominated by a single cobra-type neurotoxin that blocks the signal from nerve to muscle, backed by presynaptic neurotoxins. In people, the first signs are drooping eyelids and double vision, typically about four hours after the bite, and severe cases need breathing support. Before antivenom, about half or more of bites were fatal.

For battle ratings, the death adder is a pure ambush specialist. Its lure, camouflage and venom give it one of the roster's highest Special scores, but it is tiny, very slow and unarmored, and its venom takes hours to disable a large animal. It is dangerous to whatever walks up to it and nearly helpless against anything that sees it first.

sections.habitat: The common death adder occurs over much of eastern and coastal southern Australia, mainly Queensland, New South Wales and South Australia, and more sparsely in the Northern Territory and Western Australia. It is the only death adder in the Sydney region. Its status in Victoria is uncertain. It lives in forest, woodland, grassland and heath, hiding in loose leaf litter and debris.
sections.diet: It eats lizards, frogs, birds and small mammals, using a sit-and-wait strategy with its tail lure. It takes a broader range of prey, including fast skinks and warm-blooded animals, than most Australian elapids of similar size.
sections.social: Solitary.
sections.reproduction: It gives birth to live young in late summer. Litters usually number about 3–20 (mean litter sizes of 8–14 across death adders), with over 30 recorded. Newborns are about 12–18 cm long and fully independent. Facultative parthenogenesis (virgin birth) has been confirmed in captive southern death adders by DNA testing, the first record for any elapid.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2018 assessment, as reported by Wikipedia). Habitat loss and the spread of cane toads are concerns: toads eat young death adders, and adults that eat toads are poisoned. Field data from northern Australia show the picture is complex; one population of the related northern death adder increased after toads arrived.
sections.features:
Grub-like tail lure used for caudal luring.
Long, mobile front fangs for an elapid.
Cobra-like three-finger-toxin venom.
Broad triangular head and short, wide body.
Banded camouflage for leaf litter.
sections.humanInteraction: Death adders are not aggressive, but because they stay still rather than flee, people walking in bushland may step close to them. Before antivenom, about half or more of bites were fatal. Today deaths are rare because antivenom is widely available and paralysis develops slowly, although antivenom may not reverse paralysis that is already established. Anticholinesterase drugs can also reverse the venom's nerve block.

funFacts: It wiggles a grub-like tail tip to lure prey within striking distance.
It is not a true adder or viper but a relative of cobras and taipans.
About 59% of its venom is a single neurotoxin.
Before antivenom, about half or more of death adder bites were fatal.
It may wait in the same spot for days until a meal passes.
A litter can contain more than 30 young.
It was once thought to be deaf because it does not flee from footsteps.
Captive females have produced young without a father, the first virgin births confirmed in the cobra family.

abilities.name: Grub-Tail Lure
abilities.description: it lies hidden under leaves and wriggles its thin, pale tail tip like a grub or worm near its head. When prey comes to investigate, it strikes, injects venom and waits for the prey to die.

abilities.name: Nerve-Block Venom
abilities.description: a single long-chain three-finger neurotoxin makes up about 59% of the venom, blocking nerve-to-muscle signals, backed by presynaptic neurotoxins. In people, paralysis starts with drooping eyelids and can stop breathing hours after the bite.

traits.name: Viper-Shaped Elapid
traits.description: with its broad triangular head, short thick body and ambush habits it looks and behaves like a viper, yet it is an elapid whose venom resembles a cobra's.

traits.name: Stand-Its-Ground Ambusher
traits.description: instead of fleeing, it relies on camouflage and stays put, which makes it more likely to be stepped on and bitten than faster, more nervous snakes.

combat.weapons: The primary weapon is a fast strike through relatively long, mobile front fangs, delivering a neurotoxic venom dominated by a single potent receptor-blocking toxin, backed by presynaptic neurotoxins. The secondary tool is the caudal lure: a thin, pale, grub-like tail tip that it twitches close to its head to draw prey within range.
weaknesses: Tiny, unarmored body and very slow movement.
Venom takes hours to paralyze large animals.
Poisoned by eating cane toads; toads also eat young death adders.
Poor ability to escape once found.

common-eland.name: Common Eland
common-eland.specimen: healthy mature bull of about 700 kg, 165 cm at the shoulder and 290 cm head-body length, with full horns, dewlap and forehead brush. This sits between the commonly quoted typical bull range (500–600 kg) and the heavy old bulls of 900 kg or more.
common-eland.summary: The common eland is Africa's giant savanna antelope, a 700 kg bull with thick spiral horns, a heavy dewlap and knees that click as it walks. Slow in a sprint but almost tireless at a trot and able to leap fences from a standstill, it wins by outlasting threats rather than fighting them.
narrative: A mature eland bull is built like an ox: deep-chested, heavy-necked, with a pendulous dewlap, a dark tuft of hair on the forehead and short, thick horns wound in a tight spiral. He may weigh 700 kg or more, and as he walks his knees make a sharp click that carries across the savanna. Research on eland bulls shows that the pitch of that click tracks body size, so rivals can judge each other by sound before any contact.

For all that mass, the eland is a gentle animal. Herds drift nomadically across savanna and woodland, browsing and grazing, and bolt when startled. They are slow sprinters that tire at top speed, but they can trot for hours and live mostly on the water in their food. When cornered by a fence they simply jump it from a standstill, which is why eland farming needs very high fences.

On the ABS scale the eland is a heavyweight with a light fighting temperament. Its size and raw power put it above the kudu and sable antelope and level with the moose, while its placid nature, wrestling-style horns and slow sprint keep its Attack and Agility well below the Cape buffalo. Its standout rating is Stamina.

sections.habitat: East and Southern Africa, from Ethiopia and South Sudan to South Africa, including Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia and Angola. It uses savanna, woodland and open and montane grasslands with a wide variety of plants and avoids dense forest.
sections.diet: A mixed feeder that browses leaves, shoots and twigs and grazes grasses, shifting with the season. It uses its horns to break off branches out of reach and can live largely on the water in its food.
sections.social: Nomadic herds of up to 500 animals with separate male, female and nursery groups; females have a linear hierarchy. Old bulls often wander alone or in small groups. Elands are not territorial.
sections.reproduction: Females mature at 15–36 months and males at four to five years. Mating peaks in the rainy season. About a day after birth, mother and calf join a nursery group, where the calf stays until it is about two years old.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. The 2016 assessment estimated 90,000–110,000 mature individuals, about half in protected areas and 30% on private land, with stable or increasing populations in several countries. Numbers are slowly falling elsewhere through habitat loss and poaching for meat. It disappeared from Eswatini and Zimbabwe and has been reintroduced.
sections.features:
Thick, tightly spiralled horns in both sexes.
Large dewlap and dark forehead brush in old bulls.
Loud knee-clicks that signal body size.
Standing jumps of 1.5 m and more.
Water economy and heat control suited to dry savanna.
sections.humanInteraction: Farmed for meat and milk in South Africa, Zimbabwe, Kenya and Russia; eland milk carries 11–17% butterfat and keeps for months when properly prepared. Farmers note that elands can jump or break through high fences.

funFacts: The common eland is the slowest antelope in a sprint but can trot at about 22 km/h indefinitely.
A bull's knee-click pitch tells rivals how big he is.
Elands can clear a 1.5 m fence from a standing start.
Eland milk carries 11–17% butterfat and, properly prepared, can keep for up to eight months.
Female elands have longer horns than males; bulls' horns are thicker and more tightly twisted.
A herd can number up to 500 animals.
Elands are farmed for meat and milk in Russia as well as in southern and eastern Africa.

abilities.name: Endless Trot
abilities.description: holds a trot of about 22 km/h indefinitely and gets most of its water from food, outlasting pursuers rather than outrunning them.

abilities.name: Standing Leap
abilities.description: despite weighing around 700 kg, it can clear fences of 1.5 m or more from a standstill when startled.

traits.name: Giant Among Antelopes
traits.description: bulls commonly weigh 500–900 kg, far more than the kudu, sable, oryx or any other savanna antelope on the roster.

traits.name: Clicking Knees
traits.description: bulls' knees make a loud click as they walk, and the pitch honestly reveals body size to rivals.

combat.weapons: The eland's weapons are thick, tightly spiralled horns on a body that can weigh 700 kg or more. Bulls fight by feeling out each other's horns and then pushing with all their strength, wrestling with locked horns and butting heads. Cows use their horns to defend calves from predators. Mass gives shoving and ramming power, but the eland's temperament is mild; it has been domesticated for meat and milk, and wild animals generally avoid conflict.
weaknesses: Slow in a sprint and quick to tire at top speed.
No armor; flanks and belly are soft.
Mild temperament; usually flees rather than fights.
Horns are wrestling tools rather than lethal stabbing weapons.

corn-snake.name: Corn Snake
corn-snake.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 0.5 kg and 120.0 cm total length, representing a well-grown wild adult rather than a record animal.
corn-snake.summary: The corn snake is a slender, brightly patterned rat snake from the southeastern United States. A 0.5 kg adult male climbs trees, prowls rodent burrows at night and kills mice and rats by constriction, but it has no venom or armor and is far too small to threaten large animals. When cornered it bluffs with a buzzing tail and foul musk.
narrative: The corn snake is a quiet specialist in small places. It spends much of its life underground, sliding through the tunnels of mice and cotton rats, or tucked under loose bark and in the walls of old barns. At night it hunts by scent, flicking its tongue to follow a rodent's trail, then bites, wraps its coils around the prey and squeezes. It is just as happy in a tree, gripping branches in a stop-and-go climb to reach a bird's nest.

Its weapons stop there. Kingsnakes, which often eat other snakes, squeeze harder than corn snakes of similar size, and the corn snake has no venom and no armor. When threatened it tries to look more dangerous than it is: it shakes its tail against dry leaves to make a rattling buzz and releases a foul musk. Foxes, bobcats, weasels, opossums and hawks all eat corn snakes regardless.

In ABS terms the corn snake has low Attack and Defense, solid Agility from its climbing and burrowing, and modest Stamina. Its Intelligence is decent for a snake, supported by experiments in which young corn snakes quickly learned to find a hidden shelter. Its Special score reflects constriction, climbing and its rattle-and-musk bluff rather than any rare weapon.

sections.habitat: The corn snake lives in the southeastern United States from New Jersey to the Florida Keys and west to Louisiana, in overgrown fields, forest openings, pine and palmetto flatwoods, rocky areas and abandoned farms and buildings, from sea level to about 1,800 m. In colder areas it brumates through the winter; on the warmer coast it shelters in rock crevices and logs during cold spells.
sections.diet: Over half the diet is rodents, such as hispid cotton rats and white-footed mice, plus other small mammals like moles. It also climbs to take birds and eggs. Young snakes eat lizards, small snakes and frogs, and in Florida the diet is mainly reptiles and amphibians. It helps control rodent populations and is in turn eaten by foxes, opossums, skunks, bobcats, weasels and hawks.
sections.social: Solitary and secretive. It is active mainly at night and spends much of the day under bark, in burrows or in old buildings.
sections.reproduction: Mating follows winter brumation. About a month later the female lays 12–24 leathery eggs in a warm, damp hidden place and leaves them. The young hatch after about 10 weeks at roughly 20–38 cm long (Smithsonian and ADW figures; Wikipedia gives about 13 cm). Maturity depends on size rather than age.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. It is common across much of its range. Outside its range it is a proscribed pest in much of Australia, where authorities run eradication campaigns, and it is at risk of becoming invasive in Brazil.
sections.features:
Checkerboard black-and-white belly.
Round pupils and no heat-sensing pits.
Tail vibration and musk as defenses.
Branch-gripping concertina climbing.
Constriction to subdue prey.
sections.humanInteraction: It is one of the most popular pet snakes, second only to the ball python, prized for its calm temperament, manageable size and easy care. Decades of breeding have produced a wide range of colour morphs. In the wild it is often mistaken for the venomous copperhead, but its brighter colours, slim head and round pupils tell them apart.

funFacts: Its belly pattern looks like the kernels of Indian corn, which may be how it got its name.
The oldest known corn snake lived 32 years and 3 months in captivity.
When scared it shakes its tail against dry leaves, buzzing like a rattlesnake.
It can climb trees to raid bird nests.
Young corn snakes learned a shelter-finding maze in just 16 trials.
It is so popular as a pet that it is a banned invasive pest in parts of Australia.

abilities.name: Branch-Grip Climb
abilities.description: it climbs trees, cliffs and buildings by gripping branches in a stop-and-grip concertina movement, reaching nests and escaping ground predators.

abilities.name: Musk and Rattle Bluff
abilities.description: when threatened it vibrates its tail against dry leaves, making a rattle-like buzz, and releases a foul-smelling musk that can put off a predator.

traits.name: Maze-Learning Snake
traits.description: young corn snakes learned to find a hidden open shelter in an eight-hole arena within 16 trials, evidence that snakes can learn spatial tasks well.

traits.name: Checkerboard Belly
traits.description: its belly is patterned with alternating black and white marks like kernels of Indian corn, one explanation for its name.

combat.weapons: The corn snake is a constrictor. It bites to get a grip, then quickly coils around the prey and squeezes until it is subdued; small prey may be swallowed alive. Rodents make up over half of the diet in most areas, along with moles, birds and their eggs, lizards and frogs. A study of kingsnakes and ratsnakes, including corn snakes, found similar pulling strength in all species but significantly higher constriction pressures in kingsnakes, so the corn snake is a capable but not exceptional constrictor. Its muscles sit at lengths that favour force as the coil tightens.
weaknesses: Small, slender body with little absolute power.
No armor or venom.
Hunted by foxes, opossums, skunks, bobcats, weasels and hawks.
Constriction weaker than that of kingsnakes of similar size.

crowned-eagle.name: Crowned Eagle
crowned-eagle.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 4.0 kg, 90.0 cm total length, about 1.7 m wingspan. She is the larger and heavier sex and therefore the stronger fighting form.
crowned-eagle.summary: The Crowned Eagle is Africa's most powerful forest eagle. The canonical female weighs about 4 kg but has thick legs and massive talons that regularly kill monkeys and small antelope far heavier than herself. It attacks inside closed forest with short, broad wings, but its small absolute mass and lack of armor keep it far below large mammals in raw power and defense.
narrative: The crowned eagle packs an unusually heavy weapon system into a medium-sized raptor. At about 4 kg for the canonical female it is lighter than a golden eagle, yet its legs are thick, its toes heavy and its talons wide and strongly curved. It is built for one decisive move: a short forest attack onto a monkey or small antelope, followed by a crushing grip.

Field data support the reputation. Under two Ugandan nests over three years, primate remains dominated, and the eagles took adult male monkeys more often than expected, not just easy juveniles. Elsewhere the same bird lives on rock hyraxes, duikers and, in South African suburbs, the hyraxes and vervets of garden greenspace. That flexibility, together with selective choice of monkey prey, makes it a thoughtful predator for a raptor.

In an absolute matchup its limits are the limits of a 4 kg bird. It has no armor, a light skeleton and short wings built for forest attacks, not long chases. It wins by choosing the moment of contact inside cover. On open ground, or against a heavy grappler that survives the first strike, its advantages fade quickly.

sections.habitat: The crowned eagle occurs across sub-Saharan Africa in closed forest, riverine and gallery forest, dense woodland and wooded gorges. In southern Africa it is limited to eastern regions. A breeding population also lives in the wooded suburbs and greenspaces of Durban and Pietermaritzburg in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa.
sections.diet: It is a mammal-focused apex predator. Main prey across the range are monkeys, small antelope (duikers, chevrotains, young bushbuck), rock hyraxes, rodents and viverrids. In equatorial rainforest, estimates put monkeys at roughly 25–90% of the diet; in savanna and forest-island habitats primates are taken less often and hyraxes and duikers more often. In urban KwaZulu-Natal, rock hyrax was the main prey, and vervet monkeys were more important where hyraxes were absent.
sections.social: Adults live in territorial pairs, and no cooperative hunting was documented in the sources reviewed. The young depend on the parents for a long time after fledging.
sections.reproduction: Pairs usually raise one chick every two years, with a breeding cycle of about 500 days, because the young stay dependent for so long. The stick nest is lined with fresh green branches and reused for years; building one from scratch can take about five months.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List, with a decreasing population estimated at roughly 5,000–50,000 mature individuals. The main threats are loss and fragmentation of African forest and the bushmeat trade. Urban populations face additional human-caused threats and conflicts, reviewed in a 2021 study of urban crowned eagles.
sections.features:
Thick, heavy legs and wide, massive talons.
Short, broad, rounded wings and long tail for forest attacks.
A two-year breeding cycle with a long period of dependence for the young.
Large, long-used stick nests.
Prey choice that shifts with habitat.
sections.humanInteraction: Crowned eagles sometimes live near people in wooded suburbs. South African researchers placed time-lapse cameras at 11 urban nests to check how often prey with human associations was taken, and use GPS tracking to understand how urban pairs use space, with the aim of reducing conflict.

funFacts: In a 37-month Kibale study, primates made up the great majority of prey remains under two nests.
The eagles took male monkeys more often than females, even though males are larger and more combative.
Nests can grow to about 2.4 m across and 3 m deep after years of reuse.
A single breeding cycle lasts roughly 500 days, so a pair raises at most one young every two years.
A 4 kg female can kill antelope several times her weight; bushbuck up to about 30 kg are an exceptional record.
Urban eagles in KwaZulu-Natal live mostly on rock hyraxes.
Building a new nest from scratch can take a pair about five months.

abilities.name: Broad-Wing Forest Strike
abilities.description: short, broad, rounded wings and a long tail let the eagle attack inside closed forest, where monkeys and duikers live, instead of needing open sky. This turns forest cover into a first-strike advantage.

abilities.name: Crushing Talon Grip
abilities.description: thick legs and wide, heavy talons clamp and pierce prey until it stops moving, letting a 4 kg eagle kill monkeys and small antelope well above its own weight.

traits.name: Primate Hunter of Africa
traits.description: in Ugandan rainforest, primates made up the great majority of prey remains, and eagles took adult males more often than expected.

traits.name: Great Stick Nest
traits.description: pairs reuse and enlarge the same nest for many years; nests can reach about 2.4 m across and 3 m deep and may pass to a new pair.

combat.weapons:
The feet are the main weapon: thick legs, heavy toes and wide, strongly curved talons that crush and pierce. The hooked bill is used after the prey is controlled. Throughout its range, the main prey are monkeys, small antelope such as duikers and chevrotains, rock hyraxes, rodents and viverrids. Mammals make up most of the diet.

Evidence of weapon power comes from long-term prey studies. In a 37-month study in Kibale National Park, Uganda, prey remains collected under the nests of two pairs were mostly primates. The eagles took adult and juvenile monkeys roughly in proportion to their abundance and took males more often than females, even though the males are the larger, better-armed sex. A related taphonomic study documented the damage the eagles leave on monkey skulls and skeletons. Popular and institutional summaries describe kills of antelope weighing several times the eagle's own mass, with bushbuck up to about 30 kg as an exceptional upper record. These are extremes, not the typical kill.
weaknesses: Only about 4 kg in absolute mass.
No armor; light avian skeleton.
Short wings reduce open-country pursuit and soaring efficiency.
Loses its advantage if grounded or caught by a large terrestrial grappler.

eastern-brown-snake.name: Eastern Brown Snake
eastern-brown-snake.specimen: healthy robust adult, 1.0 kg and 150 cm total length, sex unspecified. This pass did not verify a consistent adult size difference between the sexes, so no sex-based modifier is applied.
eastern-brown-snake.summary: The eastern brown snake is a fast, slender Australian snake whose venom sets off runaway blood clotting and can cause sudden collapse. Its venom is among the most toxic of any snake, and it causes more snakebite deaths in Australia than any other species. Yet at about a kilogram it is physically fragile, and it usually warns before it strikes.
narrative: The eastern brown snake shows why venom mechanism matters more than size for snakes. At around 1.5 m and a kilogram it is light and unarmored, with almost no raw strength. What makes it dangerous is a venom that attacks the blood itself: a prothrombin activator that copies the body's own clotting enzymes, starting a runaway clotting reaction that uses up the clotting factors and can collapse circulation. Rodents injected with this protein suffered instant circulatory failure.

Its behavior is more measured than its reputation. When researchers harassed brown snakes under controlled conditions, the snakes were surprisingly tolerant, usually warned before striking, and delivered potentially serious bites in only about 15% of strikes. The raised neck display is a warning first and a launch position second.

The snake's danger to people comes from where it lives. It thrives in farmland and suburban edges full of mice and rats, so people meet it often, and bites typically happen when someone tries to kill or catch it. For battle ratings, its strengths are a fast, agile body and a venom that can drop much bigger animals. Its weaknesses are a fragile body, small and often partial venom doses, and dependence on warm weather.

sections.habitat: Eastern brown snakes live throughout much of eastern Australia and in parts of southern New Guinea. They use coastal heath, dry sclerophyll forest and woodland, and are frequently found in grassland, farmland and other disturbed land.
sections.diet: Mostly small mammals, especially introduced house mice and rats, plus frogs, reptiles, reptile eggs and birds. Farmland with abundant rodents supports good numbers of brown snakes, which in turn control pests.
sections.social: Solitary outside breeding.
sections.reproduction: Egg-laying. Sexual maturity is reached at about 2–3 years, and clutches of roughly 10–35 eggs are reported. Females develop yolking follicles from mid-September to late November and carry eggs from late October to late January.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List category was not confirmed in this pass. The species is widespread and common in eastern Australia, including heavily modified farmland. Radio-tracking in the Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area found human-related causes among the main sources of death for large elapids there, and Shine (2024) argues that farmers should not kill venomous snakes.
sections.features:
Front fangs delivering a venom with a prothrombin activator and neurotoxins.
One of the most toxic snake venoms known.
Slender, fast body.
Raised-neck warning display before striking.
Tolerance of farmland and suburban edges.
sections.humanInteraction: The eastern brown snake causes more snakebite deaths than any other species in Australia. Brown snakes accounted for 23 of 35 snakebite deaths recorded by the National Coronial Information System from January 2000 to December 2016, and about one to two deaths a year are attributed to eastern brown bites despite antivenom and first aid. Deaths are linked to venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy and early cardiovascular collapse. Most bites happen when people try to kill or handle the snake.

funFacts: Its venom has been described as the second most toxic snake venom known.
Its prothrombin activator closely copies the body's own clotting enzymes (activated factor X bound to factor V).
In harassment trials, only about 15% of its strikes had the potential to cause a serious envenomation.
It usually gives a warning display before it strikes.
Brown snakes caused 23 of 35 Australian snakebite deaths recorded from 2000 to 2016.
The largest reliably measured eastern brown snake was 2013 mm long.
It favors introduced house mice and rats, making farmland ideal habitat.

abilities.name: Clot-Cascade Venom
abilities.description: a prothrombin activator that mimics the body's own clotting enzymes sets off runaway clotting, using up clotting factors and, in rodent tests, causing instant circulatory failure. Pre- and postsynaptic neurotoxins add paralysis.

abilities.name: Warning-Then-Strike Defense
abilities.description: the snake raises its neck in a threat display and usually warns before it strikes. Many defensive strikes carry little venom, but a committed bite is extremely dangerous.

traits.name: Farmland Rat Hunter
traits.description: it thrives in farmland and disturbed land, where introduced rats and mice are its favorite prey, which puts it close to people.

traits.name: Warm-Weather Racer
traits.description: it moves surprisingly fast on hot days, and field trials show its defensive behavior changes with body temperature.

combat.weapons: The primary weapon is a front-fanged bite delivering a venom built around a prothrombin activator. It triggers runaway clotting that uses up the blood's clotting factors, and it can cause sudden cardiovascular collapse. Pre- and postsynaptic neurotoxins add paralysing effects. The secondary weapon is speed and a fast, well-aimed strike from a raised neck posture.
weaknesses: Very low body mass and no armor.
Many defensive strikes deliver little venom.
Performance drops when cold.
No constriction or mechanical weapon to hold a large opponent.

eclectus-parrot.name: Eclectus Parrot
eclectus-parrot.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 0.45 kg, 38.0 cm total length. Females are the fighting sex: they monopolize scarce nest hollows and fight other females, sometimes to the death, to hold them. ADW states the sexes are similar in size, with males tending to be larger, so the female is used without a mass penalty that matters on the roster scale.
eclectus-parrot.summary: The Eclectus Parrot is a stocky rainforest parrot from New Guinea, nearby islands and Cape York, famous because green males and red females look like different species. Females own the scarce nest hollows and will fight rivals to the death over them. In an absolute fight, though, it is a 0.45 kg bird with a hooked bill and no armor.
narrative: The eclectus parrot turns the usual bird pattern upside down. The female is the brilliant one, red with blue or purple, and she is the one who fights. Good nest hollows high in emergent rainforest trees are rare, so a female that finds one stays with it for most of the year, displaying from the entrance and driving off rival females, sometimes fatally. Males, emerald green and camouflaged in the canopy, spend their time foraging and bringing food, often several of them to one female.

Long-term field work on Cape York showed how unusual this system is. Females mate with several males, groups of males cooperate to feed one brood, and mothers can control the sex of their chicks, often removing young sons from poorer hollows within days of hatching. The male's green plumage also reflects ultraviolet light, which makes him bright to females but hard for predators to see.

In an absolute matchup the eclectus is a mid-sized parrot of about 0.45 kg. The female's readiness to fight over a hollow gives it more ferocity than most parrots, but it has no measured bite, no armor and no talons. It is dangerous only to small rivals at its nest.

sections.habitat: Eclectus parrots live in lowland rainforest from the Moluccas and New Guinea to the Bismarck Archipelago, the Solomon Islands and the tip of Cape York Peninsula, Australia, where they are restricted to rainforest in the Iron and McIlwraith ranges (Legge et al. 2004). They stay mostly in the canopy and nest in emergent trees. They have been introduced to Palau, Singapore and the Goram Islands (ADW).
sections.diet: They feed mainly on fruit and fruit pulp, plus seeds, leaf buds, blossoms, nectar, figs and nuts (Wikipedia, citing Birds of the World). Their oesophagus and proventriculus are wide and stretchy, letting them take in large amounts of food quickly.
sections.social: The breeding system is unusual for a parrot. Females mate with several males, and groups can include several males and several females. Multiple males cooperate to feed one female and her chicks. At Iron Range, Cape York, an estimated 538–596 breeding females shared the forest with 1,059–1,173 males (Legge et al. 2004).
sections.reproduction: Females lay two eggs per clutch in hollows 14–30 m up, incubate for about 28 days, and often fledge only one chick. Chicks fledge at about 13 weeks and become independent at about 6 months; both sexes mature at about 3 years (ADW). Females can bias offspring sex and in poorer hollows often remove male nestlings shortly after hatching (Heinsohn et al. 2011).
sections.conservation: The Moluccan and Papuan eclectus are both listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, though some small island populations are rarer. The Australian population is small (around 540–600 breeding females at Iron Range) and depends on scarce large nest trees, so it is considered vulnerable to habitat loss (Legge et al. 2004).
sections.features:
Most extreme male-female colour difference of any parrot.
Ultraviolet-reflecting male plumage.
Cooperative polyandry, unique among parrots.
Offspring sex control and sex-specific removal of chicks.
Dependence on high, deep rainforest nest hollows.
sections.humanInteraction: Eclectus parrots are popular pets and do well in captivity, though they were not bred in large numbers until the 1980s. Their feathers are used as decorations by people in New Guinea, and in some areas they are considered crop pests. Pet eclectus are often of Vosmaer's, Solomon Island or red-sided (Papuan) forms.

funFacts: Male and female eclectus look so different that scientists once thought they were two species.
Female eclectus parrots may fight to the death over a good nest hollow.
A female can stay at her nest hollow for up to 11 months a year while males bring her food.
Several males may cooperate to feed one female's chicks, something no other parrot is known to do.
The male's green feathers reflect ultraviolet light that females can see.
Eclectus mothers often remove newly hatched sons from poorer nest hollows.
At Iron Range in Australia, males outnumber breeding females about two to one.

abilities.name: Hollow Duelist
abilities.description: a female that owns a good nest hollow stays with it for most of the year and fights rival females, sometimes to the death, to keep it.

abilities.name: Canopy Cloak
abilities.description: the male's emerald green plumage hides him from predators while he forages in the canopy, yet its ultraviolet sheen makes him stand out to eclectus females.

traits.name: Reversed Colour Pair
traits.description: the most extreme colour difference of any parrot: red-and-blue females and green males, so different that they were once named as separate species.

traits.name: Sex-Choosing Mothers
traits.description: eclectus mothers can bias the sex of their chicks, and in poorer hollows they often remove male nestlings within three days of hatching.

combat.weapons: The bill is the only weapon. No force measurement exists, but eclectus parrots are mid-sized parrots with strongly hooked bills that open fruit, nuts and seeds. The key combat evidence is behavioral: females that own a good nest hollow stay in or near it for up to 11 months a year and fight off other females, sometimes to the death (Heinsohn 2008 as summarized on Wikipedia). This shows a willingness to fight hard over a resource, not an ability to kill larger animals.
weaknesses: About 0.45 kg in absolute mass.
No armor.
Depends on rare large nest hollows.
Low breeding success; females often fledge only one chick.

elephant-seal.name: Elephant Seal
elephant-seal.specimen: healthy mature adult male (bull), 3,000.0 kg and 460.0 cm total length, representing a harem-holding bull rather than a record giant.
elephant-seal.summary: The southern elephant seal is the largest seal and the largest carnivoran on Earth, with bulls around 3 tonnes. Rival bulls rear up and slam into each other with bites to the neck, and at sea the species makes near-continuous dives to hundreds of metres, with a record of 2,388 m. It is enormous and very hard to wear down, but slow on land and armed with little beyond teeth and mass.
narrative: On a sub-Antarctic beach in the breeding season, a harem bull is an intimidating sight. Three tonnes of blubber and muscle rears up on its fore-flippers, the swollen trunk-like nose roaring, the chest crashing down on the sand. When displays fail, rival bulls tower over each other and lunge, biting at the neck and leaning with all their weight until one gives way. Most contests are over in minutes, and older, larger bulls usually win access to the females.

At sea the same animal becomes one of the most extreme divers on the planet. For months it barely stops diving, spending up to about 90% of its time underwater and surfacing for only a couple of minutes between dives that routinely reach hundreds of metres. It has been recorded at 2,388 m. Twice the blood volume of a land mammal, extra haemoglobin and oxygen-rich muscles make this possible. The ocean has few places an elephant seal cannot go, and few animals that can follow it there.

In ABS terms the elephant seal is a titan built for endurance rather than killing. Its Stamina and Special are near the top of the roster because of its diving physiology, and its Defense is high because of its sheer mass and blubber. Its Attack is moderate because its weapons are limited to canine bites and body slams, and its Agility is low. Killer whales can still take elephant seals, especially young ones, but a full-grown bull in deep water is one of the hardest animals in the ocean to catch or wear down.

sections.habitat: Southern elephant seals breed on sub-Antarctic islands such as South Georgia, Kerguelen and Marion, and on the Península Valdés coast of Argentina. At sea they range across the Southern Ocean to the Antarctic ice edge, foraging along boundaries between water masses.
sections.diet: They eat mainly squid, including glacial squid and smooth hooked squid, and a range of fish, caught during deep dives. Killer whales prey on elephant seals, with high success against newly weaned pups and much lower success against older animals.
sections.social: On land during breeding, dominant bulls hold harems of females, from a few dozen to several hundred at large colonies, while lower-ranking males wait at the edges. At sea elephant seals travel and feed alone.
sections.reproduction: Females give birth on the breeding beaches, where dominant bulls hold harems. Weaned pups later go to sea on their own, a vulnerable stage when killer whales take many of them. Harem bulls are older and larger than other males, so only a minority of males win breeding access. Females live longer than males on average.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. The global population was estimated at about 650,000 in the mid-1990s and 664,000–740,000 in 2005, with recent summaries near 700,000, though trends differ between breeding populations. In 2023 highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 killed an estimated 17,000 southern elephant seals at Península Valdés, including at least 95–96% of pups in surveyed areas, with evidence of mammal-to-mammal spread. Population models predict a long recovery for that colony.
sections.features:
Largest body size of any seal and any carnivoran.
Inflatable proboscis in adult males.
Very large blood volume and high haemoglobin for oxygen storage.
Thick blubber for insulation and energy.
Large canines used in male contests.
Large eyes suited to dim, deep water.
sections.humanInteraction: Elephant seals were once hunted commercially for their blubber oil. Today they are major attractions for visitors to sub-Antarctic islands and Península Valdés, and they are widely studied with tags that record their dives and movements.

funFacts: The deepest dive recorded for an elephant seal is 2,388 m.
At sea elephant seals spend up to about 90% of their time underwater, taking breaks of only about two minutes.
A mature bull can weigh up to ten times as much as a female.
Elephant seals have about twice the blood volume of a land mammal their size.
Northern elephant seals, a separate species, were found to sleep only about two hours a day at sea, often while spiralling down during dives.
The 2023 bird-flu outbreak at Península Valdés killed about 17,000 southern elephant seals.

abilities.name: Abyssal Breath-Hold
abilities.description: routine dives last 20–30 minutes to 400–800 m, with a record of 2,388 m, backed by twice a land mammal's blood volume and extra haemoglobin. In a battle at sea it can simply go where an opponent cannot follow.

abilities.name: Rear-and-Slam Duel
abilities.description: bulls rear up on their fore-flippers, then crash down and lunge, biting at a rival's neck with large canines and bearing down with three tonnes of body.

traits.name: Largest Carnivoran on Earth
traits.description: the southern elephant seal is the largest pinniped and the largest member of the order Carnivora, with bulls around 3,000–3,700 kg.

traits.name: Trunk-Nosed Bull
traits.description: adult males grow an inflatable proboscis used to produce extremely loud roars in the breeding season.

combat.weapons: The elephant seal's fighting power comes from sheer mass and its canine teeth. Rival bulls rear up on their fore-flippers to tower over each other, then lunge and slam, biting at the neck and leaning their weight against the opponent. Most contests end within a few minutes when one bull retreats. Outside the breeding beach the elephant seal is not a predator of large animals; it eats squid and fish. Its offense is therefore a crushing, biting shove from a 3-tonne body, dangerous at close range but slow and short-reaching.
weaknesses: Very slow and clumsy on land.
Limited offensive weapons beyond bite and mass.
No armor; killer whales take weaned pups and occasionally larger seals.
Not a fast, agile swimmer.
Low aggression outside the breeding season.

ethiopian-wolf.name: Ethiopian Wolf
ethiopian-wolf.specimen: healthy mature adult male of about 17.0 kg, head-body about 98 cm, shoulder height about 60 cm. This is a little above the male average of 16.2 kg and well inside the 14.2–19.3 kg male range.
ethiopian-wolf.summary: The Ethiopian wolf is a rare, coyote-sized red wolf that lives only on the high plateaus of Ethiopia. At about 17 kg it is a fast, sharp-eyed rodent specialist that pounces on mole-rats and even hunts among gelada troops, but its light jaws and small size leave it outmatched by larger predators.
narrative: The Ethiopian wolf is one of the most striking canids in the world: a slender, long-legged animal with a fox-red coat, white throat and chest, and a long, narrow muzzle. A mature male weighs about 17 kg, about the same as a coyote. It lives only above about 3,000 m on Ethiopia's Afroalpine plateaus, where giant lobelias grow and the ground is honeycombed with rodent burrows.

It is a specialist in a family of generalists. Almost all of its prey are rodents, especially mole-rats, which it catches by standing motionless over a burrow and pouncing, or by digging them out. Its skull and small, widely spaced teeth suit that job well. It also uses clever tricks: it forages among cattle and among troops of gelada monkeys, where rodents seem less wary, and it licks nectar from red-hot poker flowers.

Ethiopian wolves live in close-knit packs that patrol and defend small territories together, yet they hunt alone. In a battle context the species is a light, quick canid with good senses and tactics but a weak weapon set for large opponents. It rates just below the coyote in Attack and well below the gray wolf, while its Intelligence and Agility stay in the upper band for medium canids.

sections.habitat: Endemic to the Ethiopian Highlands. It lives in Afroalpine grassland and heathland above about 3,000 m, in a mosaic of tussock grass, Euryops bushes and giant lobelias favoured by its rodent prey. More than half of the population lives in the Bale Mountains, with smaller populations in the Simien, Arsi and other ranges.
sections.diet: Almost entirely a rodent specialist: big-headed African mole-rats in Bale, Northeast African mole-rats where the larger species is absent, plus grass rats, brush-furred rats and highland hares. It occasionally hunts young antelopes and lambs in groups, scavenges, and licks nectar from Kniphofia foliosa flowers. As the top predator of the Afroalpine zone it helps control rodent numbers.
sections.social: Packs of related males with a few females share a territory, patrol it together, scent mark and greet each other with group yip-howls, but forage mainly alone. Males usually stay in their birth pack for life, while most females disperse at about two years. Mating outside the pack is common.
sections.reproduction: The dominant female gives birth once a year, between October and January. All pack members help feed the pups with regurgitated food, and subordinate females sometimes suckle the dominant female's pups. Both sexes mature in their second year.
sections.conservation: Endangered on the IUCN Red List. The 2011 estimate was 360–440 adults, and the Ethiopian Wolf Conservation Programme describes some 500 surviving in small populations. It was listed as Critically Endangered in 1994 after rabies outbreaks and shooting devastated Bale packs. Main threats are habitat loss from farming and overgrazing, disease from domestic dogs (in 2019 rabies and canine distemper struck the same population at once), road deaths and hybridisation with dogs. Habitat models project that suitable climate may shrink sharply under climate change. Conservation relies on dog vaccination, wolf vaccination, monitoring and community programmes; in 2024–25 the programme monitored 41 packs in six populations.
sections.features:
Long, narrow skull with small, widely spaced teeth.
Red coat with white throat, chest and underparts.
Bushy tail with a black tip.
High-altitude life above 3,000 m.
Long-range howls audible about 5 km away.
sections.humanInteraction: Local herders generally see it as harmless to livestock, although some surveys in Bale report it among livestock predators. The biggest human-linked risks are free-ranging dogs, which spread disease and hybridise with wolves, and habitat loss to farming and grazing. It is a flagship species for Ethiopia's mountain parks.

funFacts: It is Africa's most endangered carnivore.
Rodents made up almost 96% of its prey in one study.
It licks nectar from red-hot poker flowers and may help pollinate them.
It hunts among gelada monkey troops, which improves its rodent catch.
Its howls can be heard about 5 km away.
Even though it lives in packs, it usually hunts alone.
Subordinate females sometimes suckle the dominant female's pups.

abilities.name: Mole-Rat Pounce
abilities.description: it stands motionless over a burrow system, then pounces the moment a rodent appears, and digs furiously when it misses. Rodents made up 95.8% of prey items in one study.

abilities.name: Gelada Cover Hunt
abilities.description: it walks among grazing gelada troops and cattle herds, which hide its approach, and catches rodents far more often when hunting inside a gelada troop.

traits.name: Roof-of-Africa Wolf
traits.description: it lives only in seven isolated Ethiopian mountain ranges at about 3,000–4,500 m, with only a few hundred adults left.

traits.name: Nectar Licker
traits.description: it licks nectar from red-hot poker flowers and carries pollen on its muzzle, making it a possible pollinator, something almost unknown in large carnivores.

combat.weapons: The Ethiopian wolf is a specialist rodent hunter. Its long, narrow muzzle and small, widely spaced teeth are built for seizing small animals quickly, not for holding and tearing large prey. Rodents made up 95.8% of prey items in one study, dominated by the big-headed African mole-rat (up to about 900 g) and grass rats. It also takes highland hares and, occasionally hunting in a group, young antelopes and lambs. Against an opponent of its own size its bite is a real weapon, but it has little experience subduing large, dangerous animals.
weaknesses: Only about 17 kg, with small, widely spaced teeth.
Little experience fighting or killing large, dangerous animals.
No armor.
Susceptible to diseases carried by dogs, notably rabies and canine distemper.
