eurasian-eagle-owl.name: Eurasian Eagle-Owl
eurasian-eagle-owl.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 3.0 kg, 70.0 cm total length and about 1.8 m wingspan. She is the heavier sex and therefore the stronger fighting form.
eurasian-eagle-owl.summary: The Eurasian Eagle-Owl is one of the world's largest owls, about 3 kg in the canonical female with a wingspan near 1.8 m. It hunts at night from high perches, taking rats, rabbits and hedgehogs and even killing other birds of prey. It is powerful for a bird, but its low absolute mass and lack of armor keep it far below mammals in raw power and defense.
narrative: The Eurasian eagle-owl is the night-time counterpart of the great eagles. Females reach around 3–4 kg with wings spanning well over 1.5 m, and the species is ranked with Blakiston's fish owl as the largest owl alive. It roosts high in trees through the day, and from dusk onward it hunts across woodland edges and open country.

Its diet is extremely broad. Voles and rats make up much of it, but the owl also takes hares, rabbits, hedgehogs, waterbirds and crows, and it has a reputation among raptor researchers as a killer of other birds of prey, from buzzards and goshawks to smaller owls. Studies even show it choosing smaller rabbits when it can, a sign that it hunts with efficiency, not just raw ambition.

In an absolute matchup its strengths are timing and surprise. A 3 kg owl striking at night can kill animals much larger than most birds could handle. But it has no armor and a light skeleton, and when it has to eat large prey on the ground, foxes and other predators can steal the kill or attack the owl. In daylight open-country contests or against large, tough opponents, its advantages fall away.

sections.habitat: The Eurasian eagle-owl is found across much of Europe and Asia. The studies cited here come from southwestern Europe, Romania, goshawk and buzzard study areas in Europe, Israel's Judean region and Pakistan, which shows how widely it is distributed. It needs high perches for daytime roosting and open or edge habitat where it can hunt at night.
sections.diet: It is a top nocturnal predator with one of the broadest diets of any owl. Voles and rats are the most common prey; hares, rabbits, hedgehogs, ducks, grouse, crows, seabirds and other raptors are also taken, with rare records of foxes, marmots and young deer. Where rabbits are common they can dominate the diet, and the owl prefers smaller rabbits. In Judea, Israel, breeding success did not depend on the local prey base.
sections.social: Adults are solitary outside mating and strongly territorial, defending territories against other owls and overlapping only slightly when food is scarce. They call loudly to mark territory and are heard far more often than seen.
sections.reproduction: ADW reports a breeding season from December to April. Young leave the nest area or are driven out by the adults between September and November. Ring recoveries show wild individuals can exceed 20 years of age.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern, with a total population often summarized at about 100,000–500,000 individuals and a decreasing trend. Local declines and recoveries vary widely; in parts of Europe, expanding eagle-owl populations are now studied for their effects on other raptors.
sections.features:
Among the largest owls in the world.
Nocturnal activity with daytime roosting high in trees.
Powerful talons able to kill hares, hedgehogs and other raptors.
Loud territorial calls.
Extremely broad, flexible diet.
sections.humanInteraction: Eagle-owls can live in mixed landscapes near people, where rats and rabbits are available. As populations expand in parts of Europe, conservationists study their effect on other protected raptors such as goshawks. Rehabilitated birds are sometimes shown to the public at raptor events.

funFacts: Guinness World Records ranks it with Blakiston's fish owl as the largest owls.
It is heard far more often than seen, thanks to loud territorial calls.
It kills other birds of prey, including other owls.
Hedgehogs, which few predators tackle, are among its prey.
In a rabbit study it preferred rabbits under about 900 g, even though it can kill much larger prey.
Exceptional prey records include foxes and young deer.
Ring recoveries show wild eagle-owls can live more than 20 years.

abilities.name: Dusk Ambush
abilities.description: active from dusk through the night and roosting high in trees by day, the eagle-owl attacks in darkness when many diurnal competitors and prey cannot respond.

abilities.name: Raptor Killer
abilities.description: it kills other birds of prey, including buzzards, goshawks and other owls, and European studies have examined its effect on competing raptors. Against other birds it is often the predator, not the rival.

traits.name: Giant Among Owls
traits.description: Guinness World Records lists it with Blakiston's fish owl as the largest owls, with the largest females about 71 cm long, 190 cm across the wings and 4.2 kg.

traits.name: Spine-Proof Palate
traits.description: hedgehogs, which few other predators take, are part of its diet.

combat.weapons:
The feet and talons seize and kill; the bill tears apart prey. Everyday prey are mostly voles and rats, but the species also takes hares, rabbits, hedgehogs, ducks, grouse, crows, seabirds and other birds of prey, including other owls. Exceptional records include foxes, marmots and young deer; Wikipedia summarizes prey up to about 17 kg when taken by surprise, but these are rare extremes, not the norm.

The species also shows that a heavy predator does not always take the heaviest prey available. In a rabbit size-selection study, eagle-owls positively selected rabbits under about 900 g, and this preference was weaker in winter when rabbits were scarce.
weaknesses: Only about 3 kg in absolute mass.
No armor; light avian skeleton.
Eating large prey on the ground exposes it to foxes and theft.
Less effective in daylight open-country contests with fast diurnal raptors.

false-killer-whale.name: False Killer Whale
false-killer-whale.specimen: healthy prime adult male, 550 cm long and 1,300 kg.
false-killer-whale.summary: The false killer whale is a 1.3-tonne, thick-toothed oceanic dolphin that hunts tuna and mahi-mahi at speed, shares its catch and has attacked sperm whales and humpbacks in groups. Fast, deep-diving and armed with biosonar, it is dangerous in a pack, but one animal is far smaller than the orca it resembles.
narrative: The false killer whale looks like a slimmer, all-dark orca, and it hunts like a smaller one. A big male is about 5.5 m long and 1.3 tonnes, with thick conical teeth and a streamlined body that has been clocked at 8 m/s. It chases large, fast fish such as tuna and mahi-mahi, often leaping clear of the water at the moment of attack, and tears them apart with its teeth.

What makes it formidable is teamwork. False killer whales spread out in small groups across tens of kilometers of ocean, then converge when one finds prey, and the catch is often shared. Groups have attacked sperm whales in the Galápagos and have been reported hunting humpbacks. They echolocate, and experiments show they actively adjust their hearing while clicking so that faint echoes stay clear.

In a one-on-one battle the picture is more modest. A single false killer whale has no armor and is a fraction of an orca's size, and orcas prey on it. Its ratings therefore sit well above most marine mammals of its size in Attack, Agility and Intelligence, but clearly below the orca in every category.

sections.habitat: False killer whales live in tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide, generally in deep offshore waters over 3,300 feet (1,000 m) deep (NOAA). Some populations, such as the main Hawaiian Islands insular population, stay close to islands, rarely more than 70 km from shore.
sections.diet: They are top predators of large fish and squid, including mahi-mahi, wahoo and tuna (Wikipedia; NOAA), and sometimes attack other marine mammals, from smaller dolphins to sperm whales and humpbacks (Palacios & Mate 1996; Wikipedia). Around Hawaiʻi they dive mostly within the upper ocean but regularly go below 1,000 m, diving deeper by day and at full moon (Kratofil et al. 2026).
sections.social: False killer whales are gregarious and form strong, long-term social bonds. They travel in small subgroups linked into larger clusters and often share captured prey (NOAA). Some individuals stay together for at least 15 years, and groups appear to be centered on females (Wikipedia).
sections.reproduction: Females mature at 8 to 11 years and males 8 to 10 years later. Gestation lasts 11 to 16 months and nursing 1.5 to 2 years; births are about 7 years apart. Females enter menopause at about 44 to 55 years (NOAA).
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2018 assessment, as summarized by Wikipedia). In the US, only the main Hawaiian Islands insular population is listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act; it numbers about 140 animals and has declined about 3.5% a year for at least a decade, with fishery interactions a leading threat (NOAA).
sections.features:
Echolocation with active control of hearing during clicks.
Thick conical teeth.
Long, S-shaped flippers with a distinct hump on the leading edge (NOAA).
Strong social bonds, prey sharing and post-reproductive females.
Deep dives beyond 1,000 m.
sections.humanInteraction: False killer whales take fish and bait from fishing lines, and hooking and entanglement are among the main threats to them (NOAA). They are also taken in drive hunts in some Japanese villages and have been kept in aquariums (Wikipedia).

funFacts: The name comes from a skull that looks like an orca's, but it is a large dolphin.
Crassidens means "thick-toothed".
When one false killer whale catches a fish, others often gather round and share it.
A tagged false killer whale dove to 1,424 m.
Females can live decades after they stop reproducing, as in orcas.
Over 800 false killer whales stranded together in Argentina in 1946.

abilities.name: Gain-Control Sonar
abilities.description: the false killer whale echolocates and actively turns down its hearing of its own loud clicks while keeping faint echoes audible, so it can track prey in dark, deep water. In a battle it can find and follow an opponent without light.

abilities.name: Thick-Tooth Tear
abilities.description: rows of thick conical teeth let it grip, shake and tear large, fast fish and bite at the bodies of whales. It is the main damage tool of a large, fast predator.

traits.name: Prey-Sharing Clusters
traits.description: false killer whales spread out in small groups across tens of kilometers, then converge when one catches prey, which is often shared among several animals.

traits.name: Deep-Water Sprinter
traits.description: tagged Hawaiian animals dove to 1,424 m, and trained animals sprinted at 8 m/s, combining depth and speed in one large dolphin.

combat.weapons: The false killer whale is a large toothed predator with thick, conical teeth. It hunts big, fast fish such as mahi-mahi, wahoo and tuna (Wikipedia), and has been seen shaking prey until the head and guts come off and peeling fish with its teeth (ADW). It also attacks marine mammals: it takes smaller dolphins, has attacked sperm whales in the Galápagos (Palacios & Mate 1996), attacked a humpback calf, and in 2025 was reported hunting two humpback whales with a group of more than 50 (Wikipedia). NOAA notes it often leaps clear of the water when attacking prey.
weaknesses: No armor; blubber and muscle only.
A single animal is much smaller than the orca it resembles.
Much of its power comes from the group, which is absent in a one-on-one matchup.
Prone to mass strandings and heavily affected by fishing gear.

fancy-rat.name: Fancy Rat
fancy-rat.specimen: healthy adult male (buck) of about 0.5 kg, a typical pet male rather than an obese or record animal.
fancy-rat.summary: The fancy rat is the tame, domestic form of the brown rat: a 0.5 kg climber, swimmer and problem-solver with sharp incisors, keen ears and a strong bite for its size. Clever and resilient, it is a real threat to mice and small birds but a lightweight on the absolute scale, with no armor and little reach.
narrative: The fancy rat is the brown rat that learned to live on people's shoulders. It shares its body plan with the wild city rat: a compact, long-tailed rodent with sharp, ever-growing incisors, a keen nose, whiskers that map the dark, and hearing that extends far into ultrasound. It climbs slim poles, swims well and remembers complex routes, and it is one of the most studied learners in science.

In a fight, a rat bites fast and hard for its size and grips with its claws, and wild rats kill poultry, eggs and small wildlife. Domestication has softened its temper: pet rats are tame, box and wrestle instead of fleeing, and rarely bite people unless frightened. On the absolute ABS scale, however, even a large 0.5 kg male has very little power or protection. It scores low in Attack and Defense but high in Agility and Intelligence.

Its wild counterpart shows the species' resilience. Brown rats thrive in cities worldwide, often grow too big for cats to tackle, and have spread to islands where they threaten native animals. The pet version keeps the same senses and intelligence in a gentler package.

sections.habitat: Fancy rats live in homes worldwide. Their wild counterpart, the brown rat, lives almost everywhere people do, in cities, sewers, farms, docks, riverbanks and on islands, often near water.
sections.diet: Omnivorous: grain, seeds, fruit, vegetables, meat, insects, eggs and human food waste. Wild brown rats disperse seeds and aerate soil with their burrows, but they also kill poultry and game birds and have driven many island species toward extinction. They carry diseases and parasites that affect people and livestock.
sections.social: Large hierarchical colonies. Dominant rats outcompete subordinates for food and mates; young rats play-fight constantly. Pet rats are best kept in same-sex groups.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is rapid and can happen year-round; a female can raise successive litters without changing her food intake, and can extend pregnancy by over two weeks when food is short. Domestic rats mature and breed earlier than wild ones. Pet rats live about two to three years; most wild rats die within a year.
sections.conservation: Domesticated as the fancy rat. The wild brown rat is Least Concern and is itself one of the world's most damaging invasive mammals.
sections.features:
Continuously growing incisors.
Hearing extending well into ultrasound.
Very highly developed sense of smell.
Long, sensitive whiskers used for navigation in darkness.
Strong climbing and swimming ability.
sections.humanInteraction: The fancy rat began with the rat-catchers of 18th- and 19th-century Europe, who trapped rats for the blood sport of rat-baiting; organized rat shows started in England in 1901, and the same species became the laboratory rat. Today fancy rats are bred in many colors, coat types and ear shapes (such as "Dumbo" rats). Trainers regard them as one of the easiest animals to train. Wild rats remain major pests and disease carriers.

funFacts: Rats make ultrasonic 50 kHz chirps when tickled, which researchers compare to laughter.
Researchers bred rats for high and low "tickle laughter" in just four generations.
Brown rats on Italy's Po River learned from each other to dive for mussels.
The heaviest live brown rat on record weighed 822 g.
In a New York City study, feral cats killed only three rats in five months of filming.
Pet rats see poorly, about 20/600 vision in pigmented rats, but hear far into ultrasound.
Organized rat showing began in 1901, when Mary Douglas brought her pet rats to a National Mouse Club show in Aylesbury, England.

abilities.name: Urban Infiltrator
abilities.description: climbs slim metal poles, swims on the surface and underwater, and remembers routes through dark sewer and burrow networks, so it can reach, or escape through, places most predators cannot follow.

abilities.name: Ultrasonic Channel
abilities.description: hears well into ultrasound and communicates with calls too high for human ears, including the 50 kHz chirps rats make when played with or tickled; in a matchup this mainly aids awareness, not damage.

traits.name: Tame Twin of the City Rat
traits.description: the fancy rat is the same species as the wild brown rat but is tamer, learns faster, has lower stress-hormone levels and smaller organs, and fights by boxing rather than fleeing.

traits.name: Too Big for Most Cats
traits.description: city brown rats often exceed 300 g, and a New York study recorded feral cats killing only three rats in five months, which is why cats make poor rat control.

combat.weapons: The rat's weapons are sharp incisors backed by a strong bite for its size, plus small claws for gripping. Wild brown rats kill poultry, game birds and island wildlife and are omnivorous predators of small animals. Rats fight each other by boxing upright, biting and wrestling. Domestic rats fight differently from wild ones: wild rats almost always flee a lost fight, while caged rats spend long periods in belly-up or boxing positions. Bites can transmit rat-bite fever to people, and an early fancy-rat breeder recorded nearly dying from infected bites.
weaknesses: Tiny absolute mass and reach.
No armor.
Poor vision.
Domestic rats have lost some of the wild rat's digging and swimming ability and fear.

fighting-bull.name: Fighting Bull
fighting-bull.specimen: healthy bull of four to five years at about 520 kg, the age and weight class fought in first-rank Spanish rings, which require bulls to be at least four years old and at least 460 kg.
fighting-bull.summary: The fighting bull is a half-tonne Iberian cattle breed bred for courage: it charges again and again, hooks with long sharp horns and lifts its target off the ground. It is lighter and tires faster than wild buffalo and bison, but few animals match its willingness to attack.
narrative: The toro de lidia is a domestic animal with the temperament of a wild one. Raised free-range on the open oak pastures of Spain, Portugal and southern France, it has been bred for generations for one quality above all: the drive to charge. Breeders test cows for courage before keeping them, keep bloodlines separate, and measure behaviors such as aggressiveness, ferocity and mobility, which studies show are partly heritable.

The result is a compact, muscular bull of about half a tonne with a massive neck hump and long horns. Its attack is simple and brutal. It lowers its head, hooks with one or both horns, then drives its neck upward and swings its head in a circle, lifting and spinning whatever it has caught. Medical records from bullfighting show just how effective that is, with deep thigh and groin wounds and damaged blood vessels the typical result.

For ABS, the fighting bull's standout number is Ferocity. Its Attack sits just below the heavier bison and Cape Buffalo, and its Defense well below them, because it is lighter and has no horn boss. Its Stamina is limited: blood studies show fast metabolic stress in extended runs. It is a sprinter with horns, dangerous in the first minutes of any encounter and vulnerable to an opponent that can avoid the horns and wait it out.

sections.habitat: Raised on extensive free-range estates mainly in the west and southwest of the Iberian Peninsula, and in southern France and numerous Central and South American countries where bullfighting is organized, including Mexico and Colombia.
sections.diet: A grazing herbivore that feeds on grasses and other pasture plants on its home estate, like other domestic cattle. Its ecology is managed by ranchers rather than shaped by predators.
sections.social: Kept in free-range herds managed by ranchers. Breeding is controlled: a pardoned seed bull may be mated with some 30 cows, and bloodlines (encastes) are kept separate with little exchange of breeding animals.
sections.reproduction: Cows are tested in the tienta and, if they pass, are kept for breeding until they stop calving. A bull pardoned in the ring for exceptional performance can become a seed bull, and his offspring are later tested in the ring themselves. Ring bulls must be at least four years old.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed. Spain lists the Lidia as a native breed in its official catalogue of livestock breeds, and its genealogical book is kept by the Unión de Criadores de Toros de Lidia, founded in 1905, representing more than 300 ranches in Spain, Portugal and France. The breed's many small, isolated bloodlines are a genetic management concern.
sections.features:
Long horns in both sexes, which must be intact and even for fighting.
Heavy neck and shoulder muscle hump (morrillo).
Slightly downhill body profile with high withers.
Strong, heritable tendency to charge.
Explosive anaerobic muscle performance.
sections.humanInteraction: Fighting bulls are raised for bullfighting, bull runs and other traditional festivals, which remain controversial. They cause serious injuries: a review of 2012–2019 recorded 1,239 injured patients, with vascular injuries and back gorings the strongest predictors of death. The encierro in Pamplona sees bulls run through city streets at up to about 25 km/h.

funFacts: Spanish law sets minimum weights for bulls by ring category: 460 kg for first-rank rings.
Both bulls and cows of the breed carry long horns.
Aggressiveness in the breed is partly heritable, with estimates around 0.2 to 0.36.
The breed's genealogical book is managed by a breeders' union founded in 1905.
Bulls in the Pamplona encierro run about 850 m of streets in two to three minutes.
A bull that performs exceptionally can be pardoned and retired to breed, living 20 years or more.

abilities.name: Hook-and-Lift Goring
abilities.description: the bull lowers its head to hook the target, then drives its neck upward to lift it off the ground and swings its head in a circle, spinning the victim on the horn and causing deep wounds, most often to the thigh and groin.

abilities.name: Relentless Charge
abilities.description: the breed is bred to charge moving targets again and again without backing off, with measurable heritability for aggressiveness and ferocity.

traits.name: Bred for Bravery
traits.description: kept reproductively isolated from other cattle for generations and divided into bloodlines (encastes) chosen for aggressive behavior, with cows tested for courage before breeding.

traits.name: Ring-Standard Bull
traits.description: Spanish rules fix the fighting bull's minimum age (four years), minimum weight by ring rank (460 kg for first-rank rings), intact and even horns and fully functional vision, making it one of the most tightly specified animals on the roster.

combat.weapons: The fighting bull's weapons are its horns, driven by a fast charge and a powerful neck. Medical studies of bullfighting injuries describe the mechanism: the bull lowers its head as it charges, hooks the target with one or both horns, then extends its neck with great force, lifts the victim off the ground and swings its head in a circle so the victim spins on the horn, causing extensive tissue damage. Across Spain, Portugal and southern France, 1,239 people were treated for bull-horn injuries between 2012 and 2019; goring was the most common mechanism and the thigh and groin the most frequent sites, with vascular damage in about a fifth of thigh and groin gorings.
weaknesses: Tires quickly in prolonged fights.
No armor; flanks and hindquarters are exposed.
Charges moving targets, which a clever opponent can exploit.
Lighter than wild buffalo, bison and gaur.

fin-whale.name: Fin Whale
fin-whale.specimen: healthy physically mature adult female, 20.0 m long and 45,000 kg.
fin-whale.summary: The fin whale is a 45-tonne, 20 m rorqual built for speed: the "greyhound of the sea" can sprint to about 40 km/h and hold escape speeds that force killer whales into long chases. It has no teeth and does not fight back, so it survives on mass, endurance and running rather than weapons.
narrative: The fin whale is the second-largest animal alive, but its real signature is speed. Its body is long and slender, with a sharply V-shaped head and small pectoral fins, and it can reach about 40 km/h. Early whalers did not target it because it was too fast and lived far offshore. For killer whales the problem is the same: Ford and Reeves describe the fin whale as a "flight" species that responds to attack by swimming hard and straight, and the rare successful kills recorded took packs of orcas an hour of pursuit.

That strategy defines how it would fight. A 45-tonne fin whale has enormous raw power and great tissue depth, so a single predator struggles to injure it seriously, and it can simply leave. But it carries no teeth, and it is not known to swing its tail or flippers at attackers the way humpbacks and gray whales do. If it is cornered or overtaken by a coordinated pack, it does little to defend itself.

Its feeding is some of the most explosive behavior in the ocean. A fin whale accelerates into a school, drops its huge reinforced jaw and balloons its pleated throat to engulf a volume of water and prey approaching its own body size, then filters it out through baleen. Males broadcast long infrasonic pulses that are among the most powerful sounds any animal makes. The result is a giant with high Stamina and strong Defense, respectable Agility for its size, and an Attack held down by the lack of any weapon or will to use one.

sections.habitat: Fin whales live in all the world's oceans, mostly in deep offshore waters from temperate to polar latitudes. Many populations migrate between summer feeding grounds and winter areas, while some groups appear to be resident, for example in the Gulf of California, the East China Sea and the Mediterranean Sea (NOAA).
sections.diet: Fin whales eat krill, small schooling fish such as herring, capelin and sand lance, and squid. They lunge into prey with the mouth open, expanding 50 to 100 throat pleats, and can eat up to 2 tons of food a day (NOAA). Tagged whales off Southern California glide during descent, make a series of lunges at depth and then swim steadily back to the surface (Goldbogen et al. 2006). Feeding dives reach about 250 m and last up to around 15 minutes (ADW).
sections.social: Fin whales are often seen in groups of two to seven and sometimes gather in large mixed feeding groups with humpbacks, minke whales and Atlantic white-sided dolphins (NOAA). Only males produce the loud, repeated songs linked with breeding (Croll et al. 2002).
sections.reproduction: Males mature sexually at about 6 to 10 years and females at 7 to 12; physical maturity comes at about 25 years (NOAA). Females give birth to a single calf every 2 to 3 years; calves are about 6 m long at birth (ADW).
sections.conservation: The fin whale is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2018 assessment, as summarized by Wikipedia; the IUCN page itself was not readable in this run) and as endangered throughout its range under the US Endangered Species Act (NOAA). Commercial whaling greatly reduced populations; current threats include ship strikes, to which fin whales are among the most vulnerable species, fishing-gear entanglement and ocean noise (NOAA).
sections.features:
Long, streamlined body built for sustained high speed.
50 to 100 expandable throat pleats for engulfment feeding.
Very large, reinforced lower jaws.
Asymmetrical head coloration.
Extremely loud, low-frequency male songs.
sections.humanInteraction: Whalers did not target fin whales at first because they were fast swimmers living in open ocean (NOAA); commercial whaling later reduced their populations heavily. Today they are seen on whale-watching trips and are vulnerable to collisions with ships.

funFacts: It is the second-largest animal on Earth, after the blue whale.
It is nicknamed the "greyhound of the sea" for its speed.
The right side of its lower jaw is white and the left side dark, and the tongue is colored the opposite way.
A fin whale can eat up to 2 tons of food in a day.
US scientists who first recorded fin whale calls considered equipment faults and geophysical causes before realizing a whale was making them.
Only male fin whales sing the loud songs.

abilities.name: Greyhound Escape Sprint
abilities.description: a long, slim body built for speed lets the fin whale reach about 40 km/h and hold escape speeds that outlast pursuing killer whales. In a battle it can refuse a fight and force a long, costly chase.

abilities.name: Engulfment Lunge
abilities.description: accordion throat pleats and reinforced 3.6 m-scale jaws let it accelerate and engulf a body-sized volume of water and prey in one lunge. It is a feeding tool, but it shows the explosive power a 45-tonne rorqual can generate.

traits.name: Two-Tone Jaw
traits.description: the head is asymmetrically colored, dark on the left lower jaw and white on the right, with the reverse on the tongue, a striking asymmetry that makes the species easy to identify at the surface.

traits.name: Infrasonic Suitor
traits.description: only males make long, patterned 16–40 Hz pulses, among the lowest and most powerful sounds made by any animal, which can travel great distances through the ocean.

combat.weapons: The fin whale has no teeth, claws or horns. Its only damaging tools are the flukes and the momentum of a 45-tonne body. Unlike the humpback, it is not recorded swinging its flippers or flukes at predators. Ford & Reeves (2008) place the fin whale among the "flight" species: when killer whales approach, these whales swim rapidly away, and if overtaken and attacked they do little to defend themselves. Its practical offense is therefore collision and tail strikes from a very large body, not a willingness to press an attack.
weaknesses: No bite or cutting weapon and no habit of fighting back.
Thinner body build and no barnacle or callosity armor compared with "fight" species.
Relatively small flippers limit tight turns.
Coordinated killer whale packs can exhaust and kill adults.
Must surface to breathe; vulnerable to ship strikes (NOAA).

fisher.name: Fisher
fisher.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 5.0 kg, inside the 3.5–6.0 kg male range (Wikipedia) and the 3.5–5.0 kg male range (ADW). The largest male on record weighed 9 kg and is not used as the baseline.
fisher.summary: A long, dark forest mustelid, the fisher is one of the few predators that kills porcupines and has even ambushed Canada lynx in snowstorms. Agile in trees and bold for its size, it is still a 5 kg animal, strong for its weight but small on the absolute scale.
narrative: The fisher is a forest hunter built for persistence. A large male weighs about 5 kg and stretches over a metre with its tail, a low, muscular mustelid that runs along logs, climbs trunks and turns its hind feet backwards to come down head-first. It hunts snowshoe hares, squirrels and mice, and it is famous for tackling porcupines: circling, biting at the face again and again, and finishing the fight after up to half an hour.

Its boldness goes further. In northern Maine, biologists documented fishers killing more than a dozen Canada lynx, attacking them where they lay bedded in snowstorms with a quick bite to the neck. Fishers also kill martens, raccoons and occasionally foxes and bobcats. These feats rely on ambush, timing and relentless attack rather than raw power.

On the absolute scale the fisher remains a small predator. Its 5 kg frame sits well below badgers and honey badgers in mass, and it has no armor. In a straight fight against an alert, larger carnivore, it is at a disadvantage; against animals it can surprise or outlast, it is far more dangerous than its size suggests.

sections.habitat: Boreal and mixed deciduous-coniferous forest across Canada from Nova Scotia to British Columbia and north to Alaska, south into the northern United States, the Appalachians, the Great Lakes region, and the Pacific states. It prefers continuous forest with high canopy cover, large trees and fallen logs, and avoids clear cuts, grassland, farmland and heavily developed areas (WDFW). In the Sierra Nevada, fishers selected cooler, more forested and riparian areas during severe drought.
sections.diet: Snowshoe hares and porcupines are the main prey, supplemented by squirrels, mice, birds, carrion, insects, nuts, berries and mushrooms. Where fishers were trapped out, porcupine numbers rose and damaged timber; when fishers returned, porcupine numbers fell again. A 17-year study found that fisher predation combined with severe winters cut adult porcupine survival by as much as 44% (Ecological Applications 2015).
sections.social: Solitary and territorial. It overlaps with martens without strong separation in space or time in a 2019 Michigan camera-trap study, but it also kills martens.
sections.reproduction: Mating takes place from March to May. Implantation is delayed about ten months, active pregnancy begins around mid-February, and litters are born in spring in tree dens. Kits begin to climb at about eight weeks. Females need moderately large trees for dens.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. It recovered across much of the east after overtrapping and deforestation, but some western populations remain endangered: Washington lists it as a state endangered species and reintroduced 90 fishers to Olympic National Park in 2008–2010; the southern Sierra Nevada population is listed as federally endangered.
sections.features:
Reversible hind ankles and head-first tree descent.
Coarse hairs between foot pads for grip on slippery surfaces.
Long, flexible, muscular mustelid body.
Specialized porcupine-killing behavior.
Delayed implantation of the embryo.
sections.humanInteraction: Once heavily trapped for its fur. It sometimes raids chicken coops, and in suburban areas it has been reported killing cats and small dogs. It is useful to foresters because it controls porcupines. In California, a 2013 study examined how illegal marijuana grow sites inside fisher home ranges affect fisher survival (an average of 5.3 grow sites per home range).

funFacts: Despite its name, it rarely eats fish; the name probably comes from "fitch" or the French "fichet", words for the European polecat.
It can turn its hind feet almost backwards and climb down trees head-first.
It is one of the few animals that regularly kills porcupines.
Fishers killed at least 14 Canada lynx in one Maine study area between 1999 and 2011.
Its pregnancy lasts almost a full year because the embryo waits about ten months before implanting.
Ninety fishers from British Columbia were released in Olympic National Park between 2008 and 2010 to bring the species back.

abilities.name: Quill-Dodge Assault
abilities.description: it circles a porcupine and bites its face again and again, avoiding the quilled back, until the porcupine dies after about 25–30 minutes. Against defended prey, this patience turns a dangerous opponent into a meal.

abilities.name: Snowstorm Neck Bite
abilities.description: in northern Maine, fishers killed at least 14 Canada lynx between 1999 and 2011 by attacking them bedded down in snowstorms with a quick, powerful neck bite. It shows how ambush can let a 5 kg animal kill a much larger cat.

traits.name: Reversible Hind Feet
traits.description: its ankles rotate the hind paws almost 180°, so it can run down a tree trunk head-first like a squirrel.

traits.name: Year-Long Pregnancy
traits.description: after mating in late winter, the embryo waits about ten months before implanting, so the whole pregnancy lasts nearly a year.

combat.weapons: The fisher is a generalist forest predator whose main prey are snowshoe hares and porcupines, supplemented with smaller mammals, birds, carrion, insects, nuts, berries and mushrooms. It is one of very few predators that routinely kills porcupines: observational studies show repeated biting attacks on the porcupine's face until it dies after about 25–30 minutes (Wikipedia, citing Powell). Occasionally it kills larger animals, including wild turkeys, raccoons, foxes, martens, otters, bobcats and Canada lynx. A Journal of Wildlife Management study documented 14 fisher kills of Canada lynx in northern Maine from 1999 to 2011; the fishers attacked lynx bedded down in snowstorms with a quick, powerful bite to the neck. Local trappers and hunters in Quebec also describe the fisher as the main predator of the American marten (Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine 2017). For a 5 kg animal this is exceptional killing ability, but it depends on ambush and persistence rather than absolute strength.
weaknesses: Small absolute mass (5 kg).
No armor.
Avoids open ground, clear cuts and farmland.
Larger carnivores can kill it.

flying-fox.name: Flying Fox
flying-fox.specimen: healthy adult male, 1.0 kg, 30.0 cm head-body length, wingspan about 1.5 m, forearm about 20 cm.
flying-fox.summary: The large flying fox is a 1 kg Southeast Asian fruit bat with a 1.5 m wingspan that can fly more than 80 km in a night. It finds food by sight and smell rather than echolocation, but with only a defensive bite and fragile wings, it survives by flying away, not by fighting.
narrative: The large flying fox is one of the biggest bats alive. A healthy adult weighs about a kilogram, and its wings stretch to about 1.5 m, carried on forearms longer than a human hand. Its fox-like face, large eyes and dark mantle of fur give it its name. Unlike the small insect-eating bats, it does not echolocate. It relies on rod-rich eyes that work well at night and a strong nose to find ripe fruit and flowering trees.

Its real strength is distance. Satellite tracking in Malaysia showed bats foraging up to about 87.5 km from the roost in one night, and one bat covered 130 km in two hours. Over a year, adult males move between roosts hundreds of kilometres apart and across national borders. That range makes it an important pollinator and seed disperser for forest trees such as durian.

In a fight, though, the flying fox has very little. Its sharp canines and clawed thumbs can give a painful defensive bite or scratch, and males squabble over roosting spots and harems, but it has no predatory weapons, no armor and thin wings that are easily damaged. Its winning move against almost any opponent is to take off. Humans are its biggest threat: hunting and forest loss have pushed the species to Endangered, and its role as a natural host of Nipah virus makes it a species of public-health interest too.

sections.habitat: Found across Southeast Asia, from southern Myanmar, Thailand and Indochina through the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java, Borneo, the Philippines and the Lesser Sunda Islands. It roosts in tall trees in lowland forest, coastal forest and mangroves, and forages over forests, orchards and plantations.
sections.diet: Feeds on nectar, pollen, flowers and fruit, including coconut, durian and fig. It slices fruit rinds with its teeth and uses its long tongue to lap nectar. As a long-distance forager it disperses seeds and pollinates forest trees, including durian, whose fruit is highly valued across the region.
sections.social: Highly colonial, with roosts of up to about 15,000 individuals. Males hold roosting positions and small harems within a dominance hierarchy, and a male may mate with several females.
sections.reproduction: Females typically give birth to a single pup per year. Newborns weigh about 133 g, roughly 20–30% of the mother's mass, and cling to her for early care. Lifespan averages about 15 years in the wild by summary estimates, with captive records around 21 years.
sections.conservation: Assessed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022). Chronic over-harvesting and loss of primary forest drive declines. A 2009 study estimated about 22,000 bats were hunted legally each year in Malaysia and warned the species could disappear from Peninsular Malaysia within about 6 years if hunting continued at that rate.
sections.features:
Wingspan about 1.5 m and forearm 180–220 mm.
No echolocation; rod-dominated retinas with two cone types.
Clawed thumbs and feet for hanging and climbing.
Long tongue for nectar feeding.
Glandular neck tufts in males.
sections.humanInteraction: Hunted for food and sport across much of its range and sometimes treated as an orchard pest. It is also a natural reservoir of henipaviruses, including Nipah virus, and is suspected as the reservoir behind the 1998–1999 Nipah outbreak in pigs and people in Malaysia. Its long-distance movements across national borders make regional management important for both conservation and disease monitoring.

funFacts: Its wings span about 1.5 m, wider than many eagles'.
It does not echolocate and finds food by sight and smell instead.
One satellite-tagged bat flew 130 km in just two hours.
It can forage up to about 87.5 km from its roost in a single night.
A newborn pup weighs about 133 g, up to a third of its mother's weight.
Colonies can hold up to about 15,000 bats.
It helps pollinate durian trees.

abilities.description: flies up to about 87.5 km in a night and has been tracked covering 130 km in two hours, letting it disengage from almost any ground-bound opponent and reach distant food.

abilities.name: Echo-Free Night Vision
abilities.description: navigates without echolocation, using rod-rich eyes with two cone types and a keen nose to find fruit and flowers in the dark.

traits.name: Giant Fruit Bat
traits.description: one of the largest bats in the world, with a wingspan of about 1.5 m and a forearm up to 22 cm.

traits.name: Rainforest Pollinator
traits.description: feeds on nectar and pollen of trees such as durian and carries seeds and pollen across huge distances, supporting forest regeneration and valuable fruit crops.

combat.weapons: The large flying fox is a fruit and nectar eater, not a predator. Its canines are sharp enough to slice through fruit rinds and to give a painful defensive bite to a handler or rival, and its thumb and foot claws can scratch. None of this adds up to meaningful offensive power against animals of real size; it has no hunting behavior to draw on.
weaknesses: Almost no damaging weapons.
Fragile wings; a grounded flying fox is clumsy and exposed.
Low mass and no armor.
Heavily dependent on flowering and fruiting trees.

fossa.name: Fossa
fossa.specimen: healthy mature adult male of about 8.0 kg, head-body about 75 cm with a tail of similar length. This sits near the top of the normal male range without using exceptional heavy individuals.
fossa.summary: The fossa is Madagascar's top predator, a sleek, muscular 8 kg carnivore that hunts lemurs on the ground and high in the canopy. Rotating ankles let it run down trunks head-first, and sharp claws and a strong bite make it deadly to prey its own size, but its small mass limits it against larger fighters.
narrative: The fossa looks like a cross between a small cougar and a mongoose, with a long, low body, short dense coat, big forward-facing eyes and a tail as long as the rest of it. A mature male weighs about 8 kg. On Madagascar, where there are no native cats or dogs, it fills the role of the island's main predator, and its favourite prey is the lemur.

What sets the fossa apart in a fight is where it can fight. Its ankles rotate so it can run down a trunk head-first, it leaps between branches using the tail for balance, and it grips with sharp semi-retractile claws. That lets it follow a sifaka through the canopy, seize it with its forelimbs and finish it with a bite. Some males go further and hunt in small teams, a rare behavior for a mostly solitary carnivore.

On the absolute roster scale, though, the fossa is still a small animal. It has no armor, limited mass, and its weapons all require close contact. It rates near the top for agility and canopy control, alongside the ocelot and just below the clouded leopard, while its Attack and Defense stay in the small-carnivore band well below leopards and other big cats.

sections.habitat: The fossa lives only on Madagascar. It occurs across the island's forest types, from humid eastern rainforest to dry deciduous forest in the west and spiny forest in the south, and from sea level into the mountains. It also moves through degraded forest near villages, as tracking in Ankarafantsika National Park has shown.
sections.diet: A carnivore that eats mostly vertebrates. Lemurs are the largest part of the diet at studied sites, with tenrecs, rodents, reptiles, birds and occasionally domestic poultry also taken. Field estimates from western Madagascar suggest fossa predation removes a notable share of local sifaka and mouse lemur populations each year, making it an important pressure on lemur communities.
sections.social: Mostly solitary. Males use larger home ranges than females, and their ranges overlap more with other males. Some males form stable associations with one or two other males, and cooperative hunting by males has been observed.
sections.reproduction: Breeding centres on traditional mating trees, where a female remains for an extended period and mates repeatedly with several males. Litters are small, and young stay with the mother for many months. Juvenile females temporarily show male-like external genitalia and coat secretions, which fade as they mature; this transient masculinization was first described in this species.
sections.conservation: Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, with a decreasing population trend. Total population estimates are uncertain and vary widely between studies; regional density estimates are low. Main threats are forest loss and fragmentation, hunting and persecution in retaliation for poultry losses, and disease risks from domestic carnivores.
sections.features:
Flexible, rotating ankles that allow head-first descent.
Sharp semi-retractile claws on all feet.
Long tail used as a balance pole in trees.
Flat-footed walking gait on the ground.
Transient masculinization of juvenile females.
sections.humanInteraction: Fossa are feared and persecuted in parts of rural Madagascar because they take poultry and are the subject of local folklore. Because they are rarely seen in the wild, most people outside Madagascar know them from zoos, where they are kept in a small number of breeding programs.

funFacts: The fossa is Madagascar's largest native carnivore.
It can climb down trees head-first thanks to ankles that rotate.
Lemurs make up the largest share of its diet in field studies.
Three males were once watched hunting a single sifaka together for about 45 minutes.
Young females temporarily look male before changing as they mature.
Females mate on traditional "mating trees" where several males gather.
Its tail is about as long as its head and body combined.

abilities.name: Head-First Descent
abilities.description: highly flexible ankles rotate so the fossa can run down tree trunks head-first and leap between branches, letting it chase prey through the canopy and down to the ground without breaking contact.

abilities.name: Canopy Ambush Grapple
abilities.description: it seizes lemurs with sharp semi-retractile claws and grasping forelimbs, pins them and kills with a head or neck bite; it is the only native predator able to take the largest living lemurs.

traits.name: Madagascar's Top Carnivore
traits.description: the largest native carnivore on Madagascar and the main predator of lemurs, with lemurs making up the largest share of its diet.

traits.name: Mating-Tree Gatherings
traits.description: females mate on traditional mating trees where several males gather, and some males form lasting associations that can include hunting together.

combat.weapons: The fossa is a compact, muscular carnivore built to kill primates about its own size. It seizes prey with its forelimbs and sharp semi-retractile claws, pins it, and kills with a bite to the head or neck. Its prey list is dominated by lemurs: diet studies in western Madagascar found vertebrates make up the great majority of the diet, with lemurs the largest share, alongside tenrecs, rodents, reptiles and birds. It is the only native predator able to kill the largest living lemurs, such as sifakas.
weaknesses: Only about 8 kg; lacks the mass to overpower medium or large predators.
No armor or thick hide.
Bite and claw offense requires close contact.
Much less effective in open ground with no trees to use.

gaur.name: Gaur
gaur.specimen: healthy mature adult male (bull) of about 1,000 kg and 190 cm shoulder height, with fully grown horns and dorsal ridge. This is a representative prime bull, not a record animal.
gaur.summary: The gaur is the largest wild cattle species on Earth, a tonne-class forest bull armed with thick upcurved horns and wrapped in heavy muscle beneath a towering dorsal ridge. Usually shy, it becomes a formidable, horn-hooking brawler when surprised or cornered, strong enough to kill a tiger on occasion but still vulnerable to one.
narrative: A mature gaur bull is an imposing animal: close to two metres at the shoulder, around a tonne in weight, glossy near-black with white socks, and topped by a high muscular ridge that runs from the shoulders into the back. Its horns, present in both sexes, sweep up and inward from a broad, pale forehead. Everything about the silhouette advertises mass, and bulls use that silhouette deliberately, turning side-on to rivals so their full size is visible.

Most of the time gaur avoid trouble. They graze and browse in forest glades and hillside grasslands, retreat into cover at the first sign of danger, and in disturbed areas shift their activity into the night. When a threat is too close to escape, the response is a fast, heavy charge ending in hooking horn strikes. That reaction is why gaur injure more people than any other wild mammal around one Karnataka hospital, and why tigers usually target calves, cows and weakened animals rather than prime bulls.

For ABS calibration the gaur sits at the top of the wild-cattle group: heavier than the Cape Buffalo and Bison, with slightly higher Raw Power and Attack, but with a less aggressive temperament than the Cape Buffalo and no fused horn boss. It remains well below rhinoceros and elephant scale in size, power and defense, and it has no special mechanism beyond size, horns and display.

sections.habitat: Gaur live in South and Southeast Asia, from India and Nepal through Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam and Peninsular Malaysia. They use evergreen and deciduous forest, bamboo, forest glades and nearby grasslands, often in hilly country. About 85% of the population is in India.
sections.diet: Gaur graze on grasses and browse leaves, shoots, bamboo, bark and fruit. As large herbivores they shape forest-edge vegetation and are major prey for tigers, which rely heavily on them in some reserves.
sections.social: Herds of about 2 to 40 animals centre on females and young, typically with one breeding bull; bulls may move between herds during the breeding season or live alone. Bulls establish rank mainly by lateral display rather than all-out fights.
sections.reproduction: Females usually bear a single calf. Calves are protected within the herd and are the age class most often taken by predators. Bulls take several years to reach full body size, horn thickness and ridge height.
sections.conservation: Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, a status held since 1986. The 2016 assessment estimated roughly 6,000–21,000 mature individuals, with declines of more than 70% in parts of the range over three generations. Populations are stable or recovering in well-protected Indian reserves but face poaching, habitat loss, disease from domestic cattle, uncontrolled fire, invasive plants and disturbance elsewhere.
sections.features:
Largest living wild bovid.
Thick, upcurved horns in both sexes, 60–115 cm long.
Tall dorsal ridge over the shoulders and a prominent dewlap in bulls.
Pale "stockings" on the lower legs.
Lateral display used to settle rank.
sections.humanInteraction: Gaur are shy but increasingly enter farmland and hill towns in southern India, where encounters cause crop losses, injuries and deaths. The domestic gayal or mithun of northeast India and Myanmar was bred from gaur stock.

funFacts: Gaur are the largest wild cattle species in the world.
Despite the nickname "Indian bison", gaur are wild oxen and not bison.
Both bulls and cows carry horns up to about 115 cm long.
A Thai study of kills by 24 collared tigers found the average gaur killed weighed about 398 kg, well under half a prime bull's mass.
Gaur have been recorded killing tigers, one of very few prey animals to do so.
Near Manipal in Karnataka, gaur caused more serious injuries to people than any other wild mammal.
Bulls often size each other up side-on instead of fighting straight away.

abilities.name: Hooking Horn Sweep
abilities.description: bulls strike sideways and upward with thick, upcurved horns braced by a broad frontal ridge, backed by a tonne of body mass.

abilities.name: Lateral Size Display
abilities.description: bulls turn side-on to show their full height and ridge, settling many contests and deterring threats before contact.

traits.name: Largest Wild Cattle
traits.description: the gaur is the biggest wild bovid alive, with bulls around a tonne and up to 2.2 m at the shoulder.

traits.name: White-Stockinged Giant
traits.description: a glossy dark coat, pale lower legs, a tall dorsal ridge over the shoulders and a hanging dewlap give bulls a distinctive silhouette.

combat.weapons: The gaur's weapon system is a tonne of muscle driving a pair of thick, upcurved horns. Bulls hook sideways and upward with the horns rather than meeting head-on like a Cape buffalo; the heavy frontal ridge between the horns braces the strike. Mass, shoving and trampling add damage. The combination is lethal to people: at a tertiary hospital in Manipal, Karnataka, gaur caused more significant and life-threatening injuries than any other wild mammal in the surrounding region.
weaknesses: No true armor; flanks, belly and hindquarters are soft targets.
Heat limits prolonged exertion.
Mostly avoids a fight, giving an ambush predator the first move.
A tonne of mass limits sharp turning.
Tigers do kill adult gaur.

german-shepherd.name: German Shepherd
german-shepherd.specimen: healthy adult male working dog, 35.0 kg, 63.0 cm at the withers.
german-shepherd.summary: The German Shepherd is a 35 kg German herding and police dog built to trot all day and to finish a sprint with a hard grip. Measured police dogs reach about 42 km/h in 25 m, but their bite on a sensor sleeve is moderate, so it sits between wild dogs and heavy guardian breeds and is badly outmatched by large predators.
narrative: The German Shepherd was created in Germany from 1899, when cavalry officer Max von Stephanitz registered Horand von Grafrath as the first dog of a new breed meant to be the ideal working shepherd. A fit working male weighs about 35 kg and stands about 63 cm tall, and the breed standard describes it as a trotter whose build is judged by how well it holds up over a long working day.

Today it is best known as a police and military dog. Finnish researchers measured police German Shepherds sprinting 25 m and biting a sleeve fitted with force sensors. The dogs reached up to 42 km/h and hit with accelerations of around 7 g, but their median bite force was about 360 N, roughly the grip of an elderly man's hand. The shock of the collision matters as much as the jaws.

On the absolute scale that places it above dingoes and coyotes in attack but below the 50 kg Kangal, Rottweiler and Gray Wolf. Its trained control, stamina and nose make it a capable all-rounder, but it has no armor and a population prone to hip and spine problems, and it is far too small to stand up to bears, big cats or large hoofed animals.

sections.habitat: A domestic breed kept worldwide in homes, farms, police and military kennels. It originated in Germany.
sections.diet: Fed by its owners on commercial dog food, meat and household scraps.
sections.ecology: No wild ecological role. Working roles include herding, police patrol, detection, search-and-rescue, military work and guiding people with visual impairments.
sections.social: Bonds closely with its handler or family and is watchful toward strangers. Stanley Coren ranked it second among breeds most likely to bark as watchdogs (via Wikipedia).
sections.reproduction: Breeding is managed by breed clubs and owners. The male police GSDs measured in Finland had a median age of 58.5 months, about 4.9 years, showing that working dogs serve well into adulthood.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed. VetCompass data show GSD numbers declining in the UK, from 3.5% of the 2005 birth cohort to 2.2% in 2013.
sections.features:
Wedge-shaped head with erect ears; trunk about 10–17% longer than tall.
Dense double coat with harsh outer hair.
Smooth, ground-covering trot.
Strong scent-work and trainability.
Measured working bite about 360 N on a padded sleeve.
sections.humanInteraction: The GSD is one of the most popular and most used working breeds. Its popularity also puts it near the top of hospital-treated bite statistics in the United States. Health concerns include hip and elbow dysplasia, degenerative spinal disease and a shorter than average life.

funFacts: Horand von Grafrath, bought at a dog show in 1899, was the first dog in the German Shepherd breed register.
In Britain the breed was long called the Alsatian.
In a Finnish study, police German Shepherds hit about 42 km/h within 25 m before biting.
The same study found their median bite on a sensor sleeve was about 360 N, "lower than generally assumed".
The FCI standard describes the German Shepherd as a trotter and warns that too much hind angulation reduces stamina.
VetCompass UK recorded a median lifespan of 10.3 years for the breed.

abilities.name: Long Attack Strike
abilities.description: a sprint to about 37–42 km/h ending in a full-mouth grip, with measured accelerations around 7 g and impact decelerations over 11 g. The collision and grip can knock an opponent of similar size off balance.

abilities.name: Scent Tracker
abilities.description: follows and finds targets by smell in police, military and search-and-rescue work. In a matchup this helps it locate and follow an opponent rather than add damage.

traits.name: Tireless Trotter
traits.description: the FCI standard defines the GSD as a trotter built for a smooth, ground-covering gait and ties correct angulation directly to stamina.

traits.name: Von Stephanitz Working Dog
traits.description: founded in 1899 around Horand von Grafrath with a breed club that put working ability first; it became one of the world's most numerous and most widely used service breeds.

combat.weapons: The weapon is the canid bite. Police and protection dogs are trained to run in, take a full grip and hold. The Finnish sleeve study shows what that looks like in numbers: a sprint to about 37–42 km/h, a peak acceleration around 7 g, a deceleration spike over 11 g on impact, and a median bite of about 360 N on the sleeve. The impact is a large part of the effect, but the measured grip itself is far lower than internet figures suggest.
weaknesses: No armor; a single bite weapon.
Measured functional bite force is moderate.
Common hip, elbow and spinal problems in the population.
Far outmatched by bears, big cats and large ungulates.

gharial.name: Gharial
gharial.specimen: healthy mature adult male with a developed ghara, 180.0 kg and 450.0 cm total length.
gharial.summary: The gharial is a long, slim river crocodilian built entirely around catching fish. A mature 180 kg male sweeps its needle-toothed, pencil-thin snout sideways through the water with little drag, but it has the weakest bite of any living crocodilian and is slow and awkward on land. It is dangerous to fish, not to large animals, and it is one of the world's most endangered reptiles.
narrative: The gharial looks like a crocodile that has been stretched. Its snout is long and narrow, lined with about 110 fine interlocking teeth, and it works less like a crusher than like a pair of fishing tongs. Because a thin snout meets little resistance, the gharial can snap it sideways through the water to catch fish, and the teeth lock around slippery prey once they close.

That design comes with a clear cost. When researchers measured the bite of every living crocodilian species, the gharial came last in force. Its jaws cannot crush bone or hold down a struggling large mammal, and the long snout itself becomes a liability against a heavy biter. On land the gharial is slow, so it depends on the river for almost everything except basking and nesting.

In ABS terms the gharial is a crocodilian with most of the body armor but little of the crocodile's killing power. It keeps respectable Defense from its size and armored skin, moderate Agility in water, and a distinctive Special score for its sideways strike, needle-tooth trap and the male's buzzing ghara. Its Attack and Ferocity sit far below the alligator, Nile crocodile and saltwater crocodile, reflecting a specialist that wins against fish and loses most fights against large, heavy-jawed opponents.

sections.habitat: Gharials live in large, deep, flowing rivers with sandbanks on the northern Indian subcontinent. The main surviving populations are in India and Nepal, and the species now occupies only a small part of its former river range.
sections.diet: Adults eat mainly fish, which is why the species is also called the fish-eating crocodile. At Smithsonian's National Zoo gharials are fed a variety of fish. Young gharials take smaller aquatic animals. As a fish predator it is part of healthy river food webs.
sections.social: Gharials bask together on sandbanks. Mature males display with the ghara and buzzing calls during the breeding season and compete for access to females. Hunting is solitary.
sections.reproduction: Males reach maturity at about 15 years and 4 m, when the ghara develops. Females nest in riverside sandbanks. Late maturity and small remaining populations make every adult important for recovery.
sections.conservation: The gharial has been listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN since 2007. Fewer than 900 mature individuals are thought to remain, and numbers have fallen by as much as 98% since the 1940s, driven by hunting for traditional medicine and major changes to river habitat. The Zoological Society of London's EDGE programme lists it as a priority species, and the IUCN Crocodile Specialist Group tracks its protected-area populations.
sections.features:
Extremely long, narrow snout with little drag in water.
About 110 interlocking, needle-like teeth.
Ghara on the snout tip of mature males for sound and display.
High-set eyes and nostrils.
Armored crocodilian skin.
Powerful swimming tail.
sections.humanInteraction: Gharials are not considered a meaningful threat to people; their jaws are built for fish. The main human impacts run the other way: habitat change, fishing and hunting have pushed the species close to extinction, and conservation depends on protecting river stretches and nesting sandbanks.

funFacts: The name "gharial" comes from the ghara, a traditional Indian pot that the male's snout knob resembles.
A gharial's jaws hold about 110 interlocking teeth, more than other crocodilians.
In direct tests of every living crocodilian species, the gharial had the lowest bite force.
The ghara works as a vocal resonator, turning the male's call into a loud buzz.
Males only grow a ghara once mature, at about 15 years old and 4 m long.
Gharial numbers have fallen by as much as 98% since the 1940s.
Fewer than 900 mature gharials are thought to survive in the wild.

abilities.name: Sideways Snout Snap
abilities.description: the very long, narrow snout cuts through water with little drag, letting the gharial whip its jaws sideways to seize passing fish. Erickson's group linked this speed-for-force tradeoff to its low bite force.

abilities.name: Interlocking Needle Grip
abilities.description: about 110 sharp, interlocking teeth close like a trap, holding slippery, struggling fish that a heavier-jawed crocodile might lose.

traits.name: Ghara Resonator
traits.description: mature males grow a bulbous knob on the snout tip, named after a traditional Indian pot, which amplifies a loud buzzing call and acts as a visual signal to females.

traits.name: Light-Bite Specialist
traits.description: the gharial has the lowest measured bite force of any living crocodilian, yet its slender teeth still deliver high local pressure, a jaw built for fish rather than large prey.

combat.weapons: The gharial's weapon is a fish trap, not a bone crusher. The long, narrow snout meets little water resistance, so it can be swept sideways quickly, and the rows of interlocking needle teeth hold fish once they close. Erickson and colleagues linked this jaw shape to the gharial's very low bite force: the snout gives up leverage for speed and reach. Against a large, armored or heavy opponent the teeth can cut and grip, but the jaws cannot crush, hold a struggling large mammal or deliver the drag-and-drown attack of big crocodiles.
weaknesses: Lowest bite force among living crocodilians.
Long, slender snout that can be injured by heavy biters.
Poor land movement.
No specialization for subduing large prey.
Short bursts rather than sustained effort.

giant-forest-hog.name: Giant Forest Hog
giant-forest-hog.specimen: healthy adult boar of about 210 kg, 95 cm at the shoulder and 180 cm head-body length, with full tusks and cheek swellings. This is the median male weight reported in field guides, below the heaviest eastern boars of 225–275 kg.
giant-forest-hog.summary: The giant forest hog is the world's largest wild pig, a 210 kg shaggy black boar of African forests that fights by ramming heads hard enough to crack skulls and slashing with flared tusks. It is short-ranged and unarmored, but its temper and willingness to charge without warning make it far more dangerous than its size suggests.
narrative: A giant forest hog boar is a heavy, shaggy black pig of around 210 kg, with a broad snout disc up to 16 cm across, large naked swellings beneath the eyes and tusks that flare out to the sides. It lives in family sounders in the forests and forest edges of tropical Africa, mostly active at night, travelling up to a dozen kilometres a day to graze, root and scavenge.

Its fighting style is brutal. Rival boars line up 20 or 30 metres apart, charge and slam foreheads together; the clash can fracture skulls, and some fights end in death. The same temper is turned on threats: boars have been known to charge people without warning and to push spotted hyenas off carcasses. The whole sounder defends its piglets, but leopards and hyena clans still take forest hogs, and hunters exploit their habit of turning to fight at the edge of cover.

On the ABS scale the giant forest hog is a mid-weight brawler with high ferocity. It is heavier and far more aggressive than most forest herbivores of similar mass, such as the okapi, but lacks the armor, bulk and long weapons of true heavyweights. Its Attack reflects real danger at close range, while its modest Defense and Agility reflect a body built for a short, head-first charge.

sections.habitat: Tropical Africa in a patchy range from Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire in the west, through the Congo Basin, to the highlands of Kenya, including Mount Kenya, and Ethiopia. It uses lowland and montane forest, forest-grassland mosaics and thickets.
sections.diet: Mainly a grazer of grasses that also digs with its tusks for roots and minerals and scavenges carcasses. It is found at low densities of about 0.4–2.6 animals per km², but prime habitat can hold more than 10 per km².
sections.social: Sounders of up to 20: related females and young, typically with one old boar; boars may also form bachelor groups. Females leave to give birth and return with piglets about a week later, and every adult helps protect the young.
sections.reproduction: A mating pair leaves the sounder for a time. Piglets can nurse from any female in the group. Average wild life is about five years, with a recorded maximum of 18.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, but hunted for bushmeat across most of its range. It is so elusive that some large parks, such as Comoé in Côte d'Ivoire, have never surveyed it systematically. The small West African population has low genetic diversity. As one of Africa's four wild pig genera, it is studied as a possible host in African swine fever cycles.
sections.features:
Largest living wild pig.
Outward-flaring tusks, up to 35.9 cm in boars.
Forehead ramming that can fracture skulls.
Nasal disc up to 16 cm across.
Naked swellings under the eyes of boars, with scent glands in the cheek pads.
sections.humanInteraction: It is feared more than other African forest pigs because boars can attack without warning. It is hunted for meat and is easily tamed in captivity, but it has never been domesticated. It was only described scientifically in 1904.

funFacts: The giant forest hog is the largest wild pig in the world.
Boars charge from 20–30 m apart and crash heads like wild sheep.
A forehead clash can fracture a skull and makes a loud crack when the skull hollows meet squarely.
Its snout disc can be 16 cm across.
Piglets can suckle from any female in the sounder.
Giant forest hogs have been seen driving spotted hyenas away from carcasses.
Science did not describe the species until 1904.

abilities.name: Skull-Ram Charge
abilities.description: boars charge from 20–30 m and slam foreheads together hard enough to fracture skulls, a clash that can ring out with a loud report.

abilities.name: Flared Tusk Slash
abilities.description: outward-curving tusks up to about 36 cm slash at an opponent after the head-to-head push.

traits.name: Largest Wild Pig
traits.description: on average the biggest living member of the pig family, with eastern boars topping 225 kg.

traits.name: Giant Snout Disc
traits.description: a nasal disc up to 16 cm across and big naked swellings under the eyes of boars give it a very distinctive face.

combat.weapons: The giant forest hog has two weapon systems. The first is the head itself: boars charge at each other from 20–30 m apart and slam foreheads together, a clash violent enough to fracture skulls. The second is a pair of outward-flaring tusks, up to about 30–36 cm in boars, used to slash an opponent after head pushing. Boars are known to attack people without warning, apparently to protect their group, and have been seen driving spotted hyenas off carcasses. Fights between males that end in the death of one participant are reported as not uncommon.
weaknesses: No armor or thick hide; flanks and belly are exposed.
Tusks are modest for its size compared with a warthog's.
Short head-first charge; little reach.
Standing at bay makes it vulnerable to organized predators and hunters.

giant-otter.name: Giant Otter
giant-otter.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 30.0 kg and 160.0 cm total length, inside the male ranges of 26–32 kg and 1.5–1.7 m (Wikipedia).
giant-otter.summary: The longest member of the weasel family, the giant otter is a 30 kg river predator that lives in loud, cooperative family groups and hunts fish, snakes and even small caimans. Powerful and agile in water, it relies on a single weapon, its bite, and is much less formidable alone or on dry land.
narrative: The giant otter is the river wolf of South America. A big male weighs about 30 kg and stretches 1.6 m from nose to tail tip, with a thick neck, webbed feet and a flattened, wing-like tail. Families of three to eight patrol their stretch of river each morning, marking campsites and calling constantly; scientists have identified 22 distinct adult call types.

In the water it is fast and precise. It lunges and twists through the shallows, attacks from above or below and swivels at the last moment to catch fish in its jaws, rarely missing. It eats about 3 kg of fish a day and, when fish are scarce, will take crabs, snakes and small caimans. Some prey, such as young caimans and small anacondas, may require the group to work together, and whole families will charge intruders, including boats full of people.

On the absolute scale, a single giant otter is a strong mid-sized predator: heavier and better armed than river otters and sea otters, but relying on its bite alone and lacking the grappling claws of a similarly sized cat. Its group behavior and aquatic skill are real advantages, but in a one-on-one fight on land against a jaguar-class predator, it is outmatched.

sections.habitat: Slow-moving rivers, creeks, oxbow lakes, flooded forests and swamps in the Amazon, Orinoco and La Plata basins, the Guianas and the Brazilian Pantanal. It prefers clear water, gently sloping banks and overhanging vegetation for dens and campsites. It has vanished from much of its former range; in 2021 conservationists spotted a wild giant otter in Argentina's Bermejo River, where its presence had been uncertain.
sections.diet: Almost entirely fish, especially cichlids, perch, characins (including piranhas) and catfish, supplemented with crabs, snakes, small caimans and anacondas when fish are scarce. Hunting is most successful in shallow water under 0.6 m. As the top predator of its rivers, its status reflects the health of freshwater ecosystems.
sections.social: Extended family groups of three to eight (up to 20 when groups merge temporarily) centred on a dominant breeding pair. Older siblings help raise pups. Groups mark territory with latrines, scent and calls, and generally avoid conflict with neighbours, but fights can be serious. Some animals live as nomadic transients.
sections.reproduction: Pups are born in underground dens near the water, often in the dry season when fish are concentrated. Males and older siblings help raise them. Pups open their eyes in the fourth week, walk in the fifth, swim confidently at 12–14 weeks, are weaned by nine months, and leave the group after two to three years.
sections.conservation: Listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List since 1999, with wild populations usually estimated below 5,000; it is one of the most endangered mammals in the Neotropics. Threats include decades of poaching for its velvety pelt (1,000–3,000 pelts a year left Amazonian Brazil alone in 1959–1969), habitat loss, logging, mercury in fish from gold mining, and disturbance from poorly managed tourism. A 2024 continental study found its area of occupancy shrinking, and after the 2020 Pantanal mega-fires giant otters showed the steepest decline of any species monitored in one study area (a 2026 Pantanal study).
sections.features:
Wing-like, flattened, muscular tail and webbed feet.
Pressure-sensitive whiskers.
Individually unique throat markings.
Very large vocal repertoire.
Cooperative family groups with shared roles.
sections.humanInteraction: Heavily hunted for its velvety pelt, with poaching peaking in the 1950s and 1960s until CITES controls from 1973 cut the trade. Groups sometimes surround boats and charge them. Tourism can disturb denning and hunting. Few are kept in zoos, where poor enclosure design has historically caused high pup mortality.

funFacts: It is the longest member of the weasel family, reaching up to 1.8 m.
In Brazil it is called onça-d'água, the "water jaguar".
Every giant otter has its own unique pattern of pale throat markings.
Adults use at least 22 different calls, and each family has its own vocal signature.
It eats about 3 kg of food a day, roughly a tenth of its body weight.
Family groups sometimes kill small caimans and anacondas.
Scars on some animals suggest piranhas occasionally bite back.

abilities.name: River Wolf Pack
abilities.description: families of three to eight otters defend territory together, charge intruders as a group and can cooperate to take prey too large for one otter, such as young caimans and small anacondas. In a strict one-on-one matchup this advantage is lost.

abilities.name: Whisker Pressure Sense
abilities.description: highly sensitive whiskers track changes in water pressure and currents, helping it find and follow prey in the water alongside its sharp daytime eyesight.

traits.name: Longest Mustelid
traits.description: at up to 1.8 m, it is the longest member of the weasel family, although the sea otter may be heavier.

traits.name: Loudest Otter
traits.description: adults use at least 22 distinct call types and newborns 11, and each family has its own recognizable vocal signature.

combat.weapons: The giant otter is a fish specialist and an apex predator of South American rivers. In one Amazonian study, fish appeared in every scat, with cichlids and perch in 97% and characins such as piranhas in 86%. It chases prey in rapid, twisting lunges through the shallows, attacks from above or below, and swivels at the last instant to clamp prey in its jaws, with few misses. It eats about 10% of its body weight daily, about 3 kg. When fish are scarce it takes crabs, snakes, small caimans and anacondas; truly coordinated hunting may occur mainly when prey is too big for one otter, such as small green anacondas and young black caimans. Its only real weapon is the bite, backed by a strong neck and body; its claws are for holding prey, not for fighting.
weaknesses: The bite is its only real weapon.
No armor, and short fur gives little padding.
Much less capable on dry land.
Solitary animals and pups are much more vulnerable than groups.
Electric eels, stingrays and piranhas can injure it.
