giant-panda.name: Giant Panda
giant-panda.specimen: healthy adult male, 115.0 kg, about 160.0 cm head-body length. This is a representative wild male, not a heavy captive animal.
giant-panda.summary: The giant panda is a 100–115 kg bamboo-eating bear from the mountain forests of central China. Its broad skull gives it a bite modelled close to a lion's, and it can climb well. But it saves energy instead of spending it, rarely runs, and avoids fights unless cornered, so it has little stamina or offensive skill for a sustained battle.
narrative: The giant panda is a bear that lives almost entirely on bamboo. That single fact shapes everything about it as a fighter. To crush tough stems it has one of the broadest skulls and heaviest sets of chewing muscles among the carnivorans, and when researchers modelled its bite, the force at the canines came out close to a lion's. The pseudo-thumb, an enlarged wrist bone, lets it hold bamboo precisely while it eats for much of the day.

The other side of that diet is energy. Bamboo is poor food, and the panda copes by spending as little energy as possible. Measurements published in Science found wild pandas using only about 45% of the energy expected for a mammal their size, with low thyroid hormone levels, smaller organs and very little movement. In a fight, that means the panda has almost no reserve: it cannot chase, cannot keep up a long exchange, and generally chooses to walk away or climb a tree.

None of this makes it harmless. An adult male of around 115 kg with thick fur and a crushing bite can badly hurt anything that corners it, as visitors who entered a panda enclosure at Beijing Zoo found out. On the roster it sits near the other medium bears in size and bite, but well below them in stamina, speed and willingness to fight. It is a defensive heavyweight whose best tactic is to avoid battle, and whose worst matchups are fast, persistent predators that can wear it down.

sections.habitat: Giant pandas live only in cool, wet mountain forests with dense bamboo understory in six mountain ranges of central China (Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu provinces), usually at middle to high elevations.
sections.diet: Bamboo, eaten as shoots, stems and leaves, makes up more than 99% of the diet, with occasional small animals or carrion. Because bamboo is poor food and the panda's gut is that of a carnivore, pandas eat large quantities for most of the day and save energy the rest of the time.
sections.social: Solitary. Adults keep separate home ranges and communicate by scent marking and calls. Males and females meet briefly during the spring breeding season.
sections.reproduction: Females are fertile for only a few days each year. Newborn cubs are tiny and helpless and depend on their mother for well over a year. Twins are born fairly often, but a wild mother usually raises only one.
sections.conservation: The giant panda is assessed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, moved down from Endangered in 2016 after China's fourth national survey (2015) counted 1,864 wild pandas. Scientists have argued over whether the change was premature, because habitat fragmentation, bamboo die-offs and climate change remain threats. Panda reserves protect many other species living in the same forests.
sections.features:
Pseudo-thumb formed by an enlarged radial sesamoid bone.
Broad skull and massive chewing muscles for crushing bamboo.
Very low daily energy use and low thyroid hormone levels.
Black-and-white coat.
Good tree-climbing ability.
sections.humanInteraction: The panda is one of the best-known conservation symbols in the world and is central to China's zoo loan programmes. Attacks on people are rare and almost all involve people entering enclosures; the Beijing Zoo cases between 2006 and 2009 show that an adult panda can still cause serious bite injuries.

abilities.name: Bamboo-Crusher Bite
abilities.description: an extremely broad skull, big chewing muscles and flat crushing teeth give a canine bite force modelled at about 1,299 N, close to a lion's. A cornered panda can inflict deep, surgery-level wounds.

abilities.name: Low-Power Mode
abilities.description: wild pandas use only about 45% of the daily energy expected for their size, with low thyroid hormone levels and small internal organs. They survive on a poor-quality diet, but have almost no reserve for a long fight.

traits.name: Radial-Sesamoid Thumb
traits.description: an enlarged wrist bone under a skin pad works as a sixth digit, letting the panda grip bamboo stems precisely.

traits.name: Conservation Comeback
traits.description: China's fourth national survey counted 1,864 wild pandas, and in 2016 the IUCN moved the species from Endangered to Vulnerable.

combat.weapons: The panda's real weapon is its bite. The skull, jaw muscles and teeth are built to crush tough bamboo, and skull modelling places its canine bite force close to a lion's in absolute terms. Claws and forelimbs are strong enough for climbing and pulling bamboo but are not used to hunt. A panda does not stalk, chase or kill large animals, so its offense is defensive: a hard bite and swipes delivered when it is cornered or disturbed.
weaknesses: Very low stamina from an energy-saving physiology.
Slow, with no sprint or pursuit ability.
No real offensive technique beyond biting and swiping.
Low willingness to fight unless cornered.

goblin-shark.name: Goblin Shark
goblin-shark.specimen: healthy mature adult, 380 cm total length and 210 kg, the weighed specimen that held the species weight record until 2022 and sits at the top of the usual 3–4 m adult range.
goblin-shark.summary: The goblin shark is a pink, soft-bodied deep-sea shark whose jaws shoot forward on elastic ligaments faster and farther than any other shark's. It senses prey electrically with its long snout and snatches it in the dark, but its flabby body, weak bite and slow swimming make it a poor fighter against active predators.
narrative: The goblin shark lives on the dark slopes and seamounts of the deep ocean, hundreds of metres down. A mature adult of about 3.8 m and 210 kg has a soft, pale pink body, small fins, and a long flat snout that sticks out over its mouth like a blade. That snout is not a weapon; it is a sensor, covered underneath with electroreceptors that pick up the faint electric signals of squid, fish and crabs hidden in the darkness.

When prey comes close, the goblin shark fires its jaws. Elastic ligaments that were held taut release, and both jaws shoot forward out of the head. Filmed strikes show the lower jaw moving at 3.1 m/s and the jaws reaching almost a tenth of the shark's body length forward, farther and faster than in any other shark. Its long, nail-like front teeth snag slippery prey, and its back teeth crush crabs.

Outside that strike, the goblin shark has little to fight with. Its jaw muscles are mechanically inefficient, its body is flabby and unarmored, and it almost certainly swims slowly, drifting on neutral buoyancy instead of chasing. In the deep, dark water it calls home, that is enough. Against an active hunter it would rely on the darkness and depth that keep it out of reach.

sections.habitat: Goblin sharks have been found in scattered deep-water locations across the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, over upper continental slopes, submarine canyons and seamounts. Most records come from 270–960 m, with catches to 1,300 m, a tooth in an undersea cable at 1,370 m and sightings to about 2,000 m. Juveniles use shallower canyons, occasionally coming as shallow as 40 m.
sections.diet: A deep-water ambush predator of soft-bodied and bottom animals: rockfish such as the blackbelly rosefish, squid, pelagic octopus, crabs, shrimps and ostracods. It drifts close using neutral buoyancy and snatches prey with its projecting jaws.
sections.social: Unknown; specimens are caught singly.
sections.reproduction: Almost nothing is known. Birth size is probably about 82 cm, the length of the smallest specimen. Males mature at about 2.6 m. A pregnant 4.7 m female was landed in Taiwan in 2023. Age, growth and lifespan have not been studied.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2017) because of its wide range and low catch rate, despite its rarity. It is taken occasionally as bycatch in deep trawls, longlines and gillnets.
sections.features:
Jaws that shoot forward on elastic ligaments.
Long, flattened snout covered in electroreceptors.
Long, nail-like front teeth and flattened crushing rear teeth.
Soft, semi-translucent pink skin.
Low-density flesh and a large oily liver for neutral buoyancy.
sections.humanInteraction: Almost never seen alive; most knowledge comes from specimens brought up by deep-sea fishing gear. The first scientific report of wild goblin sharks filmed in their deep habitat was published in 2026.

funFacts: Its jaws shoot forward faster and farther than those of any other shark measured.
A goblin shark opens and closes its mouth twice during one strike, a pattern unseen in other sharks.
A goblin shark tooth was once found stuck in an undersea cable 1,370 m down.
Its pink colour comes from blood vessels showing through its skin.
Early scientists described several "new species" by mistake because preserved goblin sharks had their jaws fixed at different positions.
The first goblin sharks filmed in their natural deep habitat were seen near Jarvis Island in 2019 and in the Tonga Trench in 2024; earlier footage showed animals brought up to the surface.
A heavily pregnant 4.7 m female landed in Taiwan in 2023 weighed about 800 kg.

abilities.name: Slingshot Jaws
abilities.description: elastic ligaments fire both jaws forward at up to 3.1 m/s, reaching 8.6–9.4% of the shark's length beyond the head, the fastest and greatest jaw protrusion measured in any shark. Prey that thinks it is out of reach is not.

abilities.name: Electric Snout Radar
abilities.description: the long, flat snout is covered with ampullae of Lorenzini that sense the faint electric fields of hidden animals in total darkness.

traits.name: Pink Ghost of the Slope
traits.description: soft, semi-translucent skin lets blood vessels show through, giving adults their pink colour; young goblin sharks are almost white.

traits.name: Neutral-Buoyancy Drifter
traits.description: low-density flesh and a large oily liver let it hang in the water and drift toward prey with very little movement.

combat.weapons:
The goblin shark's weapon is its slingshot jaw. At rest the jaws sit tucked under the head. When it strikes, the lower jaw swings down and back to open a gape of up to about 116°, then elastic ligaments at the jaw joint release and both jaws fly forward. Nakaya et al. (2016) filmed the lower jaw reaching 3.1 m/s and both jaws moving forward by 8.6–9.4% of the shark's total length, by far the fastest and farthest jaw protrusion known in sharks; Wikipedia summarises the range as 2.1–9.5 times more protrusible than other sharks. It also opens and closes its mouth a second time while pulling the jaws back, something not seen in other sharks.

The long nail-like teeth snag soft, slippery prey such as squid, fish and shrimps, while the rear teeth crush crabs. Bite force is low: its jaw muscles are the least mechanically efficient among lamniform sharks. The weapon is built for a fast snatch, not for cutting large animals.
weaknesses: Soft, flabby, unarmored body.
Weak bite despite long teeth.
Probably slow, with little acceleration.
Rarely leaves the deep; shallow water is outside its normal range.

goldfish.name: Goldfish
goldfish.specimen: healthy adult common-type goldfish of 20 cm total length and about 0.1 kg. The length is ADW's average and sits at the top of Wikipedia's 12–22 cm typical wild range; the mass comes from FishBase's length-weight relationship for the species (W = 0.01148 × L^3.04, giving about 104 g at 20 cm).
goldfish.summary: The goldfish is a small East Asian carp bred for colour for more than a thousand years. It has no weapon and swims poorly, but it can see ultraviolet light, hear well, learn to navigate, and survive long spells without oxygen by turning sugar into alcohol.
narrative: Behind the bowl-and-castle image, the goldfish is a tough wild carp. Wild goldfish are olive-brown fish of East Asian ponds and ditches, where the water can turn warm, stagnant and oxygen-poor in summer and freeze over in winter. Goldfish and crucian carp cope with a metabolic trick described in no other vertebrate: when oxygen runs out, they convert pyruvate to ethanol as their metabolic end-product, and in cold water they can endure months of very low oxygen that would kill most fish within minutes.

The goldfish is also one of science's favourite fish. Its four-cone eyes see into the ultraviolet, bony Weberian ossicles give it sensitive hearing, and its Mauthner neurons have made its lightning-fast startle escape a textbook case. It learns and remembers for months, copies other goldfish, and has even learned to steer a wheeled tank toward a target on land.

None of that makes it a fighter. A healthy 20 cm goldfish weighs around 100 grams, has a toothless suction mouth for larvae and pondweed, and relies on scales, fin spines, schooling and a quick escape. Herons, otters, snakes and almost any predatory fish can eat it. Its best matchups are the ones decided by outlasting bad water, not by trading blows.

sections.habitat: Native to East Asia, including China and Japan (FishBase), in rivers, lakes, ponds and ditches with stagnant or slow-flowing, often eutrophic and weedy water (FishBase; ADW). Introduced almost worldwide, with established populations in North America, Europe, Australia, South Africa and elsewhere, where it can harm native ecosystems (FishBase; Wikipedia).
sections.diet: Opportunistic omnivore. One Quebec pond study found vegetation made up 45% of the diet, midge and mosquito larvae 21%, and small crustaceans 4%, with worms, detritus and amphibian eggs also taken (ADW). Goldfish lack a stomach and produce a lot of waste (Wikipedia). Predators include herons, river otters, water snakes, bullfrogs, cats, dogs, coyotes, bears and mountain lions (ADW).
sections.social: Schooling and gregarious, without hierarchies or territories. Injured fish release an alarm substance that puts the school on watch, and goldfish copy each other's feeding choices (ADW).
sections.reproduction: Spawning is triggered by warming water above about 10 °C in spring. Females release pheromones, males chase and bump them, and eggs stick to submerged plants or flooded meadow grass. Females spawn about 2,000–4,000 eggs at a time and may spawn several times per season; there is no parental care and adults eat eggs (ADW; FishBase). Maturity comes at 3–4 years in the wild (ADW).
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (assessed 2010, via FishBase). Outside its native range it is a potential pest and an invasive species in parts of North America and Australia (FishBase; Wikipedia).
sections.features:
Ethanol-producing metabolism that allows long survival without oxygen, and months of low oxygen in cold water.
High ammonia tolerance: 96-hour lethal concentrations about 5–6 times those of rainbow trout (Wilkie et al. 2011).
Weberian ossicles linking the swim bladder to the ear for sensitive hearing.
Four cone types including ultraviolet.
Mauthner-cell escape reflex, the textbook model for fish startle responses.
sections.humanInteraction: One of the world's most popular ornamental fish and a major laboratory species for vision, hearing and neuroscience (FishBase; Wikipedia). Goldfish kept in bowls suffer from low oxygen and high ammonia; single-tailed forms can exceed 30 cm and need large, well-filtered tanks or ponds (Wikipedia). Released pets become invasive and grow far larger than in tanks.

funFacts: Goldfish make alcohol: without oxygen they turn sugar into ethanol instead of lactic acid.
Researchers taught goldfish to drive a wheeled tank across a room toward a target.
Goldfish see ultraviolet light as well as red, green and blue.
A released goldfish caught in a South Carolina lake in 2020 weighed about 4.1 kg.
The longest-lived goldfish on record reached 43 years in captivity (ADW).
Goldfish memory lasts at least three months, not three seconds.
One radio-tagged goldfish in Australia's Murray River travelled 231 km in a year.

abilities.name: Ethanol Engine
abilities.description: without oxygen, goldfish (and crucian carp) switch to a pathway that turns pyruvate into ethanol, using a pyruvate decarboxylase like that of brewer's yeast, the first described in a vertebrate (Fagernes et al. 2017). With ethanol as the end-product they survive prolonged oxygen loss, tolerating several months of low oxygen at 2 °C (ADW), in water where most fish die within minutes.

abilities.name: Mauthner Escape
abilities.description: giant Mauthner neurons trigger a short-latency, C-shaped escape bend in response to a sudden sound or looming shadow, launching the fish away at up to about 1.2 m/s in small individuals.

traits.name: Four-Colour Eyes
traits.description: goldfish have red, green, blue and ultraviolet cones and are among the most studied colour-vision systems in fish.

traits.name: Millennium Pet
traits.description: selectively bred for colour in imperial China for more than 1,000 years; by the Song dynasty, gold and red fish were kept in dedicated ponds.

combat.weapons: The goldfish has essentially no weapon. It suction-feeds on midge and mosquito larvae, small crustaceans, pondweeds, worms and detritus (ADW) and is not aggressive toward other goldfish (ADW). In a fight it cannot injure anything larger than a tadpole or an insect larva.
weaknesses: No weapon and no meaningful bite.
Small, soft-bodied fish with only scales and fin spines for protection.
Poor sustained swimmer.
Eaten by herons, otters, snakes, bullfrogs, cats, dogs and many other predators (ADW).

goliath-tigerfish.name: Goliath Tigerfish
goliath-tigerfish.specimen: healthy large adult, 25 kg and 110 cm long, sex unspecified.
goliath-tigerfish.summary: The goliath tigerfish is the Congo River's dagger-toothed hunter: a powerful 25 kg fish armed with 32 large, interlocking teeth that it replaces in whole sets within days. It strikes hard and fast in turbulent water, but with ordinary scales and modest mass it is outclassed by crocodiles, big sharks and other heavyweights.
narrative: The goliath tigerfish is the biggest and most heavily armed of the African tigerfishes. Its jaws carry 32 large teeth that sit along the outside of the mouth like a row of daggers, meshing together when the mouth closes. When teeth break or wear, the fish sheds a whole set and grows a new one in a matter of days, so its weapons are almost always sharp.

It hunts in some of the most demanding freshwater on Earth, the fast, churning channels of the Congo River, where it holds position in the current and strikes at fish swept past. Its smaller relative, the African tigerfish, has been filmed leaping out of the water to snatch swallows in flight, a sign of how fast and precisely these fish can attack.

In a battle, the goliath tigerfish is a sharp but lightly built attacker. Against another fish of its size, its teeth and fast-water power make it very dangerous. It has no armor, however, and at around 25 kg it cannot absorb the bite of a crocodile or large shark. Many of the frightening stories about it come from popular media rather than science; the real animal is impressive enough without them.

sections.habitat: The goliath tigerfish lives in the Congo River basin, including the Lualaba River and Lake Upemba, and in Lake Tanganyika. It prefers highly oxygenated, fast-flowing water in deep river channels and open lake waters.
sections.diet: Adults are strict fish-eaters, taking smaller fish including tilapia and smaller tigerfish. Juveniles eat plankton before switching to small fish. It is one of the top predators of the Congo's rivers.
sections.social: Little is known about the social life of wild goliath tigerfish; no stable groups or cooperative hunting are documented for large adults.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is poorly studied. Reports suggest young fish grow slowly at first. No age-validated growth study was found.
sections.conservation: The goliath tigerfish is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2010 assessment). Local threats may include fishing pressure and river development, but its conservation is poorly studied.
sections.features:
32 large, interlocking, dagger-like teeth up to about 2.5 cm.
Whole-quadrant tooth replacement over a few days (documented in the genus).
Deep, powerful body suited to fast river channels.
Largest species of tigerfish.
sections.humanInteraction: The goliath tigerfish is a prized and difficult sport fish and is eaten locally. It is kept in some large public aquariums. Stories of attacks on swimmers are common in popular media but were not confirmed in scientific sources during this research.

funFacts: Its 32 dagger-like teeth are each up to about 2.5 cm long.
Tigerfish replace a whole set of teeth at once in just a few days.
A related tigerfish was filmed leaping from the water to catch swallows in flight, the first confirmed case of a freshwater fish catching flying birds.
FishBase lists a maximum length of 133 cm and a maximum published weight of 50 kg.
It lives only in the Congo River basin and Lake Tanganyika.
Adults eat smaller tigerfish as well as other fish.

abilities.name: Dagger-Tooth Slash
abilities.description: 32 large, interlocking teeth, each up to about 2.5 cm and exposed along the jaw, seize and slice prey. Against soft-bodied opponents it can remove chunks of flesh in a single strike.

abilities.name: Whitewater Strike
abilities.description: it hunts in fast, turbulent river channels, holding position and lunging at prey swept by the current. In a matchup it keeps full striking power in water that tires or unbalances many opponents.

traits.name: Five-Day Tooth Reload
traits.description: in tigerfish, a whole quadrant of teeth is shed and replaced at once over about 3–5 days, so broken weapons are quickly renewed.

traits.name: Giant of the Tigerfishes
traits.description: the largest tigerfish species, reaching up to 133 cm and 50 kg according to FishBase, and the top fish predator of the Congo's fast waters.

combat.weapons: The goliath tigerfish's weapon is a mouth full of 32 large, interlocking, dagger-like teeth, each up to about 2.5 cm, exposed along the jaw edges. They are built to seize and slice fish, and popular accounts describe tigerfish removing chunks from larger fish. The fish is a strict piscivore, eating smaller fish, including smaller tigerfish and cichlids such as tilapia. Unlike a piranha, it does not rely on a shoal; unlike a barracuda, it is deep-bodied and powerful in strong currents.
weaknesses: No armor; ordinary fish scales.
Modest mass on the full roster.
Needs well-oxygenated water.
Useless out of water.

greenland-shark.name: Greenland Shark
greenland-shark.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 400 kg and 4.0 m total length, a large adult below the 5–6 m, 1,000+ kg exceptional animals.
greenland-shark.summary: The Greenland shark is a 4-metre, 400 kg Arctic sleeper shark that can live for centuries and cuts round chunks of flesh from seals with a rolling bite. It is the slowest fish measured for its size, so it wins by stealth and patience in cold, dark water rather than by speed or agility.
narrative: The Greenland shark lives slowly. It cruises through near-freezing water at about a third of a metre per second, its tail sweeping once every several seconds, and it grows extremely slowly. Radiocarbon trapped in its eye lenses shows that some individuals are well over two centuries old, and the species may not breed until it is around 150.

It is still a real predator. Large Greenland sharks eat seals, and their jaws are made for it: thin upper teeth pin the prey while a row of interlocking lower teeth works like a blade as the shark rolls its head. Since it could never chase down an alert seal, scientists think it approaches resting or sleeping animals so slowly and quietly that they never wake. Its eyes, though often colonized by parasites, contain a rod-only retina that still works in near-darkness.

In a battle, the Greenland shark is a slow heavyweight with a dangerous bite and almost no mobility. Against a fast predator such as an orca or great white it cannot dodge, chase or flee, so it must rely on mass and toughness. Against anything that blunders into its jaws in cold, dark water, that rolling bite can do serious damage.

sections.habitat: Greenland sharks live in the cold North Atlantic and Arctic, from the surface in the far north to more than 2,000 m deep further south. They are usually found in near-freezing water and are commonest at several hundred metres depth.
sections.diet: They are generalist predators and scavengers. Small sharks mainly eat squid; larger sharks mainly eat seals and fish. They also scavenge whale carcasses and the remains of land animals, including polar bears and reindeer, that end up in the sea. They are among the largest predators in Arctic seas.
sections.social: Solitary. Individuals gather at carcasses and baited sites but are not known to form groups.
sections.reproduction: The Greenland shark gives birth to live young. It grows extremely slowly and is thought to reach maturity only at around 150 years of age. Very little is known about mating or pupping.
sections.conservation: The Greenland shark is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2020 assessment, raised from Near Threatened). The main threat is bycatch in Arctic and North Atlantic fisheries; with maturity at about 150 years, populations recover extremely slowly. The Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization adopted protections in 2022.
sections.features:
Slowest fish for its size, cruising at 0.34 m/s.
Lifespan of at least 272 years, the longest known for a vertebrate.
Rod-only retina that remains functional for centuries.
Anchoring upper teeth and a blade-like lower jaw used in a rolling bite.
TMAO-rich tissues that are toxic when eaten raw.
sections.humanInteraction: Greenland sharks are caught as bycatch and were historically fished for liver oil. The flesh is poisonous raw but is fermented and dried to make the Icelandic dish kæstur hákarl. Attacks on people are essentially unknown.

funFacts: At least one Greenland shark was estimated to be about 392 years old.
A Greenland shark's tail beats only about once every seven seconds when cruising.
The fastest burst ever measured was 0.74 m/s, slower than a brisk human walk.
Most adults carry a parasite attached to their eyes, yet their vision still works.
Their retina contains only rod cells, suited to near-darkness.
Their raw flesh is poisonous, but in Iceland it is fermented into kæstur hákarl.
Remains of polar bears and reindeer have been found in their stomachs.

abilities.name: Roll-Cut Bite
abilities.description: thin upper teeth pin the prey while the shark rolls its head so the interlocking lower blade cuts out a round chunk of flesh. It can remove large pieces from seals and whale carcasses once contact is made.

abilities.name: Silent Sleeper Approach
abilities.description: cruising at about 0.34 m/s with a slow tail beat makes very little disturbance, and researchers suggest this lets it reach seals that are asleep or resting. In a matchup it favors surprise over pursuit.

traits.name: Centuries-Old Survivor
traits.description: eye-lens radiocarbon dating shows a lifespan of at least 272 years, the longest known of any vertebrate, with maturity at about 150 years.

traits.name: Rod-Only Night Vision
traits.description: its retina holds only rod cells tuned for dim light and stays working for centuries, even though most adults carry parasitic copepods on their corneas.

combat.weapons: The Greenland shark's weapon is its jaw: anchoring upper teeth and a lower row of broad, interlocking blade-like teeth. Holding prey with the upper jaw and rolling its head, it carves out round plugs of flesh. Large Greenland sharks eat ringed, bearded and hooded seals, as well as whale tissue and large fish, and they scavenge carcasses including polar bears and reindeer that end up in the sea. The problem is delivery: a shark whose top measured burst is 0.74 m/s cannot run down a healthy seal. Watanabe et al. suggested it may instead catch seals while they sleep or rest in the water, approaching slowly and quietly. Its offense is therefore powerful on contact but hard to bring to bear on an alert, mobile opponent.
weaknesses: Extremely slow and low in acceleration.
No armor.
Cannot chase or escape.
Poor in warm water, which it avoids.

greyhound.name: Greyhound
greyhound.specimen: healthy adult male, 32.0 kg, 74.0 cm at the withers.
greyhound.summary: The Greyhound is a 32 kg sprint sighthound that reaches about 19.5 m/s within 150 m and holds its speed through tight bends. It wins by catching or escaping, not by fighting: its lean, short-coated body is easily wounded and its speed fades over longer distances, so any opponent that stands its ground has the advantage.
narrative: The Greyhound was bred in Britain to hunt by sight, running down hares in open country, and its racing and coursing studbooks go back to the 18th century. A typical male weighs about 32 kg and stands about 74 cm, with long legs, a deep chest for a large heart and a spine that flexes and extends with every stride of its double-suspension gallop.

It is one of the best-measured sprinters in the animal world. Tracking studies show racing greyhounds reach just under 19.5 m/s within 80–150 m, and biomechanics research shows their power comes mainly from huge hip-extensor muscles. They do not slow down for tight bends; their legs simply absorb about 65% more force. Their blood carries more red cells than other breeds, helping supply oxygen during the race, but speed still falls to about 16 m/s by 500–600 m.

In a fight that speed is the Greyhound's only real weapon. It can catch and kill a hare, and it can escape from almost anything on open ground, but its lean body, thin coat and gentle temperament make it one of the weakest dogs on the roster in close combat. It rates high in Agility and Special, below the cheetah and pronghorn, and low in Attack and Defense.

sections.habitat: A domestic breed from Britain, now kept worldwide as a racing dog, coursing dog and pet, mostly in homes. It was historically used for hunting by sight in open country.
sections.diet: Fed by its owners on commercial dog food, meat and household scraps.
sections.ecology: No wild ecological role. Historically used to course hares and other game in open country; later used in organised coursing and track racing.
sections.social: Usually gentle and quiet with people and often good with other dogs, though many have a strong urge to chase small animals and poor recall.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is managed by people, largely through racing and coursing studbooks. Litters of 1–12 pups are reported (Wikipedia). VetCompass UK found that most pet greyhounds are retired racers.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed.
sections.features:
Long legs, deep chest and a very flexible spine.
Double-suspension rotary gallop.
Large hip-extensor muscle mass.
High red blood cell mass and distinct blood chemistry.
Short coat with no undercoat and little body fat.
sections.humanInteraction: Greyhound racing has brought welfare scrutiny, including research on track design to reduce injuries. Many retired racers are rehomed as pets, where they are known as calm companions. Some greyhounds sleep with their eyes partly open and can startle if woken suddenly.

funFacts: Racing greyhounds typically reach top speed, just under 19.5 m/s, within 80–150 m of the start.
Greyhounds do not slow down for tight bends; their legs simply take about 65% more force.
Greyhounds have more red blood cells than other dog breeds, which can confuse vets unfamiliar with the breed.
The FCI breed standard claims that "only the cheetah tops the Greyhound for speed".
Many greyhounds sleep with their eyes partly open.
A UK study of 5,419 pet greyhounds found males averaged 32.3 kg and females 27.2 kg.

abilities.name: Double-Suspension Sprint
abilities.description: a gallop in which all four feet leave the ground twice per stride, powered by large hip-extensor muscles, taking it to about 19.5 m/s within 80–150 m. In a matchup it can close distance or escape faster than almost any other dog.

abilities.name: Bend Runner
abilities.description: keeps its foot-contact timing through tight bends and absorbs 65% higher limb forces rather than slowing, as Usherwood and Wilson showed. It turns at speed where other runners must brake.

traits.name: Red-Cell Rich Athlete
traits.description: retired racing greyhounds have higher red blood cell mass than other breeds, part of a distinct blood profile that veterinarians must account for.

traits.name: Hip-Driven Sprinter Build
traits.description: a deep chest, long legs, very flexible spine and the highest share of fast oxidative muscle fibres of any breed, with running power coming mainly from torque about the hips.

combat.weapons: The Greyhound was bred to run down game by sight and catch it, historically hares in coursing. Its weapon is the bite delivered at the end of a sprint, from a long head on a long neck. It is built to catch and kill small, fast prey, not to wrestle large or armed animals.
weaknesses: Lean, lightly protected body with no undercoat.
Speed drops off after a few hundred metres.
Poor at close grappling; no heavy musculature in the forequarters or jaw built for fighting.
Sensitive to heat and cold.
Far outmatched by any serious fighter of its size or larger.

guinea-pig.name: Guinea Pig
guinea-pig.specimen: healthy adult male (boar) of about 1.0 kg of a standard pet breed, not a 3 kg Peruvian meat-breed animal and not an obese pet.
guinea-pig.summary: The guinea pig is a 1 kg Andean grazer bred from wild cavies, with nearly all-round vision, a busy social life and a freeze-or-scatter escape plan. Its incisors are built for grass rather than fighting, so on the absolute scale it is one of the least dangerous mammals on the roster.
narrative: The guinea pig is a domestic animal with a long Andean history. People in the highlands of South America bred it from wild cavies thousands of years ago as a compact source of meat, and it still fills that role there, while elsewhere it is one of the most popular small pets. It lives in groups, talks constantly in squeaks, whistles and purrs, and keeps watch with eyes that see almost all the way around its head.

In a fight it has very little to offer. Its jaws are organized for grinding grass, and a comparative study of rodent jaw muscles found the guinea pig built for a relatively weak incisor bite. Boars do fight each other with chattering, head thrusts, leaping attacks and ear bites, but these contests matter only between guinea pigs. Against a predator, its options are to freeze, scatter with the herd, or dash for cover, and it is neither a good climber nor a good jumper.

On the absolute ABS scale the guinea pig therefore sits near the floor for Attack and Defense, below similarly sized predators and the spined hedgehog, with moderate scores for intelligence and senses. Its real distinctions are social and historical rather than martial: a herd animal that became Andean livestock, a laboratory model and a household pet.

sections.habitat: As a domestic animal the guinea pig lives worldwide in homes, laboratories and Andean farms. Its main wild source species, the montane guinea pig, lives in the high Andes from Peru to northern Chile and Argentina at about 2,000–3,800 m, in moist habitats with rocks and coarse vegetation where it makes runways through the plants.
sections.diet: Strict herbivores: grasses, hay, leafy vegetables and fruit. Like humans, and unlike most mammals, guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C and need about 10 mg a day from food. Wild cavies graze open grassy ground and shelter in other animals' burrows, rock crevices and vegetation tunnels.
sections.social: Social herd animals. Wild groups are usually one male with several females and young. Domestic groups form dominance hierarchies, with boars competing for rank and mates. Groups huddle, groom and communicate constantly by voice.
sections.reproduction: Gestation lasts about 59–72 days, and litters average about three precocial pups. Females can be fertile at about four weeks and can conceive again within hours of giving birth. Pets usually live five to eight years.
sections.conservation: Domesticated; the domestic guinea pig has no wild population to assess. Its main wild source species, the montane guinea pig, is listed as Least Concern.
sections.features:
About 340° field of vision.
Continuously growing incisors and cheek teeth.
Precocial young born furred and mobile.
Cannot synthesize vitamin C.
Large vocal repertoire, including whistles and alarm squeals.
sections.humanInteraction: Guinea pigs were domesticated for food in the Andes, where they also have roles in folk medicine and ceremonies. They became pets in Europe after the Spanish conquest, were central to early research on scurvy and infectious diseases, and gave English the phrase "guinea pig" for a test subject.

funFacts: Guinea pigs, like people, must get vitamin C from their food.
A startled group scatters in random directions to confuse predators.
Domestic guinea pigs learned a water maze faster than wild cavies, despite smaller relative brains.
Pups are born with fur, teeth and open eyes and can eat solid food almost at once.
Excited guinea pigs perform little vertical jumps called "popcorning".
The oldest guinea pig recorded by Guinness World Records lived to 14 years and 10 months.

abilities.name: Scatter Stampede
abilities.description: when a group is startled, guinea pigs bolt in haphazard directions to confuse a predator, while a lone animal freezes motionless until the threat passes. In a matchup this buys escape time but does no damage.

abilities.name: Panoramic Watch
abilities.description: laterally placed eyes give about 340° of vision, backed by alarm squeals and contact whistles, so a guinea pig rarely misses an approaching threat even while grazing.

traits.name: Andean Livestock
traits.description: first domesticated for meat in the Andes thousands of years ago, the guinea pig is still raised and eaten as cuy in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador and Colombia, where improved meat lines reach 3 kg.

traits.name: Born Ready
traits.description: unlike most rodents, guinea pig pups are born fully furred with teeth, claws and open eyes, and can run and eat solid food almost immediately.

combat.weapons: A guinea pig has incisors and small claws, but it is a grazer built for chewing grass, not for fighting. Its jaw muscles are organized for grinding rather than a hard incisor bite. Between boars, dominance is settled by chattering teeth, raised fur, head thrusts, leaping attacks and bites, especially to the ears. These fights can draw blood between guinea pigs, but they cannot seriously hurt a predator.
weaknesses: Weak incisor bite for a rodent and very low absolute power.
No armor; poor climbing and jumping.
Depends on dietary vitamin C and suffers scurvy without it.
Freezing in place can fail against a predator that has already spotted it.

gyrfalcon.name: Gyrfalcon
gyrfalcon.specimen: healthy adult female, 1.7 kg, 58.0 cm total length, wingspan about 125 cm.
gyrfalcon.summary: The gyrfalcon is the world's largest falcon, a 1.7 kg Arctic hunter that chases ptarmigan and ducks low over the tundra until they tire. It is fast, tough in the cold and armed with sharp talons and a killing bite, but its light body means it can only overpower prey far smaller than the roster's heavy hitters.
narrative: The gyrfalcon is the heavyweight of the falcon world. A female, the larger sex, weighs about 1.7 kg and spans up to 130 cm, nearly twice the weight of a male. It lives where few raptors can, nesting on Arctic cliffs and staying through the polar winter, when some birds live for weeks over sea ice hunting seabirds and ducks around open water.

Its hunting style is different from the peregrine's famous dive. Gyrfalcons usually attack low, bursting from a perch or sweeping along a ridge to surprise ptarmigan and other birds. When that first strike misses, they settle into a long tail-chase just above the ground, relying on powerful flight muscles to wear their prey down. A study of young gyrfalcons found they steer toward targets using the same rule as peregrines, but correct their heading less sharply, a match for a bigger bird built for sustained pursuit.

In a battle, the gyrfalcon is a dangerous small predator. Its talons and notched bill kill prey as large as ducks and hares, and it presses attacks with real commitment. But at under 2 kg it has no armor, and a heavy hit to its wings can end the fight. It rates highly for Agility, Stamina and senses, and modestly for Attack and Defense.

sections.habitat: Breeds across the Arctic and sub-Arctic of North America, Greenland, Iceland, Scandinavia and Russia on cliffs and outcrops in tundra, coastal and mountain landscapes. Many adults stay near breeding areas all year, while some birds, especially juveniles, move south in winter or out onto sea ice.
sections.diet: A bird specialist centered on rock and willow ptarmigan, which make up about 72% of summer diet biomass in northeast Iceland. It also takes waterfowl, seabirds, shorebirds, Arctic hares, ground squirrels and lemmings. In Iceland its breeding success rises and falls with ptarmigan numbers.
sections.social: Solitary outside the breeding season; breeding pairs hold territories around cliff nest sites and often reuse old raven or rough-legged hawk nests, as they build no nest of their own.
sections.reproduction: Breeds from about 2–3 years of age and lays a small clutch on a cliff ledge. Icelandic studies estimate annual survival at about 83% for adults and 40% for juveniles. The oldest known wild bird was at least 15 years 9 months old.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List since 2004 because of its huge range and a population estimated at about 50,000–70,000 birds. Partners in Flight estimates a global breeding population of about 70,000 and reports no evidence of long-term decline in North America. Warming that alters ptarmigan cycles and Arctic habitats is a concern for the future.
sections.features:
Largest falcon, with reversed size dimorphism.
Notched (tomial) bill for killing bites.
White, gray and dark color morphs.
Dense plumage for Arctic winter survival.
Strong flight muscles for sustained low pursuit.
sections.humanInteraction: Prized in falconry for centuries, historically reserved for royalty in parts of Europe and Asia, and still bred in captivity for falconry. Wild populations are remote and little disturbed by people.

funFacts: It is the largest falcon in the world.
Females can weigh nearly twice as much as males.
In northeast Iceland, ptarmigan make up about 72% of its summer diet by weight.
Some gyrfalcons spend weeks living over winter sea ice far from land.
One tracked juvenile female traveled nearly 3,000 miles in about 200 days, much of it over the sea.
It rarely uses the peregrine's high-speed stoop and prefers low, long chases.
The oldest known wild gyrfalcon was at least 15 years 9 months old.

abilities.name: Tundra Tail-Chase
abilities.description: when an ambush misses, it keeps chasing low over the ground, wearing down fast ptarmigan and ducks with sustained pursuit rather than a single dive.

abilities.name: Neck-Breaking Bite
abilities.description: binds prey with its talons, then kills with a bite to the neck from its notched falcon bill.

traits.name: Largest Falcon
traits.description: the biggest falcon in the world, with females reaching about 2.1 kg and a wingspan up to 130 cm.

traits.name: Sea-Ice Winterer
traits.description: some birds spend more than a month at a time over winter sea ice far from land, hunting seabirds and sea ducks around open water.

combat.weapons: The gyrfalcon kills with its feet and beak. It strikes or grabs prey with its talons, often binding to it and bringing it to the ground, then finishes it with a bite to the neck using its notched bill. Its prey is large for a falcon: ptarmigan make up the bulk of the diet in many areas, and it also takes ducks, seabirds, Arctic hares and lemmings. At 1.7 kg it is roughly 70% heavier than a female peregrine, which gives it more grip and impact against bird-sized and hare-sized prey.
weaknesses: Low absolute mass and no armor.
Flight-critical wings; a grounded falcon is badly exposed.
Less agile in tight turns than smaller falcons.
Weapons suited to bird-sized and hare-sized prey, not large animals.

house-cat.name: House Cat
house-cat.specimen: healthy mature intact adult male of about 5.0 kg, a typical non-obese tomcat rather than a giant breed or an overweight pet.
house-cat.summary: The house cat is a 5 kg pocket predator with the same toolkit as small wild cats: stealth, a lightning pounce, retractable claws and a precise killing bite, backed by superb balance and ultrasonic hearing. It is deadly to mice and birds, but on the absolute scale it is a lightweight that cannot hurt large animals.
narrative: The house cat is the most familiar predator on Earth. Bred from Near Eastern wildcat stock and carried by people across the globe, it still hunts the way small wild cats do: it watches, creeps, waits, then explodes into a short rush and pins prey with its claws before a quick bite to the neck. Very flexible spine, strong hind legs, a righting reflex and hearing that reaches about 85 kHz make it one of the most capable small hunters anywhere.

That efficiency shows up in the numbers. Free-ranging cats are estimated to kill billions of birds and mammals each year in the United States alone, and feral cats on islands have helped drive many species to extinction. In a fight, cats can be fierce: an angry tomcat fights with bites, forefoot grabs and raking hind claws, and a cornered cat is hard to handle.

For ABS the key rule is absolute scale. Pound for pound the cat is formidable, but a 5 kg animal has very little absolute power, reach or durability. It therefore sits far below the leopard and well below the 10–17 kg wild cats such as the bobcat and caracal in Attack and Defense, while scoring high in Agility and Senses, where small size is not a handicap.

sections.habitat: Worldwide, wherever people live, from city apartments to farms, deserts, tropical islands and sub-Antarctic islands. Feral cats live independently of people in many of these places.
sections.diet: Obligate carnivores. Pet cats eat prepared food, but free-roaming cats hunt small mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and insects, and scavenge. A 2013 study estimated that free-ranging cats in the contiguous United States kill about 1.3–4.0 billion birds and 6.3–22.3 billion mammals each year, most of them killed by un-owned cats.
sections.social: Solitary hunters with flexible social lives. Free-roaming cats can form colonies around food sources, where related females may nurse and guard each other's kittens. Males hold larger ranges and compete for females.
sections.reproduction: Cats can breed more than once a year, with litters of several kittens. Kittens learn hunting partly by watching their mother. Sexual maturity can come within the first year, which allows unmanaged populations to grow quickly.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated animal. Its conservation relevance is as a threat: feral and free-ranging cats are listed by IUCN among the 100 of the World's Worst Invasive Alien Species, and on islands they are implicated in at least 14% of bird, mammal and reptile extinctions and threaten at least 175 vertebrate taxa.
sections.features:
Fully retractable claws.
Very flexible spine and powerful hind legs.
Righting reflex when falling.
Hearing range of about 48 Hz to 85 kHz.
Reflective tapetum lucidum for low-light vision.
Long, sensitive whiskers.
sections.humanInteraction: Cats have lived with people for thousands of years. Genetic work on nearly 1,000 cats places their origin in Near Eastern wildcats, around the first farming villages of the Fertile Crescent, and a cat buried with a person in Cyprus about 9,500 years ago is among the earliest evidence of the partnership. Today cats are among the most popular pets in the world, and their outdoor hunting is a major wildlife management issue.

funFacts: Cats can hear sounds up to about 85 kHz, far above the human limit near 20 kHz.
A cat buried beside a person in Cyprus about 9,500 years ago is one of the oldest signs of cats living with people.
Genetic testing of 979 cats traced domestic cats to Near Eastern wildcat stock.
In one feral-cat study, males had an estimated bite force of about 206 N, around a fifth more than females.
Free-ranging cats in the contiguous US may kill billions of birds and mammals each year.
A cat's claws are fully retractable and stay sharp because they are sheathed while walking.

abilities.name: Righting Reflex
abilities.description: when a cat falls, its balance organs and flexible spine let it rotate to land feet-first, reducing injury and allowing it to recover position almost instantly.

abilities.name: Ultrasonic Ears
abilities.description: cats hear from about 48 Hz up to about 85 kHz, far above human hearing, which lets them locate rodents by their high-pitched sounds and detect threats early.

traits.name: World's Most Common Cat
traits.description: bred from Near Eastern wildcat stock and now living with people on every inhabited continent, the house cat is by far the most numerous member of the cat family.

traits.name: Island Invader
traits.description: feral cats are listed among the world's 100 worst invasive alien species and have contributed to at least 14% of bird, mammal and reptile extinctions on islands.

combat.weapons: The house cat is a small ambush hunter with the same basic kit as small wild cats: stalking, a short explosive rush, a grab with retractable claws, and a killing bite to the nape of small prey. In a fight with another cat it also rakes with the hind claws while gripping with the forefeet. Its weapons are very effective against rodents, birds, lizards and insects, which is why free-roaming cats kill vast numbers of small animals. Against anything much larger than a rabbit, however, its 5 kg body cannot deliver serious damage.
weaknesses: Very small absolute size and power.
No armor or thick hide.
Poor endurance in long chases.
Weapons cannot seriously injure large animals.

humboldt-squid.name: Humboldt Squid
humboldt-squid.specimen: healthy mature large adult female, 100 cm mantle length and 25 kg.
humboldt-squid.summary: The Humboldt squid is a 25 kg "red devil" of the eastern Pacific that hunts in shoals of hundreds, striking with elastic tentacles covered in toothed suckers and tearing with one of the hardest organic beaks known. It flashes glowing color signals in the dark, but its soft body and small size limit it against large, armored or heavy-biting opponents.
narrative: The Humboldt squid is a short-lived, fast-growing predator that makes up for its soft body with speed, weapons and numbers. A large adult has a mantle about a metre long and weighs around 25 kg. When it attacks, two elastic tentacles shoot out almost too fast to film, gripping prey with suckers ringed by hard protein teeth and pulling it to a beak so hard and stiff that materials scientists study it.

It lives by a daily commute. By day it sinks into the ocean's oxygen-poor layer, hundreds of metres down; by night it rises to hunt. There it gathers in shoals of up to 1,200, and sonar shows small groups breaking away to spiral upward together after fish. The squid communicate with rapid red-and-white flashes and patterns that they light from inside with tiny photophores, a way of signaling in near-total darkness.

In a battle the Humboldt squid is a genuine glass cannon. Its tentacle strike is quick and its beak and toothed suckers can shred fish, and it is famous for aggression, even toward its own injured shoal-mates. But a 25 kg animal with no shell cannot absorb much punishment, and against large, well-armed opponents its best weapon is its speed in escaping.

sections.habitat: Humboldt squid live in the eastern Pacific from Tierra del Fuego to California, mostly at depths of about 200 to 700 m, and have been spreading north into the waters of Oregon, Washington, British Columbia and Alaska (Wikipedia). They spend daytime in deep, oxygen-poor water and move toward the surface at night (Rosa & Seibel 2009).
sections.diet: They are voracious carnivores, eating small fish, crustaceans and other squid, including their own species. In a study of more than 2,000 squid caught off Chile, other Humboldt squid were the most common prey (Wikipedia). Off Peru, small-, medium- and large-sized groups overlap in some habitats and divide food in others (Zhao et al. 2023).
sections.social: Humboldt squid gather in shoals of up to 1,200 animals (Wikipedia). At night, small subgroups break away and hunt in coordinated spirals (Benoit-Bird & Gilly, via Deep Sea News). They communicate with pigment patterns and flashes shown selectively in foraging and social contexts (Burford & Robison 2020).
sections.reproduction: Humboldt squid live only one to two years and grow very quickly (Wikipedia). Females mature larger than males and produce large egg masses containing thousands to millions of eggs, depending on size (Wikipedia).
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the Humboldt squid as Data Deficient (as summarized by Wikipedia). It supports the most important squid fishery in the world, landed mainly in Chile, Peru and Mexico; the Gulf of California fishery collapsed in 2015 during warm-water conditions and had not recovered (Wikipedia). Warmer, more acidic water reduces its metabolic performance (Rosa & Seibel 2009).
sections.features:
Two elastic, fast-striking tentacles.
Sucker rings lined with hard protein teeth.
One of the hardest wholly organic beaks known.
Chromatophores for rapid red-white flashing, backlit by photophores in the muscle.
Tolerance of low-oxygen water during daily vertical migrations.
sections.humanInteraction: Humboldt squid are a major commercial catch and an inexpensive food in Peru and Chile (Wikipedia). They have a reputation for attacking fishers and divers, which some scientists attribute to provocation by lights or reflective gear. Their beak and sucker teeth are studied as models for tough, graded materials (Miserez et al. 2008; Rieu et al. 2016).

funFacts: Fishers in Mexico call it the "red devil" because it flashes red and white when caught.
Its beak is one of the hardest and stiffest materials made entirely by a living thing without minerals.
Every sucker is ringed with tiny teeth.
It can light up its own color patterns from inside its body to signal in the dark.
Shoals can contain up to 1,200 squid.
It usually lives only about a year.

abilities.name: Toothed Tentacle Strike
abilities.description: two elastic tentacles shoot out and retract in about a frame of video, gripping prey with suckers ringed by hard teeth and dragging it to one of the hardest organic beaks known. It is a fast, hard-to-dodge first strike.

abilities.name: Glow-Lit Flash Signals
abilities.description: the squid flashes red and white and displays pigment patterns that it lights from inside with small photophores, making its signals visible in the dark deep sea. It lets a shoal coordinate and can startle opponents.

traits.name: Red Devil Shoals
traits.description: Humboldt squid hunt in shoals of up to 1,200 and form coordinated subgroups at night; injured squid are often eaten by their shoal-mates.

traits.name: Low-Oxygen Commuter
traits.description: every day it descends into the ocean's oxygen-poor layer and returns to the surface at night to feed and recover.

combat.weapons: The Humboldt squid attacks with two long, elastic tentacles that shoot out and retract so fast that nearly the whole strike fits in one frame of normal-speed video (Wikipedia). The tentacle and arm suckers are ringed with hard teeth, and prey is drawn to an extremely hard, sharp beak (Miserez et al. 2008). Humboldt squid can strip hooked fish to the bone before fishers reel them in, and they readily attack injured members of their own shoal; about a quarter of stomachs examined in one study held remains of other Humboldt squid (Wikipedia).
weaknesses: Soft body with no armor; bites and blows cause real damage.
Small absolute mass compared with large fish and marine mammals.
Short life and sensitivity to warm, acidified water.
Cannibalism within the shoal means injured squid are attacked by their own kind.

humpback-whale.name: Humpback Whale
humpback-whale.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 30,000 kg and 14.0 m long, placed below NOAA's stated species maximum of about 60 ft and 40 tons.
humpback-whale.summary: The humpback whale is a 30-tonne, big-winged baleen giant that fights with fluke and flipper strikes rather than teeth. It is famous for charging into killer whale attacks, building bubble nets, singing learned songs and migrating across whole oceans, but without a bite it relies on mass, endurance and nerve.
narrative: The humpback is a giant with no teeth that still picks fights with killer whales. A large adult weighs around 30 tonnes and carries the longest flippers of any whale, each edged with rounded bumps that keep water flowing smoothly over the fin even when it is angled steeply. Those flippers let the humpback turn tightly enough to swim in spirals around fish schools, and they double as heavy clubs.

Researchers reviewing 115 encounters found that humpbacks usually started interactions with killer whales, almost always when mammal-eating orcas were already attacking something, and then harassed the attackers. Whether that is defense of their own calves generalised to other targets or something more, it means a humpback in a battle will not simply flee. Its weapons are blunt: a fluke or flipper strike from a 30-tonne body can do real harm, but it cannot bite or cut, so it wins by deterring, battering and outlasting rather than killing.

Its endurance and behavioral range are exceptional. Humpbacks cross whole ocean basins, one documented journey exceeding 9,800 km, and feed with techniques such as bubble nets that spread socially through populations. Males sing long, structured songs that are learned and carried from one population to another. The result is a strong defensive heavyweight with high stamina and real intelligence, held back in attack by the absence of any true weapon.

sections.habitat: Humpbacks are found in all the world's oceans. They feed in cold, productive high-latitude waters in summer and migrate to warm tropical and subtropical waters to breed and calve. They often come close to coasts, which makes them one of the most visible large whales.
sections.diet: Humpbacks are baleen filter feeders. They eat krill and small schooling fish such as herring, capelin and sand lance, lunging through prey patches with an expanding throat. Bubble-net feeding lets them corral schools; Wiley et al. (2011) identified upward-spiral and double-loop methods and found bubble nets are made within roughly the top 20 m of water. Much of the year's feeding happens in summer, and whales rely on stored energy during migration and breeding.
sections.social: Humpbacks are loosely social. They form short-term groups for feeding, travel and courtship. Some feeding groups repeatedly cooperate, and mothers stay closely with calves. Males gather in competitive groups around females on the breeding grounds.
sections.reproduction: Calves are born in warm breeding areas and travel with their mothers to feeding grounds. The long lifespan (about 80–90 years according to NOAA) and slow reproduction make populations slow to rebuild.
sections.conservation: Globally the humpback is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List after strong recoveries from commercial whaling, while NOAA manages it as distinct population segments, some of which remain protected under the US Endangered Species Act. These statuses were taken from general agency summaries and not re-verified from a retrieved assessment page in this run. Current threats include entanglement in fishing gear, ship strikes and ocean noise.
sections.features:
Exceptionally long, wing-like pectoral flippers with lift-enhancing leading-edge tubercles.
Bubble-net feeding in spiral and double-loop patterns.
Long, structured, learned songs sung by males.
Throat pleats that expand for engulfment feeding.
Record-scale migratory endurance.
sections.humanInteraction: Humpbacks are a centerpiece of whale watching worldwide because they breach, slap their flippers and tails, and approach coasts. Their flipper tubercles have inspired engineering research on wind-turbine and fan blades. Entanglement and vessel strikes are the main direct human threats.

funFacts: Megaptera means "big-winged", after the whale's long flippers.
The bumps on a humpback's flipper edge keep it generating lift at steep angles, an idea engineers have borrowed for blades.
One female was photographed off Brazil and later off Madagascar, at least 9,800 km away.
Songs spread from population to population; new song types have moved eastward across the South Pacific from Australia.
Humpbacks often charge into killer whale attacks on other species, including seals and other whales.
Bubble nets are built in the top 20 m of water, where bubbles hold together best.

abilities.name: Big-Wing Flipper Strike
abilities.description: pectoral flippers far longer than in other whales, with tubercles that keep lift at steep angles, let the humpback turn tightly and swing a heavy limb at an attacker. Combined with fluke slaps, this is its main weapon against predators.

abilities.name: Orca-Mobbing Charge
abilities.description: humpbacks deliberately approach and harass mammal-eating killer whales that are attacking prey, as shown across 115 recorded interactions. In a battle it will commit to a fight with an apex predator rather than flee.

traits.name: Bubble-Net Architect
traits.description: humpbacks blow rings and spirals of bubbles to trap fish, sometimes working in cooperative groups, and the technique spreads socially through populations.

traits.name: Ocean-Basin Songline
traits.description: males sing long, structured songs that are learned and passed between populations across whole ocean basins, and individual whales can travel more than 9,800 km between breeding areas.

combat.weapons:
The humpback has no teeth, claws or horns. Its offensive tools are the flukes and the very long pectoral flippers, swung with the force of a 30-tonne body, plus body mass itself. NOAA describes humpbacks as highly active, often slapping the surface with their flippers or tails and leaping clear of the water. These movements show the power a humpback can put behind a strike.

Its most striking documented "combat" behavior is interference with killer whales. Pitman et al. (2017) reviewed 115 interactions between humpbacks and killer whales. Humpbacks initiated most encounters (57%), almost all of the killer whales involved were mammal-eating forms (95%), and at least 87% of the killer whales approached were attacking or feeding at the time. In 55% or more of 56 detailed interactions, the humpbacks actively harassed the attacking killer whales, which the authors interpret as mobbing behavior. This shows a willingness to charge into a fight with the ocean's top predator.
weaknesses: No bite or cutting weapon; damage comes only from blunt strikes.
Must surface to breathe and does not dive to the depths toothed whales reach.
Slower and less agile than orcas and sharks.
Calves and lone animals are vulnerable to coordinated killer whale packs.
Stranded or entangled whales are helpless.

hyacinth-macaw.name: Hyacinth Macaw
hyacinth-macaw.specimen: healthy mature adult, 1.3 kg, 100.0 cm total length. Sex is left unspecified because the sexes look alike and no source read in this run gives a consistent size gap between them.
hyacinth-macaw.summary: The Hyacinth Macaw is the longest parrot in the world, about 1 m long and 1.3 kg, and it has the strongest measured bite of any bird, about 539 N. That bill cracks palm nuts that are hard to open with a hammer. In a real fight, though, it is a light, unarmored bird with one close-range weapon and no talons.
narrative: The hyacinth macaw is a specialist built around one extraordinary tool. Its huge black bill, powered by jaw muscles that produced a mean measured bite of about 539 N in live birds, lets it live almost entirely on palm nuts that few other animals can open. It holds the nut with its foot and tongue, sometimes wedges a chewed leaf against it, and chisels a line across the shell until it splits cleanly. In the Pantanal it even collects acuri nuts from cattle dung, after the cattle have eaten the fruit and passed the nuts.

Its life is tied to a few plants. It eats one or two palm species in each part of its range and nests almost only in old manduvi trees whose hollows take about 60 years to form. The toco toucan spreads most manduvi seeds and also takes about half of the macaw eggs lost to predators. Trapping for the pet trade in the 1970s and 1980s cut the wild population to a few thousand; protection by ranchers, artificial nests and the CITES Appendix I listing have helped it recover in the Pantanal.

In an absolute matchup the hyacinth has the best bite of any bird on the roster, but it sits on a 1.3 kg body with feathers for armor and feet made for holding nuts, not prey. It can deliver a crippling bite to anything small enough to be caught in it and can fly away from ground threats. Against a raptor or a carnivore that seizes it, that single weapon is not enough.

sections.habitat: The hyacinth macaw lives in central South America in three main areas: the Pantanal of Brazil with adjacent eastern Bolivia and north-eastern Paraguay; the cerrado of interior eastern Brazil; and open areas along the Tocantins, Xingu and Tapajós rivers and Marajó Island in the eastern Amazon basin. It uses palm savanna, forest edge, dry woodland with gallery forest, and swampy stands of palms such as the moriche palm. The key requirement is the presence of its food palms.
sections.diet: It feeds mainly on the nuts of a few palm species in each region. In the Pantanal the main palms are acuri (Attalea phalerata) and bocaiuva (Acrocomia aculeata); in the Amazon it uses Maximiliana, Orbignya and Astrocaryum; in north-eastern Brazil it uses Attalea funifera and Syagrus coronata (WPT). It also takes other fruit and apple snails. Its link with the toco toucan is unusual: the toucan spreads most seeds of the manduvi tree the macaw nests in, but is also its main egg predator.
sections.social: Hyacinths live in pairs, family groups or small flocks of up to about 10 birds, and are noisy and conspicuous. Peak feeding activity is in the morning and late afternoon (WPT).
sections.reproduction: Nesting runs from July to December, in tree cavities in the Pantanal and Amazon and in cliff crevices in north-eastern Brazil. About 75% of females lay two eggs, but usually only one chick survives; for every 100 eggs laid, about 25 produce a chick that leaves the nest (Guedes et al. 2022). Chicks fledge at around 110 days and depend on their parents until about six months old.
sections.conservation: The hyacinth macaw is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN and is on CITES Appendix I. WPT gives a world population of about 4,700–11,000 mature birds. The first estimate, in 1987, was about 3,000 birds, after heavy trapping: an estimated 10,000 were taken from the wild in the 1980s. Threats are trapping for the cage-bird trade, burning and clearing of habitat, and the scarcity of old nest trees. It remains locally common in the Brazilian Pantanal, where many ranchers now protect it, and the Hyacinth Macaw Project has added artificial nests to make up for lost cavities.
sections.features:
Strongest measured bite force of any bird.
Longest parrot, with a tail making up half its length.
Bright yellow bare skin around the eye and at the base of the lower bill against cobalt-blue plumage.
Dry, smooth tongue with a bone inside that helps hold and work food.
Tool use while opening nuts.
sections.humanInteraction: Hyacinths are prized in aviculture, and captive numbers were once thought to rival the wild population. Trapping drove the wild decline, and export is now banned under CITES Appendix I. As pets they need very large spaces and extremely tough chew items; WPT recommends access to an enclosure at least 15 m long for part of the year. In the Pantanal, ecotourism and rancher protection now support the species.

funFacts: A hyacinth macaw's measured bite of about 539 N is the strongest yet recorded for any bird.
It is the longest parrot in the world, and half of its 1 m length is tail.
In the Pantanal it picks acuri palm nuts out of cattle dung after the cattle have eaten the fruit.
Captive hyacinths wedge bits of leaf or wood against nuts to stop them slipping while they crack them.
The toco toucan both plants the macaw's favourite nest tree and eats many of its eggs.
Only trees older than about 60 years have hollows big enough for hyacinth macaw nests.
In the 1980s an estimated 10,000 wild birds were taken for the pet trade.

traits.name: Cattle-Dung Forager

combat.weapons: The bill is the one real weapon, and it is an exceptional one. Seven live hyacinth macaws produced a mean measured bite of about 539 N, the highest measured bite force of any bird in the published record read for this report, more than twice the measured bite of a Scarlet Macaw in the same study. The bill is built to crush and chisel palm nuts: the bird cracks the shell in one area and then breaks it cleanly in half (ADW). The same tool can badly injure a hand or a small animal. The feet grip and hold, but they are not killing talons, and the hyacinth is not a predator. Its food is almost entirely palm nuts, with some other fruit and apple snails (Pomacea) (WPT).
weaknesses: About 1.3 kg in absolute mass.
No armor; hollow-boned flying body.
Only one real weapon, delivered at close range.
Depends on one or two palm species and scarce old nest trees.
Noisy and predictable, which made it vulnerable to trapping and shooting.

indian-cobra.name: Indian Cobra
indian-cobra.specimen: healthy representative adult, 2.0 kg and 150 cm total length, sex unspecified. This pass did not verify a consistent size difference between the sexes, so no sex-based modifier is applied.
indian-cobra.summary: The Indian cobra is the spectacled cobra of South Asia, famous for its hooded threat display and its neurotoxic venom. At around 1.5 m and 2 kg it is small and unarmored, but its bite blocks the nerve signals to muscles and can stop breathing. It thrives around farms and villages hunting rats, which makes it one of the snakes behind most of India's snakebites.
narrative: The Indian cobra's reputation is built on a single, well-known image: a snake rising from the ground with its hood spread and the spectacle mark showing. That display is a real combat tool. It warns animals and people away before any contact, and if the warning fails the cobra strikes forward and down from its raised posture.

Behind the display is a venom dominated by three-finger toxins. The paralysis comes from a small fraction of them, α-neurotoxins that jam the receptors muscles use to receive nerve signals. PLA2 enzymes and other proteins add more effects, and the exact recipe changes from one region of India to another, sometimes enough to weaken antivenom treatment. For a matchup, the key point is simple: a clean bite on an unarmored animal can paralyze something far larger than the cobra.

On the absolute scale the cobra's limits are just as clear. A 2 kg snake has little strength and no armor, its fangs are short, and venom takes time. A heavy animal that crushes it fast, a raptor that strikes from above, or a mongoose whose receptors resist α-neurotoxins can beat it. Bigger snake-eaters such as the king cobra hunt it.

Its success comes from living where the food is. Farmland and village edges are full of rats, and the cobra follows them, which is also why people meet it so often. That closeness to people explains both its cultural fame and its large share of snakebite cases.

sections.habitat: The Indian cobra is found across the Indian subcontinent, including India, Sri Lanka and neighboring countries. Animal Diversity Web and other sources describe it in wild forest and cultivated land, with records from grassland, scrub, savanna-like country, mangroves and rainforest. It is common near villages and farmland.
sections.diet: It feeds mainly on rodents such as the black rat, and also takes frogs, birds, lizards and other snakes. As a rat predator in farmland it plays a real role in controlling crop and grain pests. It is itself eaten by king cobras and hunted by mongooses.
sections.social: Solitary outside breeding.
sections.reproduction: Oviparous. Females usually lay 12 to 20 eggs in a hollow tree or in the earth and guard them throughout incubation, leaving only to feed. Hatchlings emerge after about 50 days with functional venom.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. It remains widespread, though it is killed in large numbers when found near homes and is still used by snake charmers in some areas.
sections.features:
Front fangs delivering a three-finger-toxin-dominated neurotoxic venom.
Expandable hood with the spectacle-shaped mark on its back.
A wide black band on the underside of the neck.
Ability to rear and hold a large part of the body upright during threat displays.
Strong regional variation in venom composition across India.
sections.humanInteraction: India loses tens of thousands of people to snakebite each year; a nationally representative study estimated about 1.2 million deaths between 2000 and 2019, around 58,000 a year. The Indian cobra and Russell's viper cause most envenomations because they are found almost throughout the country. The cobra is central to Indian culture and folklore and is closely associated with snake charmers. Research showing that venoms from different regions respond differently to the same antivenom has pushed for better, pan-India treatments.

funFacts: The spectacle-shaped mark on the back of the hood gives the species its other name, the spectacled cobra.
Its paralysis-causing neurotoxins make up only about 1% and 3% of the venom, yet they are the only components found to cause neuromuscular paralysis.
Venom from different parts of India can differ so much that the same antivenom neutralizes some samples far better than others.
A female guards her eggs for the whole incubation, leaving only to feed.
Mongooses resist cobra neurotoxins because the toxins bind poorly to their muscle receptors.
It is one of India's "Big Four" snakes, together with the common krait, Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper.
A reference genome of the Indian cobra was published to map its full set of venom genes.

abilities.name: Receptor-Blocking Venom
abilities.description: α-neurotoxins in a three-finger-toxin-rich venom block the acetylcholine receptors of muscle, causing paralysis that can stop breathing. They are only a few percent of the venom but are its paralysis-causing core.

abilities.name: Spectacled Hood Display
abilities.description: the cobra rears, spreads its hood and shows the spectacle mark, warning threats away and striking downward from the raised position if the warning fails.

traits.name: Egg-Guarding Mother
traits.description: females lay about 12–20 eggs in a hollow tree or in the earth and guard them through incubation, leaving only to feed, until they hatch after roughly 50 days.

traits.name: Village-Edge Rat Hunter
traits.description: the cobra thrives in cultivated land and around villages where rats are common, which makes it both a pest controller and one of the "Big Four" snakes behind most snakebites in India.

combat.weapons: The main weapon is a front-fanged bite delivering venom dominated by three-finger toxins. Postsynaptic α-neurotoxins block the acetylcholine receptors of muscle, producing paralysis that can reach the breathing muscles. PLA2 enzymes and other components add further effects. The secondary weapon is the hood display: the cobra raises its forebody and spreads its neck ribs into a hood marked with the spectacle pattern, which warns off threats and gives an elevated platform for striking.
weaknesses: Low body mass and no armor.
Short fangs and delayed venom action against large opponents.
Its paralysis-causing toxins are a small share of the venom, so dose matters.
Mongooses have receptors that α-neurotoxins bind poorly, blunting its main weapon.
King cobras prey on Indian cobras.
