indian-rhinoceros.name: Indian Rhinoceros
indian-rhinoceros.specimen: healthy mature bull of about 2,100 kg, 175 cm at the shoulder and 370 cm head-body length, with fully grown lower incisor tusks and neck folds. This is a prime bull, not a record animal.
indian-rhinoceros.summary: The Indian rhinoceros is a two-tonne floodplain giant wrapped in thick, deeply folded hide. Unlike African rhinos it fights mainly with sharp lower tusks rather than its single horn, and bull fights can be deadly, making it one of the roster's most heavily built and dangerous herbivores.
narrative: A prime Indian rhino bull looks like a tank built from grey leather: great folds of hide at the neck, shoulders and rump, studded with wart-like bumps, over roughly two tonnes of muscle and bone. A single horn rises from the snout, usually about 25 cm long. The real weapons are hidden until the mouth opens: sharp lower incisor tusks that bulls use to slash one another in fights that are reported as the leading natural cause of death in the species.

Most of the time Indian rhinos graze the tall grasses of the Brahmaputra and Terai floodplains, wallow in pools, swim rivers and keep to home ranges of a few square kilometres. They hear and smell well but see poorly, and a disturbed rhino either crashes away through the grass or charges. People living beside Nepal's parks lose crops and, every year, a few lives to rhinos.

On the ABS scale the Indian rhino sits beside the white rhinoceros at the top of the rhino group. The white rhino keeps a small edge in mass, raw power and horn reach, while the Indian rhino matches it in defense through its heavier folds and adds a slashing tusk system that no African rhino has. Both remain below the common hippopotamus in Attack, and far below elephants in size.

sections.habitat: Alluvial floodplain grasslands, swamps and adjoining riverine forest of the Brahmaputra basin and the Terai of northern India and southern Nepal, usually close to water. It survives in 12 protected areas, including Kaziranga, Orang, Pobitora, Manas, Jaldapara, Gorumara and Dudhwa in India and Chitwan, Bardia, Parsa and Shuklaphanta in Nepal.
sections.diet: Mainly a grazer of tall and short grasses, also eating twigs, leaves, shrubs, flowers, fruit and aquatic plants. By grazing and wallowing it keeps floodplain grasslands open. Mynahs and egrets feed on insects around it.
sections.social: Largely solitary. Cows keep calves close for up to four years; subadults form stable groups; groups of up to 10 rhinos gather at wallows. Bulls hold overlapping home ranges of about 2–8 km² and become intolerant of rivals during breeding.
sections.reproduction: Gestation is about 15.7 months, producing one calf of 40–81 kg; birth intervals are 34–51 months. Wild females usually start breeding at about six years and bulls dominate only when much older and larger. In captivity, four rhinos lived past 40 years, the oldest to 47.
sections.conservation: Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. From about 100 animals in the early 1900s and roughly 1,870–1,895 in the early 1990s, the population grew to an estimated 4,075 in March 2025 (3,323 in India and 752 in Nepal). More than 70% live in Kaziranga National Park, so a single disaster could hit most of the species. Poaching for horn remains the main threat, along with invasive plants, shrinking grasslands and silting wetlands.
sections.features:
Sharp lower incisor tusks used as the main weapon.
Single keratin horn, typically about 25 cm, up to about 61 cm.
Thick hide in deep folds with wart-like bumps.
Excellent swimmer.
More than 10 distinct vocalizations and communal dung middens.
sections.humanInteraction: Rhinos raid crops next to protected areas and attack people, killing an average of 3.3 people a year in Nepal over two decades. They are also a flagship of Asian conservation, protected by armed patrols in Chitwan and Kaziranga.

funFacts: Indian rhinos fight mainly with their lower tusks, not their horn.
The Asian rhinos are the only living rhinos with tusk-like incisors.
They are excellent swimmers.
Bulls can spray urine 3–4 m behind them when disturbed.
Over 10 different calls have been recorded, from honks and bleats to roars and squeak-pants.
The population rose from about 100 in the early 1900s to more than 4,000 today.
No wild Indian rhino has ever been weighed; all standard weights come from zoo animals.

abilities.description: bulls fight mainly with the sharp lower incisor tusks, slashing deep wounds while the horn plays a secondary role; bull fights are the most common natural cause of death.

abilities.name: Floodplain Charge
abilities.description: a two-tonne rush from tall grass at up to 55 km/h for short bursts, backed by strong swimming that lets it use rivers and wallows as cover.

traits.name: Riveted Hide
traits.description: deep skin folds and wart-like bumps give the look that the International Rhino Foundation likens to grey armor plates with rivets.

traits.name: Comeback Rhino
traits.description: reduced to about 100 animals in the early 1900s and now over 4,000, one of Asia's major conservation recoveries.

combat.weapons: The Indian rhino fights differently from the African species. Its main weapons are the sharp lower incisor tusks, driven by a two-tonne body in slashing bites that open deep wounds. The single horn is shorter than an African rhino's front horn and is used less in fights. Charging, shoving and trampling add damage. Fights between dominant bulls are reported as the most common natural cause of death in the species, which shows how damaging the tusks are against an equally armored opponent.
weaknesses: Poor eyesight.
Thick hide is not true armor; flanks and belly can be wounded.
Heat drives it into water and limits long exertion.
Tusks require very close contact; the horn is short.
Mass limits turning.

inland-taipan.name: Inland Taipan
inland-taipan.specimen: healthy representative adult, 1.8 kg and 190 cm total length, sex unspecified. This pass did not verify a consistent adult size advantage for either sex, so no sex-based combat modifier is applied.
inland-taipan.summary: The inland taipan is a slender 2-metre snake from the remote Australian outback whose venom is the most toxic of any snake in standard lab tests. It corners rats in burrows and bites several times in quick succession, hitting nerves, blood clotting and muscle at once. At under 2 kg with no armor it is physically fragile, and it is famously shy, so its danger is all in the bite.
narrative: The inland taipan tests how far venom can carry a very small body on an absolute scale. A representative adult weighs under 2 kg and has no armor, no crushing jaws and no constriction. On raw power, protection and toughness it sits near the bottom of the vertebrate roster. What it has is a venom that laboratory assays rank above every other snake's, delivered by fixed front fangs in a burst of rapid bites.

That venom is not one toxin but a set of them. Paradoxin, a three-part PLA2 neurotoxin, disrupts the nerve signals that drive muscles. Three-finger toxins add further neurotoxic effects, and prothrombin activators push blood clotting into a runaway state that uses up clotting factors. Clinicians describe rapid coagulopathy, paralysis, muscle breakdown and kidney injury. In a matchup, a clean bite on an unarmored mammal changes everything even if the snake is a fraction of the opponent's size.

The limits are the same as for any venomous snake. It must reach the target and penetrate skin. Venom takes time, so a large animal that seizes or crushes the snake can still win. Thick armor or venom-resistant physiology can defeat the whole system. Its temperament also matters: this is a retiring snake that would rather slip into a soil crack than fight, which is why so few people have been bitten despite its reputation.

Its strongest ground is its home terrain: hot, cracking-clay plains full of fissures and burrows. There, its slender body can reach refuges that bigger animals cannot, and a confined space makes its repeated bites easy to land.

sections.habitat: The inland taipan lives in the semi-arid Channel Country of south-western Queensland and north-eastern South Australia, with records reported from adjacent parts of New South Wales and the Northern Territory. It uses cracking-clay and black-soil plains where deep fissures and animal burrows provide shelter from heat and predators. Its remote range is a main reason people rarely meet it.
sections.diet: It feeds almost entirely on small to medium mammals. The Australian Museum names the long-haired rat (Rattus villosissimus) as a key prey, plus the introduced house mouse and small dasyurid marsupials. Rodent numbers in the Channel Country rise and fall sharply with rainfall, and the snake's feeding and breeding track those boom-and-bust cycles.
sections.social: Solitary outside breeding. No group behavior is known.
sections.reproduction: The species lays eggs. Species pages report clutches of roughly one to two dozen, laid in abandoned burrows or deep cracks and hatching after about two months, with clutch size linked to food supply. A Toxicon study comparing juvenile and adult venoms found differences in biological properties with age.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Its range is remote and sparsely settled, so direct persecution is limited, but it depends on intact rodent populations and cracking-soil habitat.
sections.features:
Fixed front fangs delivering the most toxic snake venom known in mouse assays.
Multi-system venom: presynaptic PLA2 neurotoxin (paradoxin), three-finger toxins, prothrombin activators and other components.
Rapid repeated biting inside confined burrows.
Seasonal colour change for heat management.
Slender body suited to soil cracks and burrows.
sections.humanInteraction: Bites are medical emergencies with rapid systemic effects, including coagulopathy and neurotoxicity; a clinical protocol page notes envenoming can be fatal in as little as 30 minutes without treatment. Yet recorded bites are very rare: a 2024 review counted 11 well-documented envenomings, only 2 by wild snakes, with survivors treated with antivenom. One well-studied wild bite in outback South Australia left the patient with lasting paralysis of eye muscles on one side.

funFacts: It is often called the "fierce snake", yet the Australian Museum describes it as placid and shy.
Its colour changes with the seasons: darker in winter, lighter in summer.
Its venom has a mouse subcutaneous LD50 of about 0.025 mg/kg, the lowest figure usually cited for any snake.
It bites cornered prey several times in quick succession instead of striking once and waiting.
Only 2 of the 11 well-documented human envenomings reviewed in 2024 involved wild snakes.
The largest reliably measured specimen in the literature was a female with a 170 cm snout-vent length.
Its neurotoxin paradoxin is built from three subunits, like the coastal taipan's taipoxin.

abilities.name: Paradoxin Venom Cocktail
abilities.description: the venom combines the presynaptic neurotoxin paradoxin, diverse three-finger toxins and prothrombin activators, so one bite can attack neuromuscular signaling and blood clotting at the same time. Mouse assays rate it the most toxic snake venom measured, though real effect still depends on dose and target.

abilities.name: Burrow-Corner Multi-Bite
abilities.description: the snake corners rodents in burrows or soil cracks and bites several times in quick succession, stacking venom doses before the prey can escape or fight back.

traits.name: Seasonal Colour Shift
traits.description: the upper body darkens in winter and pales in summer, a documented seasonal change that helps the snake absorb heat in cold months and shed it in hot ones.

traits.name: Placid "Fierce Snake"
traits.description: despite its name and venom, the species is described by the Australian Museum as shy and placid, and very few people have ever been bitten by a wild one.

combat.weapons:
The primary weapon is a fixed front-fanged elapid bite that injects one of the most potent snake venoms known in mouse assays. The venom attacks several body systems at once: presynaptic PLA2 neurotoxins such as paradoxin disrupt neuromuscular transmission, three-finger toxins add postsynaptic neurotoxic effects, and prothrombin activators drive consumptive coagulopathy. Clinical accounts describe rapid-onset systemic envenoming with coagulopathy, paralysis risk, muscle breakdown and possible kidney injury.

The secondary weapon is delivery behavior. The Australian Museum reports that prey is usually cornered in a burrow or soil crack and bitten several times in quick succession, which raises the injected dose in a single engagement.
weaknesses: Very low body mass and almost no structural protection.
No crushing bite, constriction or large mechanical weapon.
Venom needs penetration and time; it is not an instant stop.
Ectothermic performance drops in cold conditions.
Temperament favors avoidance, so it rarely presses a fight.

jaguarundi.name: Jaguarundi
jaguarundi.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 7.0 kg, the top of the usual 3.5–7 kg range (Wikipedia) and the middle of ADW's 4.5–9.0 kg range. Individuals near 9 kg are reported but are not used as the baseline.
jaguarundi.summary: A long, low, otter-shaped wild cat of the Americas, the jaguarundi hunts birds and rodents by day, climbs, swims and leaps 2 m into the air. It is agile and versatile in habitat use, but at about 7 kg it is a small predator with modest absolute power.
narrative: The jaguarundi does not look like most cats. Its long, slender body, short legs, small flattened head and long tail give it the outline of a weasel or otter, and its coat is plain grey-brown or reddish with no spots. It is also unusual in its schedule: while ocelots and margays hunt at night, the jaguarundi is most active in daylight, peaking from late morning to noon.

It hunts mainly on the ground, pouncing on rodents, lizards and ground birds, but it climbs easily, swims across rivers and can leap two metres into the air after a bird. Radio-tracked males in Belize used ranges of up to 100 km², and the species turns up in rainforest, dry scrub and farmland alike, as long as there is dense cover and water nearby.

In a matchup, the jaguarundi is a quick, versatile small predator. At about 7 kg it is heavier than a house cat and better armed than a fox of similar weight, but it is roughly half the mass of an ocelot, the rival that suppresses it in the wild, and far below the cougar. Its best fights are against small, lightly armed animals; larger cats, dogs and big constrictors are dangerous to it.

sections.habitat: From southern Texas (where it is now very rare or gone) and Mexico through Central America to northern Argentina and Uruguay. It uses an unusually broad range of habitats for a small cat: tropical rainforest, deciduous forest, dry thorn scrub, savanna and semi-desert, usually near running water and dense cover, and it can live in reforested and farmed mosaics.
sections.diet: Mostly small animals under 1 kg: rodents, ground-feeding birds, reptiles, frogs and arthropods, with occasional poultry, fish, rabbits, marmosets and opossums. It appears to take the most abundant and easily caught prey in each area.
sections.social: Solitary or in pairs. Home ranges are large for its size: 1.4–18 km² for females and 8.5–25.3 km² for males in Brazil, and up to 88–100 km² for two males in Belize. It scent-marks by scraping, clawing logs, head rubbing and leaving feces uncovered.
sections.reproduction: Sexual maturity at one to three years. Mating occurs throughout the year, with peaks that vary across the range; after a 70–75 day gestation, one to four kittens are born in a den in a dense thicket or hollow tree. Captive individuals have lived 15 years or more.
sections.conservation: Listed as Near Threatened in the IUCN Red List's 2026 assessment as shown in Wikipedia's species box; the article text still describes its earlier Least Concern listing, noting that assessors already considered Near Threatened justified. A 2024 continental analysis found its area of occupancy has shrunk over the last two decades (Global Ecology and Conservation). It is listed as endangered in the United States and threatened in Mexico. Threats are habitat loss and fragmentation, and persecution for killing poultry.
sections.features:
Long, low, unspotted body with a long tail.
Daytime activity unusual among small cats.
Strong climbing and swimming.
Round pupils, shared with a few other cats such as the cougar.
A very large vocal repertoire.
sections.humanInteraction: Sometimes killed for raiding poultry. It tolerates light to moderate human disturbance and uses farm-forest mosaics, but road building and clearing of dense brush remain major threats. In the lower Rio Grande Valley, Texas, people are replanting native brush for jaguarundis and ocelots.

funFacts: Its name comes from the Old Guarani word for "dark jaguar".
It can leap about 2 m into the air to catch birds.
Jaguarundis have 38 chromosomes, while other small South American cats have 36.
It has 13 recorded calls, including a bird-like chirp.
It is one of the few small cats that hunts mainly by day.
One was recorded swimming across Bolivia's Tuichi River.
Grey and reddish kittens can be born in the same litter.

abilities.name: Daylight Stalker
abilities.description: unlike most small American cats it hunts mainly by day, with a peak from late morning to noon, which puts it in a different time slot from ocelots and margays and lets it surprise diurnal birds and lizards.

abilities.name: Bird-Snatch Leap
abilities.description: it can spring about 2 m into the air to knock down birds, and it climbs and swims well, so it can follow or escape an opponent across ground, branches and water.

traits.name: Otter-Shaped Cat
traits.description: a long, low body, short legs, a small flat head, small round ears and a long tail make it look more like a weasel or otter than a typical cat.

traits.name: Thirteen-Call Voice
traits.description: thirteen distinct calls have been recorded, including chattering, purring, screaming, whistling, yapping and a bird-like chirp.

combat.weapons: The jaguarundi hunts mainly on the ground for prey under 1 kg: ground-feeding birds, rodents (especially rice rats, cotton rats and cane mice), reptiles, frogs and arthropods. It also takes larger prey such as poultry, fish, marmosets, rabbits, opossums and occasionally common tapeti, and small deer have been found in its diet (possibly as carrion). It eats about 400 g of vertebrate prey a day. Its weapons are ordinary small-cat claws and bite on a slender 7 kg body; it is effective against small animals but lacks the mass or grappling power for anything much larger.
weaknesses: Low absolute mass and power.
No armor.
Outclassed by ocelots, cougars and dogs.
Small prey focus limits its practice against large, dangerous opponents.

japanese-spider-crab.name: Japanese Spider Crab
japanese-spider-crab.specimen: healthy hard-shelled adult male, 12.0 kg, 30.0 cm carapace width and about 3.0 m claw-to-claw span.
japanese-spider-crab.summary: The Japanese spider crab has the widest leg span of any arthropod, over 3 m in big males, but its long claws are weak and it is slow, gentle and unable to swim. Its spiny shell gives decent protection, yet its thin legs and weak pinch make it a poor fighter against anything with a strong bite.
narrative: The Japanese spider crab looks like a monster from the deep: a spiny, orange body the size of a dinner plate, perched on legs that can stretch more than three metres from claw to claw. It lives on the seafloor off Japan at depths of 50 to 600 m, and it keeps growing in an unusual way: the shell reaches its adult size, but the legs go on lengthening for the rest of the crab's life.

Despite the look, it is a scavenger rather than a hunter. It picks over dead fish, algae and small invertebrates, and gathers in large numbers where food falls to the bottom; researchers counted more than a thousand around one whale carcass. It is reported to have a gentle disposition, and its long claws are relatively weak, better at tearing sponges off rocks than crushing shells.

In a battle, that makes it much less dangerous than it looks. Its reach can keep a small opponent at a distance and its well-calcified, spiny carapace protects the body, but the legs are thin and easily broken, it cannot swim away, and during a molt it is helpless. It rates low in Attack and Agility, moderate in Defense, and its Special score rests on reach and camouflage rather than any real weapon.

sections.habitat: Japanese spider crabs live on sandy and rocky bottoms of the continental shelf and slope, mainly off the Pacific coast of Honshu from Tokyo Bay to Kagoshima, with outlying records from Iwate Prefecture and Taiwan (Wikipedia; ADW). They are found at 50–600 m, most often around 150–300 m (Georgia Aquarium; ADW). In Suruga Bay they are regular at 300 m, where the water is about 10 °C (Wikipedia).
sections.diet: They are omnivorous scavengers, eating dead or decaying fish, invertebrates and algae, and sometimes prying open mollusks or catching small invertebrates (Monterey Bay Aquarium). At an experimental sperm whale carcass at 500 m they were the second most abundant animal and showed day-night activity cycles (Aguzzi et al. 2019).
sections.social: They are not social in any organized way, but gather in numbers at food sources (Aguzzi et al. 2019) and move to shallower water to spawn (Monterey Bay Aquarium).
sections.reproduction: Mating takes place in early spring. Females carry fertilized eggs on the abdomen, up to about 1.5 million per season, which hatch in about 10 days (Wikipedia; ADW). Larvae pass through a brief prezoeal stage that lasts only minutes (Okamoto 1995), then zoeal and megalopa stages whose survival and length depend strongly on temperature (Okamoto 1993). Young crabs live in shallower water and move deeper as they grow (Monterey Bay Aquarium).
sections.conservation: The species has not been assessed by the IUCN in any source read for this report. The catch has declined considerably over the last 40 years, and fishing is restricted during the spring breeding season to protect it (ADW; Monterey Bay Aquarium). Warming seas may reduce larval survival and degrade seaweed beds (Monterey Bay Aquarium).
sections.features:
The widest leg span of any arthropod, over 3.5 m in the largest animals.
Well-calcified, spiny, bumpy carapace.
Long claws in males, short in females.
Legs that keep lengthening through adulthood and regrow after loss.
Decorating behavior in juveniles.
sections.humanInteraction: Japanese spider crabs are a seasonal delicacy in Japan, though their depth makes them hard to catch (Georgia Aquarium). They are popular in public aquariums worldwide; a study across six aquariums set baseline blood values and linked shell lesions to changes in blood cells (Griffioen et al. 2022). Because the legs are so long, researchers often use their tendons as a research material (ADW).

funFacts: It has the widest leg span of any known arthropod, up to about 3.7 m.
Its Japanese name, taka-ashi-gani, means "tall-legged crab".
Its shell stops growing much in adulthood, but its legs keep getting longer.
Young spider crabs dress themselves in sponges and seaweed for camouflage.
More than a thousand were counted at a single whale carcass on the seafloor at 500 m.
A female can carry up to about 1.5 million eggs in a season.

abilities.name: Record Reach
abilities.description: a big male's claw-to-claw span can pass 3 m, the widest of any arthropod, letting it touch and fend off an opponent long before that opponent reaches its body.

abilities.name: Living Disguise
abilities.description: young crabs tear off sponges, kelp and other material and attach them to hooked spines on the shell, hiding their outline on the seafloor.

traits.name: Legs That Keep Growing
traits.description: the shell stops growing much in adulthood, but the legs keep lengthening with age, and lost legs can regrow at later molts.

traits.name: Deep-Water Giant
traits.description: it lives at 50–600 m off Japan and gathers in large numbers at food falls; over a thousand were counted at one whale carcass at 500 m.

combat.weapons: The Japanese spider crab's weapons are a pair of long, slender claws, far longer in males than in females. ADW describes them as fairly weak: good for tearing up sponges or algae, prying open mollusks and warding off smaller predators, but not for crushing hard prey the way a king crab or lobster can. Its long reach is the real asset; a big male can touch an opponent from well over a metre away.
weaknesses: Weak claws and very low striking power.
Thin legs that are easily lost.
Very slow and unable to swim.
Soft and helpless during and just after molting.
Low aggression.

kangal.name: Kangal
kangal.specimen: healthy adult male working Kangal, 50.0 kg, 74.0 cm at the withers, in working condition rather than show or obese pet condition.
kangal.summary: The Kangal is a heavy-boned Turkish livestock guardian dog bred to stand between sheep and wolves. It wins by deterrence, size and a strong grip-and-shake bite rather than speed or hunting skill, putting it roughly level with a wild wolf of the same mass, but it has no armor and is badly outmatched by bears and big cats.
narrative: The Kangal comes from the high steppe of Sivas in central Anatolia, where shepherds have long kept large, pale, black-masked dogs to guard their flocks from wolves. A fit working male weighs about 50 kg and stands about 74 cm at the shoulder. Turkish field measurements put village males a little lighter, while US-registered dogs run heavier, so the canonical specimen deliberately sits between the two.

Its fighting style is defined by its job. A Kangal does not hunt; it guards. It keeps itself between the flock and danger, patrols farther out after dark, and meets a threat with a graded escalation of barking, posturing and charging that ends most encounters before teeth are used. When it does commit, it brings a strong bite on a heavy frame, and field trials in the western United States showed Kangals reducing losses to coyotes, cougars and black bears and displacing wolves.

That makes it formidable against lighter canids and small carnivores, and roughly an even contest against a wolf of similar size, where the wild wolf's hunting experience offsets the dog's heavier bone. Against bears, big cats and large ungulates it is simply too small, and without the shepherd's spiked collar its throat is as exposed as any dog's. The famous 743 PSI bite claim does not change this: no published study has measured it.

sections.habitat: The Kangal originates in the Sivas province of central Anatolia, a high steppe and upland pasture region with cold winters. It is kept across Turkey and has been exported to North America, Africa and Europe as a livestock guardian.
sections.diet: A domestic dog fed by its owners, on household scraps and prepared food in village practice or commercial diets abroad. It does not hunt for its living, although it will chase and bite intruding carnivores.
sections.ecology: In its working role the Kangal is part of a shepherd-flock-dog system, reducing losses of sheep and goats to wolves and other carnivores. Exported Kangals have been studied as a non-lethal tool for reducing conflict between ranchers and wolves, bears, cougars and coyotes.
sections.social: Kangals usually work in small groups with a flock and bond closely with the shepherd. They are territorial toward strange dogs and people and stay with the flock rather than roaming.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is managed by people. Pups are raised with livestock so they bond with the flock. Adult size and working maturity are reached at about two years, which is why the UKC measures height at maturity from two years.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed. Turkey treats the Kangal as a national breed.
sections.features:
Heavy-boned molossoid mountain-type build (FCI Group 2, Section 2.2).
Dark mask and dark ears over a pale dun coat.
Dense double coat suited to cold continental winters.
Strong protective instinct with independent decision-making.
Relaxed, economical working gait that single-tracks at speed.
sections.humanInteraction: Kangals are serious working guardians. They are generally calm with their own family and flock but suspicious of strangers and need space and training. The viral "strongest bite of any dog" claim has made the breed an internet celebrity, but that number is not supported by any published measurement.

funFacts: The FCI only recognized the Kangal as a separate breed in 2018; before that the same standard number covered the "Anatolian Shepherd Dog".
Turkish shepherds fit Kangals with spiked iron collars to protect their throats from wolf bites.
USDA researchers imported Kangals from Turkey in 2014 to test them against wolves in the western United States.
GPS collars in Sivas showed Kangals patrol farther from the flock at night than the shepherd does.
The widely shared "743 PSI" bite figure has never been traced to a published measurement.
The Kangal appears on a Turkish postage stamp as a national breed.

abilities.name: Flock Shield Stance
abilities.description: positions itself between the flock and an approaching predator and patrols farther out at night, as GPS tracking in Sivas showed. In a matchup this means it fights on its chosen ground and forces the opponent to come through it.

abilities.name: Escalating Challenge
abilities.description: a graded sequence of bark, posture, charge and bite that drives off most wolves, coyotes and even cougars and bears in field trials before a fight begins. It rewards deterrence rather than raw damage.

traits.name: Black-Masked Mountain Molosser
traits.description: a heavy-boned, broad-headed mountain-type guardian with the breed's defining dark mask and ears, heavier than wild canids of the same height.

traits.name: Sivas Working Heritage
traits.description: a Turkish national breed kept for generations by shepherds in the Sivas-Kangal region, recognized by the FCI as a distinct breed in 2018 and exported for predator-conflict programs.

combat.weapons: The Kangal's weapon is the canid bite: grip-and-hold or grip-and-shake delivered by a broad-headed, heavy-boned molossoid mountain-type dog (FCI Group 2, Section 2.2). Its fighting method against predators is escalation: stand between flock and threat, bark, posture, charge, and bite only if the intruder does not withdraw. There is no second weapon system; forelimbs brace and push but do not grapple like a felid's.
weaknesses: No armor; throat and limbs are exposed without the human-fitted collar.
A single bite weapon that requires close contact.
Less speed, turning and pursuit endurance than wild canids.
Behavior is tuned to deterrence and returning to the flock, not to finishing fights.
Far outmatched by bears, big cats and large ungulates in absolute power.

kea.name: Kea
kea.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 0.96 kg, 48.0 cm total length. Males are heavier and have a longer upper bill.
kea.summary: The Kea is a large, clever mountain parrot from New Zealand's South Island. The canonical male weighs just under 1 kg. Its long, curved bill can rip through sheep wool, and it is among the best-tested bird problem solvers, showing statistical reasoning and tool innovation. In an absolute fight, its small size and lack of armor leave it far below real predators.
narrative: The kea is a parrot that lives where parrots usually do not: on windy ridges and alpine herb-fields of the Southern Alps, nesting on the ground and breeding through the mountain winter. It survives there by being curious. Kea dig, pry, rip and test almost everything they meet, from grubs in rotten logs to rubber on cars, traps set for pests and gear left outside huts.

That curiosity is backed by measured ability. In controlled studies, kea predicted sampling outcomes from ratios of objects while taking into account physical barriers and an experimenter's bias, a combination previously shown only in great apes. A disabled kea invented his own pebble tool for preening. At the same time, experiments show limits: kea did not grasp their partner's role in a cooperation task and did not infer weight from objects moving in a breeze. The picture is of a highly capable, exploratory problem solver rather than an all-purpose genius.

In an absolute matchup, the kea's bill is a tearing tool on a bird under 1 kg. It can wound a sheep that cannot shake it off and kill a seabird chick, but it has no armor and little mass. It wins by working out what an opponent or obstacle will do, not by overpowering anything that can fight back.

sections.habitat: The kea lives only on the South Island of New Zealand, over about four million hectares along the main mountain ranges from Farewell Spit to Waitutu and in the Kaikōura Ranges. It occurs from coastal dunes and lowland valleys on the West Coast to high alpine peaks, but is most common in montane forest and the subalpine and alpine zones above it. Bones show it once lived through lowland forest on the North Island as well.
sections.diet: It is omnivorous. Kea eat shoots, fruits, leaves, nectar and seeds of more than 40 plant species; dig for insect larvae, grass grubs and plant tubers; rip open rotten logs for huhu grubs; and eat land snails. Animal food includes Hutton's shearwater chicks, mice, rabbits and carcasses of deer, chamois, tahr and sheep. Kea also spread the seeds of alpine plants.
sections.social: Adults form long-term monogamous pairs. Juveniles gather in loose, wandering flocks, which breeding adults may join as they pass through. Flocks have flexible hierarchies, and unrelated adults tolerate juveniles, which helps young kea learn.
sections.reproduction: Kea nest on the ground in natural cavities, such as rock crevices, hollow tree bases or holes under roots, mostly in native forest. Usually four eggs are laid between July and January, with a peak in August–October. The female incubates and feeds the chicks while the male brings food to her. Nests fledge on average 1.6 young.
sections.conservation: The kea is listed as Endangered by the IUCN and as Threatened–Nationally Endangered in New Zealand, with an estimated 1,000–5,000 birds (DOC). About 150,000 were killed for bounties between 1860 and 1970; protection came in stages, with full protection in 1986. Today's main threats are introduced predators (stoats, possums and cats) at nests, lead poisoning from old buildings, and conflict and accidents with people. At Aoraki / Mount Cook, all 38 live kea tested had detectable blood lead and 26 had dangerously high levels. Predator control greatly improves nest survival.
sections.features:
Long, narrow, strongly curved upper bill, longer in males.
Olive-green plumage with bright orange-red underwings.
Ground nesting and winter breeding.
High curiosity, play and problem-solving ability.
Long juvenile learning period.
sections.humanInteraction: Kea are famous for investigating people and their gear at ski-fields, huts and car parks, pulling rubber from cars and carrying off small items, which has earned the nickname "clown of the mountains". Feeding kea is harmful and discouraged. They were once killed as sheep pests; today some attacks on sheep are tolerated because the birds are protected. The kea was voted New Zealand Bird of the Year in 2017.

A kea named Bruce, who lost his upper bill, uses pebbles as tools to preen.
Hearing a recorded kea play call makes wild kea start playing.

abilities.name: Wool-Ripping Beak
abilities.description: the long, curved upper bill and gripping claws tear through thick fleece to reach fat on a live sheep's back, and dig out grubs and roots from soil and logs.

abilities.name: Mountain Puzzle Solver
abilities.description: kea combine quantities, physical barriers and social cues to make statistical predictions, innovate tools and open locks, letting them get into places and food that other animals cannot.

traits.name: Alpine Parrot
traits.description: one of very few parrots living above the treeline, it forages across mountain beech forest, subalpine scrub and alpine herb-fields, nests on the ground and breeds in winter.

traits.name: Contagious Play Call
traits.description: kea have a special play call; playing recordings of it to wild kea made both juveniles and adults play more, evidence of positive emotional contagion in a bird.

combat.weapons: The bill is the main weapon, helped by the claws. The kea's long, curved upper bill tears and pries. The clearest evidence of its offensive use is the long-disputed attacks on sheep. In 1992, nocturnal attacks were filmed, proving that at least some kea land on healthy sheep and use bill and claws to rip through the wool and eat fat from the back. The kea does not directly kill the sheep, but sheep can die from infection or from injuries while trying to escape. A few kea also prey on Hutton's shearwater chicks in the Seaward Kaikōura Range, and kea take mice and rabbits and scavenge deer, chamois, tahr and sheep carcasses.

No armor; small, light body.
Bill and claws are tearing tools, not killing weapons for large animals.
Curiosity leads to lead poisoning, traps, vehicles and other human hazards.
Ground nests are vulnerable to stoats, possums and cats.

kodiak-bear.name: Kodiak Bear
kodiak-bear.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 480.0 kg, in average active-season condition, about 140.0 cm shoulder height on all fours. This is a representative big male, not the 680 kg pre-denning peak or a record trophy animal.
kodiak-bear.summary: The Kodiak bear is a giant island brown bear from Alaska's Kodiak Archipelago, with big males weighing close to half a tonne. It wins through sheer mass, a powerful shoulder-driven swipe, long claws and a heavy bite, backed by thick fat and fur. Its weaknesses are slow turning, the lack of armor and weapons built as much for fishing and digging as for killing.
narrative: The Kodiak bear is what a brown bear becomes when food is abundant and there is no competition from other large carnivores. On the islands of the Kodiak Archipelago, rich salmon runs and berry crops support bears that routinely reach sizes the interior grizzly never approaches. A representative adult male of around 480 kg is more than twice the roster's grizzly, and in autumn a big male can carry nearly 700 kg into the den.

That size is the core of its fighting ability. A forelimb strike powered by the shoulder hump can knock down a large animal, and once on top the bear's weight and bite do the rest. Thick fat and fur and a very deep body make it hard for smaller predators to reach anything vital. But the Kodiak is a generalist rather than a killer by design. Its claws are for digging, its day is spent grazing, fishing and eating berries, and it avoids fights it does not need. Against fast, agile opponents that refuse to close, its heavy frame becomes a handicap.

Kodiak bears are also socially skilled. At salmon streams dozens of bears can feed close together, reading one another's postures to avoid costly fights. In a matchup that translates into good judgement: a Kodiak tends to test an opponent before committing, then uses its mass decisively. Against almost any land predator it holds the size advantage; only megafauna, big crocodilians in water and the polar bear meet it on equal or better terms.

sections.habitat: Kodiak bears live only on the islands of the Kodiak Archipelago in southwestern Alaska. They use almost every habitat on the islands: low-elevation salt marshes in spring, salmon streams and berry patches in summer, and alpine slopes, where they dig dens, in winter.
sections.diet: Omnivores that follow seasonal food. Sedges and other plants in spring, several salmon species during summer and autumn runs, and berries such as salmonberry, red elderberry, blueberry and devil's club fruit. Carrion, deer and occasional larger mammals add protein. Bears move salmon nutrients from streams into the surrounding forest.
sections.social: Mostly solitary but tolerant at rich food sources, where many bears gather and a dominance order forms. Males roam widely in the breeding season. Females with cubs keep away from adult males.
sections.reproduction: Mating takes place in late spring and early summer. Cubs are born in the winter den and stay with their mother for about two to three years. The main threat to cubs is adult male bears. Females are known to live longer in the wild than males.
sections.conservation: The brown bear species (Ursus arctos) is assessed as Least Concern globally; the Kodiak subspecies is not separately listed. The Kodiak population, about 3,500 bears (3,526 estimated in 2005), is healthy and closely managed by ADF&G and the Kodiak National Wildlife Refuge. Its low genetic diversity may make it more vulnerable to new diseases or parasites.
sections.features:
Very large body mass that swings strongly by season.
Shoulder hump of digging muscle.
Long, fairly straight front claws for digging.
Keen sense of smell.
Fasting and denning physiology for surviving winter without feeding.
sections.humanInteraction: Kodiak bears are a major draw for bear viewing and regulated hunting. Attacks on people are rare; most follow surprise encounters at close range or defense of cubs or food. Securing food and garbage reduces conflict.

funFacts: A large male can stand over 3 m (10 ft) tall on its hind legs.
Big males can weigh about 680 kg (1,500 lb) before denning.
The oldest known wild Kodiak female lived to 34; the oldest male to 27.
Females are about 20% smaller and 30% lighter than males.
Kodiak bears kept eating salmon even when red elderberries ripened at the same time, according to a 2023 diet study.
The whole population, around 3,500 bears, lives on one island group.

abilities.name: Hump-Powered Swipe
abilities.description: the large shoulder hump of digging muscle drives short, powerful forelimb strikes and pins, so a Kodiak can knock an opponent down or hold it before biting.

abilities.name: Salmon-Stream Diplomacy
abilities.description: a detailed language of postures, threat displays and displacement lets many large bears share one stream with few serious fights, and lets a Kodiak judge a rival before committing.

traits.name: Island Colossus
traits.description: the Kodiak Archipelago's brown bears are among the largest bears in the world, with big males reaching about 680 kg before denning.

traits.name: Isolated Island Population
traits.description: around 3,500 Kodiak bears live only on the Kodiak Archipelago, genetically isolated from mainland brown bears and with very little genetic diversity.

combat.weapons: The Kodiak bear fights with mass, forelimb strikes, long digging claws and a heavy bite. A male of nearly half a tonne can knock down, pin and bite an opponent, and the shoulder hump gives the forelimbs great power in short strikes and pulls. It is not a specialised killer like a big cat: its weapons are built as much for digging, fishing and tearing open carcasses as for subduing prey. Its offense comes from overwhelming size rather than a refined killing technique.
weaknesses: Low maneuverability and slow turns relative to cats and canids.
No armor over the face, neck and eyes.
Weapons built as much for digging and fishing as for killing.
High energy cost of bursts at nearly half a tonne.

leopard-gecko.name: Leopard Gecko
leopard-gecko.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 0.05 kg (50 g) and 22.0 cm total length, representing a well-grown wild adult.
leopard-gecko.summary: The leopard gecko is a small, spotted ground gecko from the rocky dry grasslands of South and Central Asia. A 50 g adult male hunts insects at night and fights rival males with fast bites, but it is far too small to hurt most animals. Its real trick is its fat-filled tail: it can drop it as a thrashing decoy that keeps moving for up to 30 minutes, then grow a new one.
narrative: At dusk on a rocky hillside in Pakistan, a leopard gecko slips out of a crevice where it spent the hot day. It moves slowly across the still-warm stones, then spots a cricket. Its thick tail begins to twitch, it creeps closer, and it lunges. This is the whole of its hunting life: small prey, taken at night, close to shelter.

The gecko is built for hiding and escaping rather than fighting. It has no armor, and unlike most geckos it has no sticky toe pads, so it cannot run up a smooth wall to safety. What it has is its tail. The tail stores fat for lean times, and when a predator grabs it, the gecko can shed it. The dropped tail thrashes, swings and even flips into the air for up to half an hour, a distraction that lets the gecko get away. A new tail grows back, shorter and smoother, but losing the old one costs much of its stored energy.

In ABS terms the leopard gecko sits near the floor for Attack and Defense, with moderate Agility and Stamina. Males do fight hard with one another, and they recognise rivals by skin chemicals, but those fights are gecko-scale. Its Special score is high because the decoy tail, backed by regrowth and fat storage, is a genuinely unusual survival mechanism.

sections.habitat: The leopard gecko lives in rocky, dry grassland and semi-desert with sparse vegetation and clay or gravel soils in Afghanistan, Pakistan, northwest India, western Nepal and possibly eastern Iran, where records are disputed. It reportedly avoids pure sand and shelters in crevices, burrows and under loose bark in dry forests. It was first recorded in Nepal only in 2016. Winter temperatures below about 10 °C drive it underground to live on its fat reserves.
sections.diet: It is an opportunistic predator of insects and other invertebrates, and takes small vertebrates when it can, including newborn mice, small lizards and hatchling geckos. It forages at dusk and night, when rocks still hold the day's warmth.
sections.social: Wild animals are described as living in loose colonies. Males are aggressive toward other males and court females, recognising sex by skin chemicals.
sections.reproduction: Females lay clutches of almost always two eggs, several times a season, and can store sperm. Sex depends on incubation temperature: cool (about 26–29 °C) and very warm (34–35 °C) eggs give mostly females, while intermediate temperatures (about 31–33 °C) give males. Maturity is reached at around 18 months. Hatchlings are banded rather than spotted.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Most pet leopard geckos are captive-bred, so collection pressure on wild populations is lower than for many traded reptiles.
sections.features:
Tail autotomy with a thrashing, flipping dropped tail and later regrowth.
Fat-storing tail.
Movable eyelids.
Clawed toes without adhesive pads.
About 100 teeth, each replaced every 3–4 months.
Temperature-dependent sex determination.
sections.humanInteraction: The leopard gecko is one of the most popular pet lizards, ranking behind the bearded dragon in a 2021 study of pet-trade search trends, and has been called possibly the first domesticated lizard. Decades of captive breeding have produced many colour and pattern morphs. It is also a laboratory model for studying tail regeneration.

funFacts: A dropped leopard gecko tail can keep moving for up to 30 minutes, with flips up to 3 cm high.
Its tail can hold about a quarter of its body mass as stored fat.
It replaces each of its roughly 100 teeth every three to four months.
Light can shine straight through its head from one ear opening to the other.
The temperature of the egg decides whether a leopard gecko hatches male or female.
Males tell males from females by the chemicals in their skin.

abilities.name: Decoy Tail Drop
abilities.description: the tail breaks off at built-in fracture planes with little blood loss, and the dropped tail keeps swinging and even flipping up to 3 cm into the air for up to 30 minutes. A predator that grabs or watches the tail gives the gecko time to escape, and the tail then regrows.

abilities.name: Twilight Ambush
abilities.description: it hunts at dusk and night, stalking slowly with a twitching tail before lunging at prey, while staying hidden from daytime predators.

traits.name: Fat-Storing Tail
traits.description: the thick tail holds a fat reserve, about a quarter of body mass in one study, that carries the gecko through lean periods and winter.

traits.name: Gecko With Eyelids
traits.description: unlike most geckos it has movable eyelids and clawed toes instead of sticky pads, the features that give the eyelid geckos their name.

combat.weapons: The only weapon is a small bite. It eats mainly insects and other invertebrates, and will take small vertebrates such as newborn mice, small lizards and even hatchling leopard geckos. Male-male fights involve rapid dashes and bites that can tear skin and sometimes badly injure a rival. None of this matters much against larger animals.
weaknesses: Tiny absolute size; almost any predator can kill it.
No toe pads for escaping up walls.
Losing the tail costs much of its stored energy.
Slows down in cold weather.

leopard-seal.name: Leopard Seal
leopard-seal.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 420.0 kg and 300.0 cm standard length, representing a large, fighting-fit cow rather than a record animal.
leopard-seal.summary: The leopard seal is Antarctica's top seal predator, a 420 kg, 3 m hunter with a huge head, long gripping teeth and a snake-like, agile body in the water. It ambushes penguins at the ice edge, kills other seals, and also sieves krill through its three-pointed cheek teeth. It is dangerous in the water but slow on land and has no armor.
narrative: A leopard seal at the ice edge is a problem for every penguin that has to cross it. The seal waits just under the surface where birds jump in or scramble out, and when one hits the water it is seized and thrashed against the surface until it breaks apart. The same large head and long front teeth let leopard seals take fur seal pups and other seals, and at Cape Shirreff a few big females were enough to wipe out most of a colony's pups in some seasons.

What makes the species unusual is that the same mouth also works as a strainer. Its cheek teeth have three points that interlock like a comb. When krill are plentiful, a leopard seal sucks them in and pushes the water out through that sieve, eating thousands at a time. It can therefore live at the top of the food web and near its base, switching as conditions change. Males add another surprise, filling the water under the pack ice with patterned songs for up to 13 hours a day.

In ABS terms the leopard seal is an aquatic predator with a strong bite, high Agility in water and strong tactics for a solitary animal. Its Defense is moderate because it relies on size and blubber, not armor, and it is badly outmatched by killer whales. Out of the water it is slow, but in the water it is one of the most dangerous seals in the world.

sections.habitat: Leopard seals live around Antarctica, mainly in the pack ice zone, and reach sub-Antarctic islands such as Kerguelen; wandering animals reach the coasts of southern continents, and the species appears on South Africa's national Red List. They haul out on ice floes and, at some sites, on beaches.
sections.diet: They feed at both the top and near the bottom of the Southern Ocean food web. Krill can make up anywhere from about half to most of the diet depending on place and season, and one examined seal held more than 10,000 freshly caught krill. They also kill penguins, Antarctic fur seal pups and other seals. Studies at Cape Shirreff showed that a small number of leopard seals can drive local declines of fur seals.
sections.social: Solitary. Adults haul out and hunt alone. Genomic analyses indicate that leopard seals return to the same haul-out sites across generations.
sections.reproduction: Females give birth and nurse on the pack ice. During the breeding season males sing long underwater songs. Breeding behavior is hard to study because it happens on remote pack ice.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Population size is uncertain: the most recent circumpolar estimate exceeds 35,000 animals but is considered a large underestimate, and the population trend is unknown. At Cape Shirreff, leopard seal numbers fell by about 76% from 2017 to 2023. Climate-driven change in sea ice is a commonly raised long-term concern.
sections.features:
Long, streamlined body and large head with a wide gape.
Long canine-like front teeth for gripping large prey.
Three-pointed interlocking cheek teeth that sieve krill.
Large fore-flippers for fast, agile swimming.
Loud underwater songs from males.
Spotted throat and flanks that give it its common name.
sections.humanInteraction: Leopard seals are curious and sometimes approach divers, boats and photographers. Most encounters are harmless, but the 2003 death of Kirsty Brown at Rothera led to a study of leopard seal and human interactions over the previous thirty years, which found the ice edge to be the highest-risk setting.

funFacts: Female leopard seals are larger than males, the reverse of most large seals.
One leopard seal's stomach held more than 10,000 freshly caught krill.
Males can sing underwater for up to 13 hours a day.
About 20 leopard seals at Cape Shirreff were linked to the loss of roughly 70% of fur seal pups there.
The deepest dive reported for the species is about 1,256 m, although most dives are around 30 m.
Its cheek teeth work like a sieve, the same way a baleen whale strains krill.

abilities.name: Ice-Edge Ambush
abilities.description: waits just below the water line where penguins must jump in or climb out, then seizes and shakes them apart against the surface. In a battle it strikes when an opponent is entering or leaving the water.

abilities.name: Krill Sieve
abilities.description: sucks krill into the mouth and pushes water out through interlocking three-pointed cheek teeth, the same jaws that kill penguins and seals. This lets it switch between tiny prey and large prey, so it rarely runs out of food.

traits.name: Heavier Females
traits.description: adult females outweigh males, averaging about 454 kg against 302 kg at Cape Shirreff, where the smallest adult female was heavier than the largest adult male.

traits.name: Antarctic Songster
traits.description: males sing underwater for up to 13 hours a day, with loud, patterned songs built from five call types and structured as predictably as nursery rhymes.

combat.weapons: The leopard seal is the Southern Ocean's top predator of warm-blooded prey after the killer whale. Its weapon is a large head with long canine-like teeth on a flexible, powerful neck. It seizes penguins and seals, then shakes and smashes them against the water surface to break them apart. At Cape Shirreff, about 20 leopard seals, mostly a few large females, caused the loss of roughly 70% of Antarctic fur seal pups to predation. Its bite is serious against penguins, pups and similarly sized seals, but it lacks claws or tusks as secondary weapons.
weaknesses: Slow and clumsy on land and ice.
No armor; exposed to deep bites from larger predators such as killer whales.
Single main weapon (the bite).
Short routine dives compared with deep-diving seals.
Far outmatched by killer whales and very large sharks.

maine-coon.name: Maine Coon
maine-coon.specimen: healthy mature intact male of about 7.5 kg, fully grown (the breed can take up to three years to finish growing) and in fit, non-obese condition.
maine-coon.summary: The Maine Coon is the largest non-hybrid domestic cat, a 7.5 kg shaggy "gentle giant" with snowshoe paws, a weatherproof coat and the full house-cat toolkit of claws, bite, reflexes and ultrasonic hearing. It is noticeably stronger than an ordinary cat, but on the absolute scale it remains far below wild cats such as the bobcat and lynx.
narrative: The Maine Coon grew out of the farm cats of New England, where long winters favored big, heavily coated cats with broad, tufted feet. Breeders have since selected it for size, and a mature male commonly weighs 7–9 kg, making it the heaviest non-hybrid domestic breed. It keeps every tool of the domestic cat: retractable claws, a precise neck bite, a flexible spine and righting reflex, and hearing that reaches about 85 kHz.

Its extra size matters. In cats, bite force rises with body mass, and a heavy Maine Coon male can handle larger prey and bigger opponents than an ordinary tomcat. Its thick coat gives a little padding and superb cold-weather comfort, and its snowshoe paws keep it sure-footed in snow. On the other hand, the breed's famously gentle temperament, its slower, heavier frame and its predisposition to heart and hip problems keep it from being a fighting cat in any real sense.

On the absolute ABS scale, the Maine Coon therefore sits just above the house cat in Attack and Defense, level with a red fox, and well below the 10–24 kg wild cats such as the bobcat and lynx that it superficially resembles with its tufted ears. Its Agility, Senses and Intelligence stay close to the house cat's, because it is the same species in a bigger coat.

sections.habitat: A domestic breed kept worldwide. It developed in Maine and elsewhere in New England, a region of cold, snowy forests and farmland, from cats brought by European settlers; genetic studies group the breed with Western European cats and find it most similar to random-bred cats of the northeastern United States.
sections.diet: An obligate carnivore like all cats. Pet Maine Coons eat prepared food; the breed's origins are as a farm and ship mouser hunting rodents and small animals.
sections.social: Like other domestic cats, a solitary hunter with flexible social relationships; the breed is noted for being sociable and people-oriented.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is managed by people. Maine Coons grow slowly and may take up to three years to reach full size. UK life tables give a life expectancy at birth of about 9.7 years, while Swedish insurance data give a median over 12.5 years.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed. The Maine Coon was declared "extinct" as a show breed in the 1950s, prematurely, and has since become one of the most popular breeds, ranking first in FIFe registrations in 2024 and becoming the CFA's most registered breed in 2025.
sections.features:
Largest non-hybrid domestic cat breed.
Heavy, water-resistant, shaggy coat with a ruff in some cats.
Large, round, tufted "snowshoe" paws; polydactyly in some lines.
Long, bushy, raccoon-like tail.
Large, heavily tufted ears.
sections.humanInteraction: Farmers in Maine held "Maine State Champion Coon Cat" contests at the Skowhegan Fair in the late 1860s, and a brown tabby female named Cosey was named Best in Show at the first North American cat show, at Madison Square Garden in New York in 1895. The breed gained CFA championship status in 1976 and became Maine's official state cat in 1985. Health screening focuses on hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, for which a MYBPC3 mutation is common in the breed, hip dysplasia and spinal muscular atrophy.

funFacts: A Maine Coon named Stewie held the Guinness record as the world's longest cat, 123 cm from nose to tail tip.
The breed can take up to three years to reach full size.
Many Maine Coons have extra toes; in one study of 70 cats from polydactyl lines, 48 had them, with no apparent harm to welfare.
The Maine Coon is the official state cat of Maine.
Despite the name, the breed has no raccoon in it; the raccoon story is a myth.
A female Maine Coon named Cosey was Best in Show at the first North American cat show, held at Madison Square Garden in 1895.

abilities.name: Snowshoe Paws
abilities.description: large, round paws with long tufts of fur between the toes spread its weight on snow and soft ground, and in polydactyl lines one to three extra digits per paw add grip. In a matchup this means sure footing where other small predators flounder.

abilities.name: Heavyweight Bite-and-Grab
abilities.description: the classic cat attack of pounce, claw-grip and neck bite, delivered by one of the heaviest domestic cats; in cats, estimated bite force rises with body mass, so a big Maine Coon male hits harder than an ordinary tomcat.

traits.name: Gentle Giant
traits.description: the largest non-hybrid domestic cat breed, slow to mature (up to three years), with mature males often reaching 20 lb; a Maine Coon named Stewie was the Guinness "Longest Cat" at 123 cm.

traits.name: All-Weather Coat
traits.description: a shaggy, water-resistant coat that is longest on the belly and rear, a bushy tail that wraps around the face, and heavily tufted ears suit it to Maine winters; many Maine Coons are also unusually fond of water.

combat.weapons: The Maine Coon has the standard domestic-cat kit on a larger frame: a stalk and pounce, forefoot claws to grab and hold, hind claws to rake, and a precise killing bite to the neck of small prey. Because bite force rises with body mass, a 7.5 kg male should bite harder than an ordinary 5 kg tomcat, and the breed is historically a working mouser on New England farms. Against anything much larger than a rabbit, however, it still lacks the mass and weaponry of wild cats such as the bobcat or lynx.
weaknesses: Small absolute size and power despite being a large cat.
No armor.
Poor endurance in long chases.
Breed predisposition to heart disease (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) and hind-limb joint problems.

mako-shark.name: Mako Shark
mako-shark.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 275 kg and 280 cm fork length (roughly 3 m total length), matching the median size and weight at maturity for North Atlantic females.
mako-shark.summary: The shortfin mako is the ocean's speed shark: a 3-metre, 275 kg warm-muscled hunter that bursts faster than almost any fish ever measured and leaps up to 6 metres out of the water. Its slender grasping teeth are deadly to fast fish, but it lacks the mass and cutting bite of a Great White.
narrative: The shortfin mako is built for acceleration. Its body is a stiff torpedo driven by a crescent tail and by red muscle kept warmer than the sea around it. Tags on free-swimming makos have recorded bursts above 5 metres per second, among the fastest ever directly measured in sharks, tunas and billfishes, and makos can launch themselves around 6 metres into the air. Even the skin helps: tiny scales on the flanks bristle when water starts to flow backward, keeping the flow attached as the shark turns and sprints.

That speed serves a precise weapon. The mako's long, slender teeth are made for grabbing fast, slippery fish, and it hunts bluefish, tunas, mackerels and even swordfish. The swordfish fights back: makos have been found with bills snapped off in their heads and gills. It shows the mako's style, a high-speed predator that wins by closing distance faster than its prey can react rather than by overpowering it with mass.

In a battle the mako is dangerous and elusive. It can outswim and outlast most open-water opponents and strike with little warning. Its limits are size and armor: a 275 kg shark with grasping teeth cannot carve up a much larger animal the way a Great White can, and it has no protection against a determined counterattack. Against anything it can outpace it is lethal; against giants it must rely on speed to avoid a fight it cannot win.

sections.habitat: The shortfin mako lives in tropical and temperate seas worldwide, mostly in open ocean from the surface to several hundred metres, and also along continental shelves. It avoids the coldest waters but uses warm muscles to hunt in cool water.
sections.diet: Makos are mainly fish eaters. Bluefish dominate the diet in the northwest Atlantic; elsewhere mackerels, tunas, herrings, squid, swordfish and other billfish, and smaller sharks are common. Large individuals sometimes take marine mammals. The mako is a high-level predator in open-ocean food webs.
sections.social: Makos are solitary. Sexes and size classes are often found in different areas, with large mature females less common in catches than males and juveniles.
sections.reproduction: Makos give birth to live young after the embryos feed on unfertilized eggs in the uterus. Females mature late, around 280 cm fork length, and reproduce only every few years, so populations recover slowly. Maximum known ages are 29 years for males and 32 for females.
sections.conservation: The shortfin mako is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2019 assessment), with an estimated global decline of about 47% and the highest probability of a 50–79% decline over three generations. Overfishing in longline fisheries is the main cause. NOAA completed an Endangered Species Act status review in 2022, and international fishery managers have since agreed stricter retention limits for North Atlantic makos (Oceana report).
sections.features:
Directly measured burst speed of 5.02 m/s, among the highest in pelagic fishes.
Leaps up to about 6 m high.
Flexible bristling scales on flanks and fins that control flow separation.
Regional endothermy with warm red muscle.
Long, slender, smooth-edged grasping teeth.
sections.humanInteraction: Makos are prized sport fish because of their leaps and power, and they are fished commercially for meat and fins. They are rarely involved in attacks on people but can be dangerous when hooked and brought aboard.

funFacts: The shortfin mako holds the record for the highest-leaping shark, about 6 m.
A GPS-tagged mako from New Zealand swam about 13,300 km in six months.
Mako flank scales bristle like tiny flaps when water starts to flow backward, an idea engineers are studying for aircraft wings.
Makos have been found with swordfish bills broken off inside their heads.
In one study bluefish made up about 77.5% of the diet of northwest Atlantic makos.
A 2 m female mako carried a tag that clocked a burst of 5.02 m/s.

abilities.name: Bristle-Scale Burst
abilities.description: flexible flank and fin scales bristle above 40° when water starts to flow backward over them, helping keep flow attached during fast swimming and turns. In a matchup it supports the mako's bursts, measured at 5.02 m/s, among the fastest ever directly measured in sharks, tunas and billfishes.

abilities.name: Rocket Breach
abilities.description: makos can launch up to about 6 m out of the water and have landed in boats. The same explosive power lets a mako close distance vertically and surprise opponents from below.

traits.name: Warm-Muscle Cruiser
traits.description: regional endothermy keeps the red swimming muscle warmer than the sea, supporting high performance in cool water and ocean-scale journeys such as 13,300 km in six months.

traits.name: Swordfish Hunter
traits.description: makos prey on swordfish and other billfish, and some have been found with swordfish bills embedded in their heads, a rare predator-prey duel between two high-speed fish.

combat.weapons: The mako's weapon is a fast, precise bite. Its long, slender, non-serrated teeth are built to seize slippery, fast-moving fish such as bluefish, tunas and mackerels; stomach studies also record billfish, including swordfish, and other sharks. A study of Atlantic stomachs found headless and tailless fish, consistent with makos biting off parts of prey too large to swallow whole. The mako does not have the Great White's broad cutting dentition, so it is less efficient at removing large chunks from big, tough opponents, but it delivers its bite at a speed few sharks can match.
weaknesses: No armor; a long spear such as a swordfish bill can penetrate the head and gills.
Slender grasping teeth are less effective at cutting large, tough prey than serrated teeth.
Much smaller than the Great White, so it loses head-on contests of mass.
Must keep swimming to breathe efficiently.

markhor.name: Markhor
markhor.specimen: healthy mature adult male (buck) of about 100 kg and 100 cm at the shoulder, with fully developed corkscrew horns of about 120 cm along the curve. A representative prime male, not a trophy-record animal.
markhor.summary: The markhor is a 100 kg wild goat of the Himalaya and Hindu Kush, famous for males' corkscrew horns that can pass 1.5 m. It is a cliff specialist that escapes predators by climbing where they cannot follow, and fights rivals by locking and twisting horns, but it is no heavyweight on the absolute scale.
narrative: A mature markhor buck is one of the most striking animals in the mountains: a big, grizzled goat with a long ruff of hair spilling down its chest and a pair of horns twisted like corkscrews, sometimes more than a metre and a half long. It lives on steep slopes and cliffs from northern Pakistan and Afghanistan into Central Asia, moving between high summer pastures and lower winter slopes and browsing oak, juniper and shrubs when grass is scarce.

Its life centres on terrain. Sharp eyesight and smell let it spot snow leopards and wolves at a distance, and its response is to climb onto rock faces where few predators can follow. In the rut, bucks come down to the female herds and fight by lunging, locking their horns and twisting, each trying to shove the other off balance on the slope. Those contests look dramatic, but they are wrestling matches rather than stabbing duels.

For ABS, the markhor sits beside the Alpine ibex in size and Attack, with slightly higher Agility for its cliff and slope skills, and below the Mountain Goat, which remains the roster's cliff-agility benchmark. Its horns earn a strong Weaponry score, but its mass and lack of armor keep its Attack and Defense firmly in the middle band. Its recovery story, from Endangered to Near Threatened on the back of community conservation, is one of the more hopeful in the mountains.

sections.habitat: Mountains of Central and South Asia: the Hindu Kush, Karakoram and western Himalaya, and ranges in Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Markhor use steep, rocky slopes and cliffs with scrub and open forest of oak, pine and juniper, and tend to avoid the highest ground. In Chitral Gol National Park they occurred at a mean elevation of about 2,800 m.
sections.diet: Markhor both graze and browse, eating grasses and herbs as well as leaves and twigs of shrubs and trees such as oak and juniper, especially in forested areas. They are an important prey species for snow leopards and wolves.
sections.social: Females and young live in herds; adult males are mostly solitary or in small male groups outside the rut. During the rut, which peaks from about November to January, males join the herds and compete for females.
sections.reproduction: Females give birth to their kids months after the winter rut. Males keep growing their horns throughout life, and the number of horn turns rises with age.
sections.conservation: Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List since 2015, when improved numbers led to its move down from Endangered; some subspecies and regional populations remain in more serious danger. Pakistan's population has been estimated at over 5,000, with the largest single population in Chitral Gol National Park (estimated at about 2,278 animals in 2021). Tajikistan surveys counted about 1,018 markhor in 2012 and later monitoring showed recovery. Community-based trophy hunting programs, in which most permit revenue goes to local villages that protect the herds, are credited with much of this recovery. Remaining threats include poaching, habitat loss, competition with livestock and disease.
sections.features:
Corkscrew horns up to about 165 cm in males.
Long ruff of hair on the throat and chest in mature males.
Sure-footed hooves for cliffs and narrow ledges.
Mixed grazing and browsing diet across seasons.
sections.humanInteraction: The markhor is Pakistan's national animal. Carefully limited trophy hunting, with high permit fees shared with local communities, is a well-known example of hunting revenue funding conservation. Poaching and livestock competition remain problems in parts of the range.

funFacts: The markhor is the national animal of Pakistan.
A male's horns can be over 1.5 m long, and the number of twists increases with age.
Chitral Gol National Park holds the largest known markhor population, estimated at about 2,278 in 2021.
Markhor were moved from Endangered to Near Threatened in 2015 after conservation programs took hold.
Males weigh about twice as much as females.
Rival males lock horns and twist, trying to throw each other off balance on steep slopes.

abilities.name: Corkscrew Horn Lock
abilities.description: rival males lunge, lock their spiral horns and shove and twist to throw each other off balance; the same horns and neck strength can be turned on a predator that corners a buck.

abilities.name: Cliff Refuge Escape
abilities.description: sharp eyes and smell spot snow leopards and wolves early, and the markhor retreats onto steep cliffs and ledges where few predators can follow.

traits.name: Spiral-Horned Giant
traits.description: mature males carry tightly twisted horns about 80–165 cm long, among the longest horns of any wild goat, with more turns as the animal ages.

traits.name: Hunt-Funded Comeback
traits.description: community-run trophy hunting programs in Pakistan and community conservancies in Tajikistan helped markhor numbers recover enough for the IUCN to move the species to a lower threat category in 2015.

combat.weapons: The markhor's weapons are the male's long corkscrew horns, backed by a 100 kg body. During the rut, rival males lunge at each other, lock horns and shove and twist, each trying to push the other off balance on steep ground. The horns are built for this wrestling rather than stabbing, but a lunge or horn sweep can still injure a predator or rival. Hooves give strong, precise footing for pushing on slopes.
weaknesses: Horns are wrestling tools, less suited to stabbing than a mountain goat's short horns.
No armor; light compared with large bovids.
Ordinary speed on open, flat ground.
Prefers retreat to confrontation.
