martial-eagle.name: Martial Eagle
martial-eagle.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 4.8 kg, 88.0 cm total length, about 2.1 m wingspan. Females are the heavier, stronger-footed sex and take the largest prey.
martial-eagle.summary: The Martial Eagle is Africa's largest eagle by wingspan. The canonical female weighs about 4.8 kg and hunts from a high soar, dropping in a long stoop onto hares, monitor lizards, snakes, small carnivores and even lion cubs. Large talons and very long legs make its strike dangerous, but its small absolute mass and lack of armor keep it far below large mammals in raw power and defense.
narrative: The martial eagle hunts from above. It spends much of the day circling so high over the savanna that it is hard to see, scanning ground where hares, hyraxes, game birds and monitor lizards move in the open. When it commits, it drops in a long, shallow stoop, or a steeper parachute into cover, and arrives before the prey knows it has been seen.

Its weapons match its choice of prey. Females carry hallux claws averaging about 5.6 cm, an inner claw almost as large, and the longest legs of any booted eagle, letting them strike at snakes and small carnivores without putting the body within reach. Records of lion cubs killed in Kenya and of venomous snakes, jackals and small cats in the diet show that it takes on prey that can hurt it. Vervet monkeys take the threat seriously enough to keep a separate alarm call for it.

In an absolute matchup, however, it is still a bird under 5 kg. Its wide wings suit soaring and open-country stoops, not twisting fights in dense cover, and it has no armor and a light skeleton. It wins by striking first from above. If the first strike does not end the fight, or a heavy grappler gets a grip on it, the martial eagle has little else to rely on.

sections.habitat: The martial eagle lives across sub-Saharan Africa in open and semi-open savanna, thornveld and wooded grassland with scattered large trees. It avoids dense forest. It has been recorded up to about 3,000 m but residents rarely exceed 1,500 m. It is most common in large protected areas such as Kruger and Kgalagadi in South Africa and Etosha in Namibia. In Kruger, GPS-tracked eagles preferred areas near rivers with more tree cover.
sections.diet: It is an opportunistic apex predator of mammals, birds and reptiles. Hares dominate in the Cape (about 53% of prey in the largest study), and rock hyraxes elsewhere. Other prey include larger birds (including spotted eagle-owls and white-headed vultures), monitor lizards, venomous snakes, striped polecats, jackals, medium-sized wild cats and, rarely, lion cubs. Mean prey mass is usually 1–5 kg. It rarely scavenges, but it is still killed by poisoned baits set for mammalian predators.
sections.social: Adults live in territorial pairs spread at very low density. Territories in Kruger averaged about 108 km². Non-territorial adults (floaters) wander widely. No cooperative hunting is documented.
sections.reproduction: Pairs often breed only every second year and may alternate between nests. The single chick depends on its parents for months, full independence comes at 2–3 years, and breeding begins at about 4–5 years. GPS tracking in South Africa found productivity of about 0.46 young per pair per year, higher than the 0.22 found by field nest checks, but still low.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Endangered by BirdLife International for the IUCN Red List, with continuing declines in mature individuals and range. Threats include persecution by farmers over livestock and game losses (almost certainly exaggerated), poisoned baits, electrocution and collisions with power infrastructure, and habitat fragmentation. In Kruger, three of four wide-ranging floaters died from human-related causes, and declines are occurring even inside protected areas.
sections.features:
Hallux claw about 5.6 cm in females, with a very large inner front claw.
Longest tarsus of any booted eagle.
Very broad wingspan of about 2.1 m for soaring.
Hunts mostly from a high soar with a long stoop, and can briefly hover.
Very sharp long-range vision.
sections.humanInteraction: Farmers and game managers have long shot and poisoned martial eagles for taking livestock and game, though its effect on livestock is almost certainly exaggerated. It is shy of people and prefers undisturbed land, so its future depends heavily on large protected areas and on reducing persecution in farmland.

funFacts: Its scientific name, Polemaetus bellicosus, roughly means "warlike war-eagle".
Martial eagles have been recorded killing and eating lion cubs in Kenya's Mara region.
It has been reported to spot prey from 5–6 km away.
Vervet monkeys have a special alarm call for eagles, given mainly to martial eagles.
Immature birds keep a pale plumage for years; full adult plumage comes around the seventh year.
Kruger floater eagles ranged over about 44,000 km², far beyond the park.
Unusually for such a large eagle, it can hover briefly while hunting.

abilities.name: High-Soar Stoop
abilities.description: the eagle circles high enough to be hard to see, then comes down in a long, shallow stoop or a steep parachute drop and hits prey before it can react. In open terrain this almost guarantees the first strike.

abilities.name: Snake-and-Carnivore Takedown
abilities.description: large talons, an oversized inner claw and the longest tarsus of any booted eagle let it strike from arm's length at dangerous prey such as venomous snakes, monitor lizards, jackals and lion cubs.

traits.name: Africa's Widest-Winged Eagle
traits.description: ten wild-measured birds averaged about 2.12 m in wingspan, about fourth among living eagles and the largest in Africa.

traits.name: The Vervet's Eagle Alarm
traits.description: vervet monkeys give a distinct eagle alarm call mainly to martial eagles, and young monkeys learn to aim it at the right predator.

combat.weapons:
The feet are the weapon. Large, curved talons (female hallux about 5.6 cm), an oversized inner claw and the longest tarsus of any booted eagle let it strike and hold prey on the ground, often in grass. The bill tears food after the kill. Most studies place mean prey mass between 1 and 5 kg: about 2.26 kg in the largest dietary study (Cape Province, dominated by 2.1 kg Cape hares), 2.31 kg in Tsavo East, and in the Maasai Mara 1.98 kg for males and 3.74 kg for females. Its prey range spans roughly 0.2 kg to about 7.5 kg, and ADW reports kills up to 35 kg, which should be treated as an exceptional upper claim.

The strongest evidence of weapon power is what it chooses to attack. Wikipedia's account lists monitor lizards, venomous snakes, jackals and medium-sized wild cats among its prey. A 2024 paper documented seven records of martial eagles killing or attempting to kill lion cubs in Kenya's greater Mara region, nine cubs in total, most at least partly eaten. The Peregrine Fund notes that it has taken spotted eagle-owls and white-headed vultures.
weaknesses: About 4.8 kg in absolute mass.
No armor; light avian skeleton.
Less maneuverable in dense forest and cluttered cover.
Loses most of its advantage once grounded or pinned by a heavier grappler.
Relies on surprise; a prepared, alert opponent removes its best attack.

mexican-red-knee-tarantula.name: Mexican Red-knee Tarantula
mexican-red-knee-tarantula.specimen: healthy adult female, body length about 5.3 cm and leg span about 13 cm, with an estimated mass of 15 g (0.015 kg). Seven measured females had body lengths of 52–54 mm (Wikipedia, from Mendoza and Francke); ADW gives 12.7–14 cm overall for the red-knee.
mexican-red-knee-tarantula.summary: The Mexican red-knee tarantula is a calm, long-lived burrow ambusher of western Mexico's dry forests, famous as a pet for its orange-banded legs. Its fangs and mild venom handle insects and mice, and its barbed defensive hairs deter mammals, but at around 15 grams it is fragile and weak on the absolute scale.
narrative: On the dry, thorny hillsides of Colima and Michoacán, the Mexican red-knee tarantula spends most of its life underground. A female digs or remodels a burrow beneath a log, rock or tree root, with a tunnel leading to a molting chamber and a deeper room where she rests and eats. At dusk she waits near the entrance, feeling for the vibrations of beetles, crickets or the occasional mouse, then rushes out, pins the prey, bites, and drags it below.

Her defenses are layered. Threatened, she rears up to show her fangs, then turns and kicks a cloud of barbed hairs from her abdomen, hairs that irritate skin and can injure the eyes of mammals, people included. Only as a last resort does she bite, and her venom, though deadly to insects, is mild to people. She grows slowly, moulting once a year and regrowing lost legs, and can live for 25 to 30 years, while males mature, wander in search of mates, and usually die within a few years.

In battle terms, the red-knee is a small specialist. Its fangs, venom and hairs give it a high Special rating for its size, but it weighs perhaps 15 grams, moves slowly, and has a soft, easily crushed abdomen. It wins against insects and small prey at its burrow and loses to almost any vertebrate predator large enough to shrug off a few hairs.

sections.habitat: Endemic to Mexico on the Pacific slope of the Sierra Madre Occidental and Sierra Madre del Sur, mainly Colima, north-western Michoacán and southern Jalisco (Wikipedia; Fukushima et al. 2019). It lives in subtropical dry forest, mostly thorn and deciduous secondary forest, from the coastal lowlands into the foothills up to about 2,100 m, preferring undisturbed shaded areas and places near seasonal watercourses (Fukushima et al. 2019). ADW describes red-knee habitat as dry scrubland, desert, dry thorn forest and tropical deciduous forest, often at the base of thorny plants such as cacti.
sections.diet: Nocturnal sit-and-wait predator of ground-dwelling insects, arachnids and myriapods, and occasionally small vertebrates such as frogs and mice (Fukushima et al. 2019; ADW; Wikipedia). It sucks out the liquefied body contents and wraps the remains in silk. Predators include white-nosed coatis (Wikipedia), birds and lizards (ADW), and Pepsis tarantula hawk wasps (ADW).
sections.social: Solitary. Each female keeps her own burrow; males leave their burrows to search for females in the mating season, when roads are a significant cause of male deaths (Fukushima et al. 2019).
sections.reproduction: Mating follows the male's final moult. The male hooks the female's fangs open with spurs on his front legs, transfers sperm with his palps, then retreats quickly because females can turn on males (ADW). The female lays about 200–400 eggs on a silk mat in the dry winter months, wraps them into an egg sac and guards it; young emerge about two months later and disperse before the early summer rains (ADW; Fukushima et al. 2019). Growth is slow: males mature at about 4 years, females at 6–7.
sections.conservation: Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (Fukushima et al. 2019 assessment, per Wikipedia), with an estimated extent of occurrence of about 13,000 km² and an area of occupancy of about 8,450 km², both declining through urbanisation, agriculture and roads (Fukushima et al. 2019). Listed on CITES Appendix II since 1985 (then under the name B. smithi). Illegal collection continues, especially around Colima, while legal captive breeding in Mexican management units supplies part of the pet trade (Fukushima et al. 2019). No protected area covers its range.
sections.features:
Type I urticating setae on the abdomen, kicked off in defense.
Downward-striking fangs with insecticidal venom peptides.
Deep burrows with a molting chamber and a feeding chamber, sealed with silk when molting or brooding.
Regrowth of lost legs across moults.
Exceptional female longevity of 25–30 years.
sections.humanInteraction: One of the most popular pet tarantulas because of its bright orange-banded legs and calm temperament (Wikipedia). Its hairs are the main risk to keepers, especially to the eyes (Jalink and Wisse 2021). Some local people kill the spiders with pesticides or by pouring gasoline into burrows (Wikipedia), and demand for adults drives illegal collection.

funFacts: For decades, pet "Mexican red-knees" sold as Brachypelma smithi were mostly a different species, B. hamorii; the mix-up was only settled in 2017.
Female red-knees can live 25–30 years, while males often live about five.
Its burrow tunnel is about three times the spider's leg span long and leads to a molting chamber and a separate feeding chamber.
It flicks barbed hairs at attackers instead of biting, and those hairs have caused eye injuries in people.
A tarantula even replaces its fangs when it moults, and lost legs regrow over several moults.
The male uses hooks on his front legs to hold the female's fangs open during mating.
Tarantula hawk wasps can lure it out of its burrow, paralyse it and use it as a living nursery for their young.

abilities.name: Barbed Hair Barrage
abilities.description: when threatened, the red-knee kicks type I urticating setae off its abdomen with its hind legs; the barbed hairs work into skin, nose and eyes, and have caused documented eye injuries in people. Against a mammal predator this can end a fight before contact.

abilities.name: Burrow Ambush Strike
abilities.description: it waits at the burrow mouth at night, senses prey through leg hairs and silk, rushes out to pin it with front legs and palps, strikes with downward fangs and drags the prey underground.

traits.name: Thirty-Year Spider
traits.description: females can live 25–30 years, maturing only at 6–7 years, while males rarely pass 10 and often live about 5.

traits.name: Regrowing Legs
traits.description: like all tarantulas it replaces its whole exoskeleton, including fangs, at each moult, and lost legs regrow gradually over successive moults.

combat.weapons: The red-knee waits at night near its burrow entrance and rushes out to seize passing ground-dwelling arthropods, other arachnids, myriapods and occasionally small vertebrates such as frogs and mice (Fukushima et al. 2019; ADW; Wikipedia). It holds prey with its front legs and palps, drives in its fangs, injects venom, and carries the meal back into the burrow, later wrapping the remains in silk (ADW). Against vertebrates larger than a mouse, its venom is weak and its reach tiny.
weaknesses: Tiny absolute mass; negligible raw power.
Soft abdomen and thin exoskeleton; highly vulnerable to crushing.
Poor vision and slow movement.
Mild venom against vertebrates; its hairs deter mammals but not wasps.
Tarantula hawk wasps (Pepsis) lure it from its burrow, paralyse it and lay eggs on it (ADW).

mosquito.name: Mosquito
mosquito.specimen: healthy adult female, about 2 mg and 3 mm body length. Only females bite and take blood, so the female is the combat-relevant form; males feed on plant sugars and never bite.
mosquito.summary: The African malaria mosquito weighs about 2 mg and tracks people by their breath, body heat and appearance before slipping six needle-like stylets into the skin. It cannot hurt anything directly, and any swat kills it, but the malaria parasites it carries make it one of the most dangerous animals to humans outside the battle arena.
narrative: Anopheles gambiae is a 3 mm insect weighing about 2 mg, and on the absolute battle scale it sits at the very bottom for Size, Attack and Defense. It has no jaws to bite with and no sting. Any direct hit kills it. What it has instead is a precision system for getting blood without being noticed.

A female looking for a meal follows carbon dioxide from a host's breath from tens of metres away, then uses sight and, at close range, body heat to land. Her proboscis holds six stylets; the sharp labrum and saw-edged maxillae slide into skin with micronewton forces, and saliva with anticoagulants keeps blood flowing. She can drink a meal as heavy as herself and fly off, usually at night and often indoors, when people are asleep.

The mosquito's reputation as the deadliest animal comes from what it carries, not what it does in a fight. Malaria parasites transmitted in its saliva caused an estimated 597,000 deaths in 2023, almost all in Africa. That effect appears days later and only in susceptible hosts, so the ratings credit it partly under Special while keeping Attack at the floor. In a direct contest it relies on low inertia, small size and good senses to avoid being hit.

sections.habitat: An. gambiae lives across sub-Saharan Africa, especially in humid savanna and farmland near people. Larvae grow in small, sunlit pools of fresh water such as puddles, hoof prints and rice fields. Adults rest and feed in and around houses.
sections.diet: Adults of both sexes drink plant sugars. Females also take blood, preferring humans, to develop their eggs. Larvae filter food from the water surface. Mosquitoes are prey for many animals: dragonflies, bats, birds, spiders and, as larvae, fish and other aquatic predators.
sections.social: Not social. Males form mating swarms at dusk, and females enter the swarms to mate; males and females tune their wingbeat tones to find each other.
sections.reproduction: Eggs are laid on the water surface and hatch into aquatic larvae, then pupae, then flying adults, following the standard Anopheles life cycle described by the CDC. A female takes a blood meal, digests it and lays a batch of eggs, then repeats the cycle. Larger females carry more reserves at emergence and develop eggs more readily.
sections.conservation: Not Evaluated: no IUCN Red List assessment exists for this species in the sources located. It is abundant and the target of major control efforts because of malaria.
sections.features:
Six-stylet piercing and sucking mouthparts.
Anticoagulant saliva.
Carbon dioxide, odour, visual and heat sensing used in sequence to find hosts.
Hearing tuned to wingbeat tones, used in swarm mating.
Very low mass that lets it survive raindrop impacts.
sections.humanInteraction: It is among the most important animals in human health because it transmits malaria. WHO reports that malaria control has averted billions of cases since 2000, yet 263 million cases and 597,000 deaths were estimated for 2023. Bed nets, indoor spraying and new genetic approaches all target this species. Its painless piercing mouthparts have also inspired designs for finer medical needles.

funFacts: A raindrop can weigh up to 50 times as much as a mosquito, yet the mosquito survives the hit.
Only female mosquitoes bite.
A blood meal can weigh more than the mosquito itself.
The mosquito's mouthparts are a bundle of six needle-like stylets.
It inserts them into skin with a force of only about 16.5 micronewtons.
Males and females "sing" to each other by matching wingbeat harmonics.
It can detect a person's breath from tens of metres away.

abilities.name: Breath-Tracker Homing
abilities.description: follows a host's carbon dioxide plume from about 10–50 m, switches to vision at about 5–15 m and to body heat within about a metre, landing on a target that has not noticed it.

abilities.name: Six-Needle Siphon
abilities.description: a fascicle of six stylets slides into skin with a force of about 16.5 µN while saliva with anticoagulants keeps the blood flowing, letting it drink a meal as heavy as its own body.

traits.name: Malaria Carrier
traits.description: An. gambiae is the most efficient malaria vector in Africa; WHO estimated 263 million malaria cases and 597,000 deaths worldwide in 2023, about 95% of the deaths in the WHO African Region.

traits.name: Raindrop Survivor
traits.description: at about 2 mg it is so light that a falling raindrop up to 50 times heavier barely slows on impact, so the mosquito is knocked aside and flies on.

combat.weapons: The only tool is the piercing fascicle, which draws blood rather than causing injury. Its real-world danger comes from what the saliva carries: malaria parasites (Plasmodium) that it can transmit to people. That effect takes days to weeks to appear and depends on the mosquito being infected and the host being susceptible, so it has almost no bearing on a fight in progress.
weaknesses: About 2 mg, with no physical way to harm a large animal.
Killed by any direct hit.
Short adult life.
Disease transmission is delayed and host-specific, not a battle weapon.
Weak flier in wind.

nile-crocodile.name: Nile Crocodile
nile-crocodile.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 400.0 kg and 450.0 cm total length, representing a large fighting-age bull rather than a record giant.
nile-crocodile.summary: The Nile crocodile is Africa's largest reptile and a shoreline ambush specialist. A 400 kg adult male combines a crushing crocodilian bite, gripping teeth, armored back, explosive tail-driven lunges and the seize-drag-drown tactic that makes river crossings deadly. It dominates at the water's edge but tires quickly and is far less dangerous on open dry ground.
narrative: A big male Nile crocodile fights on its own terms. It spends most of its time nearly invisible, only the eyes, ears and nostrils breaking the surface, while sensory organs across its skin pick up ripples and footsteps at the water's edge. When an antelope, zebra or wildebeest lowers its head to drink or commits to a crossing, the crocodile converts tail thrust and 400 kg of body into a short, violent lunge. Once the jaws close, the fight moves into the water, where the crocodile holds, drags, rolls and waits for the victim to drown.

This species is also more social than its reputation suggests. Crocodiles gather wherever food concentrates, jostle by size, and have been reported working together: lining up across a channel to catch fish, or anchoring a carcass so others can tear it apart. Those behaviors give it tactical options that a purely solitary ambusher would lack, though they do not approach the planning of social mammals.

In ABS terms the Nile crocodile is an asymmetric specialist. It earns elite Attack and very strong Defense from its bite, mass and armor, sitting just below the heavier saltwater crocodile and well above the American alligator. Its Agility and Stamina stay moderate because ectothermic muscles are built for bursts, not long fights, and because it cannot chase or maneuver well on land. Keep it near water and it is among the most dangerous animals on the roster; pull the fight onto open ground and much of that danger disappears.

sections.habitat: Nile crocodiles live in rivers, lakes, swamps, marshes and floodplains across much of sub-Saharan Africa, especially eastern and southern Africa, and in Madagascar. They also enter brackish estuaries and coastal lakes such as Lake St Lucia, helped by salt glands on the tongue. West African populations are now usually treated as a separate species.
sections.diet: Hatchlings eat insects, crustaceans, amphibians and small fish. Prey size increases with growth. Adults eat mostly fish, especially catfish and barbel, plus birds, reptiles and mammals ranging from impala and warthog to wildebeest, zebra and buffalo. Carrion is taken readily. Because their metabolism is slow, big crocodiles can gorge during events such as migration crossings and then go a long time between large meals.
sections.social: Adults are not territorial in every setting, but large males defend space and mating access, and dominance follows size. Crocodiles gather in numbers where food is concentrated, such as fish runs and river crossings, and can feed together on large carcasses.
sections.reproduction: Females dig nests in sandy banks and guard them. Sex is set by nest temperature: at Lake St Lucia males develop at about 31.7–34.5 °C, and females at temperatures below and above that range. Hatchling and juvenile mortality is high. Males take longer than females to reach large adult size.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List because it remains widespread and abundant across African wetlands. One widely repeated estimate puts the global population at about 50,000–70,000 mature individuals. Local populations still face habitat loss, pollution, persecution and conflict with people, and a Zimbabwe review found status varies considerably between water systems.
sections.features:
Eyes, ears and nostrils set high on the head for near-total submersion.
Dorsal osteoderms and a massive skull.
Powerful laterally flattened tail for swimming and lunging.
Whole-body integumentary sensory organs for touch and vibration.
Salt glands on the tongue for brackish water.
Conical replacement teeth for seizing and holding.
sections.humanInteraction: Nile crocodiles are widely reported to cause more attacks on people than most other crocodilians, mainly where people fish, wash or collect water at the shoreline. Management in many countries combines protection, regulated harvest and farming, and removal of problem animals.

funFacts: A study of the Mara River estimated that crocodiles in the main drowning reach eat about 150 wildebeest during the migration, roughly 2% of the carcasses entering the river.
Research on Nile crocodiles found their skin sensory organs are more sensitive to touch than human fingertips.
Nest temperature decides a hatchling's sex; at Lake St Lucia males come from a narrow middle temperature band.
Groups of crocodiles have been reported forming a living barrier across a 550 m channel at Lake St Lucia to catch migrating fish.
Crocodiles in a zoo all-male group kept fighting even when visual barriers blocked their view of each other.
The tongue carries salt glands, letting the species use brackish water despite being mainly a freshwater animal.

abilities.name: Crossing-Point Ambush
abilities.description: waits almost fully submerged at drinking points and river crossings, lunges, seizes and drags prey into deep water to drown it. This turns the shoreline into a trap for large land animals, as seen at the Mara River wildebeest crossings.

abilities.name: Fish-Dam Cooperation
abilities.description: groups have been reported lining up across narrow channels to intercept migrating fish and holding large carcasses so others can tear off pieces. In a battle this mainly adds tactical options near water rather than raw force.

traits.name: Africa's Heavyweight Reptile
traits.description: the largest crocodilian in Africa, with big males reaching roughly 225–750 kg and exceptional animals approaching a tonne.

traits.name: Fingertip-Grade Jaw Touch
traits.description: dome-shaped sensory organs in the skin, studied directly in Nile crocodiles, detect pressure and vibration with sensitivity greater than human fingertips, helping the animal find and handle prey in murky water.

combat.weapons: The jaws are the main weapon. A Nile crocodile lies almost fully submerged with only its eyes, ears and nostrils showing, closes the distance with a short tail-driven lunge, seizes with conical teeth and then drags the victim into deeper water to drown it. Large prey is broken up by jerking the head from side to side or by rolling the whole body. Species accounts list zebra, buffalo, warthog, wildebeest, impala, baboon and hyena as adult prey, with the largest males occasionally taking giraffe, young hippos or lions. Fish, especially catfish and barbel, still make up most of the diet in many areas.
weaknesses: Softer belly, eyes, throat and limb joints.
Short limbs and poor dry-land pursuit.
Offense depends on landing the first bite.
Limited sustained high-output effort.
A failed first strike against a large horned or tusked animal exposes it to heavy counterattack.

northern-goshawk.name: Northern Goshawk
northern-goshawk.specimen: healthy mature adult female of a northern or central European population, 1.3 kg, 62.0 cm total length, about 1.15 m wingspan. Females are much larger than males and take the largest prey.
northern-goshawk.summary: The Northern Goshawk is a powerful forest hawk. The canonical female weighs about 1.3 kg but kills hares and grouse up to twice her weight. Short wings and a long tail let it chase prey through dense trees with elite agility, and it defends its nest fiercely. Its small size and lack of armor keep it far below large predators in raw power and defense.
narrative: The goshawk is the forest's surprise attacker. It waits on a perch, then launches a short, hidden flight, usually under a minute and a half, through gaps in the trees. When it has been seen, it can still turn a chase into a sprint through the branches, holding its target at a fixed bearing to cut it off before switching to a direct strike.

Its power is unusual for its size. Females weighing about 1.3 kg kill mountain hares of up to 3.6 kg, and adult females have been reported taking cock capercaillie. It kills by squeezing, and the grip is backed by large gripping muscles like those of other predatory hawks. Nest defense matches this: goshawks attack intruders, people included, and one goshawk killed by a fox fatally wounded the fox in return.

In an absolute matchup, though, it is a bird of little more than a kilogram with no armor. Its best fights happen in woodland, where it can use cover and turn faster than prey can follow. In the open, against a heavier animal ready for it, or once pinned on the ground, its advantages disappear quickly.

sections.habitat: The goshawk breeds across the forests of Europe, North Africa and northern Asia to Japan. It prefers large patches of mature forest with open space beneath the canopy, but also uses farmland woods, forest edges and, increasingly since the 20th century, wooded areas in cities such as Berlin, Hamburg and Tokyo. Northern birds may move south in winter.
sections.diet: It is a generalist predator of medium-sized birds and mammals. Corvids, pigeons, grouse, pheasants, thrushes and woodpeckers dominate the bird prey; squirrels, rabbits and hares dominate the mammal prey. One goshawk needs about 120–150 g of food a day, and a kill can last one to three days. Hunting success is roughly 15–30% overall, higher on some prey. In Białowieża Forest, some males hunted in the forest while others commuted up to 20 km to hunt pigeons in town.
sections.social: Adults live as territorial pairs outside the breeding season. Each sex defends the territory mainly against its own sex. No regular group hunting is documented, though pairs occasionally hunt agile prey together.
sections.reproduction: Clutches average around three eggs; the male provides almost all the food while the female incubates and guards the nest. A brood of three needs roughly 700–950 g of food a day. Nest success is often 80–95%, with 2–3 fledglings per successful nest. Breeding typically starts at about 2 years.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern. It was heavily persecuted in the past and has recovered in many areas. In the UK, BTO atlas data show a clear increase in occupied 10-km squares, linked to reduced persecution and better access to prey. Illegal killing and loss of mature forest remain local threats.
sections.features:
Short, broad wings and a long tail for flying through dense woodland.
Large gripping muscles and strong talons.
Very strong size difference between the sexes.
Interception-based pursuit steering.
Short, hidden attack flights from perches.
sections.humanInteraction: Goshawks have been flown in falconry for centuries. They are also persecuted where they take game birds, racing pigeons or poultry, and nesting goshawks may attack people who come too close to the nest.

funFacts: A goshawk fitted with a head camera helped scientists work out how it steers to intercept fleeing prey.
Prey that jink sharply sideways are the ones most likely to break a goshawk's visual lock.
Female goshawks have killed mountain hares up to 2.4 times their own weight.
Some Białowieża Forest goshawks commuted up to 20 km to hunt pigeons in a town.
Siberian jays have a special mobbing response to goshawks, their main predator, and young jays that witness it survive better.
A goshawk killed by a fox once slashed the fox's windpipe, and the fox died soon afterwards.
Goshawks live wild in the Imperial Palace gardens in central Tokyo.

abilities.name: Interception Pursuit
abilities.description: it holds a fleeing target at a constant visual bearing to cut it off, then switches to direct pursuit for the final strike. Through dense woodland this lets it catch fast, dodging birds and squirrels at close range.

abilities.name: Crush-and-Knead Grip
abilities.description: powerful gripping muscles drive the talons in and squeeze, while the head is held back from kicks. Females have killed mountain hares weighing up to 2.4 times their own weight.

traits.name: Ghost of the Forest
traits.description: short, hidden hunting flights averaging only 83–94 seconds, from perch to strike, make it one of the most feared woodland predators of birds.

traits.name: Extreme Size Gap Between Sexes
traits.description: females can be more than twice the weight of males in some populations, so the pair hunts different prey sizes.

combat.weapons: The feet are the weapon. It kills by driving its talons into prey and squeezing, holding its head back to avoid flailing limbs, then kneading until the prey stops struggling. It takes a wide range of birds and mammals: corvids, pigeons, grouse, pheasants, thrushes and woodpeckers, and squirrels, rabbits and hares. Males have taken rabbits up to 1.6 kg, about 2.2 times their weight. Females in Fennoscandia have killed adult mountain hares of 2.7–3.6 kg, up to 2.4 times their own weight, and adult females have been reported killing cock capercaillie in winter. It sometimes preys on ravens, which are about its own size and fight back.
weaknesses: Only about 1.3 kg in absolute mass.
No armor; light skeleton.
Burst hunter; long open-country chases are not its strength.
Prey that turns sharply sideways can break its visual lock.
Vulnerable to eagle-owls, large eagles, foxes and martens when on the ground or moulting.

ocean-sunfish.name: Ocean Sunfish
ocean-sunfish.specimen: healthy mature adult, 200 cm total length (snout to the rudder-like clavus) and 400 kg, a large adult within the 247–1,000 kg range reported for mature fish, rather than the 3.3 m, 2,300 kg record.
ocean-sunfish.summary: The ocean sunfish is a 400 kg, tail-less giant that swims by flapping two tall fins like wings. Very thick skin over a stiff gelatinous capsule makes it hard to wound, but it has no weapons, swims slowly and never fights, so sea lions, sharks and orcas can prey on it.
narrative: The ocean sunfish looks like a fish that forgot to finish growing a back half. A large adult is about 2 metres long, taller than that from fin tip to fin tip, and weighs around 400 kg, yet it has no tail fin at all. Instead it beats its tall dorsal and anal fins together, side to side, generating lift like a pair of wings and steering with a frilly rudder called the clavus. Tagging shows that it swims constantly at around half a metre per second and can put on short bursts.

Much of its life happens out of sight. Sunfish dive 100–200 metres into cold water to hunt siphonophores, jellyfish, squid and small fish, then return to the surface and lie on their side to warm up, often while seabirds peck parasites from their skin. A stiff gelatinous layer under the skin keeps them neutrally buoyant without a swim bladder, and the skin itself can be over 7 centimetres thick on the belly.

In a battle the sunfish is almost entirely passive. Its small beak is made for soft prey, it has no muscular body to fight with and it cannot flee fast predators. Its thick skin and capsule make it hard for small predators to hurt, but sea lions tear at its fins and sharks and orcas eat adults. It wins by being difficult to damage, not by doing damage.

sections.habitat: Found in temperate and tropical oceans worldwide, including the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian Ocean and Mediterranean. Sunfish are often seen at the surface but spend much of their time hunting at depths below 200 m, mainly in water warmer than 10 °C. Aerial surveys in the north-east Atlantic estimated at least 12,700 sunfish in summer across about 300,000 km² (Breen et al. 2017).
sections.diet: A generalist predator of soft-bodied animals: siphonophores, jellyfish, salps and ctenophores, plus small fish, fish larvae, squid, crustaceans and other invertebrates, and sometimes eelgrass. It feeds from the surface down to deep water and sometimes near the seafloor. More than 40 species of parasites live on and in sunfish.
sections.social: Solitary, though several may gather at cleaning stations or in food-rich areas.
sections.reproduction: Spawning areas are thought to exist in all major oceans, but mating has rarely been observed. Eggs are released into the water and fertilised externally, and a female can release up to 300 million at once. The tiny, spiky larvae look more like pufferfish than adult sunfish and grow very quickly. Wild lifespan is unknown.
sections.conservation: Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, with a decreasing population. The main threat is bycatch in drift gillnets; plastic bags mistaken for jellyfish are another hazard. Sale of sunfish products is banned in the European Union, but sunfish are eaten as a delicacy in parts of East Asia.
sections.features:
No tail fin; propulsion by tall dorsal and anal fins with identical muscle mass.
Clavus, a rudder-like fringe in place of a tail.
Stiff gelatinous subcutaneous layer and no swim bladder.
Skin up to 7.3 cm thick with denticles and mucus.
Beak of fused teeth plus pharyngeal teeth.
sections.humanInteraction: Harmless to divers and a prized sight on dive trips. Few aquariums keep them because of their demanding care; Monterey Bay Aquarium and several Japanese aquariums have displayed them. Sunfish occasionally leap onto boats.

funFacts: A female sunfish can release up to 300 million eggs at once, more than any other known vertebrate.
Sunfish have no tail fin; they swim by flapping two tall fins like wings.
A sunfish's belly skin can be up to 7.3 cm thick.
After deep dives into cold water, sunfish lie on their side at the surface to warm up in the sun.
Seabirds pick parasites off sunfish basking at the surface.
The heaviest bony fish ever weighed was a 2,744 kg giant sunfish, a different sunfish species, found in the North Atlantic.
A young sunfish at Monterey Bay Aquarium increased its weight more than 14 times before release.

abilities.name: Gelatinous Armor Capsule
abilities.description: a stiff layer of watery collagen and elastin under the skin, topped by skin up to 7.3 cm thick, cushions bites and keeps the fish neutrally buoyant at any depth without a swim bladder.

abilities.name: Twin-Fin Flight
abilities.description: with no tail fin, it beats its tall dorsal and anal fins together to generate lift like wings, cruising steadily and bursting to about 2.4 m/s, and can breach up to about 3 m out of the water.

traits.name: Solar Recharger
traits.description: after feeding in cold water 100–200 m down, it basks on its side at the surface to warm up, often while seabirds and cleaner fish pick parasites from its skin.

traits.name: Egg Champion
traits.description: a female can produce up to 300 million eggs at a time, more than any other known vertebrate.

combat.weapons: The ocean sunfish has almost no offensive capability. Its beak of fused teeth and throat teeth are made for soft or slippery prey such as siphonophores, jellyfish, squid, small fish and crustaceans, and its small mouth cannot fully close. It is not known to attack anything larger than its prey. Its only incidental force is its bulk, which can injure: in 2005 a 1 m sunfish leapt onto a family boat off Wales and slightly injured a child.
weaknesses: No weapon and no attacking behavior.
Slow, with no tail fin; cannot escape fast predators.
Fins can be bitten off; sea lions, orcas and sharks prey on adults.
Struggles in cold water below about 12 °C for long.
Heavy parasite loads.

oceanic-whitetip-shark.name: Oceanic Whitetip Shark
oceanic-whitetip-shark.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 270 cm total length and 150 kg, matching FishBase's common length and the "usually up to 3 m and 150 kg" size given in secondary summaries, rather than the 4 m maximum.
oceanic-whitetip-shark.summary: The oceanic whitetip is a bold, 150 kg open-ocean shark with long paddle-like fins and fully serrated upper teeth. It cruises slowly to save energy, then bursts or breaches from deep water, and its persistence around anything that might be food makes it one of the most dangerous sharks in blue water.
narrative: The oceanic whitetip lives where food is scarce and far between. A mature female of about 2.7 m and 150 kg spends almost all her time in the warm upper 200 m of the open ocean, gliding slowly on huge, rounded pectoral fins. Motion loggers show that this leisurely style is precise economy: she swims at close to the speed that costs the least energy, holds that speed through long yo-yo dives, and can live on a kilogram or so of prey a day.

That economy hides a real predator. When something promising appears, the whitetip investigates without hesitation, and it can switch from a 0.7 m/s cruise to bursts of 4.6 m/s or a vertical rush from 160 m that carries it clear of the surface. Its broad serrated upper teeth tear flesh from tunas, turtles, seabirds and whale carcasses, and it follows pilot whales and fishing boats to find food. At feeding frenzies it pushes aside silky sharks.

In a fight, the whitetip brings persistence and a good cutting bite, but no armor and only moderate mass. Similar-sized sharks are fair contests, while larger sharks and orcas outclass it. Once so common that scientists called it perhaps the most abundant large animal on Earth, it has been reduced by fin demand and bycatch to Critically Endangered status.

sections.habitat: The oceanic whitetip lives in tropical and warm-temperate oceans worldwide, well offshore over deep water. It spends almost all its time in the upper 200 m, preferring water warmer than about 20 °C, but makes short dives into the mesopelagic zone to at least 1,082 m. It is occasionally seen near oceanic islands such as those of the Red Sea and the Bahamas.
sections.diet: An opportunistic top predator. Prey includes oceanic bony fishes such as tunas and dolphinfish, threadfins, stingrays, sea turtles, seabirds, squid, gastropods, crustaceans and the carcasses of whales, and it will eat garbage thrown from ships. Pilot fish, remoras and dolphinfish often travel with it.
sections.social: Mostly solitary, but it gathers with other sharks at concentrated food and takes part in feeding frenzies, where it dominates silky sharks.
sections.reproduction: Gives birth to live young. After a gestation of 10–12 months females give birth, usually every second year, to litters of 1–14 pups (average about 6), with larger females having more young (NOAA Fisheries). Pups are born at about 45–75 cm depending on region, and maturity comes at 4–9 years.
sections.conservation: Listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2019), with estimated declines of more than 80% over three generations and possibly around 98% in some regions. NOAA Fisheries listed it as threatened under the U.S. Endangered Species Act in 2018. It is listed on CITES Appendix II. Main threats are longline, purse-seine and gillnet bycatch and demand for its large fins.
sections.features:
Very long, rounded, paddle-like pectoral fins with white tips.
Broad, fully serrated upper teeth.
Energy-minimising yo-yo swimming at near-optimal speed.
Deep mesopelagic dives to at least 1,082 m.
Electroreceptors used to find distressed or injured prey.
sections.humanInteraction: Rarely met near shore, but divers in places such as the Red Sea and the Bahamas see it regularly. It is bold around people and boats and should be treated with caution; it has been involved in fatal incidents with swimmers and shipwreck survivors. Retention is prohibited in U.S. commercial and recreational fisheries.

funFacts: In 1969 two scientists wrote that it was perhaps the most abundant large animal on Earth; it is now Critically Endangered.
One tagged whitetip breached from 160 m below the surface, rising at about 4 m/s before leaping clear.
A 40-second breach costs about as much energy as 50 minutes of normal swimming.
An adult may need only about 1–1.5 kg of food a day.
Whitetips follow pilot whales to find squid.
Its long white-tipped pectoral fins give it the Latin name longimanus, "long hands".
Tagged sharks have dived to 1,082 m into water as cold as 7.75 °C.

abilities.name: Breach From the Deep
abilities.description: logger data recorded a whitetip accelerating vertically from 160 m at about 4 m/s and clearing the surface, one of several breaches. It can launch a surprise strike from far below an opponent at the surface.

abilities.name: Pilot Whale Shadowing
abilities.description: whitetips trail pilot whales, which find squid by echolocation, and follow tuna boats. By riding along with better finders of food, it turns empty ocean into feeding opportunities.

traits.name: Paddle-Fin Glider
traits.description: its very long, rounded pectoral fins spread wide while cruising, supporting a slow, low-cost search at 0.6–0.7 m/s.

traits.name: Open-Ocean Persistence
traits.description: a bold, hypercompetitive forager that outcompetes silky sharks at feeding frenzies and keeps investigating possible food far from land.

combat.weapons:
The oceanic whitetip's weapon is a classic requiem-shark bite: broad, fully serrated upper teeth that saw through flesh and narrower, pointed lower teeth that pin prey. The Florida Museum describes the teeth as effective for holding and tearing, and they are easily confused with bull shark teeth. It eats oceanic bony fishes, threadfins, stingrays, sea turtles, seabirds, squid, crustaceans and whale carrion (FishBase), and has been seen biting into schools of yellowfin and bigeye tuna. Sucker scars on one individual filmed off Hawaii suggest it may tackle large squid at depth.

What sets it apart is behavior. It is bold, persistent and opportunistic, investigating anything that might be food, and dominates the silky sharks it competes with at feeding events (Animal Diversity Web). No bite-force figure exists, so its offense is rated from tooth form, body mass and demonstrated prey range.
weaknesses: No armor; gills and eyes exposed.
Slow routine cruise; bursts are short.
Mass is moderate next to the largest sharks and toothed whales.
Ectothermic muscles, unlike warm-bodied makos and white sharks.

pallas-s-cat.name: Pallas's Cat
pallas-s-cat.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 4.0 kg, near the top of the usual 2.5–4.5 kg range (Wikipedia) and inside ADW's 2.5–5.0 kg range without using the heaviest records.
pallas-s-cat.summary: A stocky, heavily furred wild cat of Central Asia's cold, rocky steppes, Pallas's cat ambushes pikas and voles from behind rocks and hides rather than runs. Its dense coat and camouflage suit it to harsh winters, but at 4 kg with short legs it is slow and weak in absolute combat terms.
narrative: Pallas's cat looks larger than it is. The dense grey coat, broad flat face and low-set ears give it a round, fluffy shape, but underneath is a 4 kg cat about the size of a house cat, with short legs built for creeping between rocks rather than sprinting. It hunts pikas and voles by waiting at burrow exits, stalking, or flushing prey from cover, and it scoops rodents out of shallow tunnels with its paws.

Its strategy is concealment. It spends most of its time in rocky outcrops and ravines, chooses dens carefully and, when a fox, dog or eagle appears, it slips into a crevice or flattens and freezes against the rocks. Animal Diversity Web notes that it is probably a poor runner, which is why open steppe is so dangerous for it. Winter is the hardest season, and wild adults in one Mongolian study averaged only about 27 months of life.

On the absolute scale, Pallas's cat is a small predator with modest weapons. Its dense fur gives it a little more protection than a house cat and its cold tolerance is remarkable, but it lacks the speed and agility of most small cats. It rates below the house cat in Attack and far below the lynx and snow leopard that share some of its mountains.

sections.habitat: Rocky montane grassland, shrubland, scree slopes and ravines across Central Asia, from the Caucasus, Iran and Afghanistan through Kazakhstan, Mongolia, southern Siberia and western China to the Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau. It needs areas where continuous snow cover stays below about 15–20 cm, and shelters in rock crevices, old marmot burrows and sometimes juniper cavities.
sections.diet: A specialist predator of small mammals, above all pikas, plus voles, gerbils, ground squirrels, young marmots, small birds and insects (Wikipedia; Animals, 2025). In Mongolia's Sükhbaatar Province, Brandt's voles dominated its diet during a vole irruption in 2017–2020. It competes with red and corsac foxes and raptors for the same prey.
sections.social: Solitary. Home ranges in central Mongolia were 7.4–125.2 km² for 16 females and 20.9–207.0 km² for nine males, shrinking in winter. Males overlap several females and sometimes other males.
sections.reproduction: Litters of two to six kittens are born from late April to late May. Kittens open their eyes at about two weeks, weigh 500–600 g at two months, start hunting at about five months and reach adult size at six to seven months (Wikipedia). In European zoos, first-year mortality from all causes was 71.59% in 2006–2016, with toxoplasmosis the leading infectious cause (Journal of Zoo and Wildlife Medicine, 2020).
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List since 2020, reflecting its wide range. Some populations are threatened by poaching, poisoning of pikas and voles in rodent-control campaigns, herding dogs, habitat fragmentation from mining and roads, and continuing trade in skins and body parts. It was once hunted for more than 10,000 skins a year. It is listed as Near Threatened on the Mongolian Red List.
sections.features:
Extremely dense, long fur with longer fur on the underparts.
Low-set, rounded ears for peering over rocks.
Round pupils.
Short, stocky legs and a flat, broad face.
Heavy use of rock crevices and marmot burrows.
sections.humanInteraction: Harmless to people. Threats come from poisoning of its prey, trapping, dogs and the fur and medicine trade. It is kept in about 60 zoos in coordinated breeding programmes, where kitten survival has been a long-standing problem.

funFacts: Its fur can have up to 9,000 hairs per square centimetre.
When excited or scared it yelps like a small dog rather than meowing.
Its pupils shrink to round dots, not slits, in bright light.
It has been recorded at 5,073 m in the Himalaya and up to about 5,600 m on the Tibetan Plateau.
One Mongolian study found its cats using 101 different dens.
In European zoos, more than 70% of kittens died in their first year during 2006–2016, many from toxoplasmosis.
Its short, low-set ears let it peek over a rock while showing almost none of its head.

abilities.name: Rock-Peer Ambush
abilities.description: its low-set rounded ears let it look over a rock or ridge while exposing only a sliver of its head, so it can watch pika colonies and burrow exits unseen before pouncing. The same posture helps it avoid being spotted by foxes and eagles.

abilities.name: Crevice Vanish
abilities.description: when threatened it bolts into a rock crevice or den, or flattens and freezes beside rocks, relying on its grey coat for camouflage instead of speed. In rocky terrain this makes it hard to catch; in open ground it is exposed.

traits.name: Steppe Winter Coat
traits.description: up to 9,000 hairs per cm², with underfur about 40 mm and guard hairs up to 69 mm long, and belly fur about twice as long as the fur on its back, suited to winters on the steppe and the Tibetan Plateau.

traits.name: Round-Pupil Cat
traits.description: unlike most small cats with slit pupils, its pupils close to small round discs in bright light, a feature it shares with the cougar, jaguarundi and cheetah.

combat.weapons: Pallas's cat is a specialist ambush hunter of pikas, voles, gerbils and ground squirrels. It stalks or waits at burrow exits and also hooks rodents out of shallow burrows with its paws (Wikipedia; National Zoo). ADW describes three hunting modes: stalking, flushing and ambushing. Its weapons are ordinary small-cat claws and bite on a 4 kg frame. In Sanjiangyuan, China, its diet is dominated by plateau pikas and small rodents (Animals, 2025). It is effective against animals of a few hundred grams and weak in absolute terms against anything larger.
weaknesses: Poor runner; cannot outrun foxes, wolves, dogs or raptors in the open.
Small mass; no armor beyond thick fur.
Deep snow restricts it.
Unusually vulnerable to disease in captivity, especially toxoplasmosis in kittens.

philippine-eagle.name: Philippine Eagle
philippine-eagle.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 6.0 kg, 100.0 cm total length and roughly 2 m wingspan. The female is the heavier and longer sex and therefore the stronger fighting form.
philippine-eagle.summary: The Philippine Eagle is a critically endangered forest giant of the Philippines: about 6 kg in the canonical female, roughly a metre long, with a 2 m wingspan and a massive arched bill. It still-hunts flying lemurs, civets and monkeys from canopy perches, and pairs sometimes attack monkey troops together. Its forest ambush is formidable, but low absolute mass and no armor leave it far below large mammals in power and defense.
narrative: The Philippine Eagle is built for one of the hardest hunting problems in the tropics: finding and seizing gliding and climbing mammals in tall, dense dipterocarp forest. It sits almost motionless near the canopy for long periods, then works down through the layers of the forest from perch to perch. When a flying lemur, civet or macaque is found, the feet make the kill and the massive, deep bill finishes the job.

That toolkit is excellent on its own ground. Reported pair hunting on monkey troops, one eagle drawing attention while the other strikes from behind, adds coordination that most raptors lack. Wide forest home ranges, measured by satellite telemetry at a median of around 68 km², show a predator that covers a lot of ground patiently, not in long chases.

On the absolute roster, though, a 6 kg eagle stays a 6 kg eagle. It cannot match the grappling strength, mass or durability of medium and large mammals, and once grounded or pinned it has little protection. Its best matchups are ones where it chooses the moment and angle of contact in forest; open ground, armor, large body size and heavy grappling reverse the result.

sections.habitat: The Philippine Eagle lives only in the Philippines, on Luzon, Samar, Leyte and Mindanao. It lives mainly in remnant primary dipterocarp forest but also uses second-growth and gallery forest. A 2023 habitat model identified about 2.86 million hectares of suitable forest across its range, with Mindanao holding the largest share of breeding pairs.
sections.diet: The eagle is the top avian predator of Philippine forests. On Mindanao the Philippine flying lemur is the main prey, supplemented by palm civets, macaques, flying and tree squirrels, fruit bats, rats, snakes, monitor lizards and birds including hornbills and owls. On Luzon, where flying lemurs are absent, macaques and giant cloud rats are reported as principal prey. As a top predator with large space needs it is treated as an umbrella species for Philippine forest conservation.
sections.social: Adults live as monogamous territorial pairs, reportedly mating for life unless a partner dies. Telemetry shows a median home range around 68 km² per adult. Hunting is usually solitary, with reported cooperative hunting by pairs on monkey troops.
sections.reproduction: A full breeding cycle lasts about two years, and both parents share care of the young for roughly 20 months. A Mindanao study of five pairs (1999–2007) found average breeding success of about 60% and productivity of about 0.3 young per pair per year. During courtship, one bird presents its talons and the other rolls over in mid-air to present its own. This slow reproduction makes every lost adult significant for the population.
sections.conservation: The species is Critically Endangered. A 2023 population estimate based on habitat modelling and telemetry-measured territory size gives about 392 breeding pairs (about 784 mature individuals), higher than earlier estimates of 340 pairs (2018) and 88–221 pairs (1989). The main threats are deforestation and loss of nesting sites, accidental capture in traps set for wild pigs, and shooting, including retaliatory killing after attacks on domestic animals. The Philippine Eagle Foundation runs captive breeding, rescue, rehabilitation and release work.
sections.features:
Very deep, arched bill and powerful talons.
Long, shaggy crest of head and nape feathers.
Among the longest eagles, with a very large wing surface for its mass.
Still-hunting and perch-hunting methods suited to dense forest.
Pair-based territorial life with a two-year breeding cycle.
sections.humanInteraction: It is the national bird of the Philippines and a flagship species for forest conservation. Conflict arises when eagles take poultry or other domestic animals, and birds are still lost to shooting and to snares set for other animals. Conservation breeding, rescue and release by the Philippine Eagle Foundation are among the main responses.

funFacts: Although known as the "monkey-eating eagle", its main prey in Mindanao nest studies is the Philippine flying lemur, at 54.2% of identified prey items.
It is the national bird of the Philippines.
The Peregrine Fund calls it the largest eagle alive by length and wing surface area.
Satellite-tracked adults on Mindanao had a median home range of about 68 km².
Parents share care of a single brood for about 20 months, so pairs breed only about every two years.
Pairs have been reported hunting monkeys as a team, one bird distracting while the other strikes.
A captive eagle at the Philippine Eagle Center in Davao is reported to have lived 46 years.

abilities.name: Tag-Team Troop Ambush
abilities.description: pairs are reported to hunt monkey troops together, one eagle drawing attention from a nearby perch while the partner strikes from behind. In a matchup this adds a distraction-and-flank pattern that single raptors lack.

abilities.name: Canopy Still-Hunt
abilities.description: the eagle sits motionless near the canopy, then works down through the tree layers by gliding from perch to perch before a sudden talon strike. This keeps the first-contact advantage with the eagle.

traits.name: Colugo Specialist
traits.description: on Mindanao the Philippine flying lemur makes up more than half of identified prey in nest studies, a narrow prey specialization unusual among large eagles.

traits.name: Great Arched Bill
traits.description: a very deep, strongly curved bill, among the most massive of any eagle, used to tear apart prey the feet have secured.

combat.weapons:
The feet and talons do the killing, and the deep, arched bill tears apart prey once it is secured. Prey records show the practical reach of this weapon system: Philippine flying lemurs (colugos), Asian palm civets, macaques, flying squirrels, fruit bats, rats, hornbills and owls, snakes and monitor lizards. A five-pair Mindanao study (1999–2007) found flying lemurs made up 54.2% of identifiable prey, with at least 14 prey taxa recorded and arboreal mammals the most important prey group. Some summaries put flying lemurs as high as 90% of the diet in parts of Mindanao.

These prey show a raptor able to kill medium arboreal mammals in the canopy, but on the absolute roster a 6 kg eagle still has modest total force. Its prey-killing power is recorded mostly in Weaponry and Attack, not Raw Power.
weaknesses: Low absolute body mass compared with medium and large mammals.
No armor; hollow-boned avian body vulnerable to crushing or grappling.
Very dependent on intact forest structure.
Loses most of its advantage if grounded or forced into close contact with a larger terrestrial animal.

portuguese-man-o-war.name: Portuguese Man o' War
portuguese-man-o-war.specimen: a mature, healthy colony with a float about 20 cm long and fishing tentacles extended to about 10 m, the NOAA average. Sex is not used as a selector because it does not change colony size or weapon reach in any documented way.
portuguese-man-o-war.summary: The Portuguese man o' war is not a jellyfish but a floating colony of specialised zooids that sails on the wind under a gas-filled float. Its stinging tentacles average about 10 m and can reach 30 m, making contact extremely painful and occasionally dangerous. It cannot swim, see or chase, so it wins only when an opponent blunders into its curtain.
narrative: The Portuguese man o' war is one of the ocean's strangest fighters. What looks like a single jellyfish is a colony of genetically identical zooids, each with a job: one forms the float, some carry stinging tentacles, others digest prey or reproduce. Together they behave as one organism, drifting on the sea surface under a translucent blue or violet sail.

Its weapon is reach. Fishing tentacles average about 10 m and can trail as far as 30 m, and each carries huge numbers of nematocysts, tiny capsules that fire venom on contact. Small fish that swim into the curtain are paralysed and hauled up to the feeding polyps. For larger animals, including people, a brush with the tentacles means severe burning pain and welts; deaths have been recorded but are rare. On the absolute battle scale, that makes it a formidable passive trap rather than a killer of large animals.

Everything else is a weakness. It cannot swim, steer, see or think, and its body is soft. Its only escape trick is to deflate the float and sink for a while. Loggerhead turtles eat it through thick skin, ocean sunfish take it, blanket octopuses tear off its tentacles to use as weapons, and a small blue sea slug even recycles its stinging cells. The man o' war scores very high in Special and Weaponry, but in Agility and Intelligence it sits at the bottom of the roster.

sections.habitat: It lives at the surface of the open ocean, mainly in the Atlantic Ocean and the Indian Ocean in warm and temperate waters, and is regularly blown onto coasts. It has also appeared in the Mediterranean, where scientists have asked whether it is an occasional visitor or an established presence. Strandings are strongly driven by wind direction and strength.
sections.diet: It feeds mainly on small fish and fish larvae, plus other small drifting animals caught by the tentacles. It is itself eaten by loggerhead sea turtles, ocean sunfish, the blue sea slug Glaucus atlanticus (which stores the unfired stinging cells in its own body for defense) and blanket octopuses (which tear off tentacles and carry them as weapons). The man-of-war fish Nomeus gronovii is partly resistant to the stings and lives among the tentacles.
sections.social: Not social in the usual sense. Each colony is one organism made of many zooids. Large numbers can drift together because wind gathers them, sometimes 1,000 or more according to NOAA.
sections.reproduction: Colonies develop from a single fertilised egg; new zooids are budded off during growth, as described in detail in the Nature Scientific Reports study of its morphology and development. Specialised reproductive zooids release gametes into the water.
sections.conservation: Not Evaluated: no IUCN Red List assessment was located in this pass. The species is widespread and abundant, with frequent mass strandings.
sections.features:
Gas-filled float (pneumatophore) up to about 30 cm long that works as a sail.
Gas gland that produces carbon monoxide inside the float.
Fishing tentacles averaging 10 m, up to 30 m.
Nematocyst venom with physalitoxin as its main haemolytic toxin.
Left-handed and right-handed mirror-image forms.
Ability to deflate the float and sink briefly.
sections.humanInteraction: Stings are a common beach hazard in warm Atlantic waters and cause severe burning pain and red welts; systemic symptoms occur in some cases, and rare deaths have been reported. Stranded colonies can still sting. Medical sources note that dilute acetic acid (vinegar), proteolytic meat tenderiser or baking soda have been used to inactivate the venom, and outbreaks of stings have been documented on the coasts of Brazil and France.

funFacts: It is not one animal in the usual sense but a colony of genetically identical zooids working as one.
Its fishing tentacles average about 10 m and can reach 30 m.
It has no engine: the float is a sail, and the tentacles act as a drag anchor.
Colonies come in left-handed and right-handed forms that drift to opposite sides of the wind.
The float gas can contain up to about 13% carbon monoxide, made by the animal itself.
The blue sea slug Glaucus atlanticus eats it and reuses its unfired stinging cells for its own defense.
Blanket octopuses rip off its tentacles and wield them as weapons.

abilities.name: Ten-Meter Sting Curtain
abilities.description: fishing tentacles averaging 10 m (up to 30 m) carry vast numbers of nematocysts that fire venom on contact, then contract to haul prey up to the feeding polyps. Any opponent that swims into, bites or grabs the colony takes stings along a long stretch of skin.

abilities.name: Deflate and Dive
abilities.description: the gas-filled float can be deflated so the colony sinks briefly below the surface, a simple escape from attacks at the surface.

traits.name: Colony, Not a Jellyfish
traits.description: each man o' war is a siphonophore colony of genetically identical zooids with separate jobs (float, stinging tentacles, feeding polyps, reproductive units) that function together as one organism.

traits.name: Living Sailboat
traits.description: the float acts as a sail and the tentacles as a drag anchor, so the colony travels by wind alone; left-handed and right-handed forms drift to opposite sides of the wind, and the float gas can contain up to about 13% carbon monoxide produced by a gas gland.

combat.weapons: The only weapon is the tentacle curtain. Fishing tentacles averaging 10 m hang below the float and are loaded with nematocysts that fire on contact. After a strike, the tentacles contract and lift prey up to the gastrozooids, which digest it. There is no secondary weapon: no jaws, no beak, no spines.
weaknesses: No mobility of its own; it cannot pursue or escape except by sinking briefly.
Soft body with no armour.
Venom is rarely lethal to large animals.
Several predators ignore or exploit the stings: loggerhead turtles (skin too thick for the stings), ocean sunfish, the blue sea slug Glaucus atlanticus and blanket octopuses.
Useless on land; stranded colonies can still sting but cannot act.

pygmy-hippopotamus.name: Pygmy Hippopotamus
pygmy-hippopotamus.specimen: healthy adult of about 250 kg, 90 cm at the shoulder and 165 cm head-body length. This sits in the upper half of the 160–275 kg range without using an overweight zoo animal as the baseline.
pygmy-hippopotamus.summary: The pygmy hippopotamus is a shy, nocturnal forest hippo from West Africa, about 250 kg of dense body with thick skin and a wide mouth of ever-growing tusks. It prefers to vanish into streams rather than fight, but can bite hard when cornered, making it a sturdy mid-weight defender rather than a heavy hitter.
narrative: The pygmy hippo is what a hippo looks like when it lives under a rainforest canopy. It stands under a metre tall, weighs about a quarter of a tonne, and is shaped like a smooth, glossy barrel on short legs. By day it rests in streams or bank-side hollows; by night it walks the same worn trails through the swamp forest, browsing ferns, shoots and fallen fruit and marking the path with tail-flung dung.

Its fighting equipment is the hippo family's: a gape that opens very wide and canines that never stop growing, used for defense and contests rather than chewing. Zoo records show that adults can inflict lethal bites on small animals, and people have been attacked when they pressed too close. Yet the species' usual answer to danger is to disappear. It seals its ears and nostrils and sinks into the nearest stream, where a leopard cannot follow.

On the ABS scale that makes the pygmy hippo a compact defender with a real but modest bite. It sits close to other 250–300 kg forest herbivores such as the okapi and bongo in size and power, trades their speed for thicker skin and a biting weapon, and remains far below the common hippopotamus in every physical category. Heat and dry ground are its limits; water is its refuge.

sections.habitat: Lowland primary and secondary forest near rivers, streams and palm swamps in West Africa. The largest populations are in Liberia, with smaller ones in Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire, mostly near the Liberian border. The Niger Delta form has not been reliably recorded for decades. Its range does not overlap with the common hippopotamus.
sections.diet: A selective herbivore of the forest floor: herbs, ferns, broad-leaved plants, herbaceous shoots, forbs, sedges and fallen fruit, rarely grass or aquatic plants. It forages for about six hours a night along game trails and returns to water by day.
sections.social: Solitary or in pairs or mother-calf groups. Individuals tend to ignore each other when they meet rather than fight. Male ranges (about 1.85 km²) overlap those of several females (0.4–0.6 km²).
sections.reproduction: Sexual maturity at three to five years. Gestation is 190–210 days and usually produces a single calf of 4.5–6.2 kg, born on land or in water. Calves hide in water while the mother forages and are weaned at six to eight months. Almost all breeding data come from zoos, where the international studbook is kept by Basel Zoo.
sections.conservation: Endangered on the IUCN Red List and listed on CITES Appendix II. The main threat is loss and fragmentation of forest through logging, settlement and farming, with bushmeat hunting in Liberia as a further pressure. Camera traps in Sapo National Park, Liberia, produced the first photographs confirming the species survived the Liberian civil wars. The captive population breeds well and more than doubled between 1970 and 1991.
sections.features:
Ever-growing canines and a wide, fighting gape.
Muscular valves that close the ears and nostrils underwater.
Thick dermis coated with a pinkish, sun-screening skin secretion.
Tail-waving dung spreading to mark forest trails.
Mates and gives birth on land or in water.
sections.humanInteraction: Usually shy and seldom seen, but has attacked people on several occasions, mostly when provoked; no human deaths are recorded. It is hunted illegally for meat in Liberia. A zoo-born pygmy hippo, Moo Deng of Khao Kheow Open Zoo in Thailand, became a worldwide internet celebrity in 2024.

funFacts: Only two hippo species are alive today, and the pygmy hippo weighs less than a quarter as much as the common hippo.
Its ears and nostrils have muscular valves that seal when it dives.
Its skin secretes a pinkish fluid nicknamed "blood sweat", which is neither blood nor true sweat.
Pygmy hippos spread their dung by vigorously waving their tails, marking the trails they use.
Calves can swim almost immediately after birth.
The species was unknown outside West Africa until the 19th century.
Camera traps in Liberia's Sapo National Park provided the first proof that pygmy hippos survived the country's civil wars.

abilities.name: Hippo Gape Bite
abilities.description: a wide-opening mouth armed with ever-growing canines and forward incisors, used for defense and fighting rather than feeding; dangerous to small opponents at close range.

abilities.name: Streambed Vanish
abilities.description: closes its ears and nostrils with muscular valves and slips underwater or into bank-side resting spots, breaking contact with land predators.

traits.name: Forest Hippo
traits.description: one of only two living hippo species, and the one built for rainforest trails and swamp streams instead of open rivers and grassland.

traits.name: Blood-Sweat Skin
traits.description: thick-dermis skin coated with a pinkish secretion that helps protect it from sun, but which dries and cracks quickly without water.

combat.weapons: The pygmy hippo's weapons are its mouth: a wide gape, ever-growing canines and forward incisors that hippos use for defense and fighting rather than feeding. Behind them sits a dense, barrel-shaped 250 kg body that can shove and bowl over a smaller animal. It is a scaled-down version of the common hippo's system at roughly one-seventh of the mass, with none of the common hippo's reputation for territorial violence. Its offense is defensive in character: a cornered or startled animal bites and pushes.
weaknesses: Low absolute mass compared with the roster's large herbivores.
Short legs and rotund build limit speed and turning.
Skin dries and cracks quickly away from water.
Generally shy; tends to hide rather than fight.
Bite is the only real weapon.
