rabbit.name: Rabbit
rabbit.specimen: healthy adult buck of about 2.0 kg, a wild-type or medium pet rabbit, rather than a 1 kg dwarf breed or a 5–8 kg giant breed.
rabbit.summary: The rabbit is a 2 kg burrowing grazer built to spot danger early and sprint to cover, with nearly 360° vision, explosive hind legs and a social warren life. It kicks and bites hard enough to fight other rabbits, but its light, fragile skeleton and small size make it one of the roster's easy prey animals.
narrative: The European rabbit is a clear answer to a simple question: how does a small grazer survive in a world full of predators? Its answer is vigilance and speed. Eyes set high on the sides of the head give almost all-round vision, the ears catch the first sound of danger, and a thump of the hind feet warns the rest of the warren. When a threat comes close, the rabbit bursts away on long, powerful hind legs, jinking toward a burrow it rarely strays far from.

That escape-first body has a cost. The skeleton is unusually light and fragile, and a struggling rabbit can even break its own back with its kicks. Its weapons, incisors, claws and hind-foot rakes, are used in real fights between bucks and between does over nest sites, but they are no match for a fox, cat, lynx or eagle. On the absolute ABS scale the rabbit therefore scores low in Attack and very low in Defense, while its agility and senses are strong.

Beyond the battlefield, the rabbit is one of the most influential mammals on Earth. In Iberia it is a keystone species that feeds lynxes and eagles and engineers the landscape; elsewhere it has become one of history's most destructive invaders; and as the only domesticated rabbit it has been bred into dozens of breeds from tiny dwarfs to giants.

sections.habitat: Native to the Iberian Peninsula and southwestern France, the European rabbit prefers short grassland next to secure refuge such as burrows, boulders, hedgerows, scrub and woodland edges; in large conifer plantations it keeps to the margins and firebreaks. It has been introduced across Europe, Australia, New Zealand, Chile, many islands and parts of Africa, and domestic rabbits live worldwide.
sections.diet: Herbivorous: grasses (especially fescues), leaves and shoots, plus crops such as cereals and sugar beet, bark and berries. Grazing creates a gradient of short vegetation around warrens. In Iberia the rabbit is a keystone species, altering plant communities, fertilizing soil with latrines, providing burrows for other animals and feeding predators including the Iberian lynx and Spanish imperial eagle.
sections.social: Social groups of one to five bucks and one to eight does share a warren, with parallel dominance hierarchies. Dominant bucks sire most young, and dominant does get the best nest sites. Home ranges are small, about 4 ha.
sections.reproduction: Gestation is about 30 days; a doe may produce four or five litters a year of three to seven blind, nearly naked kittens, raised in a separate nest burrow ("stop") lined with belly fur and sealed between once-nightly nursings. Does can breed at three months. Wild mortality is very high, especially in the first year.
sections.conservation: The European rabbit is listed as Near Threatened in its native range (IUCN assessment cited by Wikipedia, 2025), after steep Iberian declines driven by myxomatosis, rabbit haemorrhagic disease and habitat change. Paradoxically it is a serious invasive pest where introduced, especially in Australia.
sections.features:
Nearly 360° field of vision.
Long, powerful hind limbs and a hopping gait.
Light skeleton, about 8% of body mass.
Two pairs of upper incisors, including small peg teeth.
Foot-thumping and white tail-flag warning signals.
sections.humanInteraction: Rabbits have been hunted since the Paleolithic and kept in enclosures since Roman times; the Romans hunted them with ferrets. Domestic rabbits are raised for meat, fur and wool and are popular pets. Where introduced, feral rabbits have caused enormous agricultural and ecological damage and have proved hard to control by physical and biological means, as in Australia.

funFacts: A rabbit's skeleton makes up only about 8% of its body weight, compared with about 13% in a cat.
Rabbits have a second, tiny pair of upper incisors hidden behind the front pair.
Warrens include emergency exits dug from the inside that drop straight down about a metre.
Genetic work shows Australia's rabbit invasion began with one 1859 release by Thomas Austin.
One domestic strain, the sauteur d'Alfort, cannot hop because of a single gene mutation and often walks on its front legs.
Rabbits flash the white underside of the tail as they flee, warning other rabbits and possibly telling the predator it has been seen.

abilities.name: Burst-to-Burrow Escape
abilities.description: long, powerful hind legs and a hopping gait give explosive acceleration and sharp turns over the short distance to cover; predators catch relatively few adults in the open. In a matchup the rabbit wins by not being there.

abilities.name: Hind-Leg Kick
abilities.description: a captured or cornered rabbit kicks out with hind limbs strong enough that veterinarians warn of serious injury, and bucks rake rivals with the hind feet. It can hurt small attackers but not deter a large one.

traits.name: Warren Engineer
traits.description: rabbits dig communal warrens with emergency exits dropping 1–1.2 m, and in Iberia their grazing, latrines and burrows shape the whole ecosystem, earning the region the label "the rabbit's ecosystem".

traits.name: World Traveler
traits.description: the only domesticated rabbit species, with breeds from under 1 kg to over 5 kg, it has been introduced to at least 800 islands and every continent except Antarctica; Australia's rabbit plague grew from a single 1859 release.

combat.weapons: The rabbit's weapons are its incisors, claws and hind-leg kicks. Rival bucks fight fiercely in the breeding season, biting and raking with the hind feet, and dominant does fight over the best nest sites, sometimes fatally. A captured rabbit kicks hard with its hind legs. None of this makes it dangerous to a predator: the rabbit is a prey animal whose weapons matter only against other rabbits and very small animals.
weaknesses: Fragile, light skeleton and very low absolute durability.
Weapons that barely matter outside rabbit-on-rabbit fights.
Poor endurance if cut off from cover.
Extremely vulnerable to diseases such as myxomatosis and rabbit haemorrhagic disease.

red-deer.name: Red Deer
red-deer.specimen: healthy mature stag in hard antler of about 180 kg, 120 cm at the shoulder and 210 cm head-body length. This represents a well-fed continental European stag; it is above typical Scottish hill and Iberian stags and well below the heaviest Carpathian and Caspian animals.
red-deer.summary: The red deer is Europe's classic antlered stag, a fast, agile 180 kg forest and mountain deer whose crowned antlers can reach over a metre. Stags size each other up by roaring before they lock antlers, and although their autumn fights are fierce, the lack of armor and a lighter frame keep them below elk and moose in raw fighting power.
narrative: A mature red deer stag in autumn is one of Europe's great wildlife sights: a russet-brown body of around 180 kg, a shaggy neck mane, and a spread of branching antlers that may measure more than a metre and end in a crown of tines. He roars across the glen at dawn and dusk, and the pitch of that roar tells other stags how big he is. When two evenly matched stags meet, they walk side by side to size each other up before crashing antlers together in a pushing, twisting struggle.

The rut is exhausting. Harem-holders stop eating, lose up to a fifth of their weight and pick up wounds; about one stag in five shows signs of injury. For the rest of the year red deer live in single-sex groups, keeping sentinels on watch and relying on speed and agility to escape wolves, the predator that kills the most calves and weakened adults in central and eastern Europe.

On the ABS scale the red deer is a mid-weight, mobile fighter. It sits between the reindeer and the North American elk in size and Attack, with antlers that make it dangerous in close quarters but no armor to take heavy blows. Its best assets are agility, senses and the ritualized assessment that lets stags avoid fights they would lose.

sections.habitat: Most of Europe, the Caucasus, Anatolia, Iran, parts of western Asia and the Atlas Mountains of North Africa, in woodland, forest edges, moorland and mountains. Introduced to Australia, New Zealand, Argentina, Chile and other countries; in some of these it is treated as a pest, and it is listed among the world's 100 worst invasive species.
sections.diet: Grazes grasses and dwarf shrubs such as heather and bilberry and takes woody browse such as tree shoots when other food is short in winter. Red deer are the main prey of wolves across much of central and eastern Europe and a key large herbivore in forest and moorland systems.
sections.social: Single-sex groups for most of the year; hind herds of up to 50 after the rut, with calves kept close by constant calls. Stags form bachelor groups once antlers are cast. In the rut, mature stags hold harems.
sections.reproduction: Hinds mature at about two years. Gestation is 240–262 days, producing one calf of about 15 kg that joins the herd after two weeks and is weaned at about two months. Calves stay with their mothers for almost a year. Stags reach peak breeding success at about eight years.
sections.conservation: Least Concern and widespread. Populations have grown in much of Europe: France's rose from about 30,000 in 1970 to about 160,000 in 2014, while North African populations have continued to decline. Reintroductions have restored red deer in parts of Portugal and the United Kingdom.
sections.features:
Branched antlers, typically 71 cm and 1 kg, up to about 115 cm and 5 kg.
Antler growth up to 2.5 cm per day.
Autumn neck mane in stags of many populations.
Deep rutting roar that signals body size.
Sharp front hooves used for forward kicks by both sexes.
sections.humanInteraction: The most prestigious quarry of medieval hunting and still a major game species; farmed for venison and antler velvet in New Zealand, China and Russia. It is the largest wild land mammal in Ireland and the United Kingdom. Red deer appear in European cave art up to about 40,000 years old.

funFacts: A red deer stag's antlers can grow about 2.5 cm in a single day.
The Barbary stag makes the red deer the only deer native to Africa.
Stags that hold harems barely eat during the rut and can lose a fifth of their body weight.
Deeper roars signal bigger stags, and rivals use them to decide whether to fight.
Red deer are the largest wild land mammals in Britain and Ireland.
Around one-fifth of rutting stags show signs of injury from fights.
France's red deer population grew more than five-fold between 1970 and 2014.

abilities.name: Roar and Parallel Walk
abilities.description: stags size up rivals first by roaring, where deeper roars mean a bigger body, then by walking side by side; many contests end without contact.

abilities.name: Crowned Antler Clash
abilities.description: branched antlers up to about 115 cm, often crowned with a cup of tines, lock with a rival's for pushing and twisting fights backed by a maned neck.

traits.name: Africa's Only Deer
traits.description: through the Barbary stag of the Atlas Mountains, the red deer is the only deer species living wild in Africa.

traits.name: Fast-Growing Bone
traits.description: antlers regrow every year and can lengthen by about 2.5 cm a day while in velvet.

combat.weapons: A stag's weapons are branched antlers backed by a heavy, maned neck. Rut fights are pushing and twisting contests with locked antlers until the weaker animal breaks away, and the tines can wound: around one-fifth of rutting males show signs of injury. Against predators, antlers and hard forward kicks with the front hooves are used by both sexes; large hinds make a stand and strike with their forelegs. The antlers are carried for more than half the year, from late summer to early spring, so stags are unarmed for part of the year.
weaknesses: No armor; the whole body is soft target apart from the skull and antlers.
Antlers are absent from spring to late summer.
Rut exhaustion and weight loss leave stags weaker afterward.
Far lighter than the roster's large bovids and moose.

red-eared-slider.name: Red-eared Slider
red-eared-slider.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 1.5 kg with a 23.0 cm straight carapace length, representing a well-grown adult rather than a record animal.
red-eared-slider.summary: The red-eared slider is a small freshwater turtle from the south-central United States, now the world's most traded reptile and a worldwide invader. A 1.5 kg adult female has only a small beak, but it can hide inside a shell that survives predator bites and can live for weeks without oxygen at the bottom of a winter pond. It is tough to kill and harmless to fight.
narrative: On a sunny log in a Louisiana pond, a row of red-eared sliders sits stretched out in the sun, some stacked on top of others. At the first sign of danger they slide into the water and vanish. That combination of basking and quick retreat is the slider's everyday life: warm up, feed on plants and small animals, and disappear under water when threatened.

As a fighter it has little to offer. The beak crops plants and catches crayfish and tadpoles, and the only fights are between males chasing and biting each other in the breeding season. Its defense is its shell, which it can close up completely, and which has been found on live sliders bearing bite marks and embedded teeth from predators, including alligators. Its bright yellow and red markings also seem to warn off some predators: largemouth bass, which hunt by sight, avoid sliders once they hatch.

Its most remarkable feature is invisible. In winter, a slider on the pond bottom can go for weeks without oxygen, slowing its heart by about 80% and using minerals from its shell to neutralise the acid that builds up in its body. In ABS terms that earns it a solid Stamina and a moderate Special, alongside a near-zero Attack, moderate Defense and modest Agility. The same toughness has made it one of the world's worst invasive species, found on every continent except Antarctica.

sections.habitat: The red-eared slider is native to the Mississippi River valley and Gulf of Mexico drainages of the south-central United States, living in ponds, lakes, swamps, creeks and slow rivers with warm, still water, abundant aquatic plants and places to climb out and bask. It can also live in brackish water. Through the pet trade it now has feral populations in Europe, Asia, Australia, Africa, the Caribbean, Bermuda and elsewhere.
sections.diet: Juveniles are mostly carnivorous, eating insects, crayfish, tadpoles, fish, snails and carrion. Adults shift to an omnivorous diet dominated by aquatic plants and algae but still take invertebrates. In southern Illinois, adult stomachs held more than 40% plant material, with females eating more molluscs than males. Predators of adults and young include alligators, snakes, gar, catfish, wading birds, crows, opossums, raccoons, mink, otters, skunks, coyotes and foxes.
sections.social: Sliders bask in groups and often stack on top of each other on the best spots, but they do not form social groups. Males court females underwater by vibrating their long front claws near the female's face.
sections.reproduction: Females lay 2–30 eggs per clutch and up to five clutches a year, digging nests on land with their hind legs. Incubation takes about 59–112 days, and some late hatchlings overwinter in the nest. Sex depends on incubation temperature: cooler nests (about 22–27 °C) produce males and warmer nests produce females. Males mature at 2–5 years and females at 5–8 years.
sections.conservation: The red-eared slider is common in its native range, and its main conservation significance is as an invader. Wikipedia, citing the IUCN Invasive Species Specialist Group (Lowe et al. 2000), lists it among the world's worst invasive alien species, and it competes with native turtles for food, nesting and basking sites and spreads parasites. The European Union has banned its import, Japan banned import and release in 2023, and Queensland has spent close to AU$1 million on eradication.
sections.features:
Red stripe behind each eye and no external ear.
Long front claws in males for courtship.
Weeks-long survival without oxygen, with shell buffering of lactic acid.
Bright markings that some predatory fish avoid.
Temperature-dependent sex determination.
Head, limbs and tail retract into the shell.
sections.humanInteraction: It is the world's most commonly traded reptile. A 1975 U.S. Food and Drug Administration rule bans the sale of turtles with shells under 10 cm because of Salmonella infections, especially in children. Many pets are later released, which is how the species spread worldwide; in Britain, the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles craze that followed the first live-action film led to a surge in pet sliders and later releases.

funFacts: It can survive for weeks without oxygen at the bottom of a frozen-over pond.
Its shell helps neutralise the lactic acid that builds up while it goes without oxygen.
Largemouth bass avoid eating sliders, apparently because of their bright warning colours.
Bite marks and embedded teeth have been found in the shells of live sliders that escaped predators, including alligators.
The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles were revealed in the comics to be red-eared sliders.
Cooler nests hatch males and warmer nests hatch females.

abilities.name: Oxygen-Free Endurance
abilities.description: at the bottom of a winter pond it can survive without oxygen for weeks, dropping heart rate and cardiac output by about 80% and buffering lactic acid with minerals from its shell. Its heart recovers from this without damage.

abilities.name: Warning-Stripe Shield
abilities.description: it pulls its head and limbs into its shell, which survives bites from predators up to alligators, and its bright yellow and red markings act as a warning: largemouth bass, which hunt by sight, avoid sliders once they hatch.

traits.name: Red Ear Stripe
traits.description: a red stripe behind each eye, where an ear would be, gives the turtle its name; brighter red stripes go with stronger immune responses.

traits.name: Six-Continent Invader
traits.description: released pets have set up populations on every continent except Antarctica, and it is listed among the world's worst invasive species.

combat.weapons: The slider's only weapon is its beak. Juveniles are mostly carnivorous, eating insects, crayfish, tadpoles, small fish, snails and carrion; adults become omnivores feeding mostly on aquatic plants, algae, stems, leaves and seeds, while still taking invertebrates when they can. Males bite, chase and display at each other. None of this is dangerous to anything larger than a small fish or crayfish.
weaknesses: Tiny beak and small body; no real offense.
Slow and exposed on land.
Many predators, from alligators and gar to raccoons, otters and foxes.
Depends on outside heat to be active.

rosy-faced-lovebird.name: Rosy-faced Lovebird
rosy-faced-lovebird.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 0.055 kg, 15.0 cm total length. Females are slightly heavier than males (ADW) and control courtship, which goes ahead only with their approval.
rosy-faced-lovebird.summary: The Rosy-faced Lovebird is a 55 g parrot from the dry south-west of Africa, a fast, acrobatic flier that can even swing along branches using only its beak. It bites hard for its size and flocks gang up to mob predators, but in an absolute fight it is one of the smallest and most fragile animals on the roster.
narrative: The rosy-faced lovebird is a small green parrot with a pink face and a blue rump that lives in the dry woodland and semi-desert of Namibia, Angola and South Africa. It must drink several times a day, so flocks gather in hundreds around pools and rivers, then scatter to feed on grass seeds and acacia pods. At night lovebirds sleep in rock crevices or inside the giant thatched nests built by sociable weavers.

For its size it is physically impressive. Force-plate tests show it bites harder than expected for a bird of 55 g, and biomechanics studies found it can climb walls with feet and beak and even move hand-over-hand beneath a thin branch using only its beak, taking about one and a half times its body weight on the bill with each swing. It is also bold: when a predator threatens, lovebirds squawk, flap and advance, and whole groups will attack a predator that refuses to leave.

In an absolute matchup, though, it weighs about as much as a large egg. Its bite can hurt a finger but cannot harm a large animal, and it has no armor. Its best weapons are speed, agility and the courage of its flock.

sections.habitat: The rosy-faced lovebird lives in dry, open country in south-western Africa, from south-western Angola across most of Namibia to the lower Orange River valley in north-western South Africa and around Lake Ngami in Botswana. It uses dry woodland, sub-desert steppe, savanna with sparse trees, and wooded belts along rivers and canyons, up to about 1,500–1,600 m, always near permanent water (WPT; ADW). Feral birds live in Phoenix and Tucson, Arizona, where they have been seen perching on air-conditioner vents in extreme heat.
sections.diet: It eats mainly seeds, especially of grasses, Albizia and Acacia, plus buds, leaves and flowers, and will take maize, sunflower and millet crops. Seeds are picked from plants or the ground and husked rapidly with tongue and bill (ADW; WPT). At night lovebirds roost in the nests of white-browed sparrow-weavers and sociable weavers.
sections.social: Very social. Groups of 5–20 are typical, with gatherings of 100 or several hundred where grass seeds ripen or at water. Pairs bond strongly and huddle together in cold weather.
sections.reproduction: Nests are cup-shaped, built in rock crevices, in chambers of the huge communal nests of sociable weavers, or in buildings and bridges. Clutches are 4–6 eggs, incubated for about 23 days; chicks fledge at about 43 days and young start forming pairs at about 2 months (ADW; WPT).
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. Heavy trapping for the cage-bird trade caused historical declines in southern Angola, but new water points and buildings have helped it spread in other areas, including towards Lake Ngami (WPT; Wikipedia).
sections.features:
Measured bite force of about 18 N, high for its size.
Beak-driven hanging locomotion ("beakiation") and wall climbing.
Females carry nesting material tucked into their rump feathers.
Coordinated group mobbing of predators.
Dependence on frequent drinking.
sections.humanInteraction: It is one of the most common pet parrots because it is small and easy to breed, and aviculturists have produced more colour mutations than in any other lovebird. Pet lovebirds can be aggressive and possessive, often bonding to one person or bird. Escaped birds have founded feral populations in Arizona and Hawaii. Lovebirds have also become a laboratory model for studies of parrot biting, gripping and climbing.

funFacts: Female lovebirds tuck strips of bark into their rump feathers and fly them back to the nest.
A lovebird can swing along under a branch using only its beak, a gait scientists named "beakiation".
Six lovebirds tested on a force plate bit with up to about 18 N, far more than most birds their size.
Feral lovebirds in Phoenix, Arizona have been seen cooling off on air-conditioner vents.
Lovebirds often sleep in the giant communal nests of sociable weavers.
In a mobbing attack, a whole group of lovebirds will fly at a predator that refuses to leave.
Pairs can form when the birds are only about two months old.

traits.name: Water-Tied Desert Parrot

Six live lovebirds bit with up to about 18 N, which is strong for a 55 g bird; lovebirds, grey parrots and monk parakeets all bite harder than expected for their size compared with other birds (Dickinson et al. 2022). In captivity lovebirds can be aggressive, bond to one individual, may not get on with other people or pets, and should not be kept with smaller birds (Wikipedia). In absolute terms the bite is a pinch that can draw blood from a finger, not a threat to anything large.

Tied to water sources; must drink several times a day.
No armor.
Bite far too weak to injure large animals.

rottweiler.name: Rottweiler
rottweiler.specimen: healthy adult male, 50.0 kg, 65.0 cm at the withers.
rottweiler.summary: The Rottweiler is a compact, heavily muscled 50 kg German drover and guard dog. It fights with a strong grip and shoulder-driving power and will challenge the dominant animal head-on, putting it close to the Kangal and Gray Wolf in attack, but it has no armor, a short coat and is heavily outclassed by bears and big cats.
narrative: The Rottweiler takes its name from Rottweil in southern Germany, where butchers used powerful black-and-tan dogs to drive cattle to market and pull carts of meat. When German police began testing breeds in the early 1900s, the Rottweiler proved so suitable that it was officially recognized as a police dog in 1910. A male weighs about 50 kg and stands about 65 cm tall, compact and heavy-boned with a broad head.

Its working style is direct. When moving cattle it picks out the dominant animal and challenges it with an intimidating charge, using its body and shoulders to push stock around. As a guard and police dog it is trained to grip and hold. That combination of mass, muscle and willingness to confront much larger animals gives it one of the stronger attack ratings among dog breeds.

It is still a 50 kg dog. It is heavier but less agile than working shepherds, lacks the long protective coat of mountain guardian breeds, and is prone to elbow and hip dysplasia and a short life. Against light wild canids it holds a clear edge; against a wolf or a heavy guardian dog it is an even contest; against bears, big cats and large hoofed animals it is simply too small.

sections.habitat: A domestic breed from southern Germany, now kept worldwide in homes, farms, police units and guard work.
sections.diet: Fed by its owners on commercial dog food, meat and household scraps.
sections.ecology: No wild ecological role. Working roles have included cattle droving, cart pulling, police work, guarding and search-and-rescue.
sections.social: Devoted to its family and handler, calm at home, and watchful toward strangers.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is managed by breed clubs and owners; the ADRK, founded in 1921, is the breed's home club.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed.
sections.features:
Compact, heavy-boned, muscular build.
Broad head with 42 teeth in a scissor bite.
Black coat with rich tan markings.
Efficient trotting gait.
Confident, protective temperament.
sections.humanInteraction: The Rottweiler is a popular guard, police and family dog. In a US study of 238 dog bite-related deaths from 1979 to 1998, pit bull-type dogs and Rottweilers were involved in more than half, though the authors warned that breed identification is unreliable and fatal attacks are rare. A later study of 2000–2009 deaths found preventable management factors in most cases and valid breed identification in few. Health problems include elbow and hip dysplasia and a short average life.

funFacts: Its German name, Rottweiler Metzgerhund, means "Rottweil butchers' dog".
The FCI standard says Rottweilers were officially recognized as police dogs in 1910.
The breed's home club, the ADRK, was formed in 1921 when several German Rottweiler clubs merged.
A working Rottweiler moving cattle picks out the dominant animal and challenges it.
The viral "328 PSI" bite figure is a television force measurement relabelled as pressure.
The FCI standard describes the Rottweiler as a trotting dog and faults sluggish movement at the trot.

abilities.name: Shoulder Drive

traits.name: Rottweil Butcher's Dog

traits.name: Black-and-Tan Powerhouse
traits.description: a compact, stalwart dog, black with sharply defined rich tan markings on the cheeks, muzzle, chest and legs, with a broad head and 42-tooth scissor bite.

combat.weapons: The weapon is the canid bite on a broad, powerful head with full 42-tooth dentition. The Rottweiler is compact and heavily muscled, and when working cattle it uses its body and shoulders as well as its teeth. As a guard and police dog it is trained to grip and hold.
weaknesses: No armor; short coat.
Heavier and slower to turn than working shepherds.
Short average lifespan and common elbow and hip dysplasia.
Far outmatched by bears, big cats and large ungulates.

russell-s-viper.name: Russell's Viper
russell-s-viper.specimen: healthy adult, 1.3 kg and 120 cm total length, sex unspecified. Wild venom-yield work found no significant difference between males and females, and this pass found no reliable size difference between the sexes, so no sex-based modifier is applied.
russell-s-viper.summary: Russell's viper is a stout, chain-patterned South Asian viper about 1.2 m long, with 16.5 mm fangs and a venom that sets off runaway clotting. It warns with a very loud hiss and strikes hard, and it is thought to cause most severe snakebites in India. Its body is still small and slow, so its danger lies almost entirely in the bite.
narrative: Russell's viper is built around one devastating weapon. At about 1.2 m and 1.3 kg it is a mid-sized viper, slow when it moves and usually content to lie still in grass or farmland. But its hinged fangs are around 16.5 mm long, and a typical adult carries about 100 mg of venom that activates clotting factors X and V, draining the blood of its ability to clot and damaging kidneys and blood vessels.

When disturbed it does not simply flee. It pulls its body into S-loops, raises the front third of its body and produces a hiss often called the loudest of any snake. If the threat continues, it strikes with enough force that a large snake can lift off the ground, sometimes holding on for several seconds. This forceful strike is behind the myth that it chases people.

In battle terms, Russell's viper has one of the strongest venom weapons among the roster's vipers, stronger in delivery than a rattlesnake of similar size. Everything else is modest: little strength, no armor, slow movement and an ectotherm's limited stamina. It wins fights that come to it, and loses fights where the opponent can stay out of reach or crush it first.

sections.habitat: Russell's viper lives in India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Nepal and Bangladesh, and possibly Bhutan. It avoids dense forest and very humid places such as swamps and rainforest, preferring open grassy or bushy areas, scrub, plantations and farmland in plains, coastal lowlands and hills. It is common in parts of Punjab, the west coast and southern India, and is often found near settlements because of the rodents that live around people.
sections.diet: Adults eat mainly rodents; juveniles eat lizards and forage actively. Other prey include small reptiles, land crabs, scorpions and other arthropods. Radio-tracking in a rural Indian community found people within 50 m of a tagged viper in about 17% of 2,066 locations, showing how closely the species lives alongside humans.
sections.social: Solitary.
sections.reproduction: Live-bearing. Mating usually occurs early in the year; gestation lasts more than six months, and young are born from May to November, mostly in June and July. Litters of 20–40 are common and up to 75 has been recorded. Sexual maturity is reached in about 2–3 years; the smallest gravid females are about 100 cm long.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2021 assessment, as reported by Wikipedia). It is common across much of its range.
sections.features:
Hinged fangs about 16.5 mm long with replacement fangs behind.
Large venom yield with clotting-factor activators.
Loud defensive hiss and S-loop posture.
Thermal-cue sensitivity without pit organs.
Chain-like blotched camouflage.
sections.humanInteraction: Russell's viper is one of India's "big four" snakes and is thought to cause the majority of clinically severe envenomings in a country with about 58,000 snakebite deaths a year (Senji Laxme et al. 2021; Suraweera et al. 2020). The Reptile Database describes it as possibly the most common dangerously venomous snake in southern Asia. Plantation workers were the most at-risk group in the radio-tracking study. Survivors can suffer long-term pituitary damage. Its venom's clotting activator is used worldwide in the dRVVT test for lupus anticoagulant.

funFacts: Its hiss is often said to be the loudest of any snake.
Large individuals can lift off the ground with the force of a strike.
A single litter of 75 young has been recorded.
A typical adult carries around 100 mg of venom, more than the estimated lethal dose for an adult human.
Hospitals use its venom in a blood test called the dilute Russell's viper venom time.
In one study, about 29% of bite survivors had pituitary damage.
The genus name Daboia is thought to come from a Hindi word meaning "the lurker".

abilities.name: Clotting-Factor Hijack
abilities.description: the venom contains activators of clotting factors X and V, setting off runaway clotting that uses up the blood's clotting capacity and leads to bleeding and kidney failure. A typical adult carries around 100 mg, above the estimated 40–70 mg lethal dose for an adult human.

abilities.name: Pressure-Cooker Hiss
abilities.description: when threatened it forms S-loops, lifts the front third of its body and gives a hiss reputed to be the loudest of any snake, then strikes with enough force that large individuals can lift off the ground.

traits.name: Chain-Link Camouflage
traits.description: three rows of dark, black-ringed spots edged in white or yellow run down a tan or brown body, breaking up its outline in grass and leaf litter; the harmless rough-scaled sand boa has a similar pattern.

traits.name: Mass Live Birth
traits.description: it gives birth to live young, with litters of 20–40 common and up to 75 recorded, each 21–26 cm long at birth.

combat.weapons: The primary weapon is a powerful strike through hinged fangs about 16.5 mm long, injecting a large dose of venom that activates clotting factors X and V, uses up the blood's clotting capacity and damages kidneys and blood vessels. The secondary weapon is intimidation: the snake forms S-loops, raises the front third of its body and produces a hiss often described as louder than any other snake's.
weaknesses: Slow-moving adults with limited escape ability.
No armor; vulnerable to crushing and to snake-eating predators.
Venom damage, though severe, builds over minutes to hours.
Needs close contact to bite.

russian-tortoise.name: Russian Tortoise
russian-tortoise.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 1.0 kg with a 20.0 cm straight carapace length, representing a well-grown wild female rather than a record animal.
russian-tortoise.summary: The Russian tortoise is a small, flat-shelled digger from the dry steppes of Central Asia. A 1 kg adult female has no real weapons, but it can seal itself inside a thick, closed shell or retreat into a burrow up to 2 m deep, and it survives by staying dormant for up to nine months a year. It is well protected for its size and hopeless as an attacker.
narrative: For most of the year the Russian tortoise is underground. On the Central Asian steppe, spring is short and summer is hot and dry, so the tortoise crams its feeding into a few weeks of green growth, then digs down and waits. Field studies have found tortoises active for only about three months a year, and even then they rest most of the time. Four stout claws on each front foot and a flat, rounded shell make it an efficient digger, and its burrows can reach 2 m deep.

As a fighter it has almost nothing to offer. The beak crops plants, and the only fights it takes part in are shoving matches between males, who ram each other and try to tip the rival over. A flipped male is in real danger from heat and predators, and males are built with longer legs and more freedom in the shell to right themselves quickly. Against a predator the tortoise simply closes up: the shell has small openings and the scaled forelimbs cover the front. That works against small attackers, but the whole package weighs about 1 kg, and a large predator can carry it off or crush it.

In ABS terms the Russian tortoise is a near-zero attacker with respectable Defense for its size, very low Agility, and solid Stamina built on patience rather than effort. Its Special score comes from its shell, its deep burrows and its long dormancy. It is also a space pioneer: two of its kind circled the Moon in 1968, before any human did.

sections.habitat: The Russian tortoise lives in dry, open steppe, semi-desert and foothill country from the Caspian Sea south through Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan and east across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan to Xinjiang, China, up to about 2,400 m. It prefers sandy or loamy soils it can dig into, and it needs some rain to soften the ground for burrowing. The climate has large daily and seasonal temperature swings and very dry summers.
sections.diet: It eats herbaceous and succulent plants, flowers, twigs and some fruit, taking most of its water from food. Lee and Smith note that it avoids grasses and often eats plants that are toxic to grazing mammals, which reduces competition with livestock; other summaries list grasses in the diet, so the point is not settled. Almost all feeding is packed into a short spring season before summer heat drives the tortoises underground.
sections.social: Tortoises visit neighbouring burrows and several may spend the night in one burrow. Males court females by head bobbing, circling and biting the female's forelegs, and males fight each other by ramming.
sections.reproduction: Growth is slow: a female may need about nine years to reach 10 cm, and maturity may take 10 to 15 years in the wild. Males mature at 10–11 cm and females at 13–14 cm carapace length. The slow growth and small clutches make wild populations very sensitive to collection of adults.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, based on a 1996 assessment by the Tortoise and Freshwater Turtle Specialist Group that is now old. It has been on CITES Appendix II since 1977. Collection for the international pet trade has been the main threat since the 1970s: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service import data summarised by Lee and Smith show 142,475 wild-caught Russian tortoises imported into the United States between 2002 and 2008, almost all for commerce.
sections.features:
Four clawed toes on each front foot.
Flattened, rounded shell with small limb openings.
Burrows up to 2 m deep.
Up to nine months a year in dormancy.
Females larger and heavier; males longer-legged and faster.
Horny beak with no teeth.
sections.humanInteraction: It is one of the most common pet tortoises in Europe and North America. A UK veterinary records study found Horsfield's tortoise made up 31.9% of pet tortoises whose species was recorded, second only to Hermann's tortoise. A survey of 1,075 tortoise keepers found that a diet of mostly grasses and weeds and outdoor enclosures gave the best health outcomes for Testudo tortoises.

funFacts: Two Russian tortoises were the first animals to fly around the Moon, on Zond 5 in 1968; each weighed only 0.34–0.4 kg before the flight.
Unlike most tortoises, it has only four toes on each front foot.
Field work found tortoises active only about three months a year, and resting 90% of the time even then.
Its burrows can reach 2 m deep.
Males often flip rivals onto their backs during fights, so males are built to right themselves faster than females.
Between 2002 and 2008, 142,475 wild-caught Russian tortoises were imported into the United States.

abilities.name: Sealed Steppe Shell
abilities.description: the flattened, rounded shell closes with small openings, and the scaled forelimbs block the front when the head is pulled in. Small predators and pecking birds face a closed box rather than a meal.

abilities.name: Deep Burrow Retreat
abilities.description: strong four-clawed forelimbs dig burrows up to 2 m deep, where the tortoise escapes midday heat, night cold, winter and many predators. In a matchup it can end contact by going underground.

traits.name: Nine-Month Sleeper
traits.description: in parts of its range it is active for only about three months a year, spending the rest in summer and winter dormancy.

traits.name: First Animals Around the Moon
traits.description: two Russian tortoises flew around the Moon aboard the Soviet Zond 5 probe in September 1968 and returned to Earth alive.

combat.weapons: The Russian tortoise is a herbivore with almost no offensive equipment. Its beak crops leaves and flowers, and its fights are ritual contests between males, who ram each other with the front of the shell and try to overturn the rival. Bonnet et al. note that these fights often end with a male flipped onto its back, where it risks overheating or predation. The same beak bites a female's forelegs during courtship. None of this is dangerous to a predator.
weaknesses: Tiny absolute mass and no weapons.
Very slow on the surface.
A 1 kg shell can be carried off, dropped or crushed by large predators.
Can be flipped; overturned animals risk overheating.

sand-cat.name: Sand Cat
sand-cat.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 2.8 kg, matching the mean of four Pakistani males (2.78 kg) and sitting inside the 2.1–3.4 kg range of Turkmen males (Cole and Wilson 2015).
sand-cat.summary: A small, broad-headed desert cat with fur-soled feet and huge ear canals, the sand cat hears prey under the sand, kills venomous vipers and goes without drinking. Superbly specialized for deserts, it is still only a 3 kg animal with little absolute power or protection.
narrative: The sand cat is built for places most predators avoid. It spends the hottest hours in a burrow and comes out at night to cover five to ten kilometres across sand and gravel, walking, listening and pausing. Its ear canals and middle ear are roughly twice the size of a domestic cat's, which lets it pick up faint sounds of rodents moving underground; it then digs them out at speed.

Its most striking hunting skill is snake killing. Saharan nomads describe it as a formidable hunter of horned vipers, and field accounts describe it stunning the snake with a flurry of paw blows before a fatal neck bite. It also has the stillness of a true desert specialist: when caught in a light beam it crouches, closes its eyes and waits, relying on its sandy coat to vanish.

In absolute combat terms, none of this changes its size. At about 2.8 kg it is lighter than a house cat and far lighter than the caracals, jackals and wolves that prey on it. It rates low in Attack and Defense, higher in Stamina for its long desert travel, and high in Special and Senses for its specialized hearing.

sections.habitat: Sandy and stony deserts with sparse grasses and shrubs across the Sahara, the Arabian Peninsula, and parts of Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Afghanistan and Pakistan. It prefers flat or undulating ground with some vegetation and avoids bare, shifting dunes where there is little prey. It shelters in burrows about 1.5 m deep, often ones dug by foxes, porcupines or gerbils. The rare Arabian subspecies has recently been recorded in Iraq (Al Sheikhly and Haba 2017) and in the central Syrian desert near Palmyra (Serra et al. 2007).
sections.diet: Small rodents (gerbils, jirds, jerboas, spiny mice), young hares, small birds such as larks, lizards such as sandfish and spiny-tailed lizards, insects and venomous snakes (Wikipedia; Cole and Wilson). It satisfies its moisture needs from prey.
sections.social: Solitary; males and females come together only to breed. Home ranges overlap. In Morocco, tracked adults used very large ranges of about 275–320 km² on average.
sections.reproduction: Two to three kittens are usually born in spring in the wild; in captivity, births can happen year-round and more than one litter a year is possible. Kittens weigh about 39–80 g at birth, reach three-quarters of adult size in five months and become independent by the end of their first year. In the studbook, 30% of young died before day 30 (Cole and Wilson).
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2016 assessment) because of its wide range, although it is rarely seen and poorly studied. Threats include habitat degradation, loss of vegetated sand habitat, uncontrolled hunting, poisoned baits set for other predators, domestic and feral dogs, and prey declines during droughts.
sections.features:
Enlarged ear canals, middle-ear spaces and auditory bullae.
Low-set ears on a broad, flat head.
Thick fur on the soles of the feet.
Very long winter coat in Central Asia.
Ability to go without drinking.
sections.humanInteraction: Harmless to people. It is threatened by habitat change, persecution and poisoned baits; in the early 1970s sand cats caught in Pakistan were exported to zoos worldwide. The Toubou people of the Sahara report sand cats coming into camps at night to drink camel milk (Wikipedia).

funFacts: Its ear canals are about twice as wide as a domestic cat's.
The soles of its feet are covered with fur up to 3 cm long.
It can sprint at about 30–40 km/h over short distances.
It kills venomous vipers by stunning them with rapid paw blows.
Shine a light on it and it crouches and closes its eyes so no eyeshine gives it away.
Sand cats in the Moroccan Sahara have been found sleeping in ravens' nests 3.5 m up in acacia trees.
It can live without drinking, getting its water from prey.

abilities.name: Underground Ear
abilities.description: ear canals about twice as wide as a domestic cat's and a greatly enlarged middle ear let it hear prey moving below the sand and then dig it out. This detection edge matters most against burrowing or hidden opponents.

abilities.name: Viper Stun
abilities.description: it stuns horned and sand vipers with rapid blows of its paws to the head, then kills with a neck bite. The technique lets a 3 kg cat deal with venomous snakes that would injure a careless predator.

traits.name: Fur-Soled Feet
traits.description: dense fur 15–30 mm long covers the soles of its feet, insulating the pads against burning sand and spreading its weight on loose sand.

traits.name: Waterless Desert Cat
traits.description: it gets the moisture it needs from its prey and can live in desert far from any water source, drinking only when water happens to be available.

combat.weapons: The sand cat hunts gerbils, jirds, jerboas, spiny mice, larks, lizards and young hares. It hunts mainly by walking, listening and pausing to look around, rarely by sitting and waiting (Cole and Wilson). It locates prey moving underground with its enlarged ears and digs rapidly to reach it. Saharan nomads describe it as a skilled hunter of horned and sand vipers: it stuns a snake with rapid paw strikes to the head before killing it with a neck bite. When it catches more than it can eat, it buries the rest for later. These are precise, well-timed small-predator weapons carried on a 2.8 kg body.
weaknesses: Tiny absolute mass and power.
No armor.
Weak climber and jumper by felid standards.
Predated by golden eagles, caracals, wolves, golden jackals, dogs and possibly large snakes; juveniles by eagle-owls and red foxes.

saw-scaled-viper.name: Saw-scaled Viper
saw-scaled-viper.specimen: healthy adult, 0.15 kg and 50 cm total length, sex unspecified. Venom-yield work on 30 wild E. c. carinatus found no difference between males and females, and this pass found no reliable size difference between the sexes, so no sex-based modifier is applied.
saw-scaled-viper.summary: The saw-scaled viper is a tiny desert viper, usually under 60 cm and about 150 g, that warns by rubbing its saw-edged scales into a sizzling hiss and strikes from a spring-like coil. Its venom destroys the blood's ability to clot. It is one of India's big four medically important snakes, but its small size and small venom doses keep its absolute combat power low.
narrative: The saw-scaled viper is proof that a snake does not need size to matter. Most adults are under 60 cm and weigh roughly 150 g, and in southern India an adult may give only a few milligrams of venom. Yet the species ranks among India's four most medically important snakes because it is common, well camouflaged on sand and rock, active at night when people walk barefoot, and quick to defend itself.

Its warning is unusual. Instead of a rattle or a loud hiss, it arranges its body into parallel C-shaped loops and rubs the angled, saw-edged scales on its flanks together. The result is a sizzling sound that speeds up as the threat grows. If the warning fails, the viper strikes from a figure-of-eight coil with its head at the center. The venom, rich in metalloproteinases, uses up clotting factors and damages blood vessels, leading to bleeding and kidney injury over hours rather than minutes.

For battle ratings, the saw-scaled viper sits near the bottom in every physical category. It has almost no mass, no armor and very little strength, and even its venom delivery is limited by dose. Its strengths are a fast strike, quick sidewinding, readiness to fight and a warning display that is one of the most distinctive on the roster.

sections.habitat: The saw-scaled viper lives in India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan, Iran, southern Iraq, Oman, the United Arab Emirates and parts of Central Asia (Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan). It uses sand, rock, soft soil and scrubland, often hiding under loose rocks, in rodent burrows, rock fissures or rotting logs, and has been recorded up to 1,982 m in Balochistan.
sections.diet: It eats rodents, lizards, frogs and many arthropods, including scorpions, centipedes and large insects. The broad diet allows high local densities. It is mostly crepuscular and nocturnal, most active after rain and on humid nights, and often climbs into shrubs.
sections.social: Solitary, though many individuals can gather in the same shrub during rain.
sections.reproduction: Indian populations give birth to live young. In northern India mating takes place in winter and young are born from April to August, usually 3–15 per litter (up to 23 recorded), each 115–152 mm long.
sections.conservation: Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2021 assessment, as reported by Wikipedia). It is common across much of its range and often lives close to farms and villages.
sections.features:
Serrated keeled flank scales used for a stridulating warning sound.
Hinged front fangs and a metalloproteinase-rich hemorrhagic venom.
Fast sidewinding locomotion.
Figure-of-eight defensive coil.
Frequent climbing into bushes, especially in rain.
sections.humanInteraction: It is one of India's "big four" snakes named in the Million Death Study as responsible for most of the country's snakebite deaths, which that study estimated at about 45,900 a year in 2001–03. A later analysis estimated about 58,000 snakebite deaths a year in India from 2000 to 2019. Bites cause severe bleeding and kidney injury; in Rajasthan, a 2019–2024 series found poor antivenom response to E. c. sochureki bites. Its venom has also given medicine useful molecules: echistatin (an anticlotting peptide), ecarin (the reagent in the ecarin clotting time test) and the design basis of the drug tirofiban.

funFacts: It warns intruders by rubbing its saw-edged scales together, making a sizzling sound like water on a hot plate.
In rain, up to 80% of adults may climb into bushes; about 20 were once seen on one shrub.
Southern Indian adults average under 3 mg of venom per extraction, yet the species is still one of India's big four.
Its venom supplied ecarin, used in a hospital blood-clotting test.
The anticlotting drug tirofiban (Aggrastat) is listed among the medicines derived from this snake's venom.
In sand it can bury itself so that only its head shows.
It gives birth to live young, unlike the egg-laying African carpet vipers.

abilities.name: Sizzling Scale Alarm
abilities.description: the snake loops into parallel C-shaped coils and rubs its angled, serrated flank scales together to make a hissing, sizzling sound that grows faster and louder as the threat continues. The sound comes from the scales, not from breath or a rattle.

abilities.name: Coil-Spring Hemorrhage Strike
abilities.description: from a figure-of-eight coil with the head in the center, it strikes like a released spring. Its metalloproteinase-rich venom causes consumption coagulopathy and bleeding, and in north-western India it is often poorly neutralized by the available antivenom.

traits.name: Sand-Swimming Sidewinder
traits.description: it moves mainly by fast sidewinding across hot sand, touching the ground at only two points, and can bury itself with only the head showing.

traits.name: Big Four's Smallest Member
traits.description: at usually under 60 cm it is the smallest of India's "big four" medically important snakes, yet it is one of them because it is common, well hidden and quick to bite.

combat.weapons: The primary weapon is a fast strike through hinged front fangs, delivering a metalloproteinase-rich venom that breaks down clotting factors and blood-vessel walls. The secondary tool is the threat display: the snake forms parallel C-shaped coils and rubs its serrated flank scales together to make a loud "sizzling" sound, speeding up as it becomes more agitated.
weaknesses: Tiny mass and no armor: any sizable predator can crush it.
Small venom yield, especially in southern populations.
Slow-acting venom: the damage comes from clotting failure over hours.
Performance drops in cold; northern populations hibernate.

south-american-coati.name: South American Coati
south-american-coati.specimen: healthy mature adult male of about 5.5 kg, head-body about 55 cm, with a ringed tail of similar length. This sits in the upper half of the published adult range without using the heaviest animals.
south-american-coati.summary: The South American coati is a 5.5 kg ring-tailed forager of South American forests that climbs down trees head-first and noses out prey with a long, mobile snout. It lives in bands that raise the alarm and scatter at danger, and it bites and claws hard when cornered, but it is far too small to stand up to real predators.
narrative: The South American coati is a slim, long-snouted relative of the raccoon, with a banded tail that it often carries straight up. A mature male weighs around 5.5 kg. Its coat varies from dark brown to orange-red, and its most noticeable feature is a long, flexible, pig-like nose that it pushes into leaf litter, soil and crevices in search of beetles, grubs and other small prey.

Coatis are built to use both the ground and the trees. Their ankles rotate so they can climb down trunks head-first, their strong front claws rip open rotten logs, and their tails help them balance as they jump from branch to branch. Females and young travel in noisy bands of up to about 30, sleeping in trees and foraging by day; at an alarm call the whole band shoots up the trees and then drops and scatters.

In battle terms the coati is a quick, well-armed small mammal rather than a fighter. Long canines and claws let males fight rivals and let any cornered coati inflict painful wounds, but it weighs little more than a large house cat and is regular prey for jaguars, ocelots and big birds of prey. It sits just below the raccoon in Attack, above it in Agility, and in the upper band for Intelligence thanks to its complex band life.

sections.habitat: Tropical and subtropical South America east of the Andes, from Colombia and the Guianas south to Uruguay and northern Argentina, mainly in lowland forest but up to about 2,500 m. It lives mainly in forest, including deciduous, evergreen and cloud forest, and its occupancy is higher where forest cover is high and lower at higher elevations. It has been introduced to Mallorca, where it is considered invasive.
sections.diet: An omnivore that eats mainly fruit and invertebrates such as beetles, grubs, ants, termites, spiders, scorpions and centipedes, plus frogs, lizards, small rodents and bird eggs. It is likely an important seed disperser and is prey for jaguars, ocelots, jaguarundis, foxes, boas and birds of prey.
sections.social: Females and young form bands of about 15–30 individuals. Most adult males live alone and join bands during the breeding season, but in this species a resident adult male often stays with a group all year. Bands do not defend exclusive territories, and home ranges overlap.
sections.reproduction: All females in a band come into heat within the same one- to two-week period. Females leave the band to give birth in a tree nest after a gestation of about 74–77 days, raising 3–7 young, and rejoin the band with their offspring 5–6 weeks later. Young can climb at 26 days and eat solid food at about four months. Females mature at about two years; males usually leave their birth group at about three years.
sections.conservation: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. It is widespread, but it depends on forest cover and is hunted by people in parts of its range. Because coatis often live close to people in parks and cities, they share parasites and pathogens with domestic animals, and many veterinary surveys focus on them.
sections.features:
Long, flexible, pig-like snout.
Ankles that rotate about 180 degrees for head-first descent.
Long, ringed, semi-prehensile tail held upright when walking.
Strong, curved front claws.
Long, sharp canines.
sections.humanInteraction: Coatis are a familiar sight at tourist sites such as Iguazú Falls, and bands may forage through hotel grounds and visitor areas. Where coatis and people interact closely, attacks can occur; a 2010 case report described a coati attacking two children in their home in Brazil, causing deep scratches and bites. People also hunt coatis in parts of their range.

funFacts: Its ankles can turn around so it can climb down trees head-first.
Solitary males were once thought to be a separate species and were called "coatimundis".
It is the only coati species whose bands keep an adult male all year.
All the females in a band come into heat within the same week or two.
Mothers give birth alone in a tree nest, then bring their young back to the band.
Coatis have been introduced to the Mediterranean island of Mallorca.

abilities.name: Reverse-Ankle Scramble
abilities.description: double-jointed ankles rotate about 180 degrees so it can run down trunks head-first, and it crosses the canopy by jumping from branch ends, using its tail for balance.

abilities.name: Band Alarm Scatter
abilities.description: when a band member gives an alarm call, the group climbs trees, then drops to the ground and scatters in many directions, making it hard for a predator to single one out.

traits.name: Snorkel Snout
traits.description: a long, flexible, pig-like snout noses through leaf litter and crevices while strong front claws rip open logs and dig out hidden prey.

traits.name: Resident Band Male
traits.description: it is the only coati species whose bands include an adult male all year; genetic tests showed resident males fathered 67–91% of their group's young.

combat.weapons: The coati's weapons are long, sharp canines and strong front claws. It is an omnivore that mostly eats fruit and invertebrates, plus small vertebrates and bird eggs, digging prey out of leaf litter, soil and rotten logs with its claws and long snout. Adult males fight each other during the mating season, and a coati that attacked two children in a Brazilian home caused deep scratches and bites, showing that its claws and teeth can wound people when it is cornered or provoked.
weaknesses: Only about 5.5 kg with no armor.
Canines and claws are effective only at close range and against small opponents.
Preyed on by jaguars, ocelots, jaguarundis, foxes, boas and large birds of prey.
Much less effective alone in open ground.

southern-ground-hornbill.name: Southern Ground Hornbill
southern-ground-hornbill.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 4.2 kg, 102.0 cm total length, about 1.5 m wingspan. Males are the larger sex with a larger casque (the ridge on top of the bill).
southern-ground-hornbill.summary: The Southern Ground Hornbill is the world's largest hornbill, a 4 kg ground-walking predator that hunts snakes, tortoises, small mammals and insects in family groups across African savanna. Its heavy bill is its only weapon, so it lacks the talons, kicks and speed of true raptors, but group foraging and long daily walks make it a persistent hunter.
narrative: The southern ground hornbill hunts on foot. A family group of up to about a dozen birds walks slowly across the grass, spending most of the day on the move and sometimes covering more than 10 km. When one bird finds something, a snake, a tortoise, a nest of chicks or a hiding mongoose, it can call the others with a low bark, and the group's heavy bills do the rest.

Its life is built around the group. Every breeding pair depends on helpers, and birds without years of experience as helpers fail to raise young. Chicks stay dependent for up to two years, and a group raises only about one chick every three years. In experiments, ground hornbills learned new foraging tricks by watching group members and adjusted to changing reward rules, evidence of solid, socially based learning.

In an absolute matchup, the hornbill is a 4 kg bird whose weapon is its bill. It has no talons, no kicking attack like the secretary bird, and no burst speed. It does well against snakes, reptiles and small mammals on open ground, but faster predators and anything larger than a mongoose can simply stay out of bill range.

sections.habitat: The southern ground hornbill lives from Kenya, Burundi and the southern Democratic Republic of the Congo south through Angola, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Mozambique and northern Namibia to northern and eastern South Africa, where it is widespread but scarce. It prefers grassland and savanna woodland with a sparse understory, from montane grassland to mopane and teak woodland. In South Africa it is now largely confined to reserves and national parks such as Kruger, where GPS-tracked groups favored grassland, open woodland and dense thicket for foraging.
sections.diet: It is carnivorous, eating mainly insects such as grasshoppers and beetles plus frogs, snakes, lizards, chameleons, tortoises, mongooses, squirrels, young hares and nestling birds. It rarely drinks. As a large ground predator it is treated as an apex predator of the savanna ground layer, and its huge territories mean that protecting one group also protects many other species.
sections.social: Groups of about 2–11 birds share a territory, with one dominant breeding pair and helpers that are usually adult males or young from earlier seasons. Groups keep contact with loud chorus calls heard up to 3 km away and defend territories of up to about 100 km².
sections.reproduction: Nests are almost always deep holes in very old trees. One or two eggs are laid; the second chick is 3–14 days younger and usually starves within weeks, so a group rarely raises more than one chick. Incubation is 40–45 days and fledging about 85 days, and the young depend on the group for one to two years. Groups therefore breed successfully only about every third year. Breeding begins around 10 years of age.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Vulnerable globally and Endangered in South Africa, Namibia, Lesotho and Eswatini. Threats include loss of big nest trees and habitat, poisoning, persecution (including for breaking windows), hunting and use in traditional medicine. Conservation programs rear the redundant second chick in captivity and reintroduce groups into former range. Hot, dry weather is linked with worse breeding results.
sections.features:
Massive 17–22 cm bill with a casque.
Long eyelashes.
Inflatable red throat pouch in adult males.
Group chorus audible up to 3 km.
Obligate cooperative breeding with helpers.
sections.humanInteraction: It is culturally important across southern Africa; in several cultures killing one is taboo. Some birds are killed after breaking windows while attacking their reflections. Kruger National Park lists it as one of its "Big Six" birds, and reintroduction projects work with landowners to restore groups.

funFacts: It is the largest hornbill in the world.
It is one of the few birds with long eyelashes.
Its group chorus can be heard up to 3 km away.
Young birds depend on their family for one to two years, longer than any other bird.
A group usually raises only one chick about every three years.
Hornbills that watched a trained group member open a puzzle box all learned to open it, while untrained birds all failed.
Captive ground hornbills have lived to about 70 years.

abilities.name: Walking Hunt Party
abilities.description: groups of hornbills comb the ground together, and a bird that finds prey can call the others with a low bark. Several heavy bills can then work on snakes, tortoises and small mammals.

abilities.name: Hammer-Bill Strike
abilities.description: a 17–22 cm bill is used to seize and dig out prey, letting a 4 kg bird handle snakes, tortoises, mongooses and young hares.

traits.name: World's Largest Hornbill
traits.description: at about 4 kg and 1 m long, it is the heaviest member of the hornbill order, and one of the few birds with prominent eyelashes.

traits.name: Helper-Run Family
traits.description: every breeding pair needs at least two helpers, and birds without years of helper experience fail to breed successfully. Young stay dependent for one to two years, longer than any other bird.

combat.weapons: The long, heavy bill is its only real weapon. It seizes prey, digs it out of the ground and dung heaps, and handles large, awkward animals. Recorded vertebrate prey includes snakes, lizards, chameleons, tortoises, frogs, mongooses, squirrels, young hares and nestling birds; invertebrates such as grasshoppers and beetles make up much of the daily food. Mammals up to the size of hares are taken. It may also snatch food from birds of prey. No quantified description of how it kills large prey was located, so weapon scoring is based on bill size and the prey list.
weaknesses: Only about 4.2 kg in absolute mass.
No talons or claws for gripping; the bill is the single weapon.
Slow on the ground compared with runners and pouncers.
No armor; bill strikes require close contact.
Slow breeding makes populations fragile.

sperm-whale.name: Sperm Whale
sperm-whale.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 35,000 kg and 15.0 m long, representing a large bull below NOAA's stated male maximum of 52 ft (15.9 m) and 45 tons (40,823 kg).
sperm-whale.summary: The largest toothed predator alive, a bull sperm whale combines a 35-tonne body, a battering-ram forehead and the loudest biosonar on Earth. It hunts squid in the dark a kilometre down on hour-long dives, but its slow routine swimming and narrow grasping jaw make it more of an unstoppable heavyweight than a fast killer.
narrative: The sperm whale is built around the deep. A mature bull weighs tens of tonnes and a large part of that mass sits in its enormous square head, which holds the spermaceti organ and junk. Those oil-filled compartments shape and focus the whale's clicks into a beam of sound so intense that no recorded animal matches it. With that beam the whale searches black water hundreds of metres down, then accelerates into a rapid buzz as it closes on a squid.

In a battle, those same traits make it a heavyweight with strange strengths. The head is not only an acoustic lens: modelling shows its internal partitions reduce the stress of an impact, fitting reports and theory that males ram one another. A charging bull brings a mass several times greater than any orca and a skull built to take its own hit. Its jaw, lined with heavy conical teeth, can seize and hold but is not designed to carve up large prey, and its routine swimming is slow. Against a small, fast opponent it may struggle to land its strike; against anything that has to absorb one, the outcome is grim.

Its deepest advantage is endurance. Where most air-breathing hunters manage a few minutes underwater, the sperm whale repeats 45-minute dives through most of the day. Add large-brained clan cultures, coordinated defense against orcas and a sensory system that works in total darkness, and it becomes one of the most complete giants in the ocean: formidable in almost any open-water matchup, vulnerable mainly to coordinated packs and to any setting that removes the deep.

sections.habitat: Sperm whales live in deep water in every ocean, typically beyond the continental shelf and along slopes and canyons where deep squid concentrate. Females and young stay mainly in warmer tropical and subtropical waters; mature males range much farther toward polar seas and return to lower latitudes to breed.
sections.diet: The diet is dominated by deep-water squid, including giant and colossal squid, with sharks, skates and fish also taken (NOAA). An adult eats about 3–3.5% of its body mass per day. Sperm whales are major predators of the deep sea, and their stomach contents have been one of the main sources of knowledge about giant squid, whose beaks accumulate inside them.
sections.social: Females and young form long-lasting social units that babysit calves at the surface while mothers dive. Units belong to larger vocal clans defined by shared coda dialects, a form of culture documented across the Pacific (Hersh et al. 2022). Mature males leave the family units and live alone or in small bachelor groups.
sections.reproduction: Males keep growing for decades and reach physical maturity at around 50 years and about 52 ft (NOAA). Females are much smaller. Long lives, slow growth and long calf dependence make populations slow to recover from losses.
sections.conservation: The sperm whale is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (Taylor et al. 2019 assessment). Commercial whaling removed very large numbers historically; current threats include ship strikes, entanglement, ocean noise, pollution and ingestion of marine debris. It is protected under the US Endangered Species Act and Marine Mammal Protection Act (NOAA).
sections.features:
Loudest biological sound recorded, used as long-range directional biosonar.
Forehead of spermaceti organ and junk, up to a quarter of body mass, with impact-reducing internal partitions.
Largest brain of any animal by mass.
Lower jaw with 18–28 functional teeth per side and a nearly toothless upper jaw.
Deep-dive physiology sustaining repeated 45-minute dives.
sections.humanInteraction: Sperm whales were hunted intensively for spermaceti oil and ambergris. Today they are a major whale-watching species in places such as the Azores, Dominica, Norway and New Zealand. Ship strikes and fishing-gear entanglement remain real risks.

funFacts: Their clicks reach up to 236 dB re 1 µPa, the loudest sound measured from any animal.
The forehead oil compartments can make up about a quarter of the whole whale's mass.
A typical foraging dive lasts about 45 minutes, with only about 9 minutes at the surface in between.
Sperm whales spend more than 72% of their time in foraging dive cycles.
Different clans use different click-pattern "dialects", and clans exaggerate the differences where they meet.
Males are about three times heavier than females: up to 45 tons against 15 tons.
When orcas attack, family groups can form a "marguerite" with heads together and tails out.

abilities.name: Abyssal Sonar Click
abilities.description: clicks of up to 236 dB re 1 µPa (rms), the loudest biological sound recorded, scan the dark water through about 81% of every dive and shift into a rapid buzz to lock onto prey. In a battle it finds and tracks opponents in complete darkness at long range.

abilities.name: Battering-Ram Forehead
abilities.description: the spermaceti organ and junk make up to a quarter of body mass, and internal partitions reduce skull stress on impact. A charging bull turns tens of tonnes of momentum into a head strike built to absorb its own recoil.

traits.name: Hour-Long Deep Diver
traits.description: average 45-minute foraging dives to several hundred metres to about a kilometre, with only 9-minute breaks, repeated through most of the day.

traits.name: Clan Coda Culture
traits.description: sperm whales belong to vocal clans marked by distinct click-pattern dialects that act as symbolic identity signals, and family units close ranks into a defensive rosette under attack.

combat.weapons:
The sperm whale has two distinct offensive systems. The first is its mass and forehead: a 35-tonne bull whose head holds up to a quarter of its body mass in the spermaceti organ and junk. Panagiotopoulou et al. (2016) modelled the forehead and found that its internal connective-tissue partitions reduce skull stress on impact, supporting the long-standing idea that males ram each other. The second is the lower jaw, a long narrow bar with 18–28 conical teeth per side that closes into sockets in the toothless upper jaw. That jaw is built to seize squid, fish, sharks and skates, not to shear chunks from large animals the way an orca or great white shark does.

In practice this makes the sperm whale devastating in collision and dangerous at the jaw, but less efficient at killing a large, mobile opponent than the roster's specialist macropredators. Its weapons are powerful but slow to deliver.
weaknesses: Must surface to breathe; a long engagement at the surface removes its depth advantage.
Slow routine swimming and a very large turning radius.
Narrow lower-jaw bite is poor for cutting large opponents.
Coordinated pack attack can isolate and wear down an individual, as orcas have shown.
Useless in any shallow-water or land setting; strandings are often fatal.
