steller-s-sea-eagle.name: Steller's Sea Eagle
steller-s-sea-eagle.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 9.0 kg, 105.0 cm total length and about 2.2 m wingspan. She is the heavier sex and therefore the stronger fighting form.
steller-s-sea-eagle.summary: Steller's Sea Eagle is the heaviest eagle in the world: about 9 kg in the canonical female, with a wingspan often over 2 m and an enormous arched yellow bill. It hunts salmon, seabirds and even foxes along the cold coasts of the Sea of Okhotsk and steals fish from smaller raptors. It is powerful for a bird, but its heavy build limits agility and it has no armor.
narrative: Steller's Sea Eagle is a heavyweight of the northern Pacific coast. Females average around 9 kg and carry a bill so large and arched it dominates the bird's silhouette. The species eats what its cold coastline provides: salmon on their spawning runs, walleye pollock, gulls, ducks and seabirds from colonies, hares, young seals, and occasionally carnivores as capable as foxes and sable.

Its combat style reflects that life. It is less a precision forest ambusher than a powerful, opportunistic coastal predator that can kill, scavenge and steal. On a salmon river its size lets it take fish from smaller raptors, and its long wings carry it between breeding coasts and wintering grounds in Kamchatka and Hokkaido.

On the absolute roster it remains a bird. Its mass gives it an edge over other eagles in food contests and a little extra durability, but it has no armor, a light skeleton and heavy, less nimble flight. Against large mammals it relies on staying out of reach. Its best matchups are over water and open coast, against prey and competitors smaller than itself.

sections.habitat: The species breeds along coasts and river valleys around the Sea of Okhotsk, on the Kamchatka Peninsula and along the lower Amur and Sakhalin. In the northern Sea of Okhotsk, about 70% of nests were found along sea coasts and the rest along rivers. In winter many birds move to Kamchatka and south to Hokkaido, with smaller numbers reaching Korea and China.
sections.diet: It is a top avian predator and scavenger of northern Pacific coasts. The diet centers on fish, especially Pacific salmon and walleye pollock, plus birds, mammals and carrion. The balance shifts by place and season: coastal pairs near seabird colonies eat mostly birds; Amur pairs eat mostly fish in summer; in Kamchatka, ducks and gulls can make up 50–70% of nestling food before salmon arrive; and dead salmon after spawning feed many wintering birds.
sections.social: Adults are solitary and territorial when breeding but gather in large numbers where food is concentrated, especially on salmon rivers and in winter.
sections.reproduction: Pairs nest in tall trees along coasts and rivers, and felling of these trees is a listed threat. Long-term monitoring in the northern Sea of Okhotsk began in 1992; coastal pairs breed more successfully than river pairs. Productivity has fallen from about 1.0 fledgling per nest in the 1980s to an average of about 0.55 fledglings per occupied nest in recent years.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Vulnerable, with a decreasing population. Published estimates put mature individuals at roughly 3,500–4,670 (about 4,600–7,000 birds in total). Threats include coastal, oil and gas, and hydroelectric development; pesticides; competition with fisheries (walleye pollock stocks have been reduced by overfishing); felling of tall nest trees; direct persecution; and lead poisoning after scavenging deer carcasses shot with lead ammunition in Japan. It is protected in Russia, Japan, South Korea and China.
sections.features:
Enormous, strongly arched yellow bill.
Dark plumage with white shoulders, thighs, forehead and wedge-shaped white tail.
The heaviest eagle, with a wingspan often over 2 m.
Flexible diet of fish, birds, mammals and carrion.
Seasonal gatherings at salmon rivers and wintering areas.
sections.humanInteraction: In Hokkaido, winter eagle gatherings draw wildlife watchers and photographers. The same region revealed a serious threat: eagles poisoned by lead fragments in deer carcasses left by hunters, which led to lead-ammunition restrictions in parts of the wintering range. Fisheries also compete with the eagle for fish such as walleye pollock.

funFacts: It is usually the heaviest eagle in the world; females average about 9 kg.
The largest recorded wingspan is about 287 cm.
It steals fish from smaller raptors.
Near seabird colonies, birds made up about 91% of the diet of nesting pairs.
Mammal prey has included Arctic foxes, red foxes, sable and American mink.
Up to about 3,500 birds may winter on Kamchatka alone.
Lead poisoning from hunted deer carcasses in Japan led to restrictions on lead ammunition in parts of its winter range.

abilities.name: Great Arched Beak
abilities.description: an enormous, strongly arched yellow bill, one of the most distinctive features of any eagle, tears apart fish, birds and mammal carcasses. In a fight it adds a powerful secondary tearing weapon to the talons.

abilities.name: Salmon-River Piracy
abilities.description: Steller's sea eagles steal fish from smaller raptors and gather in large numbers at productive salmon rivers. This size-backed piracy lets it win food contests without a costly kill.

traits.name: Heaviest Eagle
traits.description: usually the heaviest eagle in the world, with females averaging about 9 kg.

traits.name: Okhotsk Winter Gatherer
traits.description: outside the breeding season, up to about 3,500 birds winter on Kamchatka and around 2,000 on Hokkaido, often concentrating where fish are available.

combat.weapons:
The feet and talons seize prey and the enormous arched bill tears it apart. Salmon are the base of the diet in many places, but the species also takes birds (ducks, gulls, ptarmigans, capercaillies), mammals (hares, young seals, and carnivores including sable, American mink, Arctic fox and red fox) and carrion. In the northern Sea of Okhotsk, birds dominated the diet of coastal pairs (73%) and especially pairs nesting near seabird colonies (91%). Along the Amur River, summer diet was about 80% fish, 10% birds and 5% mammals. In autumn, salmon that have died after spawning become a major food for eagles wintering on inland rivers that stay unfrozen.

This record shows a large raptor able to kill foxes and seabirds, but most of its food is fish, birds and carrion, not large mammals. Attack is therefore set below the harpy eagle's specialized mammal-killing system despite the Steller's greater mass.
weaknesses: No armor; still a light-boned bird on an absolute roster.
Heavy build and long wings reduce agility in tight spaces.
Diet dependent on fish, especially salmon and walleye pollock, which makes it vulnerable to food shortages.
Loses its advantage on the ground against larger terrestrial grapplers.

stonefish.name: Stonefish
stonefish.specimen: healthy representative adult, 35 cm and 1.5 kg, sex unspecified. No consistent size difference between the sexes was documented in the sources located.
stonefish.summary: The reef stonefish is a squat, rock-like Indo-Pacific fish that lies motionless on the seabed and gulps passing prey in a split second. Its 12–14 dorsal spines carry what is often called the most potent venom of any fish, turning any bite or careless step into a painful, sometimes deadly mistake. It is a near-perfect defender but has almost no way to attack anything larger than its mouth.
narrative: The stonefish is built around doing nothing, very well. It lies still on the reef floor, often partly buried, with a lumpy body that looks like a rock. Small fish and shrimp that drift too close are sucked into its large mouth in a split second. That is its whole offense, and it only works on prey small enough to swallow.

Its defense is another matter. Along its back sit 12 to 14 stout spines, each grooved and backed by a venom gland. When a predator bites down or a foot presses on the fish, the spines drive in and venom follows. The main toxin, stonustoxin, belongs to the same family as perforin, the protein immune cells use to punch holes in infected cells, and it does something similar to the victim's cells. Verrucotoxin adds a sharp drop in blood pressure.

On the absolute battle scale, the stonefish is an extreme specialist. It scores very high in Special and respectable in Defense, because any opponent that attacks it head-on is likely to be stung. But it cannot chase, it cannot deliver venom on purpose, and it is small and slow. An opponent that simply avoids touching the spines, or attacks from below or at range, faces little danger. It wins by being attacked, not by attacking.

sections.habitat: The reef stonefish lives across the Indo-Pacific: from the Red Sea and East Africa east to French Polynesia, north to the Ryukyu and Ogasawara islands, and south to Queensland, Australia. It rests on shallow reef, rubble and sandy bottoms, often partly buried.
sections.diet: It eats small fish and crustaceans such as shrimp, taken by ambush. As a well-hidden predator it has few natural enemies because the spines deter most fish predators.
sections.social: Solitary.
sections.reproduction: Details of reproduction and growth were not documented in the sources located in this pass. A chromosome-level genome has been assembled for the species, mainly to study its stonustoxin genes.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List category was not confirmed in this pass. The species has a very wide Indo-Pacific range and appears in fisheries and the aquarium trade, according to FishBase.
sections.features:
12–14 stout, grooved dorsal spines with venom glands.
Stonustoxin, a two-part toxin built like the perforin proteins of the immune system.
Verrucotoxin, a four-part toxin that lowers blood pressure.
Rock-like body and colour with long periods of stillness.
Large mouth for suction feeding.
sections.humanInteraction: Stings usually happen when people step on stonefish in shallow water or handle them. They are excruciatingly painful and occasionally fatal. Venom research has studied the blood, nerve, blood-pressure and cell-damaging effects of the venom, and the structure of stonustoxin has helped scientists understand how perforin-like pore-forming proteins work. It is also traded as a food fish and an aquarium fish.

funFacts: It is widely described as the most venomous fish in the world.
Its main toxin, stonustoxin, is built like perforin, a protein the human immune system uses to punch holes in infected cells.
Each dorsal spine has grooves that channel venom like a syringe.
Verrucotoxin, found in the reef stonefish, lowered blood pressure and was lethal in mice.
The heaviest published reef stonefish weighed 2.4 kg.
Its range stretches from the Red Sea to French Polynesia.
Its species name, verrucosa, means "warty" in Latin, fitting its lumpy skin.

abilities.name: Spine-Syringe Venom
abilities.description: 12–14 grooved dorsal spines, each with a venom gland at its base, inject venom when pressed. Stonustoxin punches holes in cell membranes and verrucotoxin drops blood pressure, making a bite or grab very costly for any attacker.

abilities.name: Lightning Suction Gulp
abilities.description: from total stillness, the stonefish opens its large mouth in a split second, sucking in small fish and shrimp before they can react.

traits.name: Most Venomous Fish
traits.description: the Australian Museum and the Aquarium of the Pacific describe the reef stonefish as the most venomous fish in the world; stings are excruciating and can occasionally be fatal to people.

traits.name: Living Rock Disguise
traits.description: its lumpy, rock-coloured body and habit of lying still, often half-buried, make it look like part of the reef floor.

combat.weapons: The stonefish has two separate weapon systems. For feeding, it uses a sudden suction gulp that engulfs small fish and shrimp that swim within reach. For defense, it relies on 12–14 venom-loaded dorsal spines that inject venom when an attacker presses on them. The venom is not used to catch prey.
weaknesses: Almost no mobility or pursuit ability.
No active way to deliver its venom.
Small body with limited toughness if the spines are avoided.
Useless out of water.

striped-hyena.name: Striped Hyena
striped-hyena.specimen: healthy mature adult male of about 38.0 kg, head-body about 110 cm, shoulder height about 72 cm. This sits in the upper part of the normal male range (26–41 kg) without using the heaviest reported individuals.
striped-hyena.summary: The striped hyena is a shaggy, 38 kg night scavenger of Africa and Asia whose bone-cracking jaws let it feed where others cannot. It walks long distances, bluffs with a raised mane and can play dead when overpowered. It will face down a lone leopard over a carcass, but it is slow and lacks the power of big cats or spotted hyenas.
narrative: The striped hyena is the most widespread and least understood of the bone-cracking hyenas. A mature male weighs around 38 kg, stands about 72 cm at the shoulder and has the family's sloping back, big pointed ears and a coat of grey or beige barred with black stripes. Along its spine runs a long mane that it raises when threatened, suddenly looking far larger than it is.

It spends the night walking. Serengeti animals covered up to 27 km in a night at a steady 2–4 km/h, checking bushes, holes and tree bases, remembering where fruit trees and rubbish dumps are and caching what they cannot eat. It follows wolves and big cats to their kills, and its massive premolars and powerful jaw muscles let it finish bones, hooves and tortoise shells that the killers leave behind.

In a fight it relies on that bite and on its nerve. It can kill a dog with a single bite and usually wins a one-on-one dispute over a carcass with a leopard, yet it is slow, lacks claws built for fighting, and will often choose to sham death rather than keep fighting a losing battle. On the absolute roster scale it sits below the heavier spotted hyena and the gray wolf in Attack, but its toughness, endurance and odd defensive tricks make it a stubborn opponent for medium-sized animals.

sections.habitat: Found from North and East Africa through the Middle East, Turkey and the Caucasus to Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent. It prefers open habitat, thorn scrub, semi-desert, rocky hills and ravines with caves, and avoids dense forest, true sand desert centres and high cold mountains; it has been recorded to about 3,300 m in Pakistan. It tolerates people well and has been recorded close to dense human settlements in Israel.
sections.diet: Mainly a scavenger of carrion, bones and the kills of wolves, big cats and other predators. It also eats insects, fruit such as dates, melons and Balanites fruit, human refuse and small vertebrates, and in Turkmenistan it digs out tortoises. In 2024 a camera trap in Kenya photographed an adult carrying a large honeycomb, the first documented case of honey eating by a hyena. It can drink fresh, soda or salt water, or meet its water needs from melons.
sections.social: Generally described as solitary, but with more social structure than that label suggests. Pairs and small groups occur, especially in the larger populations, and several animals may meet at a carcass. Scent marking with anal-gland paste ("hyena butter") on grass stalks, stones and tree trunks communicates presence.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is not seasonal. Litters are usually two to four cubs, born with eyes and ears closed and without the adult mane. Cubs stay with their mother until they forage with her at about 10–12 months, and older daughters may act as helpers. Sexual maturity comes at two to three years.
sections.conservation: Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List. The global population is estimated at under 10,000 mature individuals. Threats include deliberate and incidental persecution (in Arabia and North Africa it is baited, tracked and trapped as a supposed grave robber), poisoning (it readily takes strychnine bait laid for wolves or jackals, and was wiped out along Israel's Mediterranean coast by a 1918–1948 rabies poisoning campaign), a shrinking prey base, and a falling supply of carcasses as the large carnivores it scavenges from decline. Camera-trap work in southern Tanzania found it at low density (about 1.4 per 100 km²).
sections.features:
Bone-cracking cheek teeth and a high sagittal crest.
Erectile dorsal mane and black mid-back patch.
Death-feigning when overpowered.
Eversible anal pouch with a pungent secretion.
Blunt, non-retractable digging claws.
sections.humanInteraction: Usually timid around people. It has long been persecuted as a grave robber and livestock killer, and it carries a heavy load of folklore across its range. Rare attacks on people, mostly on sleeping children, have been reported historically in the Caucasus, Central Asia and India, and a 2024 case report described facial injuries from a striped hyena bite in northern India. Its actual share of livestock losses is small in most surveys.

funFacts: Its raised mane can make it look about 38% bigger.
When cornered by dogs it may play dead, even while being bitten.
One striped hyena was seen digging out three hibernating tortoises in two and a half hours.
A Kenyan camera trap caught one carrying a honeycomb, the first record of a hyena eating honey.
Serengeti animals walked 7–27 km a night looking for food.
In India it usually beats a lone leopard in a dispute over a carcass.
Older daughters help their mothers raise the next litter.

abilities.name: Bone-Splitter Jaws
abilities.description: a high sagittal crest, massive premolars and strong jaw muscles let it crack bones and tortoise shells. In a fight this makes a sustained bite on a limb unusually damaging for an animal of its size.

abilities.name: Dead-Hyena Bluff
abilities.description: when overpowered by dogs or dug out by people it can sham death for long periods, even when repeatedly bitten, then recover and slip away. It can also evert its anal pouch and release a pungent secretion.

traits.name: Mane of Warning
traits.description: a long dorsal mane and black mid-back patch are raised in aggressive encounters; ADW notes the raised mane makes it appear about 38% larger. Rivals bite the throat and legs rather than the mane.

traits.name: Wolf Follower
traits.description: across the Middle East and Central Asia much of its food comes from wolf kills, and on rare occasions striped hyenas have been recorded travelling with wolf packs.

combat.weapons: The striped hyena's weapon is its bite. A high sagittal crest anchors large jaw muscles, and massive premolars crack bones, carapaces and dried carcass parts that other carnivores leave behind. It is mainly a scavenger of kills made by wolves, big cats and people, plus livestock carrion, but it also kills smaller animals. Observed hunts were a simple chase and grab, and larger individuals kill prey by seizing the flank or groin. Livestock kills are mostly goats, sheep, dogs and poultry. In a Balochistan survey of 876 livestock killed by carnivores in a year, striped hyenas accounted for only 0.6%, against 66.3% for gray wolves, which illustrates how much less of an active killer it is than a wolf.
weaknesses: Only about 38 kg; outmatched by lions, tigers, spotted hyenas and wolf packs.
Slow, with no sprinting or fast turning ability.
No armor; bite is the only serious weapon.
Tends to feign death or retreat rather than press a fight it is losing.

sun-conure.name: Sun Conure
sun-conure.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 0.12 kg, 30.0 cm total length. Males are described as slightly heavier and more strongly built, with a longer tail and a larger head and bill.
sun-conure.summary: The Sun Conure is a 120 g golden parakeet from the edge of the Guiana Shield forests, loud, fast and highly social. Its hooked bill gives a sharp bite for its size and it flies and climbs nimbly, but it has no armor and little mass. It is now Endangered in the wild because of trapping for the pet trade.
narrative: The sun conure is a bright yellow and orange parakeet that lives in flocks along forest edges and palm groves in northern Brazil and Guyana. Flocks are quiet and hard to see while feeding, sometimes blending into red and yellow flowers, but explode into screeching as they take off. Birds climb through branches using the bill as a hook, hold food in their feet, and fly fast and straight between patches of forest, sometimes covering many miles in a day.

Its beauty nearly destroyed it. Tens of thousands were exported for the pet trade, and the wild population has fallen to perhaps 1,000–2,500 mature birds, while captive-bred sun conures fill homes around the world. Wild behavior is still poorly studied: nests with several adults and chicks of different ages hint at cooperative breeding, but much of its ecology is unknown.

In an absolute matchup the sun conure is a small, light bird whose best defenses are flight, its flock and loud alarm calls. Its bite is strong for its size and painful to a person, but against anything larger that can catch it, it has no protection and very little power.

sections.habitat: The sun conure lives in a small area of north-eastern South America: northern Roraima in Brazil, southern Guyana, and possibly southern Suriname and French Guiana, with unconfirmed reports from south-eastern Venezuela. It is found mostly below 1,200 m at the edges of humid foothill forest on the Guiana Shield, in palm groves and fruiting trees, crossing open savanna mainly when moving between forest patches. Birds once reported along the Amazon are now known to be the sulphur-breasted parakeet.
sections.diet: It eats fruit, flowers, berries, blossoms, seeds, nuts and insects, including red cactus fruit, Malpighia berries and legume pods (WPT; Wikipedia). Flocks near Karasabai often feed on monkey-brush flowers. It sometimes raids crops.
sections.social: Very social, usually in flocks of about 15–30 birds, larger where fruit is plentiful (WPT). Birds rest, feed each other, preen and bathe together through the day. Pairs are monogamous.
sections.reproduction: Nests are in tree cavities, including hollows in Mauritia flexuosa palms. Clutches are 3–4 eggs, incubated by the female for about 23–27 days, with both parents feeding the chicks. Young fledge at 7–8 weeks and reach sexual maturity at about 2 years. Nests with several adults suggest cooperative breeding.
sections.conservation: The sun conure is listed as Endangered by the IUCN and on CITES Appendix II. WPT gives a world population of about 1,000–2,499 mature birds and decreasing. Trapping for the pet trade caused the collapse: more than 20,000 birds were reportedly exported to Singapore alone in 2005–2006 (Wikipedia, citing BirdLife), and numbers in Roraima fell by 50–79% over three generations. Guyana and Suriname are the only Neotropical countries that still allow capture and trade of native parrots (Romero-Vidal et al. 2022). In its Guyana stronghold, easing trapping pressure has allowed early signs of recovery.
sections.features:
Golden-yellow and orange adult plumage; green juveniles.
Very loud calls for a small bird.
Uses the bill as a climbing aid and the feet like hands.
Possible cooperative breeding.
sections.humanInteraction: The sun conure is one of the most popular pet parrots, and far more now live in homes than in the wild. It is loud, curious and affectionate with familiar people but can be territorial with visitors. Import bans on wild birds by the United States (1992), Australia (1995) and the European Union (2005) have shifted most pet supply to captive breeding, but poaching of wild birds continues.

funFacts: Far more sun conures now live as pets than in the wild, where fewer than 2,500 mature birds remain.
Young sun conures are mostly green and take up to two years to turn gold.
A lost sun conure's screams can carry for hundreds of metres to find its flock.
Feeding flocks almost disappear against red and yellow monkey-brush flowers.
More than 20,000 were reportedly exported to Singapore in just 2005–2006.
Wild nests sometimes hold several adults and chicks of different ages.

abilities.name: Hookbill Nip
abilities.description: a short, deep hooked bill gives a sharp, painful bite far stronger than a songbird of the same size could manage, used to defend the nest and deter handlers.

abilities.name: Flock Siren
abilities.description: flocks fly in with loud screeching calls, and a separated bird's high-pitched screams carry for hundreds of metres, keeping the flock together and warning of danger.

traits.name: Golden Plumage
traits.description: adults are golden-yellow with orange face and belly, but juveniles are mostly green and take up to two years to colour up; feeding flocks blend in against red and yellow flowers.

traits.name: Cooperative Nesters
traits.description: wild nests have been found holding several adults and chicks of different ages, a sign that sun conures may raise young cooperatively.

combat.weapons: The hooked bill is the only weapon. Parrots of this size bite far harder than other birds of similar mass; a related 85 g parakeet in the same genus measured about 54 N (Harrison et al. 2025). A sun conure can deliver a painful, bleeding bite to a hand, and hand-reared birds can be aggressive towards strangers (Wikipedia). But this is a 120 g bird that eats fruit, seeds, flowers and some insects, and its bite is a defensive tool, not a way to kill.
weaknesses: About 120 g in absolute mass.
No armor, fragile flying body.
Small bill with no measured force.
Heavily trapped; wild numbers are now very small.

sydney-funnel-web-spider.name: Sydney Funnel-web Spider
sydney-funnel-web-spider.specimen: healthy mature adult male, about 2.5 cm body length, estimated about 2 g live mass, with fangs about 6 mm long.
sydney-funnel-web-spider.summary: The Sydney funnel-web is a burrowing Australian spider whose wandering males carry one of the few spider venoms known to kill healthy adult humans. Its δ-hexatoxin makes nerves fire uncontrollably, and it bites repeatedly from a rearing stance. At about 2 g it is physically tiny, and many non-primate animals resist its venom far better than people do.
narrative: The Sydney funnel-web is a spider whose danger is aimed, almost by accident, at primates. Its lethal toxin, δ-hexatoxin-Ar1a, holds sodium channels open so that nerves fire over and over. Humans and other primates are exquisitely sensitive to this; many other animals are much less so. Before antivenom arrived in 1981, thirteen deaths were attributed to funnel-web bites, and in every case where the spider was sexed, it was a male.

That detail shapes the canonical fighter. Adult females are bigger but sedentary, spending years in a silk-lined burrow. Males mature in about their fifth year, leave their burrows for good, and spend the warm months walking at night in search of females, sometimes into gardens and houses. Their venom is several times more toxic than the female's, and their fangs, about 6 mm long, strike downward like picks. When cornered the spider rears up, shows its fangs, and once it bites, it holds on and bites again.

On an absolute roster the funnel-web is still a 2 g animal. It cannot absorb a blow, has poor eyesight and is slow compared with hunting spiders. Most confirmed bites of this species were not severe, and against birds, reptiles or non-primate mammals its venom is far less decisive. The profile therefore pairs a very high Special with low Attack and minimal Defense: a specialist weapon whose lethality depends heavily on who it bites.

sections.habitat: A. robustus lives in the Sydney region of New South Wales, Australia, in moist forest, bushland and suburban gardens. Burrows are lined with silk and placed in sheltered, damp ground. Wandering males are the ones people meet most often, during the warmer months (November to April).
sections.diet: An ambush predator of ground-active arthropods and other small animals that touch the silk around its burrow entrance. It spends daylight inside the burrow and hunts at night. A species-level diet study was not located in this research pass.
sections.social: Solitary. Females are highly sedentary and are thought to spend their entire lives in a single burrow. Mature males abandon their burrows permanently to search for females. A wild tracking study found males moved at night, often in zigzag paths, and were in new locations on about half of daily resightings.
sections.reproduction: Both sexes usually mature in about their fifth year. Mating typically happens in late summer to early autumn. The male carries a mating spur on his second pair of legs. After the breeding season males die, while females can live for more than eight years and breed again.
sections.conservation: No IUCN Red List assessment of A. robustus was found in this research pass, so its status is treated as Not Evaluated. It remains common around Sydney. The 2023 split into three species means older records need re-checking before they are applied to A. robustus in the narrow sense.
sections.features:
δ-hexatoxin-Ar1a, a sodium-channel toxin to which primates are exquisitely sensitive.
Large downward-striking mygalomorph fangs, about 6 mm in adult males.
Male venom 4–6 times more toxic than female venom.
Silk-lined burrow with entrance silk that transmits vibration.
Male mating spur on the second pair of legs.
sections.humanInteraction: Thirteen deaths have been attributed to funnel-web bites, all before the 1981 introduction of antivenom, with none since. Antivenom brings a complete response in almost all confirmed cases. δ-hexatoxins are also studied for their action on sodium channels.

funFacts: Male venom is 4–6 times more toxic than female venom.
No one has died from a funnel-web bite since antivenom arrived in 1981.
In a review of confirmed funnel-web bites, antivenom produced a complete response in 97% of cases.
Tracked males moved to a new spot on about half of daily checks, walking in zigzags at night.
The gene for the lethal toxin has no introns, a finding that made the title of the study that sequenced it.
In 2023 scientists split the "Sydney funnel-web" into three species.
Adult males carry a mating spur on their second pair of legs.

abilities.name: Primate-Killer Toxin
abilities.description: δ-hexatoxin-Ar1a slows sodium-channel inactivation so nerves fire uncontrollably. Primates are exquisitely sensitive, which makes this one of the few spider venoms that has killed healthy adult humans, although many non-primates are far less affected.

abilities.name: Rear-and-Grip Strike
abilities.description: the spider rears onto its hind legs with fangs raised, then drives its downward-striking fangs in, holds on and bites repeatedly. This converts a small venom dose into multiple injections.

traits.name: Deadlier Wandering Male
traits.description: the smaller male's venom is 4–6 times more toxic than the female's, and every sex-identified fatal bite came from a male. Males leave their burrows for good to search for mates at night.

traits.name: Silk-Lined Burrow Ambusher
traits.description: females spend their whole lives in one silk-lined burrow among logs, rocks or garden soil, using the entrance silk to detect prey and threats.

combat.weapons: Large downward-striking fangs deliver venom containing δ-hexatoxin-Ar1a. The toxin keeps sodium channels open for longer, so nerves fire uncontrollably. The gene for the lethal toxin has been sequenced and is intronless. In primates this can cause severe envenoming; in other animals the effect is weaker, which makes the weapon partly target-specific.
weaknesses: Tiny absolute mass and negligible raw force.
Poor eyesight.
Venom far more effective on primates than on many other animals.
Males are exposed and short-lived once they leave the burrow.
goodMatchups: Insects and other small ground-active animals.
Primates small enough to be seriously affected before they can crush the spider.
badMatchups: Birds, reptiles and non-primate mammals that are less sensitive to the venom and much larger.
Armoured or thick-coated animals that block the fangs.
Opponents that attack from range or from above.

syrian-hamster.name: Syrian Hamster
syrian-hamster.specimen: healthy adult female of about 140 g (0.14 kg) in pet or laboratory condition, not an obese pet and not one of the heavier breeder-show animals.
syrian-hamster.summary: The Syrian hamster is a 140 g solitary burrower with enormous cheek pouches, ever-growing incisors that can bite through glass and a fierce temper toward its own kind. Endangered in its small Syrian-Turkish homeland but found worldwide as a pet, it is a determined fighter at its own scale and a negligible one against anything larger.
narrative: The Syrian hamster is a small steppe rodent with an outsized reputation. In the wild it lives alone in a deep burrow in the farmland around Aleppo, slipping out in daylight for short foraging trips and stuffing seeds into cheek pouches that stretch back past its shoulders. Burrows are spaced far apart because adult hamsters do not tolerate each other, and the female, the larger sex, is the more dangerous of the two.

Its combat profile follows from that temperament. A hamster fights with its incisors, which are sharp and strong enough to chew through glass, and one fight primes it to attack again quickly. Against another hamster, a mouse or an insect this makes it formidable. Against a cat, fox, weasel, owl or snake it has nothing but speed to its burrow, and on the absolute ABS scale its 140 g body gives it almost no attack or defense.

The species also has a remarkable history. Every pet and laboratory Syrian hamster traces to a few siblings captured in 1930, while the wild population has shrunk to the point of being listed as Endangered. The pet on a child's desk is one of the world's most familiar rodents; its wild counterpart is one of the least studied.

sections.habitat: The wild range is a small arid region of northern Syria and southern Turkey around the Aleppo plateau, originally open steppe and now mostly farmland. Burrows are often in legume fields or near irrigation wells, at about 280–300 m elevation, in a climate of hot summer days, cold nights and about 336 mm of rain a year. As a pet and laboratory animal it lives worldwide.
sections.diet: Omnivorous: seeds, grain, nuts, green plants and insects, including ants and flies. Hamsters are larder hoarders, carrying food in their cheek pouches to underground stores. They disperse seeds and their abandoned burrows are used by other animals. Their rapid breeding lets wild populations withstand heavy predation.
sections.social: Solitary and territorial. Adults meet only to mate, mark territories with flank-gland secretions and keep burrows far apart. In captivity adults must usually be housed alone.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is fast, with short gestation and litters of several pups; females can be dangerous to males and will eat dead young. Adults live about two to three years in captivity and less in the wild. In cold conditions (below about 5–8 °C) hamsters enter torpor or hibernation-like states but do not fatten beforehand and must wake periodically to eat stored food.
sections.conservation: The wild species is Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022 assessment), threatened by habitat loss to agriculture and deliberate persecution as a crop pest. The domestic form is abundant.
sections.features:
Cheek pouches reaching past the shoulders.
Paired flank scent glands used for territorial marking.
Ever-growing incisors that can bite through glass.
Torpor in cold conditions.
Diurnal surface activity in the wild, nocturnal activity in captivity.
sections.humanInteraction: The Syrian hamster is the most common pet hamster in Britain and the United States and an important laboratory animal, used in research on circadian rhythms and on infections including SARS-CoV-2. Welfare research shows that hamsters given 40–80 cm of bedding dig burrows like wild ones and largely stop gnawing the cage bars.

funFacts: Wild female hamsters in Turkey were almost entirely active by day, the opposite of laboratory hamsters, spending only about 87 minutes a day above ground.
All pet and laboratory Syrian hamsters trace to a mother and litter dug up near Aleppo in 1930.
Full cheek pouches can more than double the width of a hamster's head and shoulders.
Veterinarians warn that Syrian hamsters readily bite through glass water tubes.
In the species the female is the larger and more aggressive sex.
Two expeditions in 1997 and 1999 found 30 wild burrows, and none of the inhabited ones held more than one adult.

abilities.name: Primed Aggression
abilities.description: after one attack on an intruder, a resident hamster attacks a second intruder faster and more often for about 30 minutes, a measured effect linked to the amygdala. Combined with the female's larger size and readiness to fight, it makes the hamster a relentless close-range biter against animals its own size.

abilities.name: Glass-Biting Incisors
abilities.description: ever-growing chisel incisors powerful enough that veterinarians warn hamsters readily bite through glass water tubes. This is its only damaging weapon and it requires body contact.

traits.name: Mister Saddlebags
traits.description: its cheek pouches run from the lips back past the shoulders and, when filled, more than double the width of the head and shoulders; the local Arabic name translates roughly as "mister saddlebags".

traits.name: Endangered in the Wild, Everywhere as a Pet
traits.description: the wild species is listed as Endangered and survives in a small area of northern Syria and southern Turkey, while every pet and laboratory Syrian hamster traces to siblings captured near Aleppo in 1930.

combat.weapons: The hamster's only real weapon is a bite from sharp, ever-growing incisors, driven by jaw muscles strong enough to chew through glass. It uses this bite freely against other hamsters: the species is solitary and highly territorial, and attacks between adults are commonplace. In a laboratory "resident-intruder" test, a single attack primes a resident hamster to attack a second intruder faster and more often for about half an hour. At 140 g, however, the bite can only seriously injure animals of similar or smaller size.
weaknesses: Tiny absolute mass and reach.
No armor or thick hide.
Poor sustained speed in the open.
Cannot deter any medium-sized predator.

takin.name: Takin
takin.specimen: healthy mature bull of about 320 kg, 120 cm at the shoulder and 210 cm head-body length, with full horns. This is a prime bull inside the commonly reported 300–350 kg male range, not an exceptional animal.
takin.summary: The takin is a stocky, 320 kg mountain bovid from the Himalayas and western China, with thick swept-back horns, a bulbous nose and an oily, weatherproof coat. It prefers to hide in dense cover after an alarm cough, but its bulk, horns and sure-footed climbing make it a tough, well-rounded mountain brawler.
narrative: The takin looks assembled from parts: the horns of a wildebeest, the nose of a moose, the bulk of a small bison and the climbing habits of a goat. A mature bull weighs around 320 kg and stands up to 1.4 m tall, with a heavy head, a deep chest, short strong legs and big spurred hooves that grip rocky slopes. Its long coat, thick and shaggy in winter, is slicked with an oily secretion that sheds the rain and fog of its mountain forests.

Takins spend the warm months high on the slopes in large herds, climbing to the tree line above 4,300 m, and move down into forested valleys for winter. They feed at dawn and dusk, gather for days at salt licks, and when danger appears one animal coughs loudly and the herd crashes into thick undergrowth and lies down out of sight. Bears, wolves, leopards and dholes are their only natural enemies.

On the ABS scale the takin sits beside the musk-ox as a mid-weight mountain and cold-climate bovid. It is slightly less heavily armed than the musk-ox, which has a fused horn boss and a practiced defensive ring, but it is more agile on steep ground. It remains far below heavy bovids such as the gaur or water buffalo in size and power, and far below the mountain goat in climbing agility.

sections.habitat: Forested valleys, bamboo thickets and rocky, grass-covered alpine zones from about 1,000 to 4,500 m in Bhutan, northeastern India (Arunachal Pradesh), Myanmar and central and southwestern China, including the Qinling Mountains of Shaanxi where the golden takin lives.
sections.diet: Browses and grazes leaves, grasses, bamboo shoots and flowers, feeding mostly in the early morning and late afternoon. Salt is an important part of the diet, and groups may stay at a mineral deposit for several days.
sections.social: Family groups of about 20, gathering into summer herds of up to 300; bulls are mostly solitary outside the rut. Herds are made up of cows, kids, subadults and young males.
sections.reproduction: Mating takes place in July and August. After about eight months, a single kid of 5–7 kg is born; it can follow its mother within three days, eats solid food by about two months and grows horns at about six months. Maturity comes at two to two and a half years.
sections.conservation: Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and considered Endangered in China. Threats are overhunting and habitat destruction; takin horns have been sold openly in markets in Myanmar, with 89 sets seen during surveys from 1999 to 2006. A 2010 study of Mishmi takins suggested the species is especially vulnerable to climate change.
sections.features:
Horns in both sexes that sweep out, back and up from the midline of the head.
Long, arched, swollen-looking nose.
Oily, weatherproof skin secretion.
Two-toed hooves with strongly developed spurs.
Long double coat, up to 24 cm under the head in winter.
sections.humanInteraction: The takin is the national animal of Bhutan, and takins are kept in a reserve at Thimphu. It is hunted illegally for meat and horns in parts of its range, and its horns turn up in wildlife markets.

funFacts: Its nose earned it George Schaller's description of a "bee-stung moose".
The takin is Bhutan's national animal.
Its skin oozes an oily substance that works like a raincoat in mountain storms.
Takins stand on their hind legs to reach leaves more than 3 m up.
A takin sleeps with its head resting on its outstretched front legs, like a dog.
Summer herds can reach 300 animals high on the mountain slopes.
Zoo takins have jumped 1.8 m straight up from a standing start.

abilities.name: Cough and Vanish
abilities.description: one loud alarm cough sends the whole herd into dense undergrowth, where the animals lie down and disappear from view.

abilities.name: Oil-Slick Coat
abilities.description: the skin secretes an oily, bitter-smelling substance that sheds rain and fog, over a double coat with air-filled overcoat hairs for insulation.

traits.name: Bee-Stung Moose Face
traits.description: a massive head with a long, arched, swollen-looking nose that led biologist George Schaller to compare the takin to a "bee-stung moose".

traits.name: Mountain Ox-Goat
traits.description: one of the largest and stockiest members of the goat and sheep subfamily (Caprinae), with the bulk of a small ox, standing up to 1.4 m tall yet able to climb and to feed standing on its hind legs.

combat.weapons: The takin fights with thick, ridged horns set on a massive head and a stocky 320 kg body. Bulls spar head-to-head for dominance in the summer rut and bellow during fights. The horns curve outward and back, so the most dangerous use is a butting, tossing strike: in a documented case of maternal infanticide among captive golden takins, a mother tossed her newborn into the air with her head and horns, leaving punctures in its belly. The horns are shorter and less of a spear than a sable's or an oryx's, and the takin lacks the fused boss of a musk-ox or buffalo.
weaknesses: No armor; body protection is mostly hair.
Horns shorter and less lethal than a buffalo's or oryx's.
Heavy build limits sustained speed on open ground.
Tends to hide rather than confront.

tibetan-mastiff.name: Tibetan Mastiff
tibetan-mastiff.specimen: healthy adult male working Tibetan Mastiff, 55.0 kg, 70.0 cm at the withers.
tibetan-mastiff.summary: The Tibetan Mastiff is a massive, heavily maned guardian dog from the Tibetan Plateau. It fights with a strong bite, heavy bone and a padded neck, and it carries wolf-shared gene variants that help it keep working in thin mountain air. It is slow and unarmored, and it is badly outmatched by bears and big cats.
narrative: The Tibetan Mastiff is the guardian dog of the roof of the world. For generations it watched over herders' camps, flocks, villages and monasteries on the Tibetan Plateau, often working alone and making its own decisions. A fit working male stands about 70 cm at the shoulder and weighs around 55 kg, though show and status dogs bred during China's mastiff boom were often much heavier and more heavily coated.

Its most unusual feature is invisible. Genetic studies show Tibetan Mastiffs and other highland dogs carry versions of the EPAS1 and HBB genes that match those of Tibetan gray wolves and came into the dogs through interbreeding. These variants are linked to coping with the low oxygen of the plateau, so at 4,000 m the mastiff keeps working when a lowland animal would flag. Its heavy mane is the other practical asset, padding the neck that wolves and other dogs aim for.

In a fight it is a straightforward guardian: deep bays, a charge, and a heavy bite. It is less agile than the Kangal and far less athletic than a wild wolf, so it wins by mass and persistence, not speed. Groups of abandoned mastiffs have driven snow leopards off their kills, but that is teamwork against a smaller cat. On its own, it is a strong medium-sized fighter that stays well below bears, lions and tigers.

sections.habitat: Native to the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayan highlands, including Tibet, Qinghai and neighboring mountain regions, where it guarded herders' camps, livestock, villages and monasteries. Now kept worldwide as a guardian and companion.
sections.diet: A domestic dog fed by its owners. Free-ranging abandoned mastiffs on the plateau scavenge, take livestock and wildlife, and steal kills from other predators.
sections.ecology: In traditional herding, the mastiff guarded livestock and camps against wolves and other threats. Abandoned free-ranging mastiffs have become an ecological problem, competing with snow leopards, attacking wildlife and people, and spreading disease, according to conservation and news reports.
sections.social: Kept singly or in small numbers as guardians, strongly bonded to its household and aloof with strangers. Free-ranging dogs form groups.
sections.reproduction: Females have a single estrus per year, usually in late autumn, even when kept at low altitude in mild climates. Most pups are born in December and January. The breed matures slowly.
sections.conservation: Not applicable as a wild species; it is a Domesticated breed. Its main conservation relevance is negative: abandoned free-ranging mastiffs are considered a potential threat to snow leopards on the plateau.
sections.features:
Wolf-shared EPAS1 and HBB gene variants linked to low-oxygen tolerance.
Heavy double coat with a thick neck mane.
Massive head and heavy bone.
Single breeding season per year.
Deep, booming bark.
sections.humanInteraction: Guardian and status dog. In China, a price boom in the 2000s was followed by a market collapse around 2012, leaving many dogs abandoned on the plateau. Free-ranging mastiffs have mauled people and preyed on wildlife. Owners need space, secure fencing and training.

funFacts: Tibetan Mastiffs carry high-altitude gene variants that match those of Tibetan gray wolves.
Females come into season only once a year, unlike most dogs.
Groups of abandoned mastiffs have been seen driving snow leopards off their blue sheep kills.
Researchers GPS-collared 16 stray mastiffs in Sanjiangyuan to study their effect on snow leopards.
Its bark is often described as a deep, foghorn-like bay.
Traditionally it guarded nomadic herders' camps and monasteries, often working on its own.

abilities.name: Thin-Air Engine
abilities.description: carries EPAS1 and HBB gene variants shared with Tibetan gray wolves, linked to functioning in low-oxygen air. At high altitude it keeps working when lowland opponents tire.

abilities.name: Mane Guard
abilities.description: the heavy neck and shoulder mane pads the area most canid and felid opponents target, blunting the first bites of a fight.

traits.name: Foghorn Bay
traits.description: a deep, booming bark used on night guard, a key part of its deterrence display.

traits.name: Single Yearly Season
traits.description: unlike most dog breeds, females come into season only once a year, usually in late autumn, with most pups born in December and January.

combat.weapons: A single weapon system: a large canid bite on a heavy, broad head and massive neck. The Tibetan Mastiff guards by presence, deep baying barks and charges, and bites intruders that keep coming. It has no grappling forelimbs and no specialized killing technique.
weaknesses: Heavy and relatively slow; poor at pursuit and quick turns.
One close-range weapon; no armor beneath the coat.
The heavy coat is a burden in heat.
A single dog lacks the group advantage that lets free-ranging mastiffs bully other predators.
Far below bears, big cats and large ungulates in absolute power.

titan-beetle.name: Titan Beetle
titan-beetle.specimen: healthy adult male, 15.5 cm long and 37.5 g, matching the wild male collected in French Guiana in January 2019 and measured in the first comprehensive physiological study of the species (Insects, 2020). This is a single measured individual, used because no population averages exist.
titan-beetle.summary: The titan beetle of the Amazon is one of the largest beetles on Earth, reaching almost 17 cm. It defends itself with a loud hiss and sharp mandibles said to snap pencils, but adults cannot eat and live only a few weeks on stored reserves. Huge for an insect, it is still tiny and short on stamina in any battle with vertebrates.
narrative: The titan beetle is a giant among insects. A wild male measured in 2019 was 15.5 cm long and weighed 37.5 g, and the largest reliable specimen reached 16.7 cm. It lives in the lowland rainforests of northern South America, where adults fly at night through old-growth forest and are sometimes drawn to lights.

It is also a mystery. Its larvae have never been found, though they are thought to grow inside dead wood for years. The adult stage is a short final chapter: the gut is degenerated, the fat body almost gone, and the beetle lives on reserves stored in its flight muscles. When threatened it hisses and bites with short, curved mandibles that can cut skin.

On the absolute battle scale, the titan beetle gets the highest Attack and Defense of the beetles in this batch because of its sharp jaws and heavy armour, but those scores remain very low next to vertebrates. Its biggest weakness is stamina: an animal that cannot eat cannot keep fighting, and anything larger than a small mammal can overpower it.

sections.habitat: Lowland tropical rainforest of northern South America: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, the Guianas and north-central Brazil. Its prime habitat is old-growth Amazon and Guiana forest with large trees and dead wood.
sections.diet: Adults do not feed. Larvae are thought to feed inside dead wood, possibly for several years, but have never been found, so their diet and development are inferred rather than observed. Adults are active at night, and males are drawn to lights.
sections.social: Solitary.
sections.reproduction: Adults emerge, search for mates at night and live only a few weeks on stored reserves. Males track females by scent using dense antennal sensilla. Nothing is known directly about the larvae or pupae.
sections.conservation: Not Evaluated: no IUCN Red List assessment was located in this pass. The species depends on old-growth rainforest with large dead trees, and specimens are prized by collectors.
sections.features:
One of the longest beetles in the world, up to 16.7 cm.
Sharp, curved mandibles.
Defensive hissing by stridulation.
Non-feeding adult with a degenerated gut.
Flight muscles stocked with storage fat rich in oleic acid.
Antennae packed with scent-detecting sensilla.
sections.humanInteraction: Handling a titan beetle can earn a painful, skin-cutting bite. Specimens are valuable to collectors, and night-time light traps are the main way scientists obtain adults. The 2020 study was one of the first to examine the species' biochemistry and anatomy in detail.

funFacts: The largest reliably measured titan beetle was 16.7 cm long.
A wild male from French Guiana weighed 37.5 g, about as much as a large mouse.
Its larvae have never been found.
Adults do not eat; their gut is degenerated and they live on stored fat.
Its jaws are said to snap pencils in half.
It hisses when threatened.
The scientists who studied the 2019 male caught it when it flew to a light at 1:30 in the morning.

abilities.name: Pencil-Snapping Mandibles
abilities.description: short, curved, sharp jaws that are reported to snap pencils and cut into human flesh, used to defend itself when grabbed.

abilities.name: Warning Hiss
abilities.description: when threatened, the adult rubs body parts together to make a loud hiss that warns predators before it bites.

traits.name: Giant of the Insect World
traits.description: one of the largest beetles known, with a reliable record of 16.7 cm and a measured wild male of 15.5 cm and 37.5 g.

traits.name: Adult That Never Eats
traits.description: the adult gut is degenerated and it lives entirely on reserves stored during its hidden larval life; its larvae have never been found.

combat.weapons: The primary weapon is a pair of short, curved, sharp mandibles, used defensively; they are reported to cut human skin. The secondary defense is a loud hiss that warns off predators. It has no venom, sting, horn or chemical spray.
weaknesses: Slow and clumsy on the ground.
Cannot feed as an adult, so it tires and cannot recover.
No venom or chemical defense.
Tiny in absolute terms despite being a giant among insects.

vampire-bat.name: Vampire Bat
vampire-bat.specimen: healthy adult female, 0.035 kg (35 g, unfed), 8.5 cm head-body length, wingspan about 35–40 cm.
vampire-bat.summary: The common vampire bat is a 35 g blood specialist that finds warm skin with a heat-sensing nose, cuts it with razor incisors and keeps it bleeding with anticoagulant saliva. It can even run and leap into flight from the ground, but it has almost no fighting power and survives by stealth and escape.
narrative: The common vampire bat is one of the most specialized mammals on Earth. It lives on nothing but blood, which it takes from sleeping animals, most often cattle, across the American tropics and subtropics. A typical adult weighs about 35 grams and could sit in the palm of a hand, yet it feeds on animals that can outweigh it more than ten thousand times.

Every part of its feeding method is precise. Heat-sensing pits on its nose, powered by a heat receptor tuned to about 30 °C, pick out the warm spots where blood vessels lie close to the skin. It shaves the hair, cuts a tiny wound with enamel-free incisors kept razor-sharp, and laps the blood while its saliva's anticoagulants stop the wound from clotting. Its kidneys start shedding water within minutes so it can carry a meal worth more than half its body weight back into the air.

It also moves in ways other bats cannot. On the ground it runs with a bounding gait powered by its wings, and it can spring straight up into flight in a fraction of a second if a host stirs. Back at the roost, bats that fed share blood with hungry partners, a famous case of reciprocal help. None of this makes it a fighter. In any real battle it would be crushed or eaten; its strengths are in stealth, senses and escape, and its real-world danger comes from the rabies it carries to livestock.

sections.habitat: Found from Mexico through Central America to much of South America, in tropical and subtropical forests, dry scrub, savanna and farmland. It roosts in caves, hollow trees, old mines, wells and buildings, and is most common where livestock are plentiful.
sections.diet: Exclusively blood (sanguivory), mostly from mammals. Cattle are its preferred prey in many areas; horses, pigs, wild mammals and occasionally birds and people are also bitten.
sections.ecology: The spread of cattle ranching has given vampire bats an abundant food supply. As the main reservoir of rabies for livestock in Latin America, the species has major economic and public health impact, and management programs target it in many countries.
sections.social: Colonial. Females form long-term social bonds within roosts and groom and share food with regular partners. Food sharing depends on past reciprocal help and on kinship.
sections.reproduction: Females usually raise a single pup with a long period of maternal care, including regurgitated blood before the pup can forage. Wild lifespan is around 9 years; a captive individual reached 29.2 years.
sections.conservation: Widely reported as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List because of its large range and abundance; the IUCN assessment page itself was not retrieved in this run. Locally, populations are culled to control rabies in livestock.
sections.features:
Infrared-sensing nose pits with TRPV1 channels tuned to about 30 °C.
Enamel-free, razor-sharp upper incisors.
Anticoagulant saliva (draculin, desmoteplase, desmolaris).
Forelimb-driven running and vertical jump takeoff.
Kidneys that shed water rapidly during a blood meal.
sections.humanInteraction: Vampire bats occasionally bite people, and they are the main source of rabies outbreaks in Latin American livestock, with about 450 outbreaks reported per year on average. Their saliva has inspired medical research: desmoteplase was tested as a treatment for ischemic stroke.

funFacts: A vampire bat can drink blood equal to more than half its body weight in about 30 minutes.
It starts urinating within minutes of beginning to feed to shed water from the meal.
It can run on the ground using its wings as front legs, at up to about 1.2 m/s.
It launches from the ground with a vertical jump that reaches 2.4 m/s in under 30 milliseconds.
Its nose senses heat using a pain receptor retuned to trigger at about 30 °C.
Well-fed bats regurgitate blood to hungry roost-mates, even unrelated ones.
A captive vampire bat lived for 29.2 years.

abilities.name: Heat-Seeking Nose
abilities.description: pit organs on the nose detect infrared heat through TRPV1 channels tuned to about 30 °C, letting the bat find warm blood vessels close to the skin in darkness. It is one of the very few mammals with infrared sensing.

abilities.name: Anticoagulant Bite
abilities.description: enamel-free, razor-sharp incisors cut a small wound, and saliva containing draculin, desmoteplase and desmolaris keeps it bleeding while the bat feeds.

traits.name: Running Takeoff
traits.description: one of very few bats that can run, using a forelimb-driven bounding gait, and it launches into flight from the ground with an explosive vertical jump.

traits.name: Blood-Sharing Bonds
traits.description: well-fed bats regurgitate blood to hungry roost-mates, including unrelated partners, a classic documented case of reciprocal food sharing.

combat.weapons: The vampire bat's "weapon" is a surgical incision, not a damaging bite. It lands near a sleeping host, often a cow or horse, walks or hops to a spot where blood vessels run close to the skin, shaves away hair, and cuts a small wound with its razor incisors. Saliva containing anticoagulants keeps the wound bleeding while the bat laps. The goal is to feed without waking the host, not to injure it.
weaknesses: Tiny mass and fragile wings.
No damaging weapon; its bite is designed not to be felt.
Needs to feed almost every night; starves quickly.
Poor in cold climates and in daylight.
Any awake, alert opponent of real size can crush it.

water-buffalo.name: Water Buffalo
water-buffalo.specimen: healthy mature adult male (bull) of about 900 kg and 170 cm shoulder height, with full-grown horns. This is a representative wild bull, not a record animal.
water-buffalo.summary: The wild water buffalo is a heavy, wetland-dwelling Asian bovid armed with the widest-spreading horns of any living bovid. Bulls near a tonne charge readily, hook with crescent horns and hold their ground against tigers, and the species is most dangerous in the mud and water where it lives.
narrative: A wild water buffalo bull is built for the floodplain. Standing around 1.7 m at the shoulder and weighing close to a tonne, it spends much of its day wallowing in mud and water, grazing reeds and grasses along rivers and swamps. Its horns are its signature: thick at the base and sweeping out and back in a vast crescent, they can reach about 2 m along the outer edge, more than any other living bovid.

In a fight the buffalo relies on mass, horns and temper. Bulls are reported to be more aggressive than cows and sometimes attack without provocation, while cows with calves confront tigers directly. The backward sweep of the horns means the buffalo hooks and tosses rather than stabbing forward, but a charge from a 900 kg animal can break bones regardless. Tigers do kill buffalo, including adults, and a classic study documented in detail how they seize the throat or nape, yet tigers are occasionally killed in return.

The wild buffalo is now Endangered, with only a few thousand left, most of them in Assam. Domestic buffalo bred from it far outnumber the wild form and are one of Asia's key farm animals, and hybridisation with them is a direct threat to the wild form. For ABS purposes the wild buffalo sits alongside the Cape Buffalo and Bison: similar in raw power and attack, less agile than Bison, and with a real terrain advantage in wetlands that neither of the others has.

sections.habitat: Wild water buffalo live in floodplain grasslands, marshes, swamps and riverine forest. The species survives in India, Nepal, Bhutan, Thailand, Cambodia and Myanmar, with the great majority in Assam, especially Kaziranga National Park. Its former range was far wider across South and Southeast Asia.
sections.diet: They graze grasses, reeds and sedges and eat aquatic and floodplain vegetation. Wallowing and grazing shape wetland vegetation, and buffalo are an important large prey for tigers where the two occur together.
sections.social: Cows and young form herds that bunch and face threats together; bulls live in small bachelor groups or alone and join herds to breed. Cows with calves are strongly defensive.
sections.reproduction: Females usually bear a single calf. Calves are the main target of tigers and depend on herd defense. Specific gestation and longevity data for the wild form were not captured in this research pass.
sections.conservation: Endangered on the IUCN Red List, a status held since 1986, with fewer than 4,000 mature individuals. The global population has been estimated at about 3,400, of which about 3,100 (91%) live in India, mostly in Assam. Threats are habitat loss and degradation, hunting, disease from livestock and hybridisation with domestic buffalo.
sections.features:
Widest horn spread of any living bovid.
Horns in both sexes, heavy at the base and crescent-shaped.
Heavy build suited to mud, marsh and water.
Strong wallowing and swimming behavior.
Aggressive group and calf defense against tigers.
sections.humanInteraction: The domestic water buffalo, bred from wild stock, is one of the most important livestock animals in South and Southeast Asia, used for milk, meat and draught work. Domestic and feral buffalo mix with wild herds and spread disease, and genetic studies of the wild buffalo mitochondrial genome are used to assess hybridisation. Wild bulls are dangerous to people and can attack without warning.

funFacts: Wild water buffalo have the widest horn spread of any bovid, up to about 2 m along the outer edges.
About 91% of the world's wild water buffalo live in India, mostly in Assam.
Kaziranga holds both the world's highest tiger density and the largest wild buffalo population.
Tigers are occasionally killed by water buffalo.
Both bulls and cows carry horns.
The world's domestic water buffalo were bred from this wild species.
Cows with calves are known to face tigers head-on.

abilities.name: Crescent Horn Hook
abilities.description: the widest-spreading horns of any bovid, heavy at the base, swung sideways and upward in a mass-backed charge to hook and toss attackers.

abilities.name: Wallow and Swim
abilities.description: spends long periods in water and mud and swims readily, letting it fight on wetland ground where many heavy land animals lose footing.

traits.name: Record Horn Spread
traits.description: horns in both sexes can span about 2 m along the outer edges, with a record horn just under 2 m long.

traits.name: Wild Stock of a Working Giant
traits.description: the domestic water buffalo, one of Asia's key farm animals, was bred from this wild species; hybridisation with domestic buffalo now threatens the wild form.

combat.weapons: The wild buffalo's offense is a mass-backed charge with the head lowered and the horns swung to hook and toss. Because the horns sweep sideways and backward rather than forward, the most dangerous surfaces are the heavy horn bases and the curved outer sections, used in sideways hooks and upward tosses. Body checks, shoving and trampling add damage. The sheer width of the horns also makes a frontal approach awkward for a predator.
weaknesses: No true armor; flanks, hindquarters and belly are exposed.
Backward-swept horns are less of a forward goring tool than hooked or straight horns.
Heat and water dependence limit exertion on dry ground.
No measured speed; heavy frame limits agility.
Tigers can kill adults, especially lone animals.

wedge-tailed-eagle.name: Wedge-tailed Eagle
wedge-tailed-eagle.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 4.2 kg, 100.0 cm total length, about 2.2 m wingspan. Females are the larger sex.
wedge-tailed-eagle.summary: The Wedge-tailed Eagle is Australia's largest bird of prey. The canonical female weighs about 4.2 kg and spans about 2.2 m. It has some of the sharpest measured vision of any animal and hunts rabbits, hares and wallabies, while pairs and groups can bring down adult kangaroos. Alone, its light build and modest talons keep it below the golden eagle in raw killing power.
narrative: The wedge-tailed eagle is built for wide country. Its long wings and long, wedge-shaped tail let it ride thermals to 2 km or more over the Australian interior. From there, eyes measured at 132–143 cycles per degree, close to the physical limit for a vertebrate eye, pick out rabbits, hares, lizards and carcasses far below.

Much of its daily food is ordinary: rabbits, roadkill and whatever is plentiful. What makes it stand out is cooperation. Pairs hunt in tandem, one bird drawing attention while the other strikes. Groups have been seen running down kangaroos in relays, with fresh eagles dropping in to replace tired chasers. In the Strzelecki Desert, eagles on the side of the dingo fence where kangaroos are abundant ate far more of them.

Alone in an absolute matchup, it is a 4.2 kg bird with talons a little smaller than a golden eagle's and no armor. It wins with vision, surprise and, when it has help, numbers. Against a heavy grappler that survives the first strike, one eagle has little left to use.

sections.habitat: The wedge-tailed eagle is found throughout mainland Australia and Tasmania and on many offshore islands. It uses more habitat types than perhaps any other Aquila eagle, from deserts and arid shrubland to farmland, open woodland and mountain forest with an open understory. It is common across the arid interior wherever prey and nest trees or cliffs are available.
sections.diet: It is a generalist predator and a major scavenger. Rabbits and hares are the most important live prey; macropods, lizards, birds and other mammals are also taken, and carrion, including roadkill kangaroos, makes up a large part of the diet. In the Strzelecki Desert, where dingoes are rare, eagles ate more kangaroos and bearded dragons and a wider range of species than on the other side of the dingo fence. By eating rabbits, it helps limit an invasive pest.
sections.social: Breeding adults live as long-term territorial pairs. Around each defended nest territory is a larger home range that overlaps with neighbors and non-breeding birds. Pairs, and sometimes larger groups, hunt together.
sections.reproduction: Pairs build huge stick nests that are reused for years; nests 1.8 m across, 3 m deep and weighing about 400 kg are known. Eggs are incubated for about 42–45 days, and in lean years the first-hatched chick may kill its nestmate. Plumage darkens over at least ten years. Juveniles disperse widely, one moving more than 850 km in about eight months.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern globally. Persecution was heavy in the past because of supposed lamb killing, but numbers recovered strongly, helped by rabbits and roadkill. The Tasmanian subspecies is listed federally as Endangered. Current threats include lead poisoning from ammunition in carcasses: lead was detected in 84% of 62 mainland eagle bones, at severe levels in 4.8%. Rodenticide exposure (residues in 74% of 50 Tasmanian carcasses) and collisions with vehicles while feeding on roadkill are also threats.
sections.features:
Measured visual acuity of 132–143 cycles per degree.
Very long wings and a long, wedge-shaped tail.
Legs feathered to the toes.
Cooperative and tandem hunting.
Very large, long-used stick nests.
sections.humanInteraction: It was once persecuted for killing lambs, which make up only a small share of its prey. Today it is widely admired, and it is a notorious attacker of hang gliders, paragliders and survey drones. Eagles feeding on roadkill are often hit by vehicles.

funFacts: A Tasmanian female had a verified wingspan of 284 cm, the largest measured for any eagle.
Its visual acuity was measured at 132–143 cycles per degree, close to the limit set by the optics of its eye.
Groups of wedge-tailed eagles can kill adult kangaroos.
Old nests can weigh around 400 kg.
Its scientific name audax means "bold".
It is famous for attacking hang gliders and paragliders, and eagles once knocked nine of a mining company's drones out of the sky.
Adults keep getting darker for at least their first ten years.

abilities.name: Tag-Team Kangaroo Hunt
abilities.description: pairs and groups hunt together: one eagle distracts or drives the prey while another strikes, and in large group hunts fresh pairs replace tired chasers. Together they can kill adult kangaroos that no single eagle could handle.

abilities.name: Record-Resolution Vision
abilities.description: behavioural tests measured acuity of 132–143 cycles per degree, matching the limit of its deep fovea. It can spot prey and threats from far beyond the range at which they can see the eagle.

traits.name: Widest Verified Eagle Wingspan
traits.description: a Tasmanian female measured 284 cm, the largest verified wingspan for any eagle, and the long wedge-shaped tail is unique among large Australian raptors.

traits.name: Glider Challenger
traits.description: it is the only bird with a reputation for frequently attacking hang gliders and paragliders, and it also attacks drones.

combat.weapons:
The feet and talons are the killing tools. The hallux claw (about 4.5–4.6 cm in mainland females) is somewhat smaller than a golden eagle's, but it is very sharp, and the whole foot is feathered to the toes. The bill tears carcasses and kills. Rabbits and hares are the most important live prey, and the species also takes macropods (kangaroos and wallabies), lizards such as bearded dragons, birds over about 100 g and mammals usually over 500 g. It also eats a lot of carrion, including roadkill. It kills lambs occasionally, but lambs are a small part of the diet.

Its most striking offensive behavior is cooperative. Australian Museum and BirdLife Australia both state that a group of eagles working together can kill animals as large as adult kangaroos. In one Central Australian study, about a third of 89 observed hunts were cooperative. One record describes 15 eagles hunting kangaroos, with two chasing at a time and fresh pairs taking over from the circling group.
weaknesses: About 4.2 kg in absolute mass.
Smaller talons than golden or Verreaux's eagles.
No armor; light skeleton.
Gorged birds on the ground can struggle to take off.
Heavy reliance on carrion exposes it to lead poisoning and roadkill collisions.

wels-catfish.name: Wels Catfish
wels-catfish.specimen: healthy large adult, 22 kg and 160 cm long, sex unspecified, representing the upper end of the common adult size rather than the rare 2 m-plus giants.
wels-catfish.summary: The wels catfish is Europe's giant river ambusher: a 1.6-metre, 22 kg night hunter that finds prey with electroreception and taste-covered skin, then engulfs it with a huge suction gulp. It even beaches itself to snatch pigeons, but its gripping teeth and scaleless skin leave it outmatched by armored or much larger opponents.
narrative: The wels catfish hunts by feel, taste and electricity. It spends the day in deep holes and rises at dusk, sweeping the water with long barbels. Its skin is covered in taste buds, its lateral line senses movement, and electroreceptive organs pick up the faint electric fields of other fish. In the dark, murky water where it lives, that sensory package lets it find prey that cannot see it coming.

Its attack is a gulp. The mouth is enormous, and when it opens suddenly, water and prey rush in to meet pads of hundreds of small, backward-pointing teeth. Wels have learned to use that attack in surprising ways. On the Tarn River in France, researchers filmed catfish sliding up onto gravel banks to grab pigeons before wriggling back into the water. On the Garonne, a few wels learned to wait in a fishway and caught about a third of the adult salmon passing through.

In a battle, the wels is dangerous at the water's edge and in the dark, and almost anything small enough to swallow is at risk. Its limits are just as clear: it has no scales or armor, its teeth grip rather than cut, and it is slow in open water. Against a crocodile, a large shark or a heavily armored turtle, the wels would lose.

sections.habitat: The wels catfish lives in large rivers, lakes and reservoirs of central and eastern Europe and western Asia, preferring warm, slow or still water with deep holes and cover. It has been introduced widely in western Europe, including the Ebro and Guadalquivir in Spain (the Ebro from 1974) and the Rhône, Garonne and Tarn in France, where it is now a major predator.
sections.diet: Juveniles eat invertebrates, small fish and detritus; adults eat fish, crayfish, amphibians, birds, small mammals and other available prey. Wels exploit seasonal food pulses such as migrating shad and salmon. In invaded rivers they are an apex predator and a conservation concern for native fish.
sections.social: Solitary for most of the year. Adults spend the day in deep water or cover and become active at dusk.
sections.reproduction: Wels spawn in spring and early summer in shallow, vegetated areas, where adults can become defensive. They grow quickly in warm water, which helps explain the size of fish in introduced southern European populations.
sections.conservation: The wels catfish is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, although some native populations have declined through overfishing and habitat change. Outside its native range it is an invasive species of concern, threatening salmon, shad and other native fish.
sections.features:
Very wide mouth with pads of hundreds of small gripping teeth.
Long barbels and taste buds over the barbels and skin.
Electroreceptive ampullary organs.
Scaleless, slimy skin.
Ability to beach briefly to seize prey on land.
sections.humanInteraction: The wels is a major sport fish and is farmed for food. Its spread by anglers into western European rivers has created ecological problems. Bites on swimmers are rare but real, as the 2025 Brombachsee incidents in Germany showed.

funFacts: Wels catfish in France beach themselves to catch pigeons, succeeding in about 28% of filmed attempts.
Scientists nicknamed them "freshwater killer whales".
At one River Garonne fishway, wels caught 35% of the adult salmon passing through.
Their skin is covered in taste buds, so they can taste with their whole body.
They can sense the weak electric fields of other fish.
FishBase accepts a maximum of 2.73 m and 130 kg; older claims of 5 m were errors.
In 2025 a 2 m wels bit at least five swimmers in a Bavarian lake.

abilities.name: Riverbank Lunge
abilities.description: wels in France have been filmed beaching themselves to grab pigeons at the water's edge and sliding back into the river, about 28% of attempts succeeding. In a matchup it can strike opponents that think they are safe in the shallows or on the bank.

abilities.name: Electric Barbel Radar
abilities.description: ampullary electroreceptors detect the weak electric fields of other fish, while long barbels and skin covered in taste buds track chemical and touch cues. It can find and follow an opponent in total darkness or thick mud.

traits.name: Freshwater Killer Whale
traits.description: the pigeon-beaching behavior earned wels the nickname "freshwater killer whales" in the 2012 study that documented it.

traits.name: Salmon Ambusher
traits.description: a few wels in the River Garonne learned to wait in a fishway and caught about 35% of the adult salmon passing through in 2016.

combat.weapons:
The wels catfish's weapon is its huge mouth. It attacks by sudden suction, engulfing prey and gripping it with pads of hundreds of small, inward-sloping teeth, then crushing it at the back of the mouth. The teeth grip rather than cut, so the wels swallows prey whole instead of slicing pieces off. It is an opportunist that eats fish, crayfish, amphibians, birds and small mammals.

Two studies show how effective this can be. In the Tarn River in southern France, Cucherousset et al. (2012) filmed wels catfish deliberately beaching themselves on gravel banks to grab pigeons at the water's edge, a behavior they compared to killer whales stranding to catch seals. About 28% of the filmed attempts succeeded, and only moving pigeons were attacked. In the River Garonne, Boulêtreau et al. (2018) found that wels caught 35% (14 of 39) of the adult Atlantic salmon passing through one fishway during the 2016 migration, with a few specialized individuals timing their presence to the salmon run.

The wels will also bite people. In June 2025 a wels about 2 m long and about 90 kg injured at least five swimmers at the Brombachsee lake in Bavaria before it was killed; another wels bit a swimmer there in July 2025. Fishing experts suggested the fish were near spawning grounds.
weaknesses: No armor; scaleless skin.
Teeth grip but cannot cut large prey.
Slow in open pursuit.
Stranding on land is short and risky.
