whale-shark.name: Whale Shark
whale-shark.specimen: healthy mature adult female, 12.0 m total length and 15,000 kg, representing a large adult rather than the 18.8 m record animal.
whale-shark.summary: The whale shark is the largest fish alive, a 12-metre, 15-tonne filter feeder protected by skin around 10 cm thick and even armored eyes. It is almost impossible for a lone predator to wound seriously, but it has no weapons, swims at walking pace and never fights back, so its battles are tests of endurance rather than attack.
narrative: The whale shark is a giant built for patience. A mature female stretches around 12 metres and weighs roughly 15 tonnes, yet she feeds on some of the smallest animals in the sea, cruising open-mouthed through plankton or hanging vertically to gulp fish eggs. Her hundreds of rows of tiny teeth are never used for eating; the real work is done by the filter pads behind them.

In a battle, that makes the whale shark a pure defender. Its skin is among the thickest of any animal, covered in denticles, and its eyes are armored with thousands of tiny tooth-like scales and can be pulled back into the head. A lone shark or seal-hunter would struggle to do more than scratch it. When things go badly, it can dive: tags show whale sharks plunging to around 2,000 metres, deeper than almost any opponent could follow.

What the whale shark cannot do is hurt anything on purpose. It has no bite, no spines and no fighting behavior, and it swims so slowly that a determined attacker can stay with it indefinitely. Orcas in the Gulf of California have learned exactly that, working together to open the soft pelvic region. Against a single predator the whale shark simply outlasts the attack; against a coordinated pack, its armor eventually runs out.

sections.habitat: Whale sharks live in tropical and warm-temperate seas worldwide, both far offshore and at predictable coastal feeding hotspots such as Ningaloo Reef, the Yucatán Peninsula, La Paz, Mozambique, the Philippines and the Arabian Gulf. They move between surface waters and the deep sea, occasionally diving to about 2,000 m.
sections.diet: The whale shark is a filter feeder. It eats plankton, krill, fish eggs, small schooling fish and squid, either by swimming slowly open-mouthed or by hanging vertically and sucking water in. It follows seasonal food pulses: coral spawning at Ningaloo, fish-spawn events around offshore platforms in Qatar and plankton blooms in the Gulf of California.
sections.social: Whale sharks are solitary but gather in large numbers where food is concentrated. These aggregations are feeding gatherings, not social groups, and are often dominated by juvenile males.
sections.reproduction: Whale sharks give birth to live young; little else about their breeding is known, and mating has rarely been observed. Males mature at around 8–9 m; female maturity size is less certain. Vertebral banding validated with bomb radiocarbon confirms ages of at least 50 years, and maturity may take around 30 years, making populations very slow to recover.
sections.conservation: The whale shark is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (Pierce and Norman 2016), with estimated declines of more than half over three generations in the Indo-Pacific, driven by fisheries, bycatch and ship strikes. The Atlantic subpopulation was assessed separately as Vulnerable. It is listed on the Convention on Migratory Species appendices.
sections.features:
Skin around 10 cm thick, armored with dermal denticles.
Denticle-covered eyeballs that can be retracted into the socket.
More than 300 rows of tiny unused teeth and about 20 filter pads.
Fish-record dive depth of about 2,000 m.
Unique pale spot pattern used by researchers to identify individuals.
sections.humanInteraction: Whale shark tourism supports local economies at many aggregation sites. The main threats from people are targeted fisheries (historically), bycatch in nets and collisions with ships. Encounters with swimmers are safe for the swimmer when codes of conduct are followed.

funFacts: A single whale shark eyeball can carry more than 3,000 tiny tooth-like denticles.
The whale shark can pull its eye back into its head by about half the eye's width.
Bomb radiocarbon from Cold War nuclear tests was used to confirm that one whale shark was 50 years old.
One tagged whale shark swam about 2,644 km in 37 days, and the longest recorded track topped 20,000 km.
A whale shark in the Coral Sea dived to at least 1,978 m, deeper than the old fish record of 1,928 m.
Killer whales in the Gulf of California have been filmed hunting whale sharks by targeting the pelvic area.
Female whale sharks keep growing after the males stop and end up far longer.

abilities.name: Armored Retracting Eye
abilities.description: each eyeball carries thousands of tooth-like dermal denticles and can be pulled back into the socket by about half its own diameter. Against a biting or raking opponent, the whale shark's most vulnerable sense organ is shielded and can be withdrawn.

abilities.name: Abyssal Plunge
abilities.description: tags have recorded dives to 1,928 m and, in the Coral Sea, to at least 1,978 m. A whale shark under pressure can leave the surface fight entirely for depths few opponents can follow.

traits.name: Largest Living Fish
traits.description: no other fish comes close in size; mature females average around 14 m at full growth and the largest reliably recorded individual was about 18.8 m.

traits.name: Filter-Pad Giant
traits.description: more than 300 rows of tiny teeth go unused while about 20 filter pads strain plankton, fish eggs and small fish from the water.

combat.weapons: The whale shark has no functional offensive weapon. Its hundreds of rows of tiny teeth play no part in feeding, it has no spines, no venom and no cutting jaw, and it is not known to use its tail or body against other animals. Its only real offensive asset is mass: a 15-tonne body moving through the water carries enormous momentum, and a tail sweep from an animal this size would be dangerous to anything caught by it. That is incidental force, not a weapon it deploys.
weaknesses: No weapon and no attacking behavior.
Very slow, with no documented burst speed.
Pelvic and ventral regions are vulnerable to a coordinated predator.
Docile temperament: it does not fight back.
Shallow water and stranding are dangerous for an animal this size.

wild-turkey.name: Wild Turkey
wild-turkey.specimen: healthy mature adult male (tom), 7.6 kg, 110.0 cm total length. Toms are much heavier than hens and carry leg spurs used in fights.
wild-turkey.summary: The Wild Turkey is North America's heavyweight flying gamebird. The canonical tom weighs about 7.6 kg and fights with sharp leg spurs, kicks and body slams. It can burst into flight at up to about 88 km/h or sprint away on foot. It is wary and sharp-eyed by day, but it is not a predator, and against real hunters it relies on escape more than combat.
narrative: The wild turkey is not the slow farm bird most people picture. A healthy tom weighs around 7.6 kg, runs at about 8 m/s, and can explode into the air on loud wings, reaching recorded speeds of about 88 km/h before gliding into cover or up to a roost. Keen daytime eyes and a flock full of watchers make it hard to surprise in daylight.

Its fighting is mostly among its own kind. In spring, toms strut, gobble and drum to show status and settle disputes with kicks and sharp leg spurs. Some males work in teams: subordinate brothers display beside a dominant male and help him win mates without breeding themselves. When cornered by a predator, a turkey will kick, spur, peck and ram, which is enough to drive off some mid-sized mammals, and hens defending poults have chased off hawks.

In an absolute matchup, however, it is a plant-eating bird that prefers to run or fly. Its spurs are short-range weapons without real killing power against large animals, it has no armor, and its night vision is very poor. It does well against small animals it can bully and against opponents it can outrun, but true predators usually decide the fight.

sections.habitat: Wild turkeys are native to North America, from southern Canada through much of the US to northern and central Mexico. They prefer mature hardwood forest with oak, hickory, beech, cherry and ash, mixed with clearings, fields and pasture, but they also live in montane conifer and oak woods and near farmland and suburbs. Reintroductions have restored them to most of their former range and beyond, including parts of Canada.
sections.diet: They are omnivores that feed mostly on plants: acorns and other nuts, seeds, grains, berries, buds, leaves, grass blades, roots and bulbs. They also eat insects and occasionally small salamanders, lizards and snakes. Their broad diet lets populations grow large in small areas. They are prey for many predators; poults are most vulnerable in their first two weeks.
sections.social: Turkeys live in flocks outside the breeding season, and roosting flocks of 6–40 birds may share trees. Flocks have dominance hierarchies. In spring, males display in groups and form coalitions, and most hens prefer to mate with dominant males. GPS data from 151 males and 261 females in the southeastern US showed males revisiting small display areas (about 50 ha on average) within their breeding-season ranges.
sections.reproduction: Males are polygamous. After mating, hens nest on the ground and lay clutches of 10–14 eggs, one per day. Poults leave the nest soon after hatching and hide under the hen when threatened. Mortality is high: ADW gives an average life expectancy of only 1.3–1.6 years, although some wild turkeys have lived at least 13 years.
sections.conservation: The species is listed as Least Concern and its population trend has been increasing (National Geographic). Habitat loss and market hunting drove numbers in the US as low as an estimated 30,000 by the late 1930s, and turkeys disappeared from 18 states. Protection and trap-and-transfer reintroductions restored them; current estimates put the wild population at about 7 million. Some eastern populations have recently declined, with invasive wild pigs and disease among the factors being studied.
sections.features:
Sharp leg spurs on males.
Bare, colorful head with snood and wattles that change color with excitement.
Breast "beard" of hair-like feathers that grows through life.
Fast burst flight despite its weight.
Very good daytime vision.
sections.humanInteraction: Wild turkeys are a major game bird whose recovery is a notable conservation success. Domestic turkeys were bred from wild stock by indigenous peoples of southern Mexico and Central America about 2,000 years ago. Wild toms occasionally attack people, cars or their own reflections, usually when approached too closely or during the breeding season.

funFacts: The record wild tom weighed about 17 kg.
Wild turkeys have been recorded flying at 88.5 km/h.
A tom's beard keeps growing throughout its life and can reach about 30 cm.
Toms sometimes attack their own reflection in car paint or windows.
Subordinate males, often brothers, help a dominant male court without breeding themselves.
US wild turkey numbers fell to an estimated 30,000 in the 1930s and have recovered to around 7 million.
Chased gobblers have been measured taking strides of about 1.2 m.

abilities.name: Spur Kick Brawl
abilities.description: toms fight with sharp leg spurs, powerful kicks, bill strikes and body ramming. The same toolkit can deter mid-sized predators when a turkey is cornered.

abilities.name: Rocket Take-Off
abilities.description: a turkey bursts off the ground on loud wings and can reach recorded flight speeds of about 88.5 km/h over short distances, or sprint away at about 8 m/s.

traits.name: Heavyweight Flier
traits.description: at 7.6 kg on average and sometimes over 13.8 kg, the wild turkey is among the heaviest flying birds in the world, yet it still flies fast and roosts in trees.

traits.name: Brother Display Teams
traits.description: subordinate males, often brothers, court alongside a dominant male without breeding themselves, and paired dominant males father more young than males courting alone.

combat.weapons: The tom's weapons are its legs and body. Each leg carries a sharp spur used to spar with other males. When fighting off predators, turkeys kick with their legs and spurs, bite with the bill and ram with their relatively large bodies. Wikipedia's account says this can deter predators up to the size of mid-sized mammals. Hens have been seen chasing off at least two species of hawks in flight when their poults were threatened. Turkeys are not predators of large animals; they eat mostly plants, including acorns, seeds, berries and roots, plus insects and occasionally small salamanders, lizards and snakes.
weaknesses: About 7.6 kg, with no armor.
Short bursts of flight only; heavy wing loading.
Very poor night vision; vulnerable on the ground in darkness.
Spurs and kicks are close-range weapons with little killing power against large animals.
Prefers flight to fight, so it rarely presses an attack against a dangerous opponent.

yellow-naped-amazon.name: Yellow-naped Amazon
yellow-naped-amazon.specimen: healthy mature adult male, 0.5 kg, 35.0 cm total length. The sexes look alike; males are used because captive males are the more nest-protective, biting sex in the breeding season (Wikipedia), and pair duets show clear sex-specific roles.
yellow-naped-amazon.summary: The Yellow-naped Amazon is a 0.5 kg green parrot from the Pacific side of Central America, famous as a talker and for wild vocal dialects and pair duets. Its calculated 94 N bite is strong for its size, but it is a light, unarmored bird. Poaching for the pet trade has made it Critically Endangered.
narrative: The yellow-naped amazon is a stocky green parrot with a yellow band across the back of its neck, living in the dry forests, mangroves and farm country of Central America's Pacific slope. It is one of the best-studied wild parrots because of its voice. In Costa Rica, birds from different regions use different contact calls, forming dialects with sharp borders. Young birds that move learn the local dialect within weeks, while adults tend to stay loyal to home, and over 22 years of study these dialects began to blur as populations crashed.

Pairs defend their nest territory by duetting, trading male and female notes in a fixed order. Neighbors reply with duets of their own, and occasionally these vocal contests turn into physical fights at the border. In captivity the same vocal talent makes it one of the best mimics of human speech, which is exactly why poachers take its chicks: most wild nests fail because the young are stolen, and the population has fallen by more than 92% in three generations.

In an absolute matchup it is a 0.5 kg bird with a strong bite for its size and no armor. It can hurt a hand or a small animal, but against a raptor or a carnivore it has only flight and alertness to rely on.

sections.habitat: The yellow-naped amazon lives along the Pacific slope from Oaxaca in southern Mexico to north-western Costa Rica, on the Mosquito Coast of Honduras and Nicaragua, and on the Bay Islands of Honduras. It uses deciduous and evergreen forest, clearings, savanna woodland, pine woodland on ridges, gallery forest and semi-arid woodland, and less often thorn forest, mangroves and farmland with scattered trees (WPT).
sections.diet: It eats seeds of Cochlospermum and Curatella, figs and ripening Terminalia fruit (WPT), plus other nuts, berries and fruit. Bay Island birds feed on Caribbean pine cones.
sections.social: Birds live in pairs or flocks and gather in larger groups at communal night roosts and feeding areas. Pairs are monogamous in the breeding season and defend small territories by duetting.
sections.reproduction: Nests are in large natural tree cavities; the birds chew the entrance but do not dig new holes, and dead coyol palms are a preferred site. Clutches are 2–4 eggs, laid mainly in February–March (WPT). Most nests fail because chicks are taken for the pet trade (Wikipedia).
sections.conservation: The yellow-naped amazon is listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN, after two uplistings from Vulnerable (Dahlin et al. 2024). WPT gives about 1,000–2,500 mature birds and decreasing. The population is estimated to have fallen by more than 92% over three generations, mainly from poaching of chicks for the pet trade and loss of dry forest to farming. Populations in Mexico, Guatemala and Honduras are now very small, and Costa Rica is the stronghold. The Mesoamerican Parrot Census Network, supported by WPT, monitors the species with volunteers.
sections.features:
Yellow band across the nape on otherwise green plumage.
Regional vocal dialects that young birds learn.
Syntax-based pair duets.
Excellent human-speech mimicry in captivity.
sections.humanInteraction: Yellow-naped amazons have long been prized pets for their talking ability and playful personality. They bond strongly with one person and can bite, especially males protecting a perceived nest in the breeding season. The pet trade is the main reason the species collapsed in the wild. A rare turquoise colour mutation exists.

funFacts: Yellow-naped amazons in Costa Rica speak in regional dialects, much like human accents.
A young bird moved to another dialect area switched to the local call within six weeks.
Pairs sing duets that follow rules about which notes come in which order.
Neighboring pairs sometimes "counter-duet" until the argument turns into a fight.
Its calculated bite is about 30 times the measured bite of a Cooper's hawk of similar weight.
The wild population has fallen by more than 92% in three generations.
One captive yellow-naped amazon reportedly lived 49 years.

abilities.name: Clamp-Jaw Bite
abilities.description: a calculated bite of about 94 N, roughly 30 times the measured bite of a Cooper's hawk of similar weight, makes a defending yellow-naped amazon a serious close-range biter for its size.

abilities.name: Duet Border Patrol
abilities.description: mated pairs defend their nest territory with precisely timed duets that follow rules of note order, and counter-duets with neighbors can escalate into fights.

traits.name: Parrot Dialects
traits.description: Costa Rican yellow-naped amazons speak in regional dialects with distinct contact calls, and young birds that move learn the local dialect within weeks.

traits.name: Master Mimic
traits.description: one of the parrots best known for copying human speech, which, with its playful nature, made it a top target of the pet trade.

combat.weapons: The bill is the only weapon. A calculated bite of about 94 N is strong for a 0.5 kg bird; the same study notes that a 451 g blue-fronted amazon bites with about 123 N while a Cooper's hawk of the same mass bites with only about 3 N. Captive yellow-naped amazons are known for nest-protective biting, especially males in the breeding season, and signal stress by fanning the tail and "pinning" (rapidly narrowing and widening) the pupils (Wikipedia). It is not a predator; it eats seeds, fruit, figs and nuts.
weaknesses: About 0.5 kg in absolute mass.
No armor.
Bill is its only weapon; bites are close range.
Heavy poaching of chicks; wild numbers are very low.
